Why this page

Denmark links every resident, firm, hospital visit, tax return and job to a single identifier, and lets researchers work with the whole population from the 1980s onwards. This page is a reading list of the economics that has come out of that infrastructure in the top general-interest journals and in the two leading field journals for labour and public economics: what question each paper asks, what it finds, and which registers it is built from.

The list covers 155 papers. It was assembled by searching Crossref for every article in these journals whose title or abstract mentions Denmark or Danish data, and by going through the publication lists of the main Danish research groups and authors, then checking each paper. It excludes AEA Papers and Proceedings, finance journals and papers that only use Danish data as one country among many. It will still miss papers whose abstracts do not name the country, so additions are welcome. Each paper lists its datasets, key variables, data period and sample size, and the Data & samples page puts these in one sortable table. The Themes page regroups the same papers by topic, and the Variable map lists the registers and variables they rely on, at the individual and the firm level. If a paper is missing or a summary is wrong, open an issue or a pull request on GitHub.

Subjective Earnings Risk

Andrew Caplin, Victoria Gregory, Eungik Lee, Søren Leth-Petersen and Johan Sæverud · Review of Economic Studies, 2026 · Individual

Introduces a survey instrument for earnings risk that allows for quitting and being fired, fielded to Danish workers and linked to their register earnings histories. Job transitions drive subjective risk, which is many times smaller than traditional register-based estimates even after conditioning on demographics and job history, and helps explain why many hold few liquid assets.

Data
Copenhagen Life Panel (CLP) survey, January 2021 wave, linked on CPR number, Income-tax register earnings (IND), Monthly employer-employee match and earnings data (BFL/eIndkomst), Demographic, education, household composition and household wealth registers
Key variables
  • Survey: subjective probabilities of staying, quitting and being laid off
  • Survey: subjective earnings distributions conditional on each job transition
  • Benchmark: realized job transitions, time out of work and earnings growth in 2021 (administrative)
  • Weights: population weights from a survey-participation model on 2020 administrative data
Period
Survey January 2021; administrative data through 2022
Sample
10,942 employed respondents (gross sample 14,683 respondents aged 20–65) Copenhagen Life Panel respondents aged 20–65 who were employed at the time of the January 2021 survey. source
How variables are defined (10)
  • Main monthly employer (BFL) Employment and labour force status
    From monthly eIndkomst job records (BFL), each person-month is assigned the job with the most paid hours (AJO_LOENTIMER) as the primary employer; its CVR number, wage and hours are kept. Month and year come from the job start date field AJO_JOB_START_DATO.
    Registers: BFL
    Codes: AJO_CVR_NR_FRA_PROD_JOB, AJO_SMALT_LOENBELOEB, AJO_LOENTIMER, AJO_JOB_START_DATO; primary job = max(AJO_LOENTIMER) within pnr-year-month
    replication code · script/cleaning/1_c_monthly_data.R
  • Stayer (same employer Dec 2020 to Dec 2021) Employment and labour force status
    Among workers with an employer and monthly wage above 2,000 DKK in December 2020, stay=1 if the main employer in December 2021 is the same as in December 2020, else 0. Sample restricted to ages 20-65 and 2020 annual BFL earnings of at least 24,000 DKK.
    Registers: BFL
    Codes: wage>2000 in Dec 2020; employer_g == F12.employer_g; sum_earnings>=24000
    replication code · script/analysis/fig4/preprocess_fig4a.do; paper Figure 4 note
  • Months out of work after separation Unemployment and benefits
    A separation is a month in which the worker has a main employer with monthly wage above 2,000 DKK and next month's employer differs; only the first separation per person is used. Time out of work = months until a different non-missing employer appears (capped at 24) minus one, so job-to-job moves count as 0 and returns to the same employer are not reemployment. The paper describes separations in 2020; the posted do-file's window (date<=24 from Dec 2018) covers Dec 2018-Dec 2019.
    Registers: BFL
    Codes: jan_sep = employer_g != F1employer_g; reemp = first k with F`k'employer_g != employer_g & non-missing; gap = reemp-1; cap 24
    replication code · script/analysis/fig4/preprocess_fig4b.do; paper Section 3.2 and Figure 4 note
  • Annual earnings (register) Earnings and income
    Annual earnings are wage income LOENMV_13 from the income register (IND); self-employment income is NETOVSKUD_13 kept separately. Realized earnings growth 2020-2021 is ln(earnings_2021*100/102) - ln(earnings_2020), dropping observations with earnings below 24,000 DKK in either year and trimming at the 1st/99th percentile.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: LOENMV_13 (earnings), NETOVSKUD_13 (self-employment income); threshold 24,000 DKK; deflator 100/102; winsor2 trim 1/99
    replication code · script/cleaning/1_b_annual_data.R; script/analysis/fig7/preprocess_fig7.do; paper Figure 6 note
  • Net wealth and liquid wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Net wealth = (KOEJD + BANKAKT + KURSAKT + OBLAKT + PANTAKT) - (BANKGAELD + GAELD_TIL_OFF + OBLGAELD + PANTGAELD), missing public debt set to 0. Liquid wealth = BANKAKT + KURSAKT + OBLAKT + PANTAKT. Pension wealth is the sum of PF_FORMUE across contracts in PENSFORM.
    Registers: IND, PENSFORM
    Codes: KOEJD, BANKAKT, KURSAKT, OBLAKT, PANTAKT, BANKGAELD, GAELD_TIL_OFF, OBLGAELD, PANTGAELD; PF_FORMUE
    replication code · script/cleaning/1_b_annual_data.R
  • Monthly UI, cash benefits and retirement transfers Unemployment and benefits
    From ILME monthly non-employee e-income records, amounts across A/B income fields are summed per person-month and classified by the income-type code of the largest payment: UI if VMO_INDK_ART codes 2,5,8,16,104; cash benefits if type code 6 or art codes 40,41,43,84,87; retirement if art codes 6,9,10,13,20,24,25,44,45,74,83,86,113,115.
    Registers: ILME
    Codes: VMO_INDKOMST_ART_KODE UI: 2,5,8,16,104; CB: VMO_INDKOMST_TYPE_KODE 6 or ART 40,41,43,84,87; Retirement ART: 6,9,10,13,20,24,25,44,45,74,83,86,113,115
    replication code · script/cleaning/1_c_monthly_data.R
  • Public vs private sector Sector and industry
    Main job (highest LOENTIMER in IDAN per year) is public if ARB_SEKTORKODE is non-missing and not 99, and recoded private if ARB_SEKTORKODE is in 18, 28, 89, 81, 58, 48, 42, 52. Industry groups come from DB07 ranges of ARB_HOVED_BRA_DB07 (e.g. >=840000 public services, 850000 teaching, 860000 health).
    Registers: IDAN
    Codes: ARB_SEKTORKODE private: 18,28,89,81,58,48,42,52; ARB_HOVED_BRA_DB07 6-digit DB07 ranges
    replication code · script/cleaning/1_b_annual_data.R
  • Occupation group Occupation and job hierarchy
    Main job's DISCO_KODE first digit mapped to 9 groups (1 management, 2 high knowledge, 3 medium knowledge, 4 office, 5 sales/services, 6 farming, 7 craft, 8 skilled, 9 unskilled); military (DISCO below 100000) dropped. Tenure = year - ANSAAR.
    Registers: IDAN
    Codes: DISCO_KODE first digit 1-9; DISCO_KODE<100000 excluded; ANSAAR
    replication code · script/cleaning/1_b_annual_data.R
  • Education level Education and test scores
    Highest completed education HFAUDD (latest available year) mapped through the audd format's H1 level: 10 elementary; 20, 25 high school; 30, 35 vocational; 40, 50, 60 bachelor; 65, 70 master.
    Registers: UDDA
    Codes: HFAUDD via uddan_2014_audd H1: 10; 20,25; 30,35; 40,50,60; 65,70
    replication code · script/cleaning/1_b_annual_data.R
  • Population survey weights Sample definition and timing
    Inverse predicted propensity scores from a probability model of survey participation estimated on 2020 administrative data on the demographics of Danes active in the labour market.
    paper · Footnote 10 (details in Online Appendix B)

Disaggregated Economic Accounts

Asger Lau Andersen, Kilian Huber, Niels Johannesen, Ludwig Straub and Emil Toft Vestergaard · Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2026 · Individual + firm

Builds a system of national accounts broken down into bilateral money flows between region-by-industry consumer cells, producer cells, the government and the rest of the world, and implements it for Denmark using bank transaction data and registers. Spending is locally and urban biased, and fiscal transfers raise GDP more when targeted at cells whose spending reaches cells with high unemployment.

Data
Danske Bank geo-coded transaction-level data (about 20% of Danish adult consumers), 2018–2019, Government tax and income registers (labour compensation, mixed income, interest, dividends, transfers), Employment registers linking adults to industry of main employment and region, Danish national accounts (SNA positions, input-output tables), 2018, CrediWire producer-to-producer transactions (about 5 million), Firm-level export and import data for manufacturing firms
Key variables
  • Outcome: bilateral cell-to-cell flows (consumer spending, labour and profit income, taxes, transfers, intermediates trade)
  • Unit: consumer cells (industry of main employment x region of residence)
  • Unit: producer cells (industry x region of establishments)
  • Derived: domestic spending share, gravity, urban bias and spending intensity measures
Period
2018 (consumer spending 2018–2019)
Sample
approx. 2,700 consumer cells and approx. 2,600 producer cells; around 43 million entries All Danish adults and production establishments grouped into region-by-industry cells, with consumer spending measured from Danske Bank customers. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Consumer cell (region x industry of main employment) Geography and neighbourhood
    Every adult is assigned to a region by home address at the start of 2018 (BEF), one per each of 98 municipalities, and to an industry by the NACE code of the establishment responsible for the largest part of 2018 labour income (AKM), mapped from six-digit NACE to 24 work industries. Cells with fewer than 3 individuals or establishments are censored.
    Registers: BEF, AKM
    Codes: six-digit NACE mapped to 24 DEA work industries (Table A.I); 98 municipalities
    working paper · Appendix D; Section II
  • Non-working consumer industries Employment and labour force status
    Adults without labour income are assigned to 'retired' if older than 65, 'students' if they receive a government stipend, 'long-term unemployed' if they receive unemployment or cash benefits (fully benefit-dependent with no labour income all year), and otherwise 'out of workforce'.
    Registers: BEF, IND
    working paper · Appendix D; footnote 5
  • Producer cell (establishment region x industry) Firm characteristics and productivity
    Firm establishments are assigned to 2,646 producer cells by region and production industry using the employment registers; 24 work industries plus 3 housing industries without employees (private landlords, owner-occupied housing, government-owned housing).
    Registers: BFL, IDAN
    working paper · Appendix D; Section II
  • Labour compensation flows Earnings and income
    Total annual labour compensation per individual including employer pension contributions, from IND and INPI, aggregated to consumer x producer cells and scaled by 1.01 to SNA D.1. Compensation from foreign producers (IND) scaled by 1.47; payments by Danish producers in BFL to persons not in BEF are treated as foreign employees and scaled by 1.14.
    Registers: IND, INPI, BFL, BEF
    Codes: SNA D.1; scale factors 1.01, 1.47, 1.14
    working paper · Appendix I
  • Mixed income, dividends and owner-occupied housing surplus Earnings and income
    Mixed income links sole-proprietorship establishments in IDAN (including municipality) to owners' mixed income. Dividends (SNA D.42) are allocated to consumer cells in proportion to stock dividend income in IND and to producer cells in proportion to accounting income. Owner-occupied housing surplus (B.2G) = imputed rental values in IND scaled by 0.67.
    Registers: IDAN, IND
    Codes: SNA B.3g, D.42, B.2G; scale 0.67
    working paper · Appendix J
  • Government benefits to consumers Unemployment and benefits
    Social benefits (SNA D.62) = all government income transfers plus private pension payouts from IND, scaled by 1.03. Other current transfers (D.7) allocated by BEF population shares; pension entitlement adjustment (D.8) from IND and INPI contributions net of payouts.
    Registers: IND, INPI, BEF
    Codes: SNA D.62, D.7, D.8; scale 1.03
    working paper · Appendix K
  • Disaggregated consumer spending Wealth, debt and consumption
    Danske Bank customers (main account at Danske Bank and at least one spending transaction per month in 2018-2019) assigned home region monthly from bank address records and industry from the employer paying the largest share of annual income. Merchant region from geocoded transaction-string addresses and industry from an MCC-to-ISIC/NACE crosswalk; cash withdrawals allocated in proportion to in-person card payments.
    Registers: Danske Bank transactions
    Codes: MCC to ISIC/NACE crosswalk
    working paper · Section III.A; Appendix E.A-E.C
  • Manual labour share and cell characteristics Occupation and job hierarchy
    Individual does manual labour if main occupation (AKM) is manual trades, operator and assembly, transportation, other manual labour or military. Cell averages also of university degree (UDDA), total debt, liquid financial assets (deposits, stocks, bonds, fund shares) and illiquid assets (FORMGELD).
    Registers: AKM, UDDA, FORMGELD
    working paper · Appendix M
  • Establishment output for IO disaggregation Firm characteristics and productivity
    Firm output is distributed across a firm's establishments using within-firm labour compensation shares, then aggregated to 173 subindustries combining the 117-industry national IO table and DEA industries; intermediate flows are split proportional to output shares.
    Registers: NIO1-NIO3 (statbank)
    Codes: 117 NA industries; 173 subindustries
    working paper · Appendix N.A

Replication package

Macroeconomics and expectations Firms, ownership and innovation

Beliefs About the Economy Are Excessively Sensitive to Household-Level Shocks: Evidence from Linked Survey and Administrative Data

Dmitry Taubinsky, Luigi Butera, Matteo Saccarola and Chen Lian · Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2026 · Individual

Links Statistics Denmark's consumer expectations survey to the registers to show that people's inflation forecasts and backcasts move strongly, and negatively, with their own recent and expected income changes, far more than actual inflation does. The pattern departs from Bayesian rational expectations and is consistent with affect-cued recall, where bad personal events cue pessimistic recollections.

Data
Danish Consumer Expectations Survey (Statistics Denmark Omnibus), linked on CPR, Tax registers from SKAT: income, liquid assets, net wealth, taxes (IND, formue), Civil Registration System / Population register (CPR/BEF), Education register (UDDA), National Patient Register (LPR), emergency room visits 1994–2018
Key variables
  • Outcome: inflation forecasts and backcasts (qualitative and quantitative)
  • Explanatory: recent change in household log nominal income (t-1 vs t-2)
  • Explanatory: future household income change and expected household financial situation
  • Shock: family emergency room visit in the survey month
  • Benchmark: realized inflation
Period
2012–2019 (robustness from 2008; population registers from 1991)
Sample
35050 usable responses (from 55171 survey respondents aged 25–60) Danish Consumer Expectations Survey respondents aged 25–60 in 2012–2019 without substantial self-employment income and with complete answers, linked to administrative data. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Household total income Earnings and income
    Yearly total income before taxes and labour market contributions, including labour income, public transfers, property income and most other taxable income attributable to the individual (excludes imputed rental value, pension contributions to employer schemes and lottery winnings). Household value is the average of the two spouses' values if a spouse is present in CPR, otherwise the individual value.
    Registers: IND, BEF
    Codes: PERINDKIALT_13 (income); spouse via E_FAELLE_ID
    replication code · code_dstserver/code_epinion/2_build_registries.do; NBER WP w32664 Section 1.2 and footnote 6
  • Household labour income Earnings and income
    Total taxable wage income, benefits, bonuses, severance pay and value of stock options, averaged across spouses as for total income.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: LOENMV_13 (income_work)
    replication code · code_dstserver/code_epinion/2_build_registries.do; NBER WP w32664 Section 1.2
  • Recent and future household income change Earnings and income
    For a respondent interviewed in any month of year t, recent change = log nominal household income in t-1 minus t-2; future change = log income in t+1 minus t-1. Changes are trimmed at the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: Log_Income_HH_L1L2, Log_Income_HH_F1L1; winsor2 cut(2.5 97.5) trim
    replication code · code_dstserver/analysis/A1c_sample_restrictions.do; NBER WP w32664 Section 1.3
  • Liquid assets and net wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Liquid assets follow Andersen et al. (2020): total value of bank deposits, stocks and bonds reported by financial institutions to SKAT. Net wealth is SKAT's tax-purpose measure of net household assets excluding non-deposited cash and foreign assets, with real estate at tax-assessed values; both averaged across spouses and used as asinh changes.
    Registers: IND
    working paper · Section 1.2 and footnote 7
  • Self-employment exclusion Sample definition and timing
    Exclude respondents if self-employment income exceeds one fourth of household income (in absolute value) in any year from t-4 to t+1 around the interview.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: abs(Income_selfemp_HH)/abs(Income_HH) > .25 for timestamps L4..F1
    replication code · code_dstserver/analysis/A1c_sample_restrictions.do; NBER WP footnote 11
  • Main survey sample Sample definition and timing
    Monthly survey respondents 2012-2019 (backcast analyses 2013-2019) aged 25-60, excluding high self-employment income, missing key survey answers (Do not know, refused or forecast >100 pp) and missing registry variables, after trimming income changes and inflation answers at 2.5/97.5 percentiles.
    Registers: BEF, IND, UDDA
    Codes: Age<25 | Age>60 dropped
    replication code · code_dstserver/analysis/A1c_sample_restrictions.do; NBER WP Section 1.3
  • Family emergency room visit in survey month Health care use
    Indicator equal to one if any household member (household identifier from BEF) visited the emergency room in the calendar month of the interview. An ER visit is an acute outpatient hospital contact in the NPR (recorded as patient type ER before 2014, acute outpatient from 2014). Respondents with more than 7 family ER visits over 2008-2018 are dropped.
    Registers: LPR, BEF
    Codes: has_now_visit_fam; ERvisit_count_surveysample_fam <= 7
    replication code · code_dstserver/analysis/A9_healthregs.do; NBER WP Online Appendix A.1 (Emergency Room Visits Data) and ER table notes
  • Highest education (ISCED) Education and test scores
    HFAUDD from UDDA mapped via an ISCED crosswalk to single-digit ISCED 2011 levels 1-6; code 9 (not known) set to missing.
    Registers: UDDA
    Codes: HFAUDD -> ISCED_AUDD_AFSP4L_KT first digit
    replication code · code_dstserver/code_epinion/2_build_registries.do

Fertility and Family Labor Supply

Katrine Jakobsen, Thomas H. Jørgensen and Hamish Low · American Economic Review (forthcoming), 2026 · Individual

Uses the 2009 Danish tax reform to show that higher net-of-tax wages for women reduce fertility while higher wages for men raise it. A life-cycle model of couples choosing the timing and number of children, estimated on register data, implies that allowing fertility to adjust raises women's labour supply responsiveness substantially and that human capital depreciation around births drives much of the long-run gender wage gap.

Data
Monthly payroll records (BFL/eIndkomst), Annual income tax data (IND), Population and family register (BEF), family definitions and parent links, Education register (UDDA), Labour market experience from ATP payments, Parental leave spell register (OF)
Key variables
  • Outcome: fertility (births)
  • Treatment: 2009–2018 tax reform changes in marginal net-of-tax wage rate
  • Outcome: labour market participation, part-time and full-time work from pay-slip hours
  • Outcome: annual labour income
  • Control: education (high vs less skilled), labour market experience
Period
2004–2018 (tax sample 2004–2018; estimation sample 2010–2018)
Sample
10,851,444 individual-year observations (estimation sample); 2,531,181 (tax sample) Danish individuals aged 25–60 with an opposite-sex partner, not students, self-employed, retired or on disability pension; tax sample restricted to cohabiting or married women aged 25–40. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Labour market participation, part-time and full-time work Employment and labour force status
    Participation means at least 481 annual hours (e.g. 37 hours for 13 weeks) on BFL pay slips together with annual income of at least 50,000 DKK; part time is 481-1,664 annual hours; full time is more than 1,664 hours. Monthly hours and income are scaled down by the share of the month registered on parental leave in the OF register.
    Registers: BFL (eIndkomst), OF
    Codes: thresholds 481 and 1,664 annual hours; 50,000 DKK
    working paper · Section 2; Supplemental Material A
  • Annual labour income (BFL) Earnings and income
    12-month sum of monthly labour income from BFL pay slips, by calendar year for age profiles and centred on the birth month for event-study moments (e.g. income from January-February before a March birth counts as year -1); excludes income registered while on parental leave; deflated by CPI, in 1000 DKK. Estimation sample 2010-2018.
    Registers: BFL (eIndkomst), OF
    working paper · Section 2; Supplemental Material A
  • Personal income (tax sample) Earnings and income
    Personal income from annual tax data: labour income from wage work, profits from own firms and labour market transfers; deflated by CPI.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: PERINDKP
    working paper · Supplemental Material A
  • Couples / partners Family links, fertility and household
    Partners follow Statistics Denmark's family definition, including married and cohabiting couples; cohabitants are two adults at the same address registered as parents to a child, or two opposite-sex adults with an age difference under 15 years at the same address. Constructed from EFALLE in BEF; couple age is the woman's age. Estimation sample keeps couples with at most five years age difference.
    Registers: BEF
    Codes: EFALLE; FOED_DAG; KOEN
    working paper · Section 2, footnote 8; Supplemental Material A
  • High skilled vs less skilled Education and test scores
    High skilled if at least 180 months of education (at least a bachelor's degree), measured as the highest degree earned in the sample period; less skilled otherwise.
    Registers: UDDA
    Codes: HFPRIA >= 180 months
    working paper · Section 2; Supplemental Material A
  • Labour market experience Employment and labour force status
    Statistics Denmark's experience measure based on accumulated mandatory ATP pension payments, which depend on hours worked; part-time employment counts as 2/3 of full time.
    Registers: IDAP
    Codes: ERHVER, ERHVER79
    working paper · Section 2; Supplemental Material A
  • Sample exclusions by main activity Sample definition and timing
    Individuals aged 25-60 with an opposite-sex partner; observations dropped if mainly student, self-employed, retired or on disability pension, based on main activity at end of November.
    Registers: IDAP/AKM (socio-economic status)
    Codes: SOCSTIL, SOCSTIL_KODE
    working paper · Section 2; Supplemental Material A
  • Mechanical net-of-tax rate change (instrument) Taxes and tax rates
    Four-year mechanical change log(1 - tau_{t+4}(z_t)) - log(1 - tau_t(z_t)) in the marginal net-of-tax rate, holding income and characteristics at year-t values, computed with a Danish tax simulator; used to instrument own and partner net-of-tax rate changes and virtual income. Restricted to couples where both have personal income of 50,000-600,000 DKK in the base year. Outcome is the 4-year difference in number of children born.
    Registers: IND
    working paper · Section 3; Supplemental Material A.1
  • Household wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Bank deposits, bonds, stocks and property net of loans and mortgages at end of year; registered property values raised by 10% (following Leth-Petersen 2010); deflated by CPI, in 1000 DKK.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: FORM; FORMREST_NY05 (after 1996)
    working paper · Supplemental Material A

Effects of Parental Death on Labor Market Outcomes

Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen and Ning Zhang · American Economic Review, 2026 · Individual

Uses sudden first parental deaths and matched controls in Danish administrative data. Earnings fall by about 2 percent for men and 3 percent for women, mental health worsens for both, and women with young children lose the most, around 4 percent, consistent with the loss of informal childcare from grandparents.

Data
Cause of death registers (DODSAARS/DODSAARG), Population register with parent-child links (BEF), Income and labour market registers (IND, AKM, IDAS/IDAN/IDAP), ATP-based hours proxy, Health Insurance Register for GP/psychologist/psychiatrist visits (SYSI/SSSY), National Patient Register (LPR_ADM/LPR_DIAG), Psychiatric Central Research Register (PSYK_ADM/PSYK_DIAG), Prescription register (LMDB), Childcare registers (DAGI/BOERNFB)
Key variables
  • Treatment: first sudden parental death (heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, acute respiratory infection, accidents)
  • Outcome: annual earnings (indexed to pre-death gender mean)
  • Outcome: employment and hours proxy
  • Outcome: mental health care use and prescriptions
  • Control group: matched not-yet-treated individuals
Period
1980–2019 (parental deaths 1985–2014)
Sample
Treated: 21919 daughters and 24354 sons whose mother died first; 74991 daughters and 85022 sons whose father died first (plus matched controls) Danish adults aged 25–50 with two known parents who experienced a sudden first parental death between 1985 and 2014, with matched controls. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • First sudden parental death (treatment) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    The first death of either parent, where the cause (from cause-of-death registers) is sudden/unexpected: heart disease, cerebrovascular disease, acute respiratory infections, or traffic or other external accidents. Treatment sample: first parental deaths 1985-2014, both parents known and present in the population the year before, child aged 25-50 at the death.
    Registers: DODSAARS, DODSAARG, BEF
    working paper · Section III.A-III.B
  • Matched control group Sample definition and timing
    Nearest-neighbour Mahalanobis matching of each treated individual to one control who does not experience either parent's death within five years after the treated person's event; exact matching on gender, earnings group (zero plus three quantile groups) and youngest child above/below age six one year before; NN matching on age, education, public/private sector, cohabitation, region, number of children, parental ages, youngest child's age and three years of employment and earnings history.
    Registers: BEF, IND, IDAN
    working paper · Section IV (Empirical strategy) and footnote 13
  • Indexed earnings Earnings and income
    Earnings from employment and self-employment, inflation-adjusted to 2020 levels, winsorized at 98%, and indexed by the average earnings of men and women (separately) one year before parental death so effects read as percent of the baseline mean.
    Registers: IND, AKM
    working paper · Section III.A and footnote 8
  • Participation and hours proxy (ATP) Employment and labour force status
    Participation = strictly positive ATP pension contributions; intensive margin = amount of ATP contributions, which are paid proportionally to hours worked (following Kleven, Landais and Sogaard 2019).
    Registers: IND, IDAP
    Codes: ATP contributions > 0
    working paper · Footnote 7; Figure 1 notes
  • Psychologist and psychiatrist visits Health care use
    Number of consultations per year with privately practising clinical psychologists and psychiatrists (also GPs), observed from 1990.
    Registers: SYSI, SSSY
    working paper · Section III.A; Section VI.A.A
  • Mental health prescriptions Health care use
    Any (and number of) prescriptions with ATC codes N05*, N06A*, N06B* or N06C*, available from 1995.
    Registers: LMDB
    Codes: ATC N05*, N06A*, N06B*, N06C*
    working paper · Footnote 18; Figure 3 notes
  • Opioid and alcohol-dependence prescriptions Health care use
    Opioid painkillers = prescriptions with ATC N02A*; alcohol dependence treatment = ATC N07BB* (including Antabuse).
    Registers: LMDB
    Codes: ATC N02A*; ATC N07BB*
    working paper · Footnote 19
  • Hospital visits Health care use
    In- and outpatient visits at non-psychiatric hospital wards (1994-2018); psychiatric hospital contacts observed separately from 1995.
    Registers: LPR_ADM, LPR_DIAG, PSYK_ADM, PSYK_DIAG
    working paper · Section III.A; Figure 3 notes

Family responses and insurance Labour markets, wages and sorting Health

Germs in the Family: The Short- and Long-Term Consequences of Intrahousehold Disease Spread

N. Meltem Daysal, Hui Ding, Maya Rossin-Slater and Hannes Schwandt · American Economic Review, 2026 · Individual

Shows that infant younger siblings are hospitalised for respiratory conditions two to three times as often as their older siblings were, because preschool-aged children bring disease home. Combining birth order with local variation in respiratory disease prevalence, early-life exposure lowers younger siblings' later earnings and education and worsens chronic respiratory and mental health.

Data
National Patient Register (LPR), Medical Birth Register (MFR), Population register (BEF), Register-Based Labour Force Statistics (RAS), Income Statistics Register (IND), Education Register (UDDA), Academic Achievement Register (9th grade test scores), Psychiatric Central Research Register (PCRR), Health Insurance Register (Sygesikringsregisteret), Childcare enrollment data, National Child Database (breastfeeding)
Key variables
  • Outcome: acute respiratory hospitalizations in the first year of life
  • Treatment: birth order (second-born vs first-born) interacted with municipality respiratory disease exposure index
  • Outcome: earnings, labour force participation and income rank at ages 18–32
  • Outcome: high school and college completion; 9th grade test scores
  • Outcome: chronic respiratory and mental healthcare use
Period
Children born 1981–2017; outcomes 1980–2019
Sample
1,230,180 children First- and second-born singleton siblings born in Denmark 1981–2017, at least 11 months apart, in 91 municipalities. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Acute respiratory hospitalizations (first year of life) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Number of inpatient hospitalizations in the first year of life (also split into first and second six months) with a primary diagnosis of an acute respiratory condition, from the National Patient Register (1981-2018).
    Registers: LPR
    Codes: ICD-8 starting 46, 47, 48, 490, 079, 783; ICD-10 starting J (excluding J4) or B974
    online appendix · Section 2; Appendix A
  • RSV hospitalizations Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Hospitalizations for respiratory syncytial virus, measurable only for cohorts born 1994 or later (ICD-10).
    Registers: LPR
    Codes: ICD-10 J12.1, J20.5, J21.0, B97.4
    online appendix · Appendix A
  • Chronic respiratory hospitalizations Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Inpatient visits with a primary diagnosis of a chronic respiratory condition (e.g. asthma, COPD), studied at ages 16-26.
    Registers: LPR
    Codes: ICD-8 491-493; ICD-10 J4
    online appendix · Appendix A
  • Mental healthcare visits Health care use
    Visits to psychiatric hospitals (inpatient, outpatient, ED from the Psychiatric Central Research Register) and to private psychiatric clinics (Health Insurance Register reimbursements, identified by physician specialty codes), at extensive and intensive margins, ages 16-26 (data 1997-2018).
    Registers: Psychiatric Central Research Register, Sygesikringsregisteret
    Codes: physician specialty codes 24 or 26
    online appendix · Section 2; Appendix A
  • Respiratory disease exposure index Geography and neighbourhood
    Monthly number of acute respiratory hospitalizations per 100 children aged 13-71 months in the child's municipality of residence (2007 municipality structure, via crosswalk), excluding the child's own older sibling if aged 13-71 months, summed over the 12 months of the child's first year of life (also separate indices for months 1-6 and 7-12).
    Registers: LPR, BEF
    Codes: Acute respiratory ICD codes as above
    paper · Section 4 and footnote 17
  • Sibling analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    From all 2,278,868 children born 1981-2017: drop one-child families; keep first- and second-born singletons only; require birth spacing of at least 11 months; require known municipality of birth in municipalities averaging at least 1,000 children aged 13-71 months (91 municipalities kept); drop missing parental controls and keep complete pairs. Final sample 1,230,180 children.
    Registers: MFR, BEF
    paper · Section 2 (Analysis sample), footnote 14
  • Labour force participation Employment and labour force status
    Indicator equal to 1 if in the labour force (employed or unemployed searching) and 0 if out of the labour force, based on tax-record labour market status as of November of the preceding year; ages 18-32.
    Registers: RAS
    paper · Section 2 (Labor market and income outcomes)
  • Wages, gross income and income rank Earnings and income
    Wages among the employed and gross personal income including government transfers, in 2010 USD, winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles; income rank is the percentile of gross personal income within the full Danish population of the same birth cohort and age; ages 18-32.
    Registers: IND
    paper · Section 2, footnote 12
  • Education attainment and 9th grade test scores Education and test scores
    Indicators for high school and college graduation by ages 18-32 from highest completed schooling; 9th grade Danish (reading) and mathematics scores (2001-2019) standardized within subject and test year.
    Registers: UDDA, Academic Achievement Register
    paper · Section 2 (Education outcomes)

The Direct and Indirect Effects of Online Job Search Advice

Steffen Altmann, Anita M. Glenny, Robert Mahlstedt and Alexander Sebald · Review of Economic Studies, 2026 · Individual

A large two-stage randomised experiment on the Danish public employment service's online platform gave job seekers vacancy information and occupational recommendations, with treatment intensity varying by region. Advice raises employment and earnings when few job seekers receive it, but the gains vanish at high intensity because treated job seekers crowd into the same occupations.

Data
Field experiment on jobnet.dk (Danish public employment service platform): treatment assignment and dashboard exposure, Jobnet job search profiles, vacancy information and registered job applications (with occupation codes), Statistics Denmark register data on employment, hours and earnings (12 months after start), Population registers and benefit payment records (UI recipients), Register data on the universe of unemployment-to-job occupational transitions (to build recommendations)
Key variables
  • Treatment: occupational recommendations, vacancy information, or both (individual randomization)
  • Treatment intensity: municipality cluster share of treated job seekers (two-stage randomization)
  • Outcome: working hours and earnings in the year after intervention
  • Outcome: job applications by occupation (search strategy)
Period
Intervention from March 17, 2019; outcomes over the following 12 months (before March 2020)
Sample
92,098 individuals All individuals registered as unemployed and receiving UI benefits in Denmark on March 17, 2019. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Experimental sample Sample definition and timing
    Full stock of individuals registered as unemployed and receiving UI benefits in Denmark at the start of the experiment on March 15, 2019 (92,098 individuals); welfare recipients and later entrants excluded. Outcomes measured over windows after entrydate.
    Registers: STAR experiment data
    Codes: entrydate == mdy(3,15,2019)
    replication code · _README.pdf (Subject pool); code/data_preparation.do
  • Total working hours within 6/12 months Hours worked
    Sum of paid hours (AJO_LOENTIMER) over all BFL monthly job records whose AJO_JOB_START_DATO falls after entrydate and within q x 30.42 days (q=6, 12); zero if no records.
    Registers: BFL
    Codes: AJO_LOENTIMER summed for AJO_JOB_START_DATO in (entrydate, entrydate+q*30.4167]
    replication code · code/data_preparation.do (Monthly labor market outcomes; hours4_total)
  • Total earnings within 6/12 months Earnings and income
    Sum of AJO_SMALT_LOENBELOEB over BFL records with job start date in the window after entrydate, zero if none.
    Registers: BFL
    Codes: AJO_SMALT_LOENBELOEB (earnings4_total)
    replication code · code/data_preparation.do
  • Monthly employment rate Employment and labour force status
    emp_q = 1 if cumulative BFL hours increase between month q-1 and q after entry (emp1 = any hours in month 1); employment rate over 6 or 12 months is the mean of these monthly indicators.
    Registers: BFL
    Codes: emp`x' = (hours4_total`x' - hours4_total`x-1' > 0); emp_rate12 = rmean(emp1..emp12)
    replication code · code/data_preparation.do
  • Employment in recommended / stored occupations Occupation and job hierarchy
    Hours, earnings and monthly employment in BFL jobs whose DISCO code (VMO_DISCO_KODE truncated to 4 digits) matches one of up to five recommended occupations (Alternative_DISCO mapping of the job seeker's profile occupations) or an occupation stored in the job search profile (jsjs CVFAGID), within 183 and 365 days of entry.
    Registers: BFL, STAR jsjs
    Codes: floor(VMO_DISCO_KODE/100) == floor(forslag/1000) or floor(discoams_key/1000)
    replication code · code/data_preparation.do (occupations_rec, occupations_stored)
  • Share of applications to recommended occupations Occupation and job hierarchy
    Among applications logged in Joblog within 1 or 12 months (30.25-day months) after entry, the share whose DISCO-AMS occupation equals a recommended occupation (or one stored in the profile).
    Registers: STAR Joblog
    Codes: share_recommended_t1/t12, share_stored_t1/t12
    replication code · code/data_preparation.do
  • Labour market tightness Unemployment and benefits
    Vacancies divided by job seekers per municipality x occupation in the experiment's starting week (week 1442), averaged over the occupations in the individual's search profile.
    Registers: STAR vacancies, STAR jsjs
    Codes: tightness = no_vacancies/jobseekers, week==1442
    replication code · code/data_preparation.do
  • Treatment intensity Geography and neighbourhood
    Baseline: municipality regime (10 super-control, 44 medium with 60% treated, 44 high with 90% treated). Alternatives: share treated in own plus bordering municipalities; commuting-weighted shares using the fraction of workers residing in j who commuted to m in the three prior years; and an individual measure over zip-code x 3-digit-occupation markets applied to in the two prior years.
    Registers: BFL, STAR Joblog
    Codes: geogroup 1/2/3; intensity_alt1
    online appendix · OnlineAppendix.pdf Section B.1; _README.pdf; code/data_preparation.do
  • Pre-intervention labour market history Earnings and income
    From BFL records with period start before entry: mean monthly wage (lon) and employment degree (grad) in each of the three years before entry (year t-1 excludes the last 30 days), set to zero if absent; last pre-intervention occupation is the 1-digit DISCO of the most recent BFL spell.
    Registers: BFL
    Codes: wage_tminus1-3, grad_tminus1-3; last_occ = floor(VMO_DISCO_KODE/100000)
    replication code · code/data_preparation.do

Changing Tracks: Human Capital Investment after Loss of Ability

Anders Humlum, Jakob R. Munch and Pernille Plato · American Economic Review, 2025 · Individual

Uses quasi-random work accidents in Danish administrative data to show that injured workers enrol in bachelor's programmes that build on their previous training. Exploiting differences in how stackable degrees are, higher education moves injured workers from disability benefits into full-time jobs paying 25 percent more than before injury, and reskilling subsidies pay for themselves four times over.

Data
Industrial Injury Register (Arbejdsskaderegisteret) / workers' compensation claims from AES, National Patient Register (LPR), Health Insurance Register (Sygesikringsregisteret), Prescription Drug Database (LMDB), Education Register (UDDA), Course Participant Register (VEUV), Danish Register for Evaluation of Marginalization (DREAM), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), linked to O*NET, Population register (BEF/POP)
Key variables
  • Treatment: work accident causing loss of earning capacity (vs. matched non-injured workers)
  • Outcome: enrollment in and completion of formal degrees and courses
  • Outcome: earnings, hours and occupation (task content)
  • Outcome: disability and other social transfers
  • Severity: assessed earning capacity loss and personal impairment
Period
1995–2017 (work injury claims 1998–2017)
Sample
14,481 injury events (14,369 distinct individuals); 4,568 events (4,528 individuals) for workers with vocational degrees with access to higher education Full-time employed Danish workers (excluding military) who suffered an accepted physical work accident with positive earning capacity loss, compared with matched non-injured workers. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Work accident causing loss of earning capacity (treatment) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Work accidents recorded by the Labour Market Insurance (AES) that caused a loss of earning capacity, restricted to physical (not psychological) injuries, non-military workers, and workers with full-time employment in each of the three years before the accident. An injury qualifies for compensation if personal impairment exceeds 5% or earning capacity loss exceeds 15%.
    Registers: Industrial Injury Register (Arbejdsskaderegisteret, AES), IDA
    working paper · Sections 2.1, 2.2.1 and 3.1
  • Injury severity (earning capacity loss, personal impairment) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Earning capacity loss is assessed by AES industry specialists as the loss of work capacity in the worker's occupation; personal impairment is based solely on the injury diagnosis, independent of occupation, age or earnings.
    Registers: Industrial Injury Register (Arbejdsskaderegisteret, AES)
    working paper · Section 2.1
  • Matched non-injured control workers Sample definition and timing
    For each injured worker, a one-to-one random match among workers satisfying the pre-event employment requirements but not injured in the event year, with the same three-digit ISCO occupation, two-digit NACE industry, education level, age and gender in the year before the accident.
    Registers: IDA, UDDA, POP
    Codes: ISCO 3-digit; NACE 2-digit
    working paper · Section 3.1; Table 2 notes
  • Access to higher education (instrument) Education and test scores
    Workers whose initial education gives direct access to higher degrees: high school graduates and workers whose vocational degree provides direct access to specific higher-education programmes (e.g. carpentry gives access to a Construction Architecture bachelor; landscape gardening does not). Access and no-access groups are balanced by inverse probability weighting on health, age, gender, years of schooling and occupation.
    Registers: UDDA
    working paper · Section 4.1, footnote 18 (list in Appendix Table A.3)
  • Degree and course enrolment/completion Education and test scores
    Enrolment in and completion of formal degrees from UDDA (six-digit programme codes covering basic, vocational and post-secondary education) and of non-degree courses from VEUV (five-digit course codes; subsidy-eligible courses, all attendees).
    Registers: UDDA, VEUV
    Codes: UDDA six-digit programme codes; VEUV five-digit course codes (specific values not given)
    working paper · Section 2.2.3
  • Disability and other social transfers Unemployment and benefits
    Receipt of social transfers including unemployment, rehabilitation, disability benefits and public pensions, from DREAM.
    Registers: DREAM
    working paper · Section 2.2.4
  • Occupational task content / physical ability Occupation and job hierarchy
    IDA occupations (six-digit ISCO, linked in week 48 of each year) linked to O*NET; Physical Ability is the average importance of Static, Explosive, Dynamic and Trunk Strength and Stamina. Career clusters follow O*NET.
    Registers: IDA, O*NET
    Codes: ISCO six-digit
    working paper · Section 2.2.5; footnotes 14 and 21
  • Health care utilisation (incl. antidepressant use) Health care use
    Hospitalisations (inpatient and outpatient) with diagnoses from LPR, contacts with primary-care physicians and specialists from the Health Insurance Register, and prescription drug purchases (e.g. antidepressants, painkillers/opioids) from LMDB, 1995-2017.
    Registers: LPR, Sygesikringsregisteret, LMDB
    working paper · Section 2.2.2; Section 3.1

Micro versus Macro Labor Supply Elasticities: The Role of Dynamic Returns to Effort

Henrik Kleven, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Kristian Larsen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard · American Economic Review, 2025 · Individual

Builds a model in which effort today raises earnings tomorrow, so responses to taxes are delayed and mediated by job switches. Danish administrative data confirm the model's life-cycle predictions for earnings and hours, and a quasi-experimental design based on job switchers finds a long-run earnings elasticity around 0.5, against a short-run elasticity of about 0.2.

Data
Linked administrative registers on earnings, occupation (DISCO), firm and demographics, full population, Employer-employee matched data (firm x occupation job cells), ATP pension contribution-based hours measure (1980–2018), Monthly uncapped hours measure (from 2008), Income tax records (2009 tax reform variation)
Key variables
  • Outcome: earnings (log earnings changes)
  • Treatment: 2009 tax reform change in marginal net-of-tax rate
  • Instrument: simulated net-of-tax rate change at baseline income
  • Mediator: job switches (firm x occupation cell), incl. mass-layoff switches
  • Outcome: hours worked
Period
1980–2018
Sample
N = 2,501,126 and 2,428,411 in the main elasticity regressions (Table 1) Full Danish population; tax-reform analysis uses taxpayers with baseline income between 250,000 and 1,000,000 DKK. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • ATP-based hours (1980-2018) Hours worked
    Hours inferred from mandatory ATP pension contributions, which employers pay based on a binned measure of hours; for monthly-paid workers annual contributions depend on monthly hours in four bins, giving 37 annual hours bins. Capped at full time in all 12 months.
    Registers: ATP pension contributions
    working paper · Section 3, footnotes 17-18
  • Monthly uncapped hours (from 2008) Hours worked
    Uncapped hours worked for all workers at monthly level, available from 2008; used where precise hours variation is needed (aggregated to quarters in the promotion event study).
    Registers: Monthly payroll records
    working paper · Section 3; Section 4 Fact 3
  • Job (firm x occupation cell) and job switch Occupation and job hierarchy
    Job is a firm x occupation cell; a switcher moves between firm x occupation cells after the reform. Occupations use DISCO-08 from 2010 (563 occupations), DISCO-88 1991-2009 (372) bridged with the Humlum (2021) crosswalk, and an older Danish classification before 1991 (299). Switches where more than 50% of an individual's coworkers move to the same job cell in the same year are dropped.
    Registers: Employer-employee matched data
    Codes: DISCO-08; DISCO-88; pre-1991 Danish occupation codes
    working paper · Section 3, footnote 15; Section 5.1
  • Mass layoff switchers Firm characteristics and productivity
    Workers who move firm following a mass layoff in their original firm; a mass layoff requires the firm to reduce its workforce by at least 30% on a base of at least 20 employees.
    Registers: Employer-employee matched data
    working paper · Figure 6 notes (mass-layoff panel)
  • Labour earnings outcome Earnings and income
    Total labour compensation, including contributions to employer-administered retirement savings plans; outcome is the log change between 2008 and 2010 (placebo 2006-2008).
    Registers: Income tax records
    working paper · Section 5.1, footnote 26
  • Reform treatment and simulated net-of-tax rate instrument Taxes and tax rates
    Treatment assigned by pre-reform baseline taxable income (labour income, transfers, pensions, alimony and certain capital income) in bins relative to the 2009 reform threshold (around the 70th percentile). The instrument is the simulated log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate from tax code changes, holding income at baseline (Gruber-Saez). Baseline sample: taxpayers with baseline income 250,000-1,000,000 DKK.
    Registers: Income tax records
    working paper · Section 5.1, footnote 27; Table 2 notes
  • Promotion Occupation and job hierarchy
    Within-firm switch to an occupation cell whose median earnings are at least 10% higher (robustness 5% and 20%); promoted workers matched to unpromoted co-workers in the same firm.
    Registers: Employer-employee matched data, Monthly payroll records
    working paper · Section 4, Fact 3

Taxation and public finance Labour markets, wages and sorting

Untying the Knot: How Child Support and Alimony Affect Couples' Dynamic Decisions and Welfare

Hanno Foerster · Review of Economic Studies, 2024 · Individual

Estimates a dynamic model of family labour supply, home production, saving and divorce on Danish register and survey data to study post-marital maintenance payments. Alimony carries larger labour supply disincentives and insures consumption less efficiently than child support, so welfare rises when child support is increased and alimony reduced.

Data
Danish register data on income, labour force status and hours worked, Marital histories and birth register (BEF/family links), Maintenance (child support and alimony) payment records and child residence after divorce, Danish Time Use Survey 2001 (DTUS)
Key variables
  • Outcome: labour supply (employer-recorded hours bins) and annual labour income
  • Outcome: divorce
  • Policy: child support and alimony (maintenance) payments
  • Survey: housework hours and relative consumption in couples (DTUS)
Period
1980–2013
Sample
322,732 couples (645,464 individuals) and 4,312,826 couple-year observations; DTUS 2,105 households Danish couples in their first marriage, both spouses aged 25–58, at least one working, excluding couples with children from previous relationships. source
How variables are defined (10)
  • Marriage and divorce events Family links, fertility and household
    Marriage event when marital status is unmarried in year t and married in t+1; divorce event when married in t and divorced in t+1. Marital status from CIVST (G=1 married, U=0 unmarried, F=2 divorced, D=3, E=4, L=5, O=6, P=7), with CIV_VFRA giving the date since status.
    Registers: BEF (personer)
    Codes: CIVST in {G,U,F,D,E,L,O,P}; marriage: CIVST U->G; divorce: G->F; CIV_VFRA
    replication code · code/assembledat_untying.sas (marital status recode and event definitions)
  • Household dissolution (divorce year) Family links, fertility and household
    Divorce year is the minimum of the formal divorce year and the first year, within 6 years before formal divorce, in which a married, never-divorced person's partner ID (FAELLE_NR) changes to a new partner or no partner.
    Registers: BEF
    Codes: FAELLE_NR (parid); divyear=min(fdivyear, firstparswitch_year), parswitch window t_ref_fdiv in [-6,0]
    replication code · code/datprep_untying.do (Define year of household dissolution)
  • Couples sample Sample definition and timing
    Individuals observed from the start of their first marriage (first observed marriage event with missing prior marital-status date and no prior divorce), years 1980-2013, ages 28-58; individuals or partners with children from previous relationships are dropped.
    Registers: BEF, Fertility database (ftdb_father, ftdb_mother)
    Codes: age 28-58; year 1980-2013; other_kids==0 & other_kids_par==0
    replication code · code/assembledat_untying.sas (sel_IDS); code/datprep_untying.do
  • Weekly work hours bins Hours worked
    IDA job attachment code TILKNYT recoded into weekly hours per the Statistics Denmark key: codes 0/10/20/30 -> 0, 5/15/25/35 -> 5, 4/14/24/34 -> 15, 3/13/23/33 -> 25, 2/12/22/32 -> 34, 1/11/21/31 -> 38 hours. Set to 0 for those out of the labour force with missing hours.
    Registers: IDAN
    Codes: TILKNYT: {0,10,20,30}=0; {5,15,25,35}=5; {4,14,24,34}=15; {3,13,23,33}=25; {2,12,22,32}=34; {1,11,21,31}=38
    replication code · code/datprep_untying.do lines 1-20; assembledat_untying.sas (work_vars1)
  • Labour income (model-consistent) Earnings and income
    Weekly hours (from TILKNYT bins) times 49 weeks times hourly wage TIMELON; zero if hours are zero. Register labour income LONIND is also assembled (earnings), with negative values truncated to 0.
    Registers: IDAN, IDAP
    Codes: TIMELON (hourly wage), TILKNYT; LONIND (earnings); labor_income = work_hours*49*wage
    replication code · code/datprep_untying.do lines 309-316
  • Out of labour force / participation Employment and labour force status
    Out of the labour force if IDA labour force status PSTILL is in 40, 41, 50, 52, 90, 92, 93 or 95; labour force participation is the complement.
    Registers: IDAP
    Codes: PSTILL in 40,41,50,52,90,92,93,95 = out of labour force
    replication code · code/datprep_untying.do (Define out of the labor force)
  • Maintenance payments (observed) Family links, fertility and household
    Post-marital maintenance paid (child support and alimony) from the income register variable UNDERHOL, deflated to 2004 prices; an indicator for any positive payment is also used.
    Registers: IND (indh)
    Codes: UNDERHOL
    replication code · code/assembledat_untying.sas (inc_vars1); code/datprep_untying.do; code/maint_imp.do
  • Custody and imputed child support/alimony Family links, fertility and household
    Custody counts children under 19 living in the same family ID after a divorce. Child support imputed from 2004 rules: 10,608 DKK per child times an earnings-dependent multiplier (thresholds 320k/340k/370k/500k/900k for one child, higher for 2-3 children) for children in the ex-partner's custody; alimony = 20% of (payer earnings minus child support minus max(ex-partner earnings, 90,000)), capped, only if ex-partner not remarried; total maintenance capped at one third of earnings. Earnings base = labour income + UI benefits (ARBLHU, KONTHJ, KONT_GL) in 2004 prices.
    Registers: IND (indk, indh), FAMILIE, IDAN
    Codes: ARBLHU, KONTHJ (pre-1993), KONT_GL (post-1993); FAMILIE_ID; cs_normal2004=10608
    replication code · code/maint_imp.do
  • Assets Wealth, debt and consumption
    Individual and household assets from the income register wealth variables: FORM before 1997 and FORMREST_NY05 after 1997; household assets are the sum of own and partner's post-1997 assets in DKK 1000s.
    Registers: IND (indh)
    Codes: FORM (assets before 1997), FORMREST_NY05 (assets post 1997)
    replication code · code/assembledat_untying.sas (inc_vars1); code/datprep_untying.do
  • Births and child identifiers Family links, fertility and household
    Children linked to fathers and mothers via the fertility database (PNRF, PNRM, PNRB) with birth year from FOED_DAG; first, second and third child IDs are assigned sequentially; birth event = child born in that year. Number of children and persons in the family from the family register.

    Codes: PNRF, PNRM, PNRB, FOED_DAG; C_ANTBOERNF, C_ANTPERSF

On the Family Origins of Human Capital Formation: Evidence from Donor Children

Petter Lundborg, Erik Plug and Astrid Würtz Rasmussen · Review of Economic Studies, 2024 · Individual

Uses Danish children conceived through sperm and egg donation to separate nurture from genetic transmission, since donors are not selected on parental traits. Only mothers' education matters once genes are removed: fathers' schooling has no effect on children's test scores, while mothers' schooling raises reading scores as much as among non-donor children.

Data
Danish IVF register (Danish Health Data Authority), Danish Education Register (UDDA), National test scores in reading and math (from 2010), Administrative registers on demographics and labour market (birth year, gender, marital status, children, earnings)
Key variables
  • Outcome: child average standardized national test score (reading and math)
  • Explanatory: mother's and father's years of schooling
  • Variation: donor sperm / donor egg conception (genetically unrelated parent)
  • Controls: month of first donor treatment and clinic fixed effects (waiting-list assignment)
Period
IVF treatments 1994–2007; demographics 1991–2016; labour market 1991–2012; tests from 2010
Sample
19,509 non-donor IVF children, 820 sperm donor children and 157 egg donor children (97 matched to egg donors) Children conceived through IVF treatments in Denmark 1994–2007 with at least one national test score, compared with 30% random samples of non-adopted (650,930) and adopted (2,674) children. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Child average standardized test score Education and test scores
    Scores from nationwide math and reading tests in primary and lower secondary school (2010-2020), each standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 within cohort; for each child the average over all available standardized reading and math scores. Math covers numbers and algebra, geometry and applied mathematics; reading covers language comprehension, decoding and reading comprehension. Grade-specific scores: reading grades 2, 4, 6, 8; math grades 3, 6.
    Registers: National test data (STIL)
    Codes: overall_grade; lang2 lang4 lang6 lang8 math3 math6
    replication code · Read_me.pdf, Table 1 variable description
  • Parental years of schooling and college Education and test scores
    Years of schooling of highest completed education of mother and father (and of egg donor, imputed when missing). College indicator equals 1 if more than 14 years of completed education.
    Registers: UDDA, IDAPALL
    Codes: yr_edu, yr_eduf, yr_edu_donor(_imputed); univ_m/univ_f = years > 14
    replication code · Read_me.pdf, Table 1
  • Donor-conception samples Family links, fertility and household
    Children conceived by IVF are split into a non-donor IVF sample, an egg-donor sample and a sperm-donor sample; treatment timing is captured by the calendar month of first IVF treatment and clinic dummies.
    Registers: IVF register (Danish Health Data Authority), BOERN, FTDK
    Codes: one_de_ds (non-donor), de (egg donor), ds (sperm donor); first_year_month_linear; clinic
    replication code · Read_me.pdf, Table 1; Table_1_do.do
  • Pre-birth parental labour income Earnings and income
    Average annual labour income (in 10,000 DKK) of mother/father (or egg donor) over the 4 years preceding the child's birth year; post-minus-pre log income change uses average labour income over the 5 years following the birth year.
    Registers: IDAPALL
    Codes: lonind_beforem4, lonind_beforef4, dif_logincm, dif_logincf
    replication code · Read_me.pdf, Table 1
  • Parental leave days Family links, fertility and household

Survey 2019 (income for 2017); register income histories

9,415 respondents (from 50,100 invited) Danish-born people born 1969–1973 (aged 45–50), randomly drawn by Statistics Denmark, who completed the survey. source

Inequality and fairness

The Anatomy of Sorting: Evidence from Danish Data

Rasmus Lentz, Suphanit Piyapromdee and Jean-Marc Robin · Econometrica, 2023 · Individual + firm

Estimates a flexible model of worker and firm heterogeneity in wages and job mobility on Danish matched employer-employee data. Workers and firms sort positively, with sorting operating through both wages and non-wage amenities, and worker heterogeneity accounts for the bulk of wage dispersion.

Data
Matched employer-employee register data (IDA) with annual wages, Weekly labour market spell/mobility data built from Statistics Denmark registers
Key variables
  • Outcome: log wage rate
  • Job-to-job mobility and transitions to and from non-employment (weekly)
  • Latent worker and firm types (finite mixture, classification EM)
  • Controls: gender, education, potential experience, tenure, calendar time
  • Sorting channels: job preferences, segmentation, layoffs, job finding
Period
1985–2013 (analysis panel starts 1987)
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Danish workers after completing education, employment spells starting before age 50, followed weekly across employers from 1987 to 2013 (read from the 2018 predecessor working paper). source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Log wage rate Earnings and income
    Annual total salary declared by the employer to the tax authorities divided by total hours worked by the worker in that year; assigned to the first week of the year or the first week of a new employment spell starting within the year. Hours are inferred by Statistics Denmark from mandatory pension contributions that depend on weekly hours.
    Registers: Danish matched employer-employee data (MEE)
    working paper · Section 2, footnote 7
  • Full-time employment vs non-employment spell Employment and labour force status
    Weekly employment and non-employment spells 1985-2013; spells with less than an average of 25 work hours per week are treated as non-employment spells (to keep only full-time workers). Non-employment is coded as firm ID 0.
    Registers: Danish matched employer-employee data (MEE)
    working paper · Section 2 and footnote 6; Appendix E.1
  • Analysis panel Sample definition and timing
    Panel starts in 1987 (1985-1986 used to classify tenure of the 1987 stock of jobs); only employment spells starting after the individual finished the highest level of education are kept, and spells starting after age 50 are removed. Workers are drawn from the 1987 working-age population or enter in the first week of the year after their last year of schooling. About 4 million workers and 400,000 firms.
    Registers: Danish matched employer-employee data (MEE)
    working paper · Section 2; Appendix E.1
  • Education groups Education and test scores
    Based on normed years of education of the highest completed degree: low is below 12 years, medium is exactly 12 years, high is above 12 years.
    Registers: Education register
    working paper · Section 5
  • Tenure and potential experience groups Sample definition and timing
    Short tenure is less than 100 weeks of employment (26 weeks for non-employment spells). Potential experience is time since leaving school (age minus age upon leaving school), grouped as under 5, 5-10, 11-15 and over 15 years; calendar time in 3-year intervals (9 groups 1987-2013), giving 72 covariate cells.
    Registers: Danish matched employer-employee data (MEE)
    working paper · Section 2; Section 5
  • Public/private status of firm Sector and industry
    Time-invariant firm characteristic indicating public or private status, used as observed firm covariate.
    Registers: Danish matched employer-employee data (MEE)
    working paper · Section 5

Equilibrium Trade in Automobiles

Kenneth Gillingham, Fedor Iskhakov, Anders Munk-Nielsen, John Rust and Bertel Schjerning · Journal of Political Economy, 2022 · Individual

Develops and estimates a dynamic equilibrium model of the market for new and used cars with heterogeneous households on the universe of Danish car ownership records, which record every vehicle's owner, age and scrappage. The model is used to evaluate Denmark's very high registration taxes and fuel taxes, showing how tax changes propagate through used-car prices and the age distribution of the fleet.

Data
Car ownership register covering all privately owned cars (Statistics Denmark extract), Odometer readings from mandatory vehicle inspections (driving), Demographic and income registers for all Danish households, Tax deduction for commuting distance (work distance), Fuel prices from eof.dk
Key variables
  • Outcome: car ownership transitions (keep, trade, buy new, scrap)
  • Car types: four classes by weight and fuel efficiency, 25 age groups
  • Household types: couple/single, high/low income, high/low work distance
  • Outcome: kilometres driven
  • Policy variable: new car registration tax and fuel tax
Period
1996–2008 (estimation 1997–2008)
Sample
nearly 39 million observations on car ownership transitions All Danish households and all cars owned by private individuals, 1996–2008. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Car types (green/brown x heavy/light) Other
    Cars are split by whether weight is above or below the median for the car's vintage cohort, then within each half by whether fuel efficiency is above (green) or below (brown) the median, giving four types; attributes are averaged within type. Cars are grouped into 25 age groups from new to 24+ years (cars over 22 years dropped from estimation).
    Registers: Car ownership register (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Appendix F.1 (Car types); Section 6.2
  • Household types Family links, fertility and household
    Eight household types from couple vs single, high vs low work distance, and high vs low income, where the income split is at the median income within the demographic cell.
    Registers: Demographic and income registers
    working paper · Appendix F.1 (Household types); Table 2
  • High work distance Geography and neighbourhood
    Based on the Danish tax deduction for travel distance to work, which applies only to full-time workers living more than 12 km (each way) from their workplace; households with the deduction are classed as high work distance (slightly under half of Danes).
    Registers: Tax records (commuting deduction)
    working paper · Appendix F.1 (Household types)
  • Kilometres driven Other
    Driving measured from odometer readings recorded at mandatory vehicle inspections, which occur biannually from car age 4 (ages 4, 6, 8, 10, ...).
    Registers: Vehicle inspection odometer data
    working paper · Appendix F.1 and footnote 32
  • Scrappage Other
    Scrappage is not observed directly: a vehicle is defined as scrapped if an ownership spell ends and no other ownership spell ever begins afterwards (ownership register extract from September 2011, last sample year 2008, so at least about 3 years without an owner). Accidents are not observed.
    Registers: Car ownership register
    working paper · Appendix F.1
  • New car registration tax Taxes and tax rates
    T(P) = 1.25 x [tau1 x min(P, K) + tau2 x max(P - K, 0)], with 25% VAT on the price including tax; in 2008 K = DKK 81,000, tau1 = 105% and tau2 = 180%. Fuel prices are country averages from eof.dk.
    Registers: Fuel prices (eof.dk)
    working paper · Appendix F.1
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Universe of Danish households and all privately owned cars, 1996-2008 (estimation on holdings 1997-2008, about 39 million household-year observations of car ownership transitions).
    Registers: Demographic registers, Car ownership register
    working paper · Appendix F.1; Section 6
