Reference Dependence in the Housing Market

Steffen Andersen, Cristian Badarinza, Lu Liu, Julie Marx and Tarun Ramadorai · American Economic Review, 2022 · Individual

Combines Danish housing listings and transactions with register data on owners to estimate a structural model of listing and sale decisions with loss aversion and financial constraints. Households derive utility from gains over the original purchase price and weigh losses about 2.5 times more than gains, which helps explain the co-movement of house prices and turnover.

Data
Property ownership and transaction register from SKAT and the Building and Housing Register (BBR), 1992–2016, Tax-assessed property values (SKAT), Property listings data from RealView, 2008–2016, Loan-level mortgage data from Danmarks Nationalbank, 2009–2016, Civil Registration System (CPR/BEF) for demographics and household links, Income and wealth records from SKAT (IND/formue)
Key variables
  • Outcome: listing decision and listing premium relative to hedonic value
  • Main regressor: potential gain or loss relative to original purchase price (reference point)
  • Potential home equity relative to down-payment constraint
  • Expected house value from hedonic pricing model
  • Structural parameter: loss aversion
Period
2009–2016 (transactions from 1992)
Sample
214,103 listings (191,507 unique households, 178,933 unique properties); housing stock of 5,538,052 observations of 807,345 properties Listings of Danish owner-occupied housing between 2009 and 2016, both sold and retracted, matched to mortgages and household finances. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Hedonic expected house value Wealth, debt and consumption
    Log sale price of sold listings regressed on year x municipality fixed effects (98 municipalities), an apartment indicator interacted with ln(lot size), ln(interior size), rooms, bathrooms, showers, unoccupied-at-sale dummy, ln(building age), rural and historic dummies, ln(distance to nearest major city), and a third-order polynomial (plus square-root term) of the previous-year tax-assessed value; predicted for all listed properties.
    Registers: SKAT property register, BBR, RealView
    paper · Section 3.6, eq. (6); Online Appendix E.1
  • Listing premium Wealth, debt and consumption
    l = ln(L) - predicted ln(P), where L is the initial listing price and predicted ln(P) is from the hedonic model.
    Registers: RealView, SKAT, BBR
    paper · Section 4.1
  • Potential gain (vs reference price) Wealth, debt and consumption
    G = predicted ln(P) - ln(R), where R is the nominal original purchase price of the property; measurable only for properties bought in 1992 or later.
    Registers: SKAT property transactions, BBR
    paper · Sections 3.5 and 4.1
  • Potential home equity Wealth, debt and consumption
    H = predicted ln(P) - ln(M), where M is the outstanding mortgage balance reported by the household's mortgage bank that year (multiple mortgages on a property summed; LTV and rate weighted); sellers with H < 20% are classed as potentially facing a binding down-payment constraint.
    Registers: Danmarks Nationalbank mortgage data
    paper · Sections 3.3 and 4.1
  • Listings sample Sample definition and timing
    Listings 2009-2016 with known owner and household id, purchase since 1992; excludes foreclosures, properties with registered size 0, prices below DKK 100,000 or above DKK 20 million (2015) or flagged extreme, within-family sales, anomalous transactions, sales to government/companies/organisations, summer houses, and households owning more than three properties. Includes sold and retracted listings.
    Registers: SKAT, BBR, RealView, Danmarks Nationalbank mortgage data, CPR
    paper · Section 3.5; Online Appendix C.5
  • Household Family links, fertility and household
    Household defined by the family identification number in CPR/SKAT records, used to aggregate individual income and wealth to household level.
    Registers: CPR, SKAT income and wealth
    paper · Section 3.4

Housing Household finance, saving and consumption

Globalization, Gender, and the Family

Wolfgang Keller and Hale Utar · Review of Economic Studies, 2022 · Individual + firm

Men and women hit by the same import shock from China adjust differently. Women in their late thirties who are displaced respond by having a child, especially high earners and those who would need to retrain, so a gender-neutral trade shock produces a long-run gender gap through the biological clock.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Central Population Register (CPR/BEF) for births, marriages, divorces and cohabitation, Domestic production database by 10-digit product (Industrial commodity statistics, VARS) to identify firms making quota goods, Industry-level imports from China and other advanced countries (instrument), Parental leave records
Key variables
  • Outcome: new births, marriage, divorce, parental leave
  • Outcome: earnings, hours, unemployment
  • Treatment: 1999 employer produces goods subject to MFA quota removal for China after WTO entry
  • Treatment (economy-wide): industry import penetration from China, instrumented with other countries' imports
  • Heterogeneity: gender and age (biological clock)
Period
1999–2007
Sample
about 1,600,000 workers; about 10,000 textile and clothing workers The 1999 cohort of full-time Danish private-sector workers aged 18–56, followed through 2007. source
How variables are defined (11)
  • Exposure to MFA quota removal (treatment) Trade and offshoring
    A firm is exposed (treated) if as of 1999 it had domestic production in any 8-digit CN good for which China would no longer face a quota upon WTO entry; quota categories are matched to 8-digit CN goods and firms producing quota goods are identified from the domestic production database reporting establishment sales by 10-digit product. Workers are exposed if employed by such a firm in 1999.
    Registers: IDA, VARS (domestic production / industrial commodity statistics)
    Codes: Stata variable affwd (1=Exposed, 0=Non-exposed); clustering on cvrnr99 (1999 firm id)
    working paper · Section 2.1; Analysis1.do lines 25-26
  • 1999 full-time private-sector worker cohort Sample definition and timing
    Cohort of workers who in 1999 were full-time employed in Denmark's private sector, had positive wages and were aged 18-56; part-time workers are excluded. IDA covers persons aged 15-70, establishments with at least one employee and jobs active in the last week of November. The textile sample is the roughly 10,000 such workers employed in the textile and clothing industry in 1999; the economy-wide sample excludes public administration, education and health.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 2.2 and footnote 49
  • Birth event Family links, fertility and household
    Indicator for whether a worker fathers or mothers a newborn baby in a given year (for the IV specification: parent of a new child over 2000-2007). Child births come from Statistics Denmark's Fertility Database, which links parents' personal IDs to every child born in Denmark.
    Registers: Fertility Database (Statistics Denmark)
    Codes: Stata variable DBirth
    working paper · Section 2.3; Table 1 notes; Section 6 eq. (4)
  • Marriage and divorce events Family links, fertility and household
    Indicators for whether a worker marries or divorces in a given year, taken from the Central Population Register and linked by personal identifier. The divorce analysis uses workers married as of 1999; marriage analysis uses workers unmarried in 1999 (1999 dropped from marriage-rate plots). Cohabiting partners are distinguished from married spouses.
    Registers: CPR (Central Population Register)
    Codes: Stata variables EMARA (marriage), EDIVA (divorce), mar99
    working paper · Section 2.3; Table 1 notes; Analysis1.do labels
  • Parental leave take Family links, fertility and household
    Indicator for taking childcare/parental leave in a year, from childcare leave spells in Statistics Denmark's social benefits statistics, part of the income statistics registers.
    Registers: SHSS (Sammenhaengende socialstatistik), OF (Offentligt forsoergede)
    Codes: Stata variable DParL
    working paper · Section 2.3
  • Fertile age Family links, fertility and household
    Fertile-age sample is women below 37 and men below 46 years as of 1999 (fertile age limit taken as 36 for women and 45 for men). The published-version code instead uses an age 18-39 indicator (age1839) for fertility heterogeneity.
    Registers: IDA, BEF
    working paper · Footnote 25; Table 4 notes
  • Unemployment and UI benefits Unemployment and benefits
    Unemployment is the percentage of annual time in unemployment. UI benefits are the sum of unemployment insurance, education allowance for the unemployed and other UI benefits, deflated by CPI and expressed relative to the worker's average 1996-1999 monthly earnings.
    Registers: IDA, IND
    Codes: arblhu (unemployment insurance), quddydl (education allowance for unemployed), andakas (other UI benefits); normalised by normsal9699
    replication code · Analysis1.do lines 684-705 (Table A5); WP Table 8 notes
  • Earnings and personal income Earnings and income
    Annual labour earnings (salary) and personal income, the latter including unemployment insurance and government transfers; in the cumulative textile-worker regressions both are expressed as multiples of the worker's own 1999 value. Earnings at the 1999 firm are also analysed separately.
    Registers: IDA, IND
    Codes: Stata variables anrsalary, anrsal99, anrperinc, anrperinc99
    working paper · Table 8 notes; Analysis1.do Table 3
  • Occupation groups (manager, machine operator) Occupation and job hierarchy
    1999 occupation grouped from DISCO-88 major groups: 1 Managers; 2-3 Professionals and technicians; 4-5 Clerks and service workers; 7 Craft workers; 8 Operators; 9 Labourers; set missing if 2-digit code is 99. Machine operator is DISCO 2-digit group 82.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: DISCO-88 1-digit (disc1_99) groups {1},{2,3},{4,5},{7},{8},{9}; disc2_99==82 machine operator; disc2_99==99 missing
    replication code · Analysis1.do lines 7-22
  • Industry import penetration from China (economy-wide) Trade and offshoring
    Change in Chinese import penetration at the six-digit industry level, instrumented with Chinese imports in other advanced countries (Australia, Finland, Germany, Japan, Netherlands, New Zealand, Switzerland, USA), log average distance of Denmark's import partners in 1996, and the share of retail trading firms; two-digit industry fixed effects included.

  • Firm separation rate Firm characteristics and productivity

    Registers: IDA

The Returns to Nursing: Evidence from a Parental-Leave Program

Benjamin U. Friedrich and Martin B. Hackmann · Review of Economic Studies, 2021 · Individual + firm

A Danish parental-leave programme offering up to a year off per child aged 0 to 8 induced a nurse shortage that hospitals and nursing homes could not replace. Nurse employment fell by 15 percent in hospitals and 10 percent in nursing homes, 30-day readmissions of heart attack patients rose, and nursing home mortality increased sharply.

Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) for health workers, plants and industries, Population register (BEF) for children's ages, residence and household characteristics, Social benefits records of parental leave spells (from 1995), National Patient Register (LPR), inpatient hospitalisations 1990–2000, Register of Causes of Death (DAR), 1991–2000
Key variables
  • Treatment: 1994 parental leave programme; exposure = share of nurses eligible times estimated take-up, by health sector and county
  • Outcome: nurse employment in hospitals and nursing homes
  • Outcome: 30-day hospital readmission rates and other quality-of-care measures
  • Outcome: nursing home (elderly) mortality
  • Eligibility: having a youngest child aged 8 or younger

1990–2000
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Danish nurses, nursing assistants and doctors, and hospital patients and nursing home residents, aggregated to health sector by county, 1990–2000. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Skilled nurse / unskilled nurse / doctor (by education) Occupation and job hierarchy
    Health workers are classified by vocational education code in IDAP: skilled nurses (general nurse BSc, specialist nurse training, midwife BSc, nurse MSc); unskilled nurses (health and care workers); medical doctors (MD, PhD; medical BSc 7172 excluded). Doctors' first 7 years of experience are treated as residency and not counted as doctors.
    Registers: IDAP (IDAPALL)
    Codes: ERHAUDD (or HFAUDD in SAS extract): skilled nurse 5166-5173, 5175, 5180, 5181, 8634; unskilled nurse 5146-5150, 5152; doctor 7170, 7180
    replication code · programs/sas/dataprep.sas; programs/stata/Prepare_microdata_healthworkers_by_industry.do; Prepare_aggregate_county_exposure.do

Missing codes are filled backwards within establishment and, for nursing homes, backwards by person within the same firm (CVRNR); other employed = other sectors; no workplace type = unemployment/nonparticipation. New freelancers (missing LBNR) among unskilled nurses keep their previous sector.
    Registers: IDAS, IDAP
    Codes: BRANCHE 851100 = hospital; BRANCHE 853140, 853150 = nursing home
    replication code · programs/stata/Prepare_microdata_healthworkers_by_industry.do (steps 0-4)
  • Eligibility: young children Family links, fertility and household

    Codes: youngkids = ageyoungest <= 8 (C_ALDYNGST / ALDYNGST)
    replication code · programs/stata/Prepare_microdata_healthworkers_by_industry.do
  • Leave take-up and exposure Unemployment and benefits
    Leave = worker with an establishment in t-1 has none in t, or is on maternity leave at end of November (SHSS maternity benefit months: November value 30, or positive in both November and December). Individual take-up is estimated by regressing leave on age-of-youngest-child dummies interacted with 1995 vs 1993; predicted take-up is assigned to workers based on prior-year child age, and county-sector exposure = summed expected take-up / number of active workers of that type in 1993.
    Registers: SHSS, IDAP, FAMILIE
    Codes: SHSS: BEL_BAR, VARMMSF11, VARMMSF12; child-care leave VAR_ORL_BP, VARMMO1-12
    replication code · programs/stata/Prepare_microdata_healthworkers_by_industry.do; Prepare_estimates_individual_takeup.do; Prepare_aggregate_county_exposure.do
  • County Geography and neighbourhood
    County assigned from workplace municipality (AKOM) for employed workers, otherwise residence municipality, using pre-2007 municipality code ranges mapped to 15 counties.
    Registers: IDAP
    Codes: Municipality codes 101-147 = county 1; 151-189 = 2; 201-237 = 3; 251-271 = 4; 301-345 = 5; 351-397 = 6; 400-409 = 7; 421-499 = 8; 501-545 = 9; 551-577 = 10; 601-631 = 11; 651-685 = 12; 701-751 = 13; 761-793 = 14; 801-861 = 15
    replication code · programs/stata/Prepare_aggregate_county_exposure.do
  • 30-day readmission Health care use
    Among inpatient (patient type 0) stays of 100 days or less, a readmission occurs if the next admission (or scheduled referral date) of the same person is within 30 days after discharge, starting at least one day after discharge; same-day readmission counts only if referred by a GP to the same hospital. Set to missing if the patient died before discharge.
    Registers: LPR
    Codes: C_PATTYPE == 0; D_INDDTO, D_UDDTO, D_HENDTO, C_UDM == 1, C_SGH
    replication code · programs/stata/Prepare_hospitalsample_PartA.do
  • AMI 30-day readmission and mortality Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Patients aged 65+ with primary diagnosis acute myocardial infarction; index admissions exclude those with an ischemic heart admission in the preceding 365 days. 30-day mortality = death within 30 days of admission (DAR).
    Registers: LPR, DAR
    Codes: AMI: ICD-8 4109, 41099; ICD-10 DI21, DI22. Ischemic: ICD-8 410-414; ICD-10 DI20-DI25
    replication code · programs/stata/Prepare_hospitalsample_PartA.do
  • Nursing home residents and mortality Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Nursing home addresses are identified from deaths registered in a nursing home (place-of-death institution code 2) 1990-2000, using the first 14 characters of the address code (BOPIKOM) within municipality, keeping addresses where no children live; residents aged 60+ living at those addresses are nursing home residents, and their mortality is the outcome.

Child's Gender, Young Fathers' Crime, and Spillover Effects in Criminal Behavior

Christian Dustmann and Rasmus Landersø · Journal of Political Economy, 2021 · Individual

Uses the gender of a first-born child as a natural experiment for young fathers in Denmark. Having a son rather than a daughter lowers the father's subsequent criminal behaviour, and the reduction spills over to the father's peers and later to the child, which identifies both a direct parenting response and network effects in crime.

Data
Birth register (child's gender, parent links), Population register (BEF) for demographics and family links, Central Police Register crime data (charges and convictions), Victim register (from 2001), Income, education and occupation registers, Residential register with neighbourhood classification
Key variables
  • Outcome: young father's crime convictions and charges
  • Treatment: first child is a son vs a daughter
  • Spillover outcome: crime of male peers in the father's neighbourhood
  • Peer group: males within ±3 years of father's age in the same neighbourhood
  • Outcome: neighbourhood crime victimisation
Period
Children born 1991–2004; crime data from 1990
Sample
2,803 first-time fathers aged 20 or younger; 101,132 male peers in 2,114 neighbourhoods Danish men who fathered their first child at age 20 or younger between 1991 and 2004, plus male peers in their neighbourhoods. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Crime (convictions and charges) Crime
    Charges or convictions for offences against the criminal code from the Central Police Register, excluding traffic offences; convictions (court rulings of guilt) are the preferred measure. Charges and convictions are dated by the date the crime was committed (exact crime dates available from 1990); records are observed even after deletion from the individual's criminal record.
    Registers: Central Police Register (crime register)
    paper · Section II.A and footnote 7
  • Crime categories Crime
    Property crime: theft, fencing, aggravated vandalism, fraud, burglary, forgery, economic crimes. Violent crime: simple violence (assault), severe or life-threatening violence, threats, violence against or obstructing a public servant, failure to help a person in danger, coercion, attempted murder or homicide. Other crime: drug possession and sale, possession of weapons/explosives, false testimony, sexual crimes.
    Registers: Central Police Register
    paper · Footnote 8; online Table A1 (code breakdown, not read)
  • Young first-time father sample / treatment Family links, fertility and household
    Males who father their first child at age 20 or younger, children born 1991-2004 (birth and demographic registers), with information on both parents from the birth for up to 5 subsequent years, matched uniquely to a neighbourhood; treatment is the first child being a son. Fathers in neighbourhoods with more than one young father having a first child in the same year are excluded.
    Registers: Birth register, BEF
    paper · Section II.B and footnote 9
  • Neighbourhood Geography and neighbourhood
    Neighbourhoods follow the classification documented in Damm and Schultz-Nielsen (2008), constructed in 2004, linked to individuals through anonymised home address identifiers in the residential register; the largest and smallest 5% of neighbourhoods are excluded from most analyses.
    Registers: Residential register, BEF
    paper · Section II.B
  • Peer group and peer crime Crime
    Peers are all males within +/-3 years of the focal father's age living in the father's neighbourhood on January 1 of the year the child is born (alternatively all males aged 14-25 at the birth), regardless of later moves; the father and his family members are excluded. Peer crime is their convictions/charges.
    Registers: Residential register, BEF, Central Police Register
    paper · Section II.B; footnote 5
  • Neighbourhood victimisation Crime
    Based on individuals who report having been the victim of a crime (register available from 2001); victim sample includes all individuals living in the father's neighbourhood at the time of the birth, counting the number of victims in each neighbourhood.
    Registers: Victim register
    paper · Section II.B (victim sample) and footnote 10

Crime Family responses and insurance Children, intergenerational mobility and skills

Estimation of a Roy/Search/Compensating Differential Model of the Labor Market

Christopher Taber and Rune Vejlin · Econometrica, 2020 · Individual + firm

Combines a Roy model, search frictions, compensating differentials and on-the-job human capital accumulation in one framework, establishes what is non-parametrically identified, and estimates it on Danish matched data. Pre-market skills account for most wage variation, while preferences for non-wage job attributes and search frictions matter greatly for turnover and for which jobs workers choose.

Data
Weekly labour market spell data built from Statistics Denmark registers (all individuals aged 15–74), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) with hourly wage measure, Danish Work Environment Cohort Study surveys (1995 and 2000) on reasons for job separation
Key variables
  • Outcome: log hourly wage (detrended)
  • Job-to-job transitions between establishments (revealed preference)
  • Employment and non-employment spell durations
  • Worker skill/education group and labour market experience
  • Decomposition of wage variance into skill, search, compensating differential and human capital components
Period
1985–2003
Sample
2,969,454 workers, 25,630,532 spells and 467,983 establishments (estimation sample) Danish workers after labour market entry and up to age 55, followed in weekly spell data across establishments, 1985–2003. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Weekly labour market state Employment and labour force status
    Weekly spell data 1985-2003 for all individuals aged 15-74 with states employed, unemployed, self-employed, retired and non-participation. Unemployment = receiving unemployment insurance benefits or social assistance; non-participation is the residual (not observed in any register). Unemployment and non-participation are aggregated into non-employment.
    Registers: Weekly spell data (built from Statistics Denmark registers), IDA
    working paper · IZA DP 9975, Section 6 (Data)
  • Hourly wage Earnings and income
    Hourly wage measure of Lund and Vejlin (2015), which improves on IDA's annual average hourly wage for the job held in the last week of November; log wages are detrended by gender-education groups conditional on experience.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 6, footnote 21; Section 6.1
  • Establishment (job type) Firm characteristics and productivity
    Job types are establishments (not firms). Statistics Denmark's establishment identifier is the same across years if one of three criteria is met: same owner and industry; same owner and workforce; or same workforce and either same address or same industry. A job is an employment spell within an establishment.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 6, footnote 22
  • Job-to-job transition Employment and labour force status
    Transition between two establishments with a very short intermediate non-employment spell: non-employment spells of 2 weeks or less are allocated to the first employment spell; non-employment spells of 12 weeks or less between jobs at the same establishment are overwritten as employment (recalls). Transitions to/from establishments with missing ID and from closing or mass-layoff establishments are ignored.
    Registers: Weekly spell data, IDA
    working paper · Section 6 and 6.1
  • Mass layoff / closing establishment Firm characteristics and productivity
    Mass layoff: establishment has more than 15 workers in year t and less than 30 percent of them left in year t+1. Closing: establishment no longer observed in the data.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 6.1, footnote 28
  • Involuntary separation (survey) Unemployment and benefits
    From the Danish Work Environment Cohort Study (1995 and 2000), whether the job spell in November 5 years earlier ended due to the employer or the employee; matched to register data to form a moment identifying the probability of an immediate offer after job destruction.
    Registers: Danish Work Environment Cohort Study, IDA
    working paper · Section 6
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Workers censored after age 55 and when entering retirement or self-employment; spells before labour market entry (time of highest completed education, not observed in education later, or age 19) dropped; workers with errors in education information or gaps in spell histories (e.g. missing IDA year) dropped.
    Registers: Weekly spell data, IDA
    working paper · Section 6.1

Labour markets, wages and sorting

Wealth Taxation and Wealth Accumulation: Theory and Evidence from Denmark

Katrine Jakobsen, Kristian Jakobsen, Henrik Kleven and Gabriel Zucman · Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2020 · Individual

Exploits the 1989 Danish wealth tax reform, which cut rates sharply for the wealthy, to estimate long-run effects of wealth taxes on wealth accumulation. Responses are sizable for the very wealthy (top one percent) and small for the moderately wealthy, with effects that keep growing over a decade.

Data
Administrative wealth registry (third-party reported assets and debts, since 1980), Income registers and socio-economic registers (occupation, family composition)
Key variables
  • Outcome: log taxable wealth and third-party reported wealth
  • Treatment: 1989 wealth tax cut (unbound vs bound by tax ceiling: ceiling DD)
  • Treatment: doubling of couples' exemption threshold (couples DD)
  • Running variable for bunching: taxable wealth around exemption threshold
  • Controls: pre-reform portfolio shares and income deciles
Period
Wealth data since 1980; quasi-experimental panel 1985–1996
Sample
138,384 observations (ceiling DD) and 520,452 observations (couples DD, couples vs couples) Balanced panels of Danish households in the top 1% (ceiling DD) or married couples in the top 5% (couples DD) of the wealth distribution before the 1989 reform. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Household (tax unit) and married status Family links, fertility and household
    Household id is the family id when the person's spouse id equals the cohabitation partner id and civil status is in the married range (up to 2007, from FAIN); from 2008 from BEF using spouse id = partner id and civil status G or P. Persons not so linked form their own household. Only persons aged 20+ are kept and wealth is summed within household.
    Registers: FAIN, BEF
    Codes: FAIN (<=2007): aegtefaelle_id == c_faelle_id, c_status 2-5, hhid = c_familie_id; BEF (>=2008): aegte_id == efalle, civst in {G, P}; alder >= 20
    replication code · Empirical Analysis/DD_make_hh_ids.do
  • Household taxable wealth (outcome) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Household net taxable wealth = sum over household members aged 20+ of the wealth variable FORM from the income-tax register (INDH); outcome is log(FORM). Portfolio shares use INDK components: equity share = listed stocks / total assets, housing share = (mortgage deeds + real estate value) / total assets.
    Registers: INDH, INDK
    Codes: FORM (INDH); share_tx_equities = KURSAKT/QAKTIVF; share_tx_housing = (KURSPANT+KOEJD)/QAKTIVF; other INDK fields: FORMSK, LOFTFORM, QPASSIV, PRIGALD, KONTANT, KURSOBL, INDESTPI
    replication code · Empirical Analysis/DD_base_data.do, section 1
  • Wealth tax exemption threshold and marginal wealth tax Taxes and tax rates
    Annual exemption threshold (allowance) by year; for couples it equals 2 x single allowance, except 1989-1992 when couples' allowance uses a separate married allowance x 2. Household marginal wealth tax rate tau_it = statutory rate if FORM exceeds the household allowance, else 0. Bunching analysis uses distance b = FORM - allowance, deflated, in DKK 20,000 bins from -540,000 to 540,000.
    Registers: INDH
    Codes: Allowance (DKK): 1980-81 1,000,000; 1982 1,083,000; 1983 1,158,900; 1984 1,204,900; 1985 1,229,200; 1986 1,253,500; 1987 1,278,700; 1988 1,329,900; 1989 1,383,600; 1990 1,424,500; 1991 1,452,700; 1992 1,482,100; 1993 1,534,500; 1994 1,580,500; 1995 1,592,000; 1996 2,400,000; married: 1989-90 811,500x2, 1991 1,249,600x2, 1992-96 2x single
    replication code · Empirical Analysis/DD_base_data.do section 2.2; bunching_base_data.do
  • Ceiling DD treatment (unbound by tax ceiling) Taxes and tax rates
    X = wealth tax actually paid (FORMSK) / theoretical wealth tax ((FORM - allowance) x tax rate). Treatment: household in top 1% of the wealth distribution with X > 0.99 in every pre-reform year of the window (e.g. 1982-1988), i.e. not bound by the tax ceiling; control: top 1% with X < 0.80 (bound by ceiling). Households above the 99.99th percentile excluded. In the panel, status is re-coded post-reform using X, LOFTFORM > 0 and wealth relative to allowance.
    Registers: INDK, INDH, FAIN
    Codes: treatmt_2e_X80: X > .99 and top1 in 1982-1988; control_2e_X80: X < .80 and top1; drop form_pctile > .9999
    replication code · Empirical Analysis/DD_balance_and_treatment_status.do section 3.4; DD_base_data.do section 2.3
  • Couples DD treatment Taxes and tax rates
    Treatment: married households with wealth between the (single) allowance and 2 x allowance in each pre-reform year (1988 and earlier years depending on window), which became exempt when the couples' threshold doubled in 1989; controls: (c1) singles with wealth in the same band, (c4) married couples in the top 5% with wealth below the allowance, or (c5) singles with wealth between allowance/2 and allowance.
    Registers: INDH, FAIN
    Codes: treatmt_c1*: married & allowance <= FORM <= 2*allowance; control_c1*: unmarried, same band; control_c4*: married & FORM < allowance & top5; control_c5*: unmarried & allowance/2 <= FORM <= allowance
    replication code · Empirical Analysis/DD_balance_and_treatment_status.do section 3.3
  • Balanced panel 1980-1996 Sample definition and timing
    Households (persons 20+ aggregated by household id) observed with strictly positive aggregate wealth FORM in all 17 years 1980-1996.
    Registers: INDH, FAIN
    Codes: drop if form <= 0 | missing; keep if _N == 17 (balanced_1980_96)
    replication code · Empirical Analysis/DD_balance_and_treatment_status.do section 2
  • Self-employment / business income indicator (bunching) Earnings and income
    Household flagged as self-employed if business profit (NETOVSKUD_GL) is nonzero; a broader 'ext' flag also uses nonzero values of EGNKAPVK, UDLFKURS, UDLIND2 or UDLIND3 (foreign/business-related components).
    Registers: INDH, INDK
    Codes: selv = netovskud_gl != 0; ext = netovskud_gl!=0 | egnkapvk!=0 | udlfkurs!=0 | udlind2!=0 | udlind3!=0
    replication code · Empirical Analysis/bunching_base_data.do

Sources of Inaction in Household Finance: Evidence from the Danish Mortgage Market

Steffen Andersen, John Y. Campbell, Kasper Meisner Nielsen and Tarun Ramadorai · American Economic Review, 2020 · Individual

Many Danish households fail to refinance fixed-rate mortgages when it is clearly profitable. A model with inattention and psychological refinancing costs fits the data, and both frictions are stronger for households with less education, income and financial wealth.

Data
Loan-level mortgage data for all Danish mortgages from Danmarks Nationalbank (via mortgage bank associations), Civil Registration System / population register (CPR/BEF) for demographics and household links, Income and wealth data from the Danish Tax Authority (SKAT) (IND/formue), Education register (UDDA)
Key variables
  • Outcome: refinancing of a fixed-rate mortgage in a quarter
  • Incentive: financial gain from refinancing given coupon and market rates
  • Structural parameters: probability of inattention and psychological refinancing cost
  • Household characteristics: age, education, income, housing and financial wealth
Period
2009–2017
Sample
2,376,815 household observations (9,351,183 household-quarters); 378,421 refinancings Danish households holding a single fixed-rate mortgage observed in consecutive years, 2009–2017. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Refinancing event Wealth, debt and consumption
    A refinancing occurs when a household changes from one fixed-rate mortgage to another mortgage (fixed- or adjustable-rate) on the same property; terminations from moves, death or divorce are handled separately as mortgage termination. Annual loan data are expanded to quarters using mortgage issue dates.
    Registers: Danmarks Nationalbank mortgage data, CPR
    working paper · Section 2.2.B Sample selection
  • Cash-out refinancing Wealth, debt and consumption
    A refinancing associated with an increase in mortgage principal of 10% or more.
    Registers: Danmarks Nationalbank mortgage data
    working paper · Section 2.1
  • Refinancing incentive (ADL threshold) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Incentive I = (coupon on old mortgage - yield on new mortgage) - O, where O is the Agarwal-Driscoll-Laibson optimal threshold with sigma = 0.0074, tau = 0.33, rho = 0.05, monetary cost kappa(m) = 3000 + max(0.002m, 4000) + 0.001m DKK (winsorised at the 99th percentile), and lambda = predicted termination hazard + nominal principal paydown + past-year CPI inflation.
    Registers: Danmarks Nationalbank mortgage data
    working paper · Section 3.1, eqs. (1), (4)-(7)
  • Household Family links, fertility and household
    One or two adults living at the same postal address; the household must have an unchanging number of adult members over two subsequent years.
    Registers: CPR
    working paper · Section 2.2.B
  • Single fixed-rate mortgage sample Sample definition and timing
    Year by year 2009-2017: households holding any mortgage, then those with a single mortgage observed in two consecutive years, then those whose mortgage is fixed-rate; expanded to household-quarters.
    Registers: Danmarks Nationalbank mortgage data, CPR
    working paper · Section 2.2.B
  • Financial literacy Education and test scores
    At least one household member has a degree in finance or economics or professional training in finance; a broader measure counts extended family members (non-resident parents, siblings, in-laws, children).
    Registers: Education register (Ministry of Education), CPR
    working paper · Section 3.4
  • Ranked household characteristics Wealth, debt and consumption
    Age, years of schooling (computed from highest education level), income, financial wealth and housing wealth enter as demeaned ranks. Wealth is from SKAT third-party reports and excludes unbanked cash, cars, private debts, defined-contribution pensions and private businesses, so net financial wealth can be negative.
    Registers: SKAT income and wealth, Education register
    working paper · Sections 2.2.A and 3.4

Household finance, saving and consumption

Time Discounting and Wealth Inequality

Thomas Epper, Ernst Fehr, Helga Fehr-Duda, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, David Dreyer Lassen, Søren Leth-Petersen and Gregers Nytoft Rasmussen · American Economic Review, 2020 · Individual

Links incentivised time-discounting experiments to the wealth positions of a large sample of middle-aged Danes in the registers. Patient individuals sit markedly higher in the wealth distribution, and the association survives controls for education, income profiles, school grades, initial and parental wealth, credit constraints and risk preferences, which points to saving behaviour as the channel.

Data
Incentivised online convex time budget experiment (February 2015) linked on CPR, Income and wealth registers based on third-party reports (1980–2015), Population register (BEF) for sampling and demographics, Education and family registers, Survey of time discounting for the 1952–1955 cohorts at ages 18–21
Key variables
  • Outcome: individual's percentile rank in the net wealth distribution
  • Main regressor: experimentally measured patience (time discounting)
  • Controls: education, income, parental wealth, risk attitudes
  • Heterogeneity: credit-constrained vs unconstrained individuals
Period
Experiment in 2015; register data 1980–2015 (wealth ranks tracked 2001–2015)
Sample
3,620 experiment participants (of 27,613 invited); 2,548 survey subjects in the 1952–1955 cohorts Danes born 1973–1983 who lived in Copenhagen municipality at age seven and completed the online experiment. source
How variables are defined (10)
  • Net wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    End-of-year value of real estate (tax-assessed value adjusted by the average market-price-to-assessed-value ratio among traded houses of the same property class, location and price range), deposits, listed stocks, bonds, mortgage deeds in deposit, cars and pension accounts, minus all debt except debt to private persons. Pension and car values are available only from 2014; results robust to including them.
    Registers: Tax-based income and wealth registers (third-party reports)
    working paper · Section 2, 'Register data information on wealth'; Table 1 notes
  • Wealth percentile rank Wealth, debt and consumption
    Individual's percentile rank in the within cohort x year wealth distribution of the sample (main outcome measured in 2015).
    Registers: Tax-based wealth register
    working paper · Section 3 and footnote 1; Figure 3 notes
  • Credit-constrained indicator Wealth, debt and consumption
    Individual holds liquid assets worth less than one month's disposable income in 2014 (alternative: share of years 2001-2015 observed with liquid assets below one month's disposable income).
    Registers: Tax-based income and wealth registers
    working paper · Table 2 notes; Section 3; Appendix figure notes
  • Marginal interest rate (interest on marginal liquidity) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Imputed per account from yearly interest payments and end-of-year balances; for people with debt accounts, the highest debt-account interest rate; for people without debt, the lowest deposit-account interest rate.
    Registers: Account-level debt and deposit data (tax reports)
    working paper · Section 3 (Table 2 col. 7 discussion); details in Online Appendix C.4
  • Stock market return Wealth, debt and consumption
    (Dividend income + realised capital gains/losses during the year) / market value of stocks, averaged over 2008-2014; plus an indicator for owning stocks during the period.
    Registers: Tax-based income and wealth registers
    working paper · Section 3 (Table 2 col. 7 discussion)
  • Parental wealth / initial wealth deciles Family links, fertility and household
    Parental wealth decile = parents' position in the parental wealth distribution measured within the respondent's cohort when the respondent was 18; initial wealth decile = own position in the within-cohort wealth distribution at age 18.
    Registers: Wealth register, Population register (parent links)
    working paper · Table 2 notes; Figure 3 notes
  • Income controls Earnings and income
    Decile indicators of within-cohort gross income excluding capital income in 2015, of observed income growth from age 25-27 to age 30-32, and of expected income growth 2014-2016 from the experiment survey.
    Registers: Income register
    working paper · Table 2 notes
  • Experiment sample Sample definition and timing
    Individuals drawn from the population register born 1973-1983 who lived in the municipality of Copenhagen at age seven; invited by letter to an online experiment in February 2015; respondents without required register data or with gender/birth-year mismatch excluded.
    Registers: BEF (population register)
    working paper · Section 2, Sample and recruitment; footnote 6
  • Patience index Other
    Mean share of 10 blocks saved for later receipt across the five convex-time-budget choices between t1 = 8 weeks and t2 = 16 weeks; takes values in [0,1] in steps of 1/50.
    Registers: Experiment data
    working paper · Section 2, eq. (4)
  • Years of education Education and test scores
    Years of completed education in 2015; regressions use indicators for 12 education lengths in years in the Danish system.
    Registers: Education register
    working paper · Figure 3 notes; Table 2 notes

Household finance, saving and consumption Inequality and fairness

Tax Evasion and Inequality

Annette Alstadsæter, Niels Johannesen and Gabriel Zucman · American Economic Review, 2019 · Individual

Matches leaked offshore account data (HSBC Switzerland, Panama Papers) and tax amnesty records to Scandinavian wealth registers. Tax evasion rises steeply with wealth: the top 0.01 percent evade about a quarter of their taxes, which materially raises measured top wealth shares.

Data
Leaked HSBC Switzerland client list (Swiss Leaks, 2007) matched to tax records in Denmark, Norway and Sweden, Panama Papers / Mossack Fonseca leak matched to Norwegian and Swedish wealth data (not Denmark), Tax amnesty voluntary disclosures in Norway and Sweden, Population-wide administrative wealth and income tax records for Norway, Sweden and Denmark, Danish stratified random tax audits by SKAT (tax years 2008, 2010, 2012), National accounts household wealth totals
Key variables
  • Outcome: taxes evaded (share of taxes owed) by wealth group
  • Ranking variable: household net wealth including imputed pension wealth
  • Indicator: owning an undeclared HSBC account / Panama Papers shell / amnesty participation
  • Outcome (event study): reported wealth and income after amnesty
  • Random-audit detected evasion (domestic evasion)
Period
HSBC leak 2006–2007; amnesties since 2006; Danish random audits for tax years 2008, 2010, 2012
Sample
520 HSBC households; 165 Panama Papers households; 1,422 amnesty taxpayers in Norway and 6,811 in Sweden; 18,985 randomly audited Danish taxpayers Scandinavian households appearing in offshore leaks or tax amnesties, ranked in the full population wealth distribution, combined with Danish random audits. source
How variables are defined (4)
  • Household (unit of analysis) Family links, fertility and household
    A household is either a single person aged 20 or above or a married couple, in both cases with dependent children if any; fractiles are defined relative to the total number of households, including those not liable to wealth tax.
    Registers: Administrative wealth and income records
    online appendix · Online Appendix A.1.2
  • Household net wealth (ranking variable) Wealth, debt and consumption
    100% of national-accounts household wealth at market value distributed to households: all non-financial and financial assets minus debts, including funded pensions, excluding durables and valuables. Pension wealth imputed (40% to wage earners pro rata wage income, 60% to retirees pro rata pension income); unlisted equity imputed by capitalizing unlisted dividends and non-corporate business assets by capitalizing business income. Danish distribution taken from Jakobsen et al. (2018), based on individual wealth records.
    Registers: Danish individual wealth records, National accounts
    working paper · Section 3.2; Online Appendix A and D
  • HSBC undeclared account holder Taxes and tax rates
    Households who owned at least one account at HSBC Switzerland (including via shell companies with identified beneficial owners), declared themselves taxable in Scandinavia in 2006 and could be matched to a tax return (2006/2007 records); non-residents excluded; for Denmark all matched households are treated as evaders (about 95% of matched Danish accounts were undeclared).
    Registers: Leaked HSBC list (Danish tax authority version), Tax returns
    working paper · Section 3.1.1, footnotes 13-16; Online Appendix E
  • Random-audit detected evasion Taxes and tax rates
    SKAT stratified random audits for tax years 2008, 2010 and 2012 (18,985 taxpayers; self-employed and complex returns oversampled), every line item examined; main results include all errors; deliberate evaders are those rated 0-2 on SKAT's 0-6 compliance scale. Evasion rate = taxes evaded / (taxes paid + taxes evaded) by wealth group, weighted by audit weights.
    Registers: SKAT random audit data
    Codes: SKAT compliance rating 0-2 = deliberate evasion
    online appendix · Section 4 (Random Audit Data); Online Appendix H.1-H.2

Refugee Migration and Electoral Outcomes

Christian Dustmann, Kristine Vasiljeva and Anna Piil Damm · Review of Economic Studies, 2019 · Individual

Using the quasi-random refugee dispersal policy, refugee allocation raised vote shares for anti-immigration parties in rural municipalities and lowered them in the largest urban municipalities. Effects are strongest where refugees are few relative to natives and where crime rises after allocation.

Data
Population register (BEF) to identify refugees and municipality of initial placement, Income, education, labour force and socio-economic registers for 1985 municipality characteristics, Statistics Denmark municipal and parliamentary election results, Danish National Election Survey (DNES) 1990–98
Key variables
  • Outcome: change in vote share of anti-immigration parties (Progress Party, Danish People's Party)
  • Treatment: cumulative share of allocated refugees in municipal population (1986 base)
  • Source of variation: Danish Spatial Dispersal Policy allocation of refugees 1986–98
  • Heterogeneity: urban vs rural municipality
  • Controls: 1985 municipality characteristics
Period
Refugee allocation 1986–1998; parliamentary elections 1990–98 and municipal elections 1989–97
Sample
275 municipalities (550 observations for parliamentary elections); 76,673 refugees allocated 1986–98 All 275 Danish municipalities observed across election cycles during the 1986–98 refugee dispersal policy. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Allocated refugees Immigration and origin
    Refugees received in 1986-1998 who initially received a permanent residence permit, from Lebanon, Iran, Iraq, Somalia, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Afghanistan, Ethiopia, or without citizenship; municipality of initial placement identified from the population register. Refugees from former Yugoslavia (special 1993 policy) and family-reunified spouses/children arriving more than 12 months after the refugee are excluded.
    Registers: BEF (population register)
    paper · Sections 2.4-2.5, footnotes 19-20
  • Refugee share (treatment) Immigration and origin
    Cumulative number of refugees allocated to the municipality from 1986 until the year preceding each election, divided by the municipal population at the beginning of 1986; regressor is its change between consecutive election years (RS_it).
    Registers: BEF
    paper · Section 2.4 and Section 3.2, eq. (3.1)
  • Vote share changes by party group Other
    Percentage-point change in municipal vote shares between election years t-1 and t (1989-98: three parliamentary and three municipal elections) for anti-immigration parties (Progress Party and Danish People's Party), centre-right, centre-left and small centre parties; seat shares also computed.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark election results
    paper · Sections 2.1 and 3.2, Table 1
  • Urban municipality Geography and neighbourhood
    Municipalities above the 95th percentile of municipal population size are labelled urban.
    Registers: BEF
    paper · Introduction
  • Share of rich (1985 municipal control) Earnings and income
    Share of adults whose disposable income as a household member is above 50% of the Danish median (one of several 1985 municipal characteristics with immigrant share, mean log gross earnings, crime rate, church-tax payers, unemployment rate, tertiary education share, immigrant welfare dependency).
    Registers: Income registers, Population, education, labour force and socio-economic registers
    paper · Section 2.4, footnote 22
  • Non-employment Employment and labour force status
    Being unemployed or not in the labour force at ages 18-65.
    Registers: Labour force registers
    paper · Section 2, footnote 23

Migration, neighbourhoods and refugees Political economy

Consumption Network Effects

Giacomo De Giorgi, Anders Frederiksen and Luigi Pistaferri · Review of Economic Studies, 2019 · Individual + firm

Measures household consumption from Danish tax records on income and assets and defines peer groups by workplace using matched employer-employee data. Instrumenting peers' consumption with shocks to their own non-overlapping networks and firms, the paper finds sizeable consumption spillovers that can generate macro multipliers, operating through both intertemporal and intratemporal channels.

Data
Administrative income and wealth tax records (tax registry incl. wealth tax data), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) for plant IDs and coworker networks, Danish Expenditure Survey (DES) 1994–1996
Key variables
  • Outcome: household consumption imputed from income and change in assets
  • Endogenous regressor: average consumption of coworkers' households (peer consumption)
  • Instruments: firm-level shocks to distance-3 (non-overlapping) network members
  • Network definition: coworkers in the same plant
  • Mechanisms: budget shares of visible goods (DES)
Period
1980–1996
Sample
757,439 households Danish households with head aged 18–65 where both spouses are working employees, linked to spouses' coworkers. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Imputed household consumption Wealth, debt and consumption
    Annual household consumption (spending) imputed from the budget constraint as C = Y - T - dA, where Y = gross income from all sources (labour and capital) + housing support + child support - implicit tax on the consumption value of owned housing, T = total taxes paid, and dA = change in assets (cash, bank deposits, stocks and shares, property value, cars and other vehicles, minus liabilities). Values in 2000 DKr.
    Registers: Tax records (income and wealth tax data)
    working paper · Section 2.1, eq. (1)
  • Co-worker network (weighted) Firm characteristics and productivity
    Co-workers are individuals working in the same plant (for public employees, the physical address of the workplace) from IDA. Baseline weights favour similar workers: with five education groups and three occupation groups (blue collar, white collar, manager), degree of separation d = |E_i - E_j| + |O_i - O_j| and weight (d+1)^-2; peers' consumption is the weighted average of co-workers' household log consumption.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 2.1; Section 5.1, eq. (11)
  • Distance-3 peers Family links, fertility and household
    Starting from households where both spouses work, distance-1 peers are co-workers, distance-2 peers are the working spouses of co-workers, and distance-3 peers are the co-workers of the spouses of co-workers. Couples working in the same plant are excluded and feedback cases (where own household would serve as instrument for the peer) are discarded.
    Registers: IDA, Tax records
    working paper · Sections 4.1.2 and 5.1
  • Firm instruments (distance-3 firm shocks) Firm characteristics and productivity
    Weighted averages over distance-3 peers of their firm's size, firm-specific change in employment, firm type dummies (publicly traded, limited liability, other) and a public-sector dummy, all expressed in first differences. A separate set uses distance-3 peers' demographics (age, age squared, years of schooling, share women, occupation shares, kids 0-6 and 7-13).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 5.2 (text before Table 4); Table 1
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Households 1980-1996 whose head is aged 18-65 and where both spouses work as employees (not self-employed); households are dropped from the year one or both members stop working or become self-employed. Peers' consumption is computed using all workers, including singles and one-earner households.
    Registers: Tax records, IDA
    working paper · Section 2.1; Online Appendix Table A1 (selection steps)
  • Visible / neutral / non-visible spending (DES) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Spending in the Danish Expenditure Survey is split using the Heffetz (2011) visibility index: visible = tobacco and alcohol, food away from home, clothing, furniture and home goods, electrics/appliances, vehicles, entertainment, books, education, personal care; neutral = food at home; everything else (insurance, rent, etc.) non-visible.
    Registers: DES (Danish Expenditure Survey)
    working paper · Section 2.2; Table A6

Family Health Behaviors

Itzik Fadlon and Torben Heien Nielsen · American Economic Review, 2019 · Individual

A severe health shock to one family member, such as a heart attack or stroke, makes spouses and adult children raise their own preventive behaviour: more check-ups, more preventive medication and lifestyle changes. Responses are sharp, immediate and persistent, and they reflect updating about one's own risk.

Data
Prescription Drug Database (LMDB), 1995–2011, Health Insurance Registry (SSR, primary-care and specialist contacts), 1985–2011, National Patient Registry (LPR), inpatient 1980–2011 and outpatient 1994–2011, Cause of Death Registry (DAR), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) for demographics, education and coworker links, Family links (spouses, parents–children) from population registers
Key variables
  • Treatment: family member's first heart attack or stroke (non-fatal), or death (fatal shock)
  • Outcome: statin and other cardiovascular drug take-up
  • Outcome: preventive care such as GP visits and cholesterol testing
  • Control group: households experiencing the same shock five years later
  • Exposure groups: spouses, adult biological children, siblings, in-laws, coworkers
Period
1980–2011 (shocks between 1985 and 2011)
Sample
Non-fatal shocks, spouses: 20,381 treated and 28,699 control (prime age 25–55), 37,828 treated and 36,392 control (older 55–85); biological children: 63,323 treated and 68,437 control (25–40), 39,783 treated and 32,926 control (40–65) Family members and close coworkers of all Danish individuals who had a first heart attack or stroke (or died) between 1985 and 2011. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Non-fatal cardiovascular shock Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    First-time heart attack or stroke (identified from the National Patient Registry, ICD diagnoses) between 1985 and 2011 where the individual survived the four-year analysis horizon (three years for stepchildren, children-in-law and coworker samples). Household matches based on period t = -1.
    Registers: LPR, Cause of Death Registry
    working paper · Sections 3.1-3.2
  • Fatal shock Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Death of a family member between 1985 and 2011, from the Cause of Death Registry (exact death dates and causes).
    Registers: Cause of Death Registry
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Treatment and control groups (shock timing) Sample definition and timing
    Treatment: family members of households experiencing the shock in year tau; control: family members from the same cohorts in households experiencing the same shock in year tau + Delta (main Delta = 5, giving effects up to four years), combined in a dynamic difference-in-differences.
    Registers: LPR, Population registers
    working paper · Section 2 and Section 3.2
  • Statin consumption and cholesterol tests Health care use
    Indicator for purchasing statins (cholesterol-lowering prescription drugs) from the Prescription Drug Database (ATC classified, 1995-2011); indicator for blood tests of cholesterol levels from health care utilization records.
    Registers: LMDB, Health Insurance Registry
    working paper · Sections 3.1 and 4.1
  • Urgent care contacts Health care use
    Non-hospital contacts with on-call local doctors or nurses initiated outside regular working hours (8 am to 4 pm).
    Registers: Health Insurance Registry
    working paper · Section 4.2, footnote 31
  • Addiction treatment drugs and opioid doses Health care use
    Indicator for purchasing nicotine/alcohol dependence medication; prescription opioid consumption measured in WHO defined daily doses (DDD), i.e. prescription day equivalents (spouses only, dosage data excluded for adult children).
    Registers: LMDB
    Codes: ATC N07BA, N07BB (dependence treatment)
    working paper · Section 4.2, footnotes 29, 32
  • Family circles (spouses, children, siblings, stepchildren, in-laws) Family links, fertility and household
    Spouses: married and cohabiting couples (spousal links available for cohorts 1910-1970); adult biological children via parent links for those born after 1960; siblings share biological parents; stepchild = person neither of whose biological parents is the shocked individual but one of whom is that individual's spouse; children-in-law are spouses of biological children.
    Registers: Population registers (family links)
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Close coworkers Occupation and job hierarchy
    Coworkers in the same physical establishment during t = -4 to t = -1 in workplaces with employees at or below the sample 25th percentile (about 20), in the same Statistics Denmark ISCO-based occupation class (managers vs non-managers by low/medium/high skill) and within 5 years of age; family members excluded.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.2, footnotes 14-16
  • Predicted cardiovascular risk Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Annual predicted probability of a cardiovascular shock from population data using age, gender, hypertension and diabetes (proxied by lagged indicators for condition-specific prescriptions) and education; spouses split at the population median of risk at t = -1.
    Registers: LMDB, IDA, LPR
    working paper · Section 4.1.1

Health Family responses and insurance

An Empirical Model of Wage Dispersion with Sorting

Jesper Bagger and Rasmus Lentz · Review of Economic Studies, 2019 · Individual + firm

Estimates an equilibrium search model with endogenous search intensity and two-sided heterogeneity on Danish matched data. Finds positive assortative matching between worker and firm productivity, and quantifies how much of wage dispersion is due to sorting versus search frictions.

Data
Weekly labour market spell data from administrative registers (jobs reported to tax authorities, public transfers, mandatory pension contributions), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA): education, hourly wages and firm sector
Key variables
  • Outcome: hourly wage (last week of November)
  • Key variable: job-to-job transitions and unemployment spells
  • Estimated: worker skill and firm productivity types (sorting)
  • Decomposition: log-wage variance into worker heterogeneity, firm heterogeneity, frictions and sorting
Period
1994–2003 (spell data available 1985–2003)
Sample
6,815,884 observations; 782,951 individuals; 1,698,990 job spells; 117,847 firms (NBER 2014 version) Danish workers up to age 55, after labour market entry, never observed in public-sector employment, self-employment, retirement or agriculture. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Weekly labour market spells Employment and labour force status
    Weekly spells 1985-2003 for the population aged 15-70 constructed from registers on public transfers, hourly wages, employer-reported job start/end dates and mandatory employer pension contributions; five states (employment, unemployment, retirement, self-employment, non-participation), with non-participation a residual state (neither employed, self-employed nor receiving a transfer classifying the person as unemployed or retired).
    Registers: Spell data (administrative registers), IDA
    working paper · Section 5 (Data sources)
  • Unemployment spell (broad) and recall recoding Unemployment and benefits
    Non-participation recoded as unemployment; unemployment spells of 13 weeks or less followed by recall to the same employer are recoded as part of the original employment spell; unemployment spells of 2 weeks or less between employment spells with different employers are treated as a job-to-job transition.
    Registers: Spell data
    working paper · Section 5 (Analysis panel), footnotes 10-11
  • Hourly wage Earnings and income
    IDA estimate of the average hourly wage for jobs active in the last week of November (no wage for spells not overlapping it); trimmed at 1st and 99th percentiles annually and trended to 2003 levels using implicit deflators.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 5
  • Analysis panel Sample definition and timing
    1994-2003; histories truncated at age 55 and starting at graduation from highest completed education; workers ever observed in public-sector employment, self-employment, retirement or agriculture are discarded.
    Registers: Spell data, IDA
    working paper · Section 5 (Analysis panel)
  • Firm inflow (poaching) rank Firm characteristics and productivity
    For each firm, the fraction of all hires over the 10-year window that come directly from other firms (job-to-job); measured only for firms with more than 15 hires and at least one hire from unemployment; used as a firm productivity rank.
    Registers: Spell data
    working paper · Section 6 (moments), footnote 17
  • Education strata Education and test scores
    Robustness estimation splits workers into less than 15 and more than 15 years of education.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section on education-stratified estimation

Labour markets, wages and sorting

Occupations and Import Competition: Evidence from Denmark

Sharon Traiberman · American Economic Review, 2019 · Individual + firm

Estimates a dynamic occupational choice model on Danish worker histories in which workers accumulate occupation-specific human capital that is lost when they switch. Occupations explain 57 percent of the dispersion in worker outcomes from trade, sectors only 16 percent, and rising import competition from 1995 to 2005 lowered lifetime earnings for about 5 percent of workers.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA/IDAS) with ISCO occupation codes, Firm and establishment statistics (FIRE, FIRM) for industry codes, Customs trade data (UHDI), UN Comtrade (CEPII BACI), Danish national accounts, Danish CPI, LIBOR
Key variables
  • Outcome: annual salary income from November employer
  • Choice variable: two-digit occupation by sector
  • Shock: import prices / import competition by industry
  • Worker skill groups: low, medium, high education
  • Occupational tenure
Period
1996–2007 worker panel (tenure built from 1990–1996); import competition 1995–2005
Sample
18,513,301 observations in sample frame (33,502,593 in raw data) Danish individuals aged 23–59 in IDA, 1996–2007, used to estimate an occupational choice model. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Two-digit occupation (cleaned) Occupation and job hierarchy
    Two-digit ISCO (DISCO) code taken from the four-digit occupation code in IDA, using only codes whose quality flag indicates they come from administrative surveys or pension funds (not imputation or lagged information). Missing codes are imputed if the worker has the same occupation at t-1 and t+1, or from t+2 after a firm switch; managerial codes 10-13 are combined into one, legislators and military are dropped, and small occupations are merged by skill group (e.g. 52 into 51, 92 into 61 for all skill groups).
    Registers: IDA, IDAS
    Codes: DISCO/ISCO two-digit; quality flag codes 1, 2, 4, 10 kept; ISCO 10-13 combined; high-skilled merges 42->41, 52->51, 72->71/74, 81->82/83, 91->93 per Appendix table; 21/22 merged for low/medium skill
    online appendix · Online Appendix D.1, Data Cleaning: Occupations (and footnote 11)
  • Four-sector industry aggregation Sector and industry
    NACE 1.1 four-digit industry codes assigned to plants (FIRE; firm-level FIRM data used when plant data not available) and matched to workers, aggregated into four sectors: Manufacturing (incl. construction, agriculture, utilities), FIRE, Public Services (labelled Health & Education), and Other Services.
    Registers: FIRE, FIRM, IDA
    Codes: NACE 1 2-digit 0-45 = Manufacturing; 64-74 = FIRE; 75, 80, 85-90 = Public Services; all remaining = Other Services
    online appendix · Online Appendix D.1, Data Cleaning: Industry (full mapping in appendix Table 16)
  • Skill group Education and test scores
    Three skill groups from completed education in IDA: low = high school or short-cycle education; medium = vocational or medium-cycle education; high = bachelor's degree or more. Education is never allowed to decrease (higher earlier level imputed) and missing values are filled from the previous year, else the next reported year.
    Registers: IDA
    online appendix · Online Appendix D.1, Data Cleaning: Skill
  • Occupational tenure Occupation and job hierarchy
    Tenure measured at the occupation-sector pair level, constructed for early cohorts using data from 1990-1996, and censored above at 6 years to keep the measure comparable across cohorts; tenure resets upon switching occupations.
    Registers: IDA
    online appendix · Online Appendix D.1, Occupational Tenure; Appendix model section
  • Annual income (November job) Earnings and income
    Total salary-based income reported by IDA in November of each year, covering the worker's primary and any secondary occupation; all of it is attributed to the reported (primary) occupation. Hours are not used because they are often imputed. Deflated by the 2000 Danish CPI (1000s DKK).
    Registers: IDA
    online appendix · Online Appendix D.1, Income; notes to Table A.7
  • Employed Employment and labour force status
    A worker is counted as employed in year t if employed in November of t (IDA November position).
    Registers: IDA
    online appendix · Online Appendix D.1, Employment
  • Sample frame Sample definition and timing
    Raw data are all individuals in IDAS aged 23-59 in 1996-2007; the final sample applies the occupation/education imputation and cleaning and drops workers non-employed for the whole sample period.
    Registers: IDAS
    online appendix · Online Appendix Table A.7 notes; D.1
  • Foreign (import) price index by industry Trade and offshoring
    Variety-corrected CES import price index per industry built following Broda-Weinstein/Feenstra (Sato-Vartia weights on the common set of goods, adjusted for new and disappearing varieties) from customs data aggregated to the country-product level; a similar index is built from Comtrade, and the geometric mean of the customs, Comtrade and national-accounts indices is used as the path of foreign prices.
    Registers: UHDI, Comtrade (CEPII BACI), National accounts
    online appendix · Online Appendix, calibration of labour demand side (foreign prices, incl. footnote 14)

Trade and offshoring Labour markets, wages and sorting

Can Women Have Children and a Career? IV Evidence from IVF Treatments

Petter Lundborg, Erik Plug and Astrid Würtz Rasmussen · American Economic Review, 2017 · Individual

Uses success in in vitro fertilisation treatment among childless Danish women as an instrument for having children, since IVF success is unrelated to labour market history. Children lower women's earnings substantially and persistently, mostly through hourly earnings rather than hours, and the effect is much larger for the first child than for later ones.

Data
IVF register held by the Danish National Board of Health (all IVF treatments in public and private clinics, 1994–2005), Linked administrative registers on education, age, marital status and number of children, Linked labour market registers: labour force status, hours worked, hourly wages, annual earnings, occupation, sector and firm
Key variables
  • Instrument: success of the first IVF treatment
  • Endogenous treatment: having children (fertility at the extensive margin)
  • Outcome: annual earnings
  • Outcome: hourly wages and hours worked / employment
  • Mechanisms: occupation, sector and firm changes
Period
1991–2009 (IVF treatments 1995–2005)
Sample
18,538 treated women Childless women entering their first IVF treatment with embryo implants between 1995 and 2005. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • IVF treatment success (instrument) Family links, fertility and household
    Equals 1 if the first IVF treatment with embryo implants (in a sequence of treatments) led to a childbirth, 0 otherwise; treatment outcome (birth, abortion, stillbirth, failure) and dates from the IVF register (mandatory reporting 1994-2005).
    Registers: IVF register (Danish National Board of Health)
    paper · Section III (model) and Section II.B
  • Having children (endogenous treatment) Family links, fertility and household
    Indicator equal to 1 if the woman has children and 0 otherwise, measured over periods t = 0-1, 2-5 and 6-10 after the (potential) childbirth.
    Registers: Population registers
    paper · Section III and Table 2 notes
  • IVF sample and potential childbirth year Sample definition and timing
    Childless women (no children observed the year before first treatment) in their first IVF treatment with positive embryo implants, first treatment in 1995 or later (to avoid misclassified treatment order since the register starts 1994), matched to other registers: 18,538 women. Year of (potential) childbirth = date of embryo transfer plus nine months; outcomes followed up to ten years after; pretreatment outcomes averaged over years 1-4 before first treatment.
    Registers: IVF register, Population and labour market registers
    paper · Section II.E and table notes
  • Annual earnings Earnings and income
    Annual labour earnings from tax and employer-employee registers, including parental leave and sickness benefits, in 2008 DKK.
    Registers: Tax registers, Employer-employee registers
    paper · Section I and Table 1 notes
  • Job changes and job characteristics Occupation and job hierarchy
    Dummies for any workplace change and any (four-digit) occupation change in the short, medium and long run; job characteristics are averages of earnings, hours and log hourly wages by workplace and four-digit occupation over the study period computed in a representative sample of Danish women, plus workplace percent female, public sector and home-work distance.
    Registers: Employer-employee registers
    Codes: Four-digit occupation code
    paper · Section IV.C and Table 4 notes
  • Depression Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Measured as antidepressant medication use (data complete only from 1994 onward).
    Registers: Prescription registry
    paper · Section IV and Table 2 notes

The Consumption Effects of the 2007–2008 Financial Crisis: Evidence from Households in Denmark

Thais Lærkholm Jensen and Niels Johannesen · American Economic Review, 2017 · Individual

Customers of banks that were hit hard by the crisis cut consumption more than customers of healthier banks. The channel is reduced credit availability: exposed households borrowed less and spent less, which shows how bank distress transmits to the real economy through households.

Data
Tax authority third-party reports of all individuals' loan and deposit account balances, linked to bank identity via branch numbers (Nets lists), Bank balance sheet data from the Danish Central Bank (MFI statistics), Administrative registers on demographics, education, labour market and income, Income and wealth registers (capital income, social transfers, stock portfolios, pension accounts), Motor vehicle register and real estate register
Key variables
  • Treatment: primary bank's 2007 loan-to-deposit ratio (above vs below median exposure)
  • Outcome: individual borrowing (loan balances by account)
  • Outcome: imputed spending = disposable income minus change in net wealth
  • Outcome: car ownership (motor vehicle register)
  • Separate analysis: customers of banks that failed 2008–2011
Period
2003–2011
Sample
around 440,000 individuals, almost 3.5 million individual-years and more than 5.7 million individual-account-years 25% random sample of non-self-employed Danish residents aged 20–50 in 2007 whose primary bank did not fail during 2008–2011. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Bank-account link (bank identity) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Year-end loan and deposit account balances reported by financial institutions to the tax authorities; the first four digits of each account number identify the bank branch, mapped to bank identity using hand-collected Nets lists of branch id-numbers for each year 2003-2011.
    Registers: Tax authority third-party account reports, Nets branch lists
    Codes: First four digits of account number = branch id
    working paper · Section 3.1, footnote 5
  • Primary bank (2007) Wealth, debt and consumption
    If one bank relation in 2007, that bank; if multiple relations but a loan in only one, that bank; if loans in multiple banks, the bank with the largest loan balance; if no loans, the bank with the largest deposit balance. Always a bank, never a mortgage institution.
    Registers: Tax authority third-party account reports
    working paper · Section 3.3 and footnote 6
  • Exposed bank Firm characteristics and productivity
    Individuals ordered by the 2007 loan-to-deposit ratio of their primary bank and split at the median individual: above-median primary bank = exposed (approximately equal numbers in each group).
    Registers: Danish Central Bank bank balance sheets
    working paper · Section 3.3
  • Imputed spending Wealth, debt and consumption
    Spending = disposable income minus change in net wealth. Disposable income = total realized income - taxes - interest payments + payments from private pension accounts (net of taxes) + imputed capital gains on stocks (start-of-period stock value times growth in stock price index). Net wealth = market value of securities + savings and checking accounts - mortgage loans - bank debt - other loans; real estate excluded (so spending includes real estate purchases). Main regressions exclude stock owners.
    Registers: Income registers, Wealth registers
    online appendix · Online Appendix Table A1; WP Section 3.2
  • Pension withdrawals (borrowing-constraint indicator) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Withdrawals (liquidations) from tax-favoured pension savings accounts, which carry a 60% penalty before pension age, used as an indicator of borrowing constraints.
    Registers: Income and wealth registers
    working paper · Section 5 (Table 4, col. 3)
  • Car ownership Wealth, debt and consumption
    Number of cars owned, indicators for owning at least one and at least two cars, and average car weight, from the auto register (weight and production year of each registered automobile).
    Registers: Motor vehicle register
    working paper · Sections 3.1 and 6
  • Baseline sample Sample definition and timing
    Residents 2003-2011 aged 20-50 in 2007, excluding self-employed and individuals whose 2007 primary bank failed in 2008-2011 (analysed separately), 25% random sample (about 440,000 individuals); DKK variables winsorized at 1st and 99th percentiles.
    Registers: Tax records, Population registers
    working paper · Sections 3.1 and 3.3
  • Unemployment controls/outcome Unemployment and benefits
    Control: dummy for unemployment spells during 2006-2007; outcome: fraction of the year spent in unemployment.
    Registers: Labour market registers
    working paper · Section 4 controls; Table A-notes
