Does Growing Up in a High Crime Neighborhood Affect Youth Criminal Behavior?

Anna Piil Damm and Christian Dustmann · American Economic Review, 2014 · Individual

Refugees arriving between 1986 and 1998 were allocated to municipalities quasi-randomly. Boys placed in neighbourhoods with a higher share of youth criminals were later more likely to be convicted, especially for violent crime, which identifies a causal neighbourhood effect on criminal behaviour.

Data
Central Police Register: crime charges and convictions for the full population, Administrative registers: age, residence, parents' IDs, country of origin, immigrant status and date of immigration, Educational Institution Register and surveys, Municipality-level crime and socio-economic measures built from the registers
Key variables
  • Treatment: youth crime conviction rate (share of 15–25-year-olds convicted) in the municipality of assignment
  • Identification: quasi-random assignment of refugee families under the 1986–1998 spatial dispersal policy
  • Outcome: criminal conviction and charge between ages 15 and 21 (by crime type)
  • Longer-term outcomes: education and employment
  • Controls: family background, country of origin, municipality characteristics at assignment
Period
1980–2006
Sample
4,425 children Refugee children from eight source countries who arrived in Denmark before age 15 with at least one refugee parent between 1986 and 1998 and are observed to age 21. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Conviction Crime
    Court ruling that the suspect is guilty of the charge, signalled by a sentence (fine, conditional withdrawal of charge, or suspended or unsuspended prison sentence); 'not guilty' if a not-guilty verdict was recorded or the indictment dropped. Convictions are linked to the start date of committing the offence; all charges and convictions are observed even after deletion from the criminal record.
    Registers: Central Police Register
    working paper · Section II.B and footnote 17
  • Offence categories Crime
    The register's eight offence types (sexual assault, violent crime, property crime, other penal code, Traffic Act, Drugs Act, Arms Act, Tax/other special acts) are recombined, omitting Traffic Act offences, into property crimes, violent crimes (including sexual assault), drug crimes and other offences.
    Registers: Central Police Register
    working paper · Section II.B (details in online Table A4, not accessed)
  • Individual crime outcomes ages 15-21 Crime
    Indicators/counts of charges and convictions for offences committed between ages 15 and 21, split into ages 15-17 and 18-21, by offence category.
    Registers: Central Police Register
    working paper · Section II.B
  • Youth crime conviction rate of municipality Crime
    Share of individuals aged 15-25 living in municipality r who were convicted of a crime committed in calendar year t (t = year of assignment); also computed by crime type (violent, property) and other age ranges. Alternatives: reported crimes per capita and reported violent crimes per 10,000 inhabitants.
    Registers: Central Police Register, Population registers
    working paper · Section II.C
  • Refugee (dispersal policy sample) Immigration and origin
    Individual who immigrated 1986-1998 from Lebanon, Iran, Iraq, Somalia, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Afghanistan or Ethiopia and, at the year of receiving a residence permit, was not married to someone from a non-refugee sending country or to a refugee-country immigrant who arrived at least one year earlier; former Yugoslavia excluded.
    Registers: Administrative population registers
    working paper · Section II.C and footnote 18
  • Refugee children sample Sample definition and timing
    Refugees under 15 at assignment with at least one refugee parent residing in Denmark, immigrating at most one year after the parent(s), and observed in the registers every year until age 21 (4,425 children); treatment measured in the initial assignment municipality.
    Registers: Administrative population registers
    working paper · Section II.C and footnote 19
  • Municipal poverty rate Geography and neighbourhood
    Share of adults in the municipality living in a household with disposable household income below 50% of the national equivalence-scaled median disposable household income (OECD relative poverty).
    Registers: Income registers
    working paper · Section II.C, footnote 22
  • Policing measures Crime
    Police officers per 1,000 inhabitants in the municipality and the crime detection rate, computed as charges relative to reported crimes from administrative police statistics.
    Registers: Police statistics
    working paper · Section II.C (details in online Table A5.B, not accessed)

Migration, neighbourhoods and refugees Crime Children, intergenerational mobility and skills

The Wage Effects of Offshoring: Evidence from Danish Matched Worker-Firm Data

David Hummels, Rasmus Jørgensen, Jakob Munch and Chong Xiang · American Economic Review, 2014 · Individual + firm

Links product-level firm imports and exports to worker wages. Offshoring raises wages of high-skilled workers and lowers wages of low-skilled workers within job spells, while exporting raises wages for all. Tasks that are routine or easily offshored lose the most.

Data
Firm Statistics Register (FirmStat/FIRM), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Firm-worker link (FIDA), Foreign Trade Statistics Register, Extrastat and Intrastat (UHDI), UN COMTRADE world trade data for instruments, Firm accounts and other firm registers (Data Appendix)
Key variables
  • Outcome: log hourly wage of workers within job spells
  • Treatment: firm offshoring (imports of inputs)
  • Treatment: firm exports
  • Instruments: world export supply and world import demand shocks by product and country (COMTRADE) and transport costs
  • Heterogeneity: worker skill type (high vs low skilled)
  • Outcome: earnings losses of displaced workers
Period
1995–2006 (trade data 1990–2006)
Sample
about 1.95 million worker-firm-year and 9,800 firm-year observations Manufacturing workers in Danish firms that both import and export, excluding single-year job spells, workers changing skill level, and firms with fewer than 50 employees and less than 0.6 million DKK in imports. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Hourly wage Earnings and income
    Annual labour income plus mandatory pension fund payments divided by annual hours (IDA); full-time workers; annual hours do not capture overtime.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section II.2 and footnote 7
  • High- vs low-skilled worker Education and test scores
    High-skilled: tertiary education in the two highest ISCED categories (5 and 6); all others low-skilled. Workers whose skill level changes during the sample are dropped.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: ISCED 5-6 = high-skilled
    working paper · Section II.2 and footnote 8
  • Broad offshoring Trade and offshoring
    Total value of imports by a given manufacturing firm in a given year, from the Foreign Trade Statistics Register (Extrastat and Intrastat), recorded at CN8 and aggregated to HS6.
    Registers: Foreign Trade Statistics Register (UHDI)
    working paper · Section II.3
  • Narrow offshoring Trade and offshoring
    Sum of the firm's imports in the same HS4 category as goods the firm sells domestically or exports (HS2 variant as robustness); raw materials are counted in broad but omitted from narrow offshoring.
    Registers: Foreign Trade Statistics Register (UHDI)
    Codes: Raw materials = HS chapters 01-15, 25-27, 31, 41
    working paper · Section II.3, Table 2, footnote 14
  • World export supply and world import demand instruments Trade and offshoring
    WES: country c's total supply of HS6 product k to the world market minus its supply to Denmark in year t; WID: country c's total purchases of product k from the world market less purchases from Denmark; both from COMTRADE and weighted by pre-sample firm input/output shares; plus exchange rates and transport costs fitted from US imports data.
    Registers: UN COMTRADE, Foreign Trade Statistics Register
    working paper · Section III and Data Appendix section 2
  • Estimation sample (firms) Sample definition and timing
    Manufacturing worker-firm-years 1995-2006 linked via FIDA (week 48 employment); drops one-year job spells, workers whose skill changes, and firms with fewer than 50 employees and less than DKK 0.6 million imports; firms kept in years they both import and export, with first trading year treated as pre-sample.
    Registers: FirmStat, IDA, FIDA, Foreign Trade Statistics Register
    working paper · Section II.2
  • Firm controls Firm characteristics and productivity
    Employees as full-time equivalents from FirmStat; capital stock (land, buildings, machines, equipment, inventory) from the Accounting Statistics register; gross output net of taxes from the VAT register; firm skill intensity aggregated from IDA education via FIDA.
    Registers: FirmStat, Accounting Statistics, VAT register, IDA, FIDA
    working paper · Data Appendix section 1
  • Routine / non-routine task intensity Occupation and job hierarchy
    O*NET 13 (2008) characteristics mapped to ISCO-88 occupation codes in IDA; non-routine = principal component of O*NET items 1.A.1.c.1, 1.A.2.b.3, 1.A.3.c.3, 2.A.1.e, 4.A.2.b.2, 4.A.2.b.6; routine = 1.A.2.a.2, 1.A.2.a.3, 1.A.2.b.2, 4.A.2.a.2, 4.A.2.a.3 (similar lists for social science, natural science, communication, hazards).
    Registers: IDA, O*NET
    Codes: ISCO-88 occupation; O*NET ids as listed
    working paper · Data Appendix section 1
  • Mass-layoff displacement and offshorer Employment and labour force status
    Displaced workers separate from firms where at least 30% of the initial-year workers are not employed by the firm the following year (gross flows). Offshorers are displaced from firms whose predicted offshoring (first stage) rose at least 10% between predisplacement and displacement year. Sample: manufacturing workers with at least six years tenure in some year 1997-2000, not dying, emigrating or turning 61 in 1995-2006, at firms importing at least DKK 600,000 with 50+ employees.
    Registers: IDA, FIDA, FirmStat
    working paper · Section VI, footnotes 32-34, Data Appendix section 3

Migration and Wage Effects of Taxing Top Earners: Evidence from the Foreigners' Tax Scheme in Denmark

Henrik Jacobsen Kleven, Camille Landais, Emmanuel Saez and Esben Schultz · Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2014 · Individual

The 1991 preferential tax scheme for high-earning foreigners roughly doubled the number of highly paid foreigners in Denmark. The implied elasticity of migration with respect to the net-of-tax rate is above one, far larger than domestic labour supply elasticities, and the scheme generated modest wage spillovers.

Data
Administrative tax and payroll records for all residents (income tax register), Civil registration (CPR) citizenship and migration records with dates of entry and exit, Foreigners' tax scheme beneficiary records (contract start and end dates), Employer links at firm and establishment level with industry
Key variables
  • Treatment: eligibility for the preferential foreigners' tax scheme (earnings above threshold)
  • Outcome: number of foreigners above vs below the earnings threshold (migration response)
  • Outcome: earnings of scheme beneficiaries (wage effects / bunching at the threshold)
  • Outcome: spillovers on native top earners' employment and earnings
  • Key variable: citizenship and years of presence in Denmark
Period
1980–2010 (tax data since 1980; scheme introduced 1992)
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked All foreigners and natives resident in Denmark, focusing on foreigners with earnings around the scheme eligibility threshold (researchers excluded). source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Scheme earnings eligibility threshold Taxes and tax rates
    Foreigners' scheme requires annual wage earnings with the requesting employer above a threshold that grows roughly with average earnings and lies between the 99.2th and 99.4th percentile of the Danish wage earnings distribution (DKK 765,600 in 2009); it must be met on an annualized basis (e.g. a 6-month contract needs half the annual threshold). For pre-1991 years the threshold is imputed by holding the threshold-to-average-earnings ratio at its 1991 value, with average earnings computed over all workers with positive earnings.
    Registers: Administrative tax and payroll records
    working paper · Section 2.1 and footnote 14
  • Scheme eligibility (prior tax liability) Taxes and tax rates
    To be eligible the taxpayer must have been recruited abroad and not have been tax liable in Denmark in the 3 years before going on the scheme (applied to each scheme spell separately; prior scheme time not counted); citizenship plays no formal role, so Danish citizens tax-resident abroad for 3+ years qualify. Scheme lasts at most 36 months.
    Registers: Foreigners' tax scheme beneficiary records
    working paper · Section 2.1 and footnote 12
  • Annualized earnings Earnings and income
    Earnings of part-year residents are annualized based on duration of stay in the year, with duration of stay measured from the migration database (daily dates of entry and exit from CPR records).
    Registers: Administrative tax records, CPR migration records
    working paper · Section 4.1, footnote 23
  • Treatment and control groups of foreigners (migration DiD) Immigration and origin
    Treatment: foreigners with (annualized) earnings above the eligibility threshold; controls: foreigners with earnings between 80% and 90% (control 1) and between 90% and 99.5% (control 2) of the threshold, series normalized to 1990. In the elasticity regressions controls are foreigners between 80% and 99% of the threshold; an alternative uses the 99.5-100th percentile vs the 95-97th and 97-99th percentiles of the full earnings distribution.
    Registers: Administrative tax records, CPR citizenship records
    working paper · Section 4.1, Figures 4-5, Table 2
  • Citizenship groups and expatriates Immigration and origin
    Nordic foreigners: citizens of Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden; English-speaking: Australia, Canada, Ireland, New Zealand, South Africa, UK, US. Expatriates are Danish citizens returning after a spell of at least three years abroad.
    Registers: CPR citizenship records
    working paper · Section 4.1, Table 2 Panels A5-A7
  • Wage-effect repeated cross-section sample Sample definition and timing
    For year t, foreigners who arrived in Denmark in year t-1 and stayed the full calendar year t; earnings between 70-95% (below) and 105-400% (above) of the threshold, excluding 95-105% (bunchers) and above 400%; years 1991-1994 excluded because scheme earnings are not computerized.
    Registers: Administrative tax records, CPR migration records, Scheme beneficiary records
    working paper · Section 4.2, Figure 8, Table 3, footnote 30
  • Top natives and top foreign employees (spillovers) Earnings and income
    Top natives: native workers with earnings above 75% of the scheme eligibility threshold (about the top 3% of native earnings). Top foreign employees: foreign employees with less than 3 years of presence in Denmark and annualized earnings above the threshold; industry scheme use = growth in top foreign employees between 1980-1990 and 1991-2000 divided by top native employees in 1980-1990.
    Registers: Administrative tax and payroll records, Employer links with 2-digit industry
    working paper · Section 4.3 (industry-level spillovers), footnote 35

Tenure, Experience, Human Capital, and Wages: A Tractable Equilibrium Search Model of Wage Dynamics

Jesper Bagger, François Fontaine, Fabien Postel-Vinay and Jean-Marc Robin · American Economic Review, 2014 · Individual + firm

Builds and estimates an equilibrium search model with on-the-job search and human capital accumulation using Danish career histories. Human capital accumulation drives most early-career wage growth, while job-to-job mobility and employer competition explain the later part of wage profiles.

Data
Weekly labour market spell data built from administrative registers (employment, unemployment, non-participation, self-employment, retirement), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA): hourly wages, education, experience, ownership, ATP pension contributions used to measure actual experience since 1964, Firm accounts survey (Accounts Statistics) 1999–2003 with value added and hours
Key variables
  • Outcome: hourly wage of jobs active in the last week of November
  • Key variable: job tenure and actual labour market experience
  • Key variable: firm productivity measured by value added (accounting data)
  • Key variable: job-to-job, employment-to-unemployment transitions (spell data)
  • Stratification: three schooling levels (7–11, 12–14, 15–20 years)
Period
1985–2003
Sample
168,649, 320,638 and 66,155 workers (2,534,203, 4,344,288 and 663,362 observations) in the three education groups Danish private-sector male workers born in 1948 or later, at least two years past graduation, with histories truncated at entry into retirement, self-employment, the public sector or industries lacking value-added data. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Weekly labour market states (spell data) Employment and labour force status
    Weekly firm-level spell data built from several administrative registers, with spells classified as employment, self-employment, unemployment, non-participation and retirement; non-participation is a residual state. Short (13 weeks or shorter) non-employment, non-retirement spells between job spells with the same employer are recoded as employment.
    Registers: Spell data (administrative registers), IDA
    working paper · Section 3 (Data) and Appendix B
  • Hourly wage Earnings and income
    IDA average hourly wage for jobs active in the last week of November, deflated to 2003 prices with Statistics Denmark's CPI.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3 and Appendix B
  • Actual labour market experience Employment and labour force status
    Actual experience at end of calendar year constructed from mandatory ATP pension payments back to 1 January 1964; pre-1980 experience measured in years and post-1980 in 1/1000 of a year's full-time work. Workers dropped if pre-1980 experience changes over 1985-2003, if experience falls or rises by more than two years in a year, or exceeds age minus 15.
    Registers: IDA, ATP
    working paper · Section 3, footnote 11, Appendix B
  • Firm productivity (hourly value added) Firm characteristics and productivity
    Value added per FTE from Statistics Denmark's firm accounts survey 1999-2003, converted to hourly by dividing by 12 x 166.33 hours; top and bottom 1% within strata set to missing; moments reweighted by empirical sampling probabilities by firm size bins 0-9, 10-19, 20-49, >49 employees.
    Registers: Accounts Statistics (firm accounts survey)
    working paper · Appendix B and Table 7
  • Private-sector employment Sector and industry
    Ownership code of the employing establishment in IDA identifies private-sector establishments; histories are truncated at entry into a public sector job, self-employment, retirement or an industry without accounting data. Firm industry and ownership taken from its largest establishment.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3, footnote 10, Appendix B
  • Schooling strata Education and test scores
    Years of education computed from type of highest completed education, grouped as 7-11 years (primary), 12-14 years (high school or vocational) and 15-20 years (bachelor or higher); workers enter two years after graduation and are dropped if ever observed in education afterwards or if years of education exceed age minus seven.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3 and Appendix B
  • Analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    Men born on or after 1 January 1948 (so experience from 1964 is complete), 1985-2003, dropping firms with missing ID, ownership or industry and workers with gaps in observed histories.
    Registers: Spell data, IDA
    working paper · Appendix B

Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark

Raj Chetty, John N. Friedman, Søren Leth-Petersen, Torben Heien Nielsen and Tore Olsen · Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2014 · Individual

Uses the universe of Danish savings records to show that tax subsidies for retirement accounts mostly shift saving between accounts: each krone of subsidy raises total saving by about one øre. Automatic employer contributions, by contrast, raise total saving almost one for one, because roughly 85 percent of individuals are passive savers who do not re-optimise.

Data
Income tax register with third-party reported earnings and pension contributions (IND), Third-party reported wealth: end-of-year assets and liabilities in taxable accounts, Population register (BEF), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Key variables
  • Outcome: contributions to employer and individual retirement accounts
  • Outcome: taxable saving (change in taxable assets), gross and net
  • Treatment: employer pension contribution changes at job switches (automatic contributions)
  • Treatment: 1999 reduction in tax subsidy for capital pensions for top-bracket taxpayers (price subsidy)
  • Treatment: government mandatory savings plan (SP) contributions
Period
1995–2009
Sample
approximately 41 million observations for 4 million individuals Danish population aged 18–60, excluding observations with self-employment income (unbalanced panel). source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Primary analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    Danish population 1995-2009 from merged income tax register, population register and IDA, excluding observations below age 18 or above 60 and observations with self-employment income (about 41 million observations on 4 million individuals).
    Registers: IND (income tax register), BEF, IDA
    working paper · Section III (Sample and Variable Definitions)
  • Taxable saving (gross and net) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Gross taxable saving = change in third-party reported end-of-year assets in taxable accounts; net saving = gross saving minus change in liabilities, where liabilities cover secured and unsecured debt except home mortgages. Saving measures and rates below the 1st or above the 99th percentile in the estimation sample are set to missing.
    Registers: Third-party reported wealth data (tax authority)
    working paper · Section III
  • Pension contributions by account Retirement and pensions
    Annual employer and individual contributions to capital pension (lump-sum) and annuity pension accounts as reported by employers and pension funds; contributions above the 99th percentile are top-coded at the 99th percentile in each account and year.
    Registers: IND (income tax register)
    working paper · Section III
  • Income concepts Earnings and income
    Labor income = labor earnings before taxes excluding contributions to employer-administered pensions; total compensation = labor earnings plus employer and employee contributions to employer-administered accounts; taxable income = labor income plus other income (e.g., UI) affecting tax liability. Measured at the individual level, with joint-account balances split equally.
    Registers: IND (income tax register)
    working paper · Section III
  • Firm switch Employment and labour force status
    Individual switches firms in year t if he has earnings from two distinct firms in t and t-1 (primary job for multiple jobholders); switches where earnings fell by more than half or more than doubled are excluded; set missing in 2003, 2005 and 2007 when firm identifiers changed. Event studies require at least 4 years of data before and after.
    Registers: IDA, IND
    working paper · Section IV.A, footnotes 9-10
  • Mandatory Savings Plan (MSP) contribution Retirement and pensions
    From 1998 individuals with labor income at or above DKr 34,500 were required to contribute 1% of earnings (DKr 345 at the cutoff); RD on changes in pension contributions/saving from 1997 to 1998 for individuals within DKr 25,000 of the cutoff.
    Registers: IND (income tax register)
    Codes: cutoff Y >= DKr 34,500; bandwidth DKr 25,000
    working paper · Section IV.B, equation (6)
  • 1999 capital pension subsidy reduction Taxes and tax rates
    From 1999 the deduction for capital pension contributions fell from 59 to 45 cents per DKr for individuals in the top income tax bracket (cutoff DKr 251,200 in 1998); treatment group: taxable income DKr 25,000-75,000 above the top-tax cutoff; control: DKr 25,000-75,000 below.
    Registers: IND (income tax register)
    working paper · Section V, V.A (Estimator 1)

Household finance, saving and consumption Taxation and public finance

Unwilling or Unable to Cheat? Evidence from a Tax Audit Experiment in Denmark

Henrik Jacobsen Kleven, Martin B. Knudsen, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Pedersen and Emmanuel Saez · Econometrica, 2011 · Individual

A randomised field experiment with the Danish tax authority on about 40,000 taxpayers. Evasion is close to zero for third-party reported income but substantial for self-reported income, and audit threat letters raise reported self-reported income. Information, not morality, is what makes modern tax systems work.

Data
Randomized tax audit experiment implemented by the Danish tax authority (SKAT), SKAT Business Object Database: third-party information reports, pre-populated returns, filed returns and after-audit returns, item by item, SKAT computer-generated audit flags, Basic socio-economic variables and employer industry/size from SKAT records
Key variables
  • Treatment: random assignment to 100% vs 0% unannounced audit group (2007 filing season)
  • Treatment: random threat-of-audit letters (100%, 50%, none) before the 2008 filing deadline
  • Outcome: detected tax evasion (audit adjustments to net income and tax)
  • Outcome: change in reported income in the following year
  • Heterogeneity: self-reported vs third-party reported income
Period
2006–2007 income years (2007 and 2008 filing seasons)
Sample
25,020 employees and 17,764 self-employed Stratified random sample of Danish taxpayers (employees, including transfer recipients, and self-employed) selected by SKAT for the audit experiment. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Audit treatment (stage 1) Taxes and tax rates
    Stratified random sample of 25,020 employees and 17,764 self-employed (strata: employee/self-employed, light/heavy return complexity, 30 regional tax centres) randomly split into a 100% group subjected to unannounced comprehensive audits of returns filed in 2007 (2006 income) and a 0% group never audited; effects are intent-to-treat (actual audit rates 98.7% employees, 92% self-employed).
    Registers: SKAT Business Object Database
    working paper · Section 4.2
  • Threat-of-audit letters (stage 2) Taxes and tax rates
    Employees in both audit groups randomly assigned (thirds) to receive a letter one month before the 1 May 2008 filing deadline stating that the return would certainly be audited (100% letter), that half of the group would be audited (50% letter), or no letter. Outcome is the probability of self-reported adjustments (upward/downward) relative to the latest return at the time the letter was received.
    Registers: SKAT Business Object Database
    working paper · Section 4.2; Section 7 and footnote 38; Table 8
  • Detected tax evasion (audit adjustments) Taxes and tax rates
    Net audit adjustment = after-audit return (A) minus filed return (F), split into under-reporting (upward adjustments raising tax liability) and over-reporting (downward adjustments), for net income, total tax and income components.
    Registers: SKAT Business Object Database
    Codes: Returns: information report (I), pre-populated (P), filed (F), after-audit (A)
    working paper · Section 4.3; Section 5.1; Table 2 notes
  • Third-party vs self-reported income and evasion Taxes and tax rates
    Third-party income comes from information reports; self-reported income = total reported income minus third-party income. For always-positive line items, third-party under-reporting = A-F if F<A<I, = I-F if F<I<=A, zero otherwise; self-reported under-reporting is total upward adjustment net of third-party under-reporting. Third-party under-reporting is defined only for positive items.
    Registers: SKAT Business Object Database
    Codes: F<A<I: A-F; F<I<=A: I-F; else 0
    working paper · Section 5.2; Table 2 notes
  • Net income and components Earnings and income
    Net income = personal income + capital income + stock income + self-employment income + foreign income - deductions. Personal income: earnings, pensions, alimony minus some retirement contributions; capital income: interest income, bond returns, net rents minus interest payments; stock income: dividends and realised capital gains on stocks; self-employment income: net profits of unincorporated businesses.
    Registers: SKAT Business Object Database
    working paper · Table 2 notes; Table 1
  • Audit flags Taxes and tax rates
    Presence and number of computer-generated audit flags, a deterministic function of the return characteristics that SKAT normally uses to select returns for examiner review.
    Registers: SKAT audit flag system
    working paper · Section 4.1; Section 4.3

Taxation and public finance

Adjustment Costs, Firm Responses, and Micro vs. Macro Labor Supply Elasticities: Evidence from Danish Tax Records

Raj Chetty, John N. Friedman, Tore Olsen and Luigi Pistaferri · Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2011 · Individual + firm

Uses bunching at kinks in the Danish tax schedule to show that observed earnings responses are shaped by search costs and by firms coordinating hours around tax thresholds. Once adjustment frictions are accounted for, the structural labour supply elasticity is around 0.3, far above the small elasticities from individual-level micro studies, which helps reconcile micro and macro estimates.

Data
Income tax register / Income Statistics Register (IND), Population register (BEF), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) with firm ID and occupation
Key variables
  • Outcome: bunching (excess mass) of taxable income at the top-tax kink
  • Treatment: marginal tax rate changes at bracket cutoffs (tax simulator)
  • Key variable: firm and occupation-level bunching (hours constraints / firm responses)
  • Key variable: size of tax change across kinks
  • Comparison: wage earners vs self-employed
Period
1994–2001
Sample
17.9 million observations of wage earners (6.8 million within DKr 50,000 of the top tax cutoff; 1.8 million self-employed observations) Danish wage earners aged 15–70, excluding the self-employed and pensioners, with self-employed studied separately. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Wage earner sample Employment and labour force status
    Individuals aged 15-70 in the tax register 1994-2001 classified as wage earners by IDA employment status, excluding self-employed, pensioners, wage earners with self-employment income and wage earners with unemployment; much of the analysis uses wage earners within DKr 50,000 of the top tax cutoff. Self-employed analysed separately.
    Registers: IND (tax register), IDA
    Codes: BESKST=4 (robustness: BESKST in 4, 5, 7, 8)
    working paper · Section 4; Appendix B
  • Tax simulator and marginal tax rates Taxes and tax rates
    Authors' tax simulator computing tax liabilities and marginal tax rates from own and spouse's tax variables and previous-year municipality of residence; it matches actual municipal, regional, bottom, middle and top taxes within DKr 5 for 95% of observations.
    Registers: IND (tax register)
    Codes: pnr, henv (spouse), glskkmnr (municipality), pfrdst, berfrdst (personal exemption), perindkp, berpi (personal income), kapindkp, berkap (capital income), lignfrdp (special deductions), kappens, fosfufrd (individual pension contributions), arbpen14, arbpen15 (employer capital pension contributions), underhol (alimony)
    working paper · Appendix B
  • Wage earnings and net deductions Earnings and income
    Wage earnings from the tax register; net deductions = deductions minus non-wage income (accounting for spousal deductions), equivalently wage earnings minus taxable income; in the top-tax base, net deductions = wage earnings needed to start paying top tax minus the statutory top tax cutoff. Small-deduction group: net deductions below DKr 7,500 in magnitude.
    Registers: IND (tax register)
    Codes: wage earnings qlontmp2; self-employment profits qovskvir, virkordind
    working paper · Section 4; Appendix B
  • Bunching (excess mass) at kinks Taxes and tax rates
    Excess mass b = number of individuals in a window around the kink in excess of a counterfactual density, relative to the average counterfactual density in the window; the counterfactual is a seventh-degree polynomial fitted to binned counts of the earnings distribution excluding a DKr 15,000 window centred on the kink (q=7, R=7).
    Registers: IND (tax register)
    Codes: q=7 (polynomial degree), R=7 (bins on each side), excluded window DKr 15,000
    working paper · Section 4, equations (15)-(16)
  • Firm bunching and occupation earnings modes Occupation and job hierarchy
    Occupation-year modes = DKr 5,000 wage-earnings bin with most workers in each 4-digit ISCO occupation-year (occupation-years with under 7,000 workers excluded). Firm bunching b_F = excess mass at the statutory top-tax cutoff for workers with more than DKr 20,000 in deductions; individual bunching b_I = excess mass at the pension kink for the same group; compared across 2-digit ISCO occupations.
    Registers: IDA, IND
    Codes: occupation discok (ISCO 4-digit; 2-digit for Figure 18); deductions > DKr 20,000
    working paper · Section 6 (Predictions 2 and 3); Appendix B; Figures 14, 18
  • Pension-driven kink Retirement and pensions
    Cap on tax-deductible pension contributions (about DKr 33,000 on average) means workers contributing up to the cap enter the top bracket at wage earnings about DKr 33,000 above the statutory cutoff; bunching there is used to measure individual (job-search) bunching.
    Registers: IND (tax register)
    working paper · Introduction; Section 6

Intertemporal Consumption and Credit Constraints: Does Total Expenditure Respond to an Exogenous Shock to Credit?

Søren Leth-Petersen · American Economic Review, 2010 · Individual

The 1992 reform that let Danish homeowners borrow against housing equity provides an exogenous credit shock. Total expenditure responded only modestly on average, with the response concentrated among young households with little liquid wealth, which indicates that credit constraints bind for a minority.

Data
Income tax register: taxable income, transfers, final taxes, Wealth tax register: third-party reported assets and liabilities (housing, shares, mortgage deeds, cash, bonds, debt), Administrative registers on family composition and dwelling characteristics, Danish Family Expenditure Survey (DES) 1994–1996, used to validate the expenditure imputation
Key variables
  • Outcome: total household expenditure imputed from income minus change in wealth
  • Treatment: 1992 credit market reform allowing home equity to be used as collateral for consumption loans
  • Treatment group: homeowners (renters as comparison/consistency check)
  • Credit-constraint proxy: low liquid (non-housing) assets in 1991 relative to monthly disposable income
Period
1987–1996
Sample
38,486 households, of which 25,275 live in owner-occupied housing (working-paper version) Households from a 10% random sample of the Danish population, aged 18–75, not self-employed, non-movers observed in all years 1987–1996. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • Imputed total household expenditure Wealth, debt and consumption
    Total expenditure imputed from tax registers as disposable income (taxable income plus some non-taxable components and transfers, minus final taxes) minus the change in net wealth from the end of one tax year to the end of the next, following Browning and Leth-Petersen (2003); capital gains are not netted out except for housing. Households with negative imputed expenditure are dropped.
    Registers: Income tax register, Wealth tax register
    Codes: c_t = y_t - dW_t (equation 14), with allowance for housing capital gains
    working paper · Section 4.1, equation (14); Section 4.2
  • Wealth components Wealth, debt and consumption
    Third-party reported assets in six pre-reform categories (housing assets at tax-assessed cash value, shares, deposited mortgage deeds, cash holdings, bonds, other assets incl. self-reported non-deposited bonds, ship shares and high-value objects) and total liabilities; mortgage debt is separately available only up to 1993, so only total liabilities are consistent across years. Employer pension funds are not observed.
    Registers: Wealth tax register
    working paper · Section 4.2; Appendix figure A2
  • Credit-constrained (low liquid assets) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Households whose liquid (non-housing) assets in 1991, the year before the reform, are worth less than one month of disposable income (split D1) or at most two months of disposable income (split D2).
    Registers: Wealth tax register, Income tax register
    working paper · Section 4.3, Table 1
  • Credit reform exposure Wealth, debt and consumption
    The 1992 mortgage reform allowed mortgage loans to finance non-housing purposes, up to 60% of the house value, and extended the maximum maturity from 20 to 30 years; homeowners are treated and renters serve as a consistency check.
    Registers: Administrative dwelling registers
    working paper · Section 2; Section 4.3
  • Household panel sample Sample definition and timing
    Drawn from a 10% random population sample 1987-1996: excludes self-employed, persons living with parents or in a common household, requires age 18-75, no move during the period, no negative imputed expenditure, and observation in all years 1987-1996; 38,486 households, of which 25,275 owner-occupiers.
    Registers: Income tax register, Wealth tax register, Population and dwelling registers
    working paper · Section 4.3

Household finance, saving and consumption

An Empirical Model of Growth Through Product Innovation

Rasmus Lentz and Dale T. Mortensen · Econometrica, 2008 · Firm

Estimates a Schumpeterian model of firm growth through product innovation on a Danish firm panel. Reallocation of labour from less to more innovative firms accounts for roughly half of aggregate productivity growth, with the remainder coming from innovation within firms.

Data
Danish Business Statistics Register: annual panel of privately owned firms (value added, total wage bill, full-time equivalent employment)
Key variables
  • Firm value added (Y)
  • Total wage bill (W) used to build quality-adjusted employment
  • Full-time equivalent employment (N)
  • Labor productivity: value added per worker and per quality-adjusted worker
  • Moments: firm growth rates including exit, and productivity growth decomposition (within, between, cross, exit)
Period
1992–1997
Sample
unbalanced panel of 4,872 firms All privately owned Danish firms existing in 1992 with more than 20 workers, followed through 1997, excluding later entrants. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • Firm panel Sample definition and timing
    Unbalanced annual panel 1992-1997 of privately owned firms from the Danish Business Statistics Register: all firms existing in 1992 with more than 20 workers, followed over time; entrants after 1992 excluded (about 4,872 firms).
    Registers: Danish Business Statistics Register
    working paper · Section 2 (Danish Firm Data); Section 5 (Danish Firm Data)
  • Quality-adjusted employment Firm characteristics and productivity
    N* of firm j equals its total wage bill W_j divided by the economy-wide average wage per worker (sum of W over sum of N); for firms observed in several years the implied labour quality is averaged over time.
    Registers: Danish Business Statistics Register
    Codes: N*_j = W_j / w, w = sum_j W_j / sum_j N_j
    working paper · Section 2, equation (1) and footnote 2
  • Labour productivity Firm characteristics and productivity
    Value added per worker (Y/N) and value added per quality-adjusted worker (Y/N*), with Y in DKK.
    Registers: Danish Business Statistics Register
    working paper · Section 2, Figure 1
  • Firm growth including exit Firm characteristics and productivity
    Firm growth rate in value added (dY/Y) where an exiting firm contributes an observation of -1.
    Registers: Danish Business Statistics Register
    working paper · Section 5, Table 2
  • Productivity growth decomposition Firm characteristics and productivity
    Growth in aggregate value added per worker decomposed following Foster, Haltiwanger and Krizan (2001) into within, between, cross, entry and exit terms, with firm employment shares as weights; no entry term because entrants are excluded.
    Registers: Danish Business Statistics Register
    Codes: P_t = sum_e s_et p_et, p_et = Y_et/N_et, s_et = N_et/N_t
    working paper · Section 5, equation (19), Table 3

Inside the Family Firm: The Role of Families in Succession Decisions and Performance

Morten Bennedsen, Kasper Meisner Nielsen, Francisco Pérez-González and Daniel Wolfenzon · Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2007 · Individual + firm

Uses the gender of a departing CEO's first-born child as an instrument for family succession in Danish firms. Family CEOs hurt performance: operating profitability falls by at least four percentage points relative to firms that hire outside CEOs, with the largest costs in fast-growing industries and large firms.

Data
Købmandsstandens Oplysningsbureau (KOB) firm financial and management data (private, from annual reports), Danish Civil Registration System (CPR) with family links, Danish Commerce and Companies Agency (Erhvervs- og Selskabsstyrelsen) management/board records with CPR numbers, Industry-level data from Statistics Denmark and OECD STAN
Key variables
  • Outcome: operating return on assets (OROA) around CEO transitions
  • Treatment: family CEO succession (incoming CEO related by blood or marriage)
  • Instrument: gender of the departing CEO's firstborn child
  • Heterogeneity: industry growth, skill intensity and firm size
Period
1994–2002 (management data); financial data 1991–2003
Sample
5,334 successions CEO successions in Danish limited liability (public and private) firms between 1994 and 2002, first transition per firm. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Operating return on assets (OROA) Firm characteristics and productivity
    Ratio of earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT) to the book value of assets, from annual reports of limited liability firms (KOB). Performance change is the three-year average after succession minus the three-year average before, omitting the succession year.
    Registers: KOB
    working paper · Section II.B; footnote 13; Table IV notes
  • Industry-adjusted OROA Firm characteristics and productivity
    OROA minus the equally weighted average OROA of all active firms (including non-event firms) in the same industry and year; four-digit NACE industries are used if they contain at least 20 non-event firms in a year, otherwise three- or two-digit groupings.
    Registers: KOB
    Codes: NACE 4-digit, falling back to 3- or 2-digit; minimum 20 non-event firms
    working paper · Section II.B
  • Industry-and-performance-adjusted OROA Firm characteristics and productivity
    OROA adjusted using as control firms in the same industry and the same industry-adjusted performance decile in the year before succession (Barber and Lyon, 1996).
    Registers: KOB
    working paper · Section IV.A
  • Family CEO succession Family links, fertility and household
    Indicator equal to one if the incoming CEO is related by blood or marriage to the departing CEO according to family trees built from the Civil Registration System (parents, siblings, children, marital history), zero otherwise; family successions split into children and other relatives.
    Registers: CPR, Erhvervs- og Selskabsstyrelsen (ES) management records
    working paper · Section II.A, II.C; equation (2)
  • Gender of firstborn child (instrument) Family links, fertility and household
    Indicator equal to one if the departing CEO's first child is male and zero if female; used as an instrument for family succession in a linear first stage.
    Registers: CPR
    working paper · Section III, equation (2)
  • CEO succession sample Sample definition and timing
    CEO successions 1994-2002 in Danish limited liability firms, kept when the departing (incoming) CEO had been (stayed) in the position at least two years, CEO names were matched to CPR numbers via the ES dataset, matching KOB financial data existed around the transition and employment (where available) was non-zero; only the first transition per firm is kept (5,334 successions).
    Registers: KOB, ES, CPR
    working paper · Section II.A
  • Industry heterogeneity measures Sector and industry
    Sample split at the median of industry production growth, output volatility (value of production), labour compensation per employee and import penetration (Statistics Denmark), workers' schooling (authors' calculation from individual schooling and industry of employment), and R&D (industries reporting R&D expenses in OECD STAN).
    Registers: Statistics Denmark industry statistics, OECD STAN
    working paper · Section V, footnote 11
  • Return on capital employed and net income to assets Firm characteristics and productivity
    ROCE is operating income divided by book equity plus book debt; net income to assets is after-tax profits over book value of assets; assets measured as log assets in 2000 DKK.
    Registers: KOB
    working paper · Section II.B; footnote 13

Reskilling and Resilience

Anders Humlum and Pernille Plato · AER: Insights (forthcoming), 2026 · Individual

Studies how retraining shapes workers' resilience to labour market shocks in Danish administrative data, extending the authors' work on human capital investment after injury to the question of which workers reskill and how reskilling protects earnings when jobs disappear.

Data
Work accident reports from Labour Market Insurance (AES), Education Register (UDDA), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), National Patient Registry (hospitalizations), Health Insurance Registry (primary care and specialist visits), Prescription Drug Database, Population register (BEF) for partner linkages
Key variables
  • Shock: work accident causing permanent loss of earning capacity
  • Treatment/moderator: access to reskilling (vocational degree granting direct entry to higher education)
  • Outcome: antidepressant use and other mental health measures
  • Outcome: partner labour market and health outcomes
  • Outcome: earnings and employment of injured workers
Period
1995–2017 (work accidents 1998–2017)
Sample
2,915 injury events (male craft workers); 2,103 stable partners Male craft workers with vocational degrees and full-time employment in the three years before a physical work accident causing permanent loss of earning capacity, and their partners. source
How variables are defined (12)
  • Work accident with permanent earning-capacity loss Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Work accident reports from Labour Market Insurance (AES) with an estimated earning capacity loss (ECL) > 0, excluding psychological shocks; collapsed to person-year. Earning capacity loss is estimated upfront by AES. Milder accidents without permanent loss serve as placebo.
    Registers: AES
    working paper · Section 1.3; footnote 7; Appendix Table A.2
  • Access to reskilling Education and test scores
    Indicator that the worker's vocational degree grants direct entry to relevant higher education programmes (e.g. carpenters, electricians, welders) versus comparable trades that require three years of high school first (e.g. blacksmiths, iron and metal workers, manufacturing technicians). Reskilling = participation in higher education by year +10.
    Registers: UDDA
    working paper · Section 2.2; Figure 1 notes
  • Antidepressant use Health care use
    Dummy indicating a prescription for drugs in ATC class N06A (Antidepressants) in the year.
    Registers: Prescription Drug Database (LMDB)
    Codes: ATC N06A
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, row 19
  • Opioid use Health care use
    Dummy indicating a prescription for drugs in ATC class N02A (Opioids).
    Registers: Prescription Drug Database (LMDB)
    Codes: ATC N02A
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, row 25
  • Alcohol diagnoses Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Accumulated number of hospital diagnoses related to alcohol following Browning and Heinesen (2012): alcohol poisoning, addiction syndrome, delirious abstinence, alcohol psychosis, oesophageal varices, alcoholic liver disease, alcoholic pancreatic disease.
    Registers: LPR
    Codes: ICD-10 F100, F102, F104, F105, I85, K70, K860, T500, T510
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, row 24
  • Cardiovascular / respiratory diagnoses; suicide attempts Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Accumulated number of hospital diagnoses in ICD-10 chapter I (circulatory) or J (respiratory); accumulated hospitalisations where the reason for contact is registered as a suicide attempt (or accident).
    Registers: LPR
    Codes: ICD-10 chapter I; ICD-10 chapter J
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, rows 21-23, 26
  • Full-time and employment Employment and labour force status
    Full-time = full-time work according to RAS, defined by normal working hours above 32 hours/week. Employment = full-time work while not enrolled in a post-secondary programme and not receiving DI (DI = any weeks in the year on disability insurance). Stable pre-injury employment = full-time in all three years before the accident.
    Registers: RAS, IDA
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, rows 10, 15-17; Section 1.3
  • Hours worked (FTE) Hours worked
    2008-2017: yearly number of paid hours; 1995-2007: yearly labour income divided by hourly wage rate (November job). Divided by 1,924 full-time-equivalent yearly hours (37 hours/week).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, rows 11-12
  • Labour income Earnings and income
    Total labour market income including bonuses, fringe benefits, wages paid during sick and parental leave, and employer pension contributions.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, row 9
  • Stable partner / partner retention Family links, fertility and household
    Stable partner = cohabiting (including married) with the same partner for 3 consecutive years; partners are the initial partner in the year before the accident, followed regardless of separation; outcome = share still in the relationship.
    Registers: BEF
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, row 3; Section 2.1; Figure 3 notes
  • Physical-cognitive ability gap Occupation and job hierarchy
    ln(Physical Ability Requirements / Cognitive Ability Requirements) of the occupation, using O*NET importance of strength and stamina items vs. reasoning and idea items; both normalised.
    Registers: IDA, O*NET
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, row 18
  • Union membership Employment and labour force status
    Dummy for a positive deductible union-fee amount reported by unions to the tax authorities.
    Registers: IND
    working paper · Appendix Table A.1, row 14

Survivors' Mental Health and the Protective Role of Income Stability

Itzik Fadlon, Astrid Sophie Fugleholm and Torben Heien Nielsen · AER: Insights, 2026 · Individual

Documents the immediate, large and lingering rise in mental health medication after a spouse's death across the universe of Danish households. A large share of the spike is explained by the income loss the death imposes, so safety-net liquidity protects survivors' mental health.

Data
Population Registry (BEF) with family linkages, Death Registry, National Patient Registry (LPR), Income Registry (earnings, transfers, pension payouts, capital income), Education Registry, Pharmaceutical Database / prescription register (LMDB), Health Insurance Registry (psychiatrist visits)
Key variables
  • Treatment: spouse's fatal heart attack or stroke (death within 12 months), treated vs later-event control group
  • Outcome: take-up of mental health medication (ATC N05, N06)
  • Mechanism: household income loss from spousal death (instrumented by deceased spouse's earnings share)
  • Heterogeneity: baseline income, net wealth and insurance (DI/OAP, sick pay)
Period
1995–2018
Sample
12,637 treatment and 15,212 control households Danish couples aged 45–80 in which one spouse had a heart attack or stroke between 1999 and 2018 and died within 12 months, excluding the self-employed, balanced four years before and after. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Fatal heart attack or stroke (death event) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Index event = first time a spouse is recorded with a heart attack or stroke in the National Patient Registry (hospital admission); restricted to fatal events where the spouse dies within twelve months of the index admission (death date from the Death Registry). Calendar year of the shock is r = 0. Robustness: cause of death must match the event.
    Registers: LPR, LPR-DIAG, Death Registry
    working paper · Section I (Variable definitions); footnote 3
  • Mental health medication take-up Health care use
    Indicator for redeeming a prescription for psychotropic drugs classified as psycholeptics (ATC N05) or psychoanaleptics (ATC N06) by the surviving spouse, measured at monthly and annual frequency (extensive margin).
    Registers: LMDB
    Codes: ATC N05, N06
    working paper · Section I (Variable definitions)
  • Household income loss Earnings and income
    Percent change in household income from the last full year before the shock (r = -1) to the first full year after (r = 1), normalised by r = -1 household income. Household income covers labour earnings, DI and old-age pension, sick pay, other government benefits, private pension payouts, capital income and other income of both spouses.
    Registers: Income Registry (IND)
    working paper · Section I (Variable definitions); Appendix Table B.4
  • Deceased's income share (instrument) Earnings and income
    Share of overall household income earned by the deceased spouse in the baseline year r = -1; used to instrument household income loss.
    Registers: Income Registry (IND)
    working paper · Section I (Variable definitions); Section II.B
  • Treatment/control by event timing Sample definition and timing
    Treatment: spouse has a fatal event in year tau (1999-2013); control: spouse has a fatal event in tau + 5 (2004-2018) and is assigned a placebo event in tau (Delta = 5, robustness 3-7). Couples defined by marriage or cohabitation five years before the event; both spouses Danish residents aged 45-80 in the event year; self-employed excluded; sample balanced from four years before to four years after.
    Registers: BEF, LPR, Death Registry, IND
    working paper · Section II.A (Quasi-Experiment, Analysis Sample); Appendix Table B.1 notes
  • Baseline psychiatric treatment Health care use
    Indicator for whether the surviving spouse had psychiatric treatment (visits to psychiatrists recorded in the Health Insurance Registry from 1990), used as a heterogeneity/control variable.
    Registers: SSSY, SYSI
    working paper · Section I (Data); Section III.B robustness

Taxing the Wealth of the Poor: Evidence from the Danish Old-Age Support Asset Test

Niels Johannesen, Johan Sæverud and Emmanuel Saez · AER: Insights, 2026 · Individual

The asset test for Danish old-age support creates diffuse but large excess mass in liquid assets just below the threshold among the eligible, relative to comparable ineligible groups. Cohort analysis suggests the test reduces liquid assets by about 20 percent near the threshold, and high-frequency bank data show the responses are permanent rather than timed around the test date.

Data
Administrative registers on assets, income and demographics (Statistics Denmark): third-party reported and self-reported liquid wealth, Danske Bank customer data: monthly spending, cash withdrawals and account balances (2014–2016)
Key variables
  • Running variable: liquid wealth relative to the old-age check asset test threshold
  • Outcome: bunching / excess mass of liquid wealth below the threshold
  • Outcome: year-end spending and cash withdrawals (bank data)
  • Eligibility: age 65+ and low income
Period
2014–2018 (main cross-section); bank data 2014–2016
Sample
2,526,421 observations of singles aged 60+ (2,054,987 aged 65+; 1,283,721 low-income 65+), pooled 2014–2018; bank sample 461,471 observations, 2014–2016 Single individuals aged 60 and over in Denmark, with a linked Danske Bank subsample of about 20 percent of the elderly population. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Default liquid wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Third-party-reported year-end value of current accounts, savings accounts and securities accounts (bank deposits and listed securities); excludes durables, real estate and pension accounts and does not net out debt. Available for the full population; mirrors the 'default wealth' the authorities use for the old-age check asset test.
    Registers: IND, Statistics Denmark administrative wealth registers
    paper · Section I.A and I.C; Table 1 notes; Figure 1 notes
  • Reported liquid wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Default liquid wealth plus self-reported corrections submitted via the government website (e.g. adding cash, reducing account balances); available only for individuals above the statutory retirement age. The variable available to the authors does not capture corrections made close to year-end.
    Registers: SOCP, IND
    paper · Section I.A and I.C; Table 1 notes
  • Total wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Default liquid wealth plus pension wealth and housing wealth, net of liabilities (approximates total net wealth for the low-income elderly).
    Registers: IND, PENSFORM
    paper · Figure 1 notes (panel B)
  • Old-age check eligibility (age and income) Retirement and pensions
    Age-eligible = aged 65 or older (statutory retirement age in the sample period). Low-income (income-eligible) = income, net of social security and before self-reported corrections, below the threshold at which the old-age check is fully phased out (disregard DKK 42,000, phase-out rate 34% for singles in 2020). Asset test: check lost entirely when liquid wealth at end of t-1 exceeds DKK 90,000 (2020 value; threshold raised 15% in 2010). For the 2001-2007 reform analysis the 2003 income threshold is applied throughout.
    Registers: IND, SOCP, BEF
    paper · Section I.A; Figure 1 and 2 notes; Supplemental Appendix Figure A.4 notes
  • Treatment and control groups for bunching Sample definition and timing
    Treated: low-income singles aged 65+. Controls: low-income singles aged 60-64 (age-ineligible) and singles aged 65+ with incomes between 150% and 200% of the full phase-out income threshold. Sample restricted to singles; main cross-section pools 2014-2018 (2014-2016 for bank data).
    Registers: BEF, IND
    paper · Section I.C (Sample); Figure 1 notes (panel C)
  • Excess mass below asset-test threshold Wealth, debt and consumption
    Fraction of individuals with liquid wealth between 50% and 100% of the asset test threshold, compared across eligible and control groups and periods; wealth inflated to 2020 values with the average wage index used to index the tax-transfer system so the threshold is the 2020 value for all observations; densities in DKK 5,000 bins.
    Registers: IND
    paper · Table 1 Panel B1 notes; Section I.C (Indexing)
  • Cohort-approach counterfactual Sample definition and timing
    For single income-eligible individuals born 1941-1945, compare the indexed liquid wealth distribution at ages 70-74 (five to nine years into eligibility) with ages 60-64 (before eligibility); only those income-eligible in a given year are included (unbalanced panel).
    Registers: IND, BEF
    paper · Section II (Cohort Approach); Table 1 Panel B2 notes
  • Bank liquid wealth, spending and cash withdrawals Wealth, debt and consumption
    From Danske Bank customer data linked by personal identifier, 2014-2016: bank liquid wealth = value of deposits and listed securities in the bank; monthly spending (excluding cash), cash withdrawals and changes in consumer debt. Bank sample restricted to individuals with at least one spending transaction through the bank in every month of the year (about 20% of the elderly). A robustness measure adds all December cash withdrawals back to end-of-December liquid wealth.
    Registers: Danske Bank customer data
    paper · Section I.C (Bank Data); Section III; Table 1 notes; Supplemental Figure A.4

Dynamic Spending Responses to Wealth Shocks: Evidence from Quasi Lotteries on the Stock Market

Asger Lau Andersen, Niels Johannesen and Adam Sheridan · AER: Insights, 2024 · Individual

Uses lottery-like variation in stock market gains across investors with similar portfolios, observed in granular bank data, to trace spending responses. Responses are immediate and persistent, cumulating to a marginal propensity to consume of 4.4 percent over one year and 16 percent over three, consistent with the permanent income hypothesis with some inattention.

Data
Danske Bank customer records: transaction-level spending, securities portfolios and online logins (2009–2016), Population register (household identifiers, age), Tax register: income and banks' year-end account-level reports, Employment register (employer links), Education register
Key variables
  • Treatment: monthly stock market gains, with quasi-random variation across investors with similar portfolio characteristics
  • Outcome: monthly household consumer spending (card, bill, mobile payments, cash withdrawals)
  • Heterogeneity: liquidity
  • Heterogeneity: financial attention (frequency of account logins)
Period
2009–2016
Sample
around 13.5 million household-month observations comprising 390,000 distinct households Danske Bank households with stock portfolios of at least 100 DKK and at least five spending transactions per month, excluding employee-shareholders and holders of only Danske Bank shares. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Monthly household consumer spending Wealth, debt and consumption
    Monthly sum over household members of debit and credit card purchases, bill payments, in-store mobile payments and cash withdrawals from Danske Bank transaction records. Transactions not associated with consumption (e.g. debt service, tax payments) are excluded using Merchant Category Codes and a proprietary register of bill creditors, as are housing expenditures such as rent.
    Registers: Danske Bank transaction data, Population register (household identifiers)
    Codes: Merchant Category Codes (MCC) used to exclude non-consumption
    working paper · Section 2.1 (Bank data)
  • Stock market gains Wealth, debt and consumption
    Monthly gain G = sum over days in the month and securities of the payout-adjusted daily price change times the number of units held (adjusted for splits, mergers and dividends, so it includes dividends). The portfolio covers direct equity and mutual fund shares in all liquid securities accounts, excluding bonds, deposits and retirement accounts.
    Registers: Danske Bank portfolio and price data
    working paper · Section 2.1, eq. (1)
  • Passive gains (instrument) and portfolio controls Wealth, debt and consumption
    Passive gains are the gains earned in the month by the portfolio held at the beginning of the month, used to instrument actual gains. Controls are full interactions of portfolio size (stock value on the last day of the previous month), risk (SD of portfolio returns over the past 12 months) and expected return (mean monthly return over the past 12 months).
    Registers: Danske Bank portfolio and price data
    working paper · Sections 2.1 and 3
  • Net investment in stocks Wealth, debt and consumption
    Gross purchases net of gross sales, computed residually as the total change in portfolio value minus the change due to capital gains.
    Registers: Danske Bank portfolio data
    working paper · Section 2.1
  • Liquidity Wealth, debt and consumption
    Liquid assets (deposits, stocks and other securities) at the beginning of the month relative to average monthly income; household-months are ranked within month and split into terciles.
    Registers: Danske Bank data, Tax register (income)
    working paper · Section 4.3 (Heterogeneity)
  • Financial attention (logins) Other
    Number of days in a month on which a household member logs into any Danske Bank account (not only brokerage), averaged over months, and split into within-month terciles.
    Registers: Danske Bank online login data
    working paper · Sections 2.1 and 4.3
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Households with Danske Bank securities accounts, 2009-2016, excluding those with portfolios under 100 DKK, those with fewer than five spending transactions in the month, those holding shares in the primary employer of a household member (identified via an employer-ISIN crosswalk to the employment register), and those whose only stock holding is Danske Bank shares (about 390,000 households). A robustness subsample keeps exclusive Danske Bank customers, i.e. households with no accounts at other banks in banks' year-end reports to the tax authority.
    Registers: Danske Bank data, Employment register, Tax register (bank account reports)
    working paper · Sections 2.2 and 2.3
  • Household aggregation and controls Family links, fertility and household
    Households are formed from population-register identifiers linking cohabiting couples and dependants; spending, income and stock variables are summed within household. Controls: age of the oldest member, number of children, and highest education in the household (primary, high school, college, graduate).
    Registers: Population register, Education register
    working paper · Section 2.2; Section 3.3

Household finance, saving and consumption

Does Biology Drive Child Penalties? Evidence from Biological and Adoptive Families

Henrik Kleven, Camille Landais and Jakob Egholt Søgaard · AER: Insights, 2021 · Individual

Compares event-study child penalties for biological and adoptive mothers using almost 40 years of Danish adoption data. Short-run penalties are slightly larger for biological mothers, but long-run penalties are virtually identical, so biology is not a key driver of child-related gender gaps.

Data
Statistics Denmark administrative registers covering the full population 1980–2017, linked with family identifiers, Adoption registry of Statistics Denmark (1988–2009), augmented with foreign adoptions identified via country of origin and Central Person Register immigration records, Earnings and labour-supply registers incl. hours from the ATP mandated pension scheme, Education registers
Key variables
  • Event: arrival of first child (by birth or adoption)
  • Outcome: annual earnings (wages, salaries, self-employment)
  • Outcome: labour force participation, hours worked, wage rates
  • Comparison group: biological vs adoptive families (biological sample reweighted to match adoptive families)
Period
1980–2017
Sample
around 527,000 first births (biological sample) and around 4,600 first arrivals (adoptive sample) Danish parents whose first child arrived by birth or foreign adoption (before age 5) between 1985 and 2007, with both parents known, alive and resident in Denmark from 5 years before to 10 years after. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Foreign adoptee Family links, fertility and household
    Individuals who (1) were born in a non-western country, (2) have two known parents born in a western country, (3) whose parents both had a legal address in Denmark with no emigration record at the child's birth, and (4) have an immigration record into the Central Person Register after the date of birth. This supplements Statistics Denmark's adoption registry (1988-2009 only) and is validated against it.
    Registers: CPR, BEF, Adoption registry (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 2 (Data); Online Appendix Figure A.I
  • Event sample (first child arrival) Sample definition and timing
    Parents whose first child arrives (by birth or adoption) between 1985 and 2007. Both parents must be known, alive and resident in Denmark in every year t = -5 to +10, with no restriction on relationship status. All subsequent children must be of the same type as the first (purely biological or purely adoptive) and adoptees must arrive before age 5. Baseline event time is centred on arrival rather than birth.
    Registers: BEF, CPR
    working paper · Section 2 (Data and Empirical Strategy)
  • Annual earnings Earnings and income
    Annual income from wages, salaries and self-employment.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark income registers
    working paper · Section 2 (Data)
  • Hours worked and wage rate Hours worked
    Hours worked from administrative, third-party-reported data on contributions to the mandated ATP (Arbejdsmarkedets Tillaegspension) pension scheme, which employers pay based on employees' individual hours worked. The wage rate is earnings divided by hours worked.
    Registers: ATP
    working paper · Section 2 (Data)
  • Reweighting of biological families Sample definition and timing
    The biological sample is reweighted by f(xA)/f(xB) to match the adoptive sample's distribution, in bins, of year of first child arrival, years to second child, total number of children, mother's age at first child, and mother's pre-child education and earnings.
    Registers: BEF, UDDA, IND
    working paper · Section 2 (Empirical Strategy)
  • Relative female earnings potential Earnings and income
    Potential earnings predicted from Mincer regressions estimated on men only within each of 140 education fields: log earnings on six education-level dummies, experience (years since graduation), experience squared and year dummies. Families are split by the mother's potential relative to the father's at event time -1 (median or quartiles).
    Registers: UDDA, IND
    working paper · Section 3.2, eq. (3)

The Welfare Magnet Hypothesis: Evidence from an Immigrant Welfare Scheme in Denmark

Ole Agersnap, Amalie Sofie Jensen and Henrik Kleven · AER: Insights, 2020 · Individual

The 2002 cut in benefits for non-EU immigrants, its repeal and its reintroduction provide repeated quasi-experiments on the welfare magnet hypothesis. The cut reduced net immigration by about 5,000 people a year and the repeal reversed it almost exactly, implying a migration elasticity with respect to benefits of 1.3.

Data
Danish administrative registers on the full population 1980–2017 (immigrant status, country of origin, demographics, family links), Residence permit data by permit type (asylum, family, work/study; available from 1997), Central Person Register (CPR) migration records, National statistics bureaus of other Nordic countries and OECD International Migration Database (1991–2017)
Key variables
  • Treatment: maximum monthly welfare benefit for non-EU immigrants (2002 introduction, 2012 repeal, 2015 reintroduction of the immigrant welfare scheme)
  • Outcome: net immigration flow by welfare benefit group, scaled by pre-scheme stock
  • Outcome: gross inflow by residence permit type
  • Comparison: EU vs non-EU immigrants; Denmark vs other Nordic countries
Period
1980–2017
Sample
444 group-year observations (12 welfare benefit groups) Immigrant flows to Denmark aged at least 30 (baseline), collapsed into 12 benefit-eligibility groups by EU/non-EU origin, marital status and number of children. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Treated (non-EU) immigrants Immigration and origin
    First-generation immigrants from outside the EU and the four EFTA countries (Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway, Switzerland), who are subject to the immigrant welfare scheme. 'Inside the EU' is defined by member countries in the pre-scheme year 2001, to avoid confounding from later EU enlargements.
    Registers: CPR, BEF
    Codes: EU membership as of 2001 + EFTA
    working paper · Section 2.1 and footnote 6
  • Net immigration flow Immigration and origin
    Year-to-year change in the stock of first-generation immigrants residing in Denmark according to the Central Person Register, by group, scaled by the group's pre-scheme (2001) immigrant stock and residualized on a linear group-specific trend estimated on 1980-2001.
    Registers: CPR
    working paper · Section 3, footnote 11 and eq. (1)
  • Inflow by residence permit type Immigration and origin
    Immigration flows by type of residence permit granted (asylum, family, work, study; available from 1997). Asylum and family permit holders are treated as potentially welfare-eligible; work/study permit holders as untreated. Asylum applications are used as a supplementary measure.
    Registers: Residence permit data (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 3, Figure 3, footnote 12
  • Welfare benefit groups and maximum monthly benefit Unemployment and benefits
    Twelve groups relevant for benefit eligibility: married vs unmarried, with 0, 1 or 2+ children, from outside vs inside the EU. Each group's maximum monthly cash benefit (converted to 2018 USD at the 31 Dec 2018 DKK-USD rate) is computed for non-employed households at age 40 out of work for three months, with children aged 10 and 8, from STAR (scheme) and the OECD tax-benefit calculator. It covers cash welfare only, excluding UI and in-kind benefits such as housing support; reform years use the yearly average.
    Registers: STAR scheme rules, OECD tax-benefit calculator
    working paper · Section 3 eq. (1), footnote 15; Appendix Figure A.II notes
  • Age restriction (24-Year Rule) Sample definition and timing
    Main within-country specification restricts to immigrants at least 30 years old, to avoid confounding from the 2002 '24-Year Rule' requiring both spouses to be at least 24 for marriage-based residency. The cross-country analysis has no age restriction.
    Registers: CPR, BEF
    working paper · Section 2.1 and footnote 7
  • Synthetic Denmark (cross-country control) Immigration and origin
    Weighted average of Finland (0.468), Norway (0.361) and Sweden (0.171), chosen to match 1991-2001 non-EU/EFTA net immigration flows normalized by each country's 2001 non-EU/EFTA immigrant stock. Immigrants from the former Yugoslavia are dropped throughout to remove the Bosnia shock.
    Registers: Nordic national statistics bureaus, OECD International Migration Database
    working paper · Section 3 (cross-country strategy), footnote 18; Appendix Figure A.IV notes
