Breaking Bad: How Health Shocks Prompt Crime

Steffen Andersen, Elin Colmsjö, Gianpaolo Parise and Kim Peijnenburg · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2026 · Individual

Uses plausibly exogenous timing of cancer diagnoses in Danish registers to show that a health shock raises the probability of committing a crime, both first offences and re-offences, persistently. Patients replace lost legal income with illegal income and face a lower expected cost of punishment because of reduced survival, and welfare programmes that cushion the income loss dampen the effect.

Data
Danish administrative registers on cancer diagnoses (timing of diagnosis), Crime registers (first crimes and re-offenses), Income and welfare program registers
Key variables
  • Treatment: timing of a cancer diagnosis (health shock)
  • Outcome: probability of committing a crime (first crimes and re-offenses)
  • Mechanism: loss of legal income
  • Mechanism: survival probability (expected cost of punishment)
  • Heterogeneity: welfare program coverage
Period
Not stated in the sources checked
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Danish individuals diagnosed with cancer, using variation in the timing of diagnosis. source (abstract)
How variables are defined (7)
  • Crime (conviction for offence committed in year t) Crime
    Indicator equal to one if the individual is convicted of a crime committed in year t, dated by offence year and scaled to 100 in event-study figures. Offence types are classified as economic/non-economic and as property/sexual/violent (the latter following Statistics Denmark's system), covering 4,732,529 crimes 1980-2018.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark crime registers
    Codes: Offence classification in Online Appendix Table I.I
    online appendix · Online Appendix H eq. (15)-(16); Table I.I; Figure I.6 notes
  • Time from offence to apprehension Crime
    Log of one plus the days between when a crime is committed and when the perpetrator is apprehended, using the median time if the person commits multiple crimes in a year; only observations in the offence year are used.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark crime registers
    online appendix · Online Appendix Table I.IX notes
  • Decline in 5-year survival probability due to cancer Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Logit of dying within 5 years, estimated on people aged 18-62 in 1980-2013 (diagnosed plus up to ten exactly matched controls per case) with cancer-type indicators (14 types plus multiple), age polynomial interactions, post-cancer, gender and marriage controls, separately for 1980-1992, 1993-2003 and 2004-2013. The decline is predicted probability minus the counterfactual with no diagnosis. Low survival means an above-median decline within gender (also split by quintile).
    Registers: Cancer register, Death register, Population registers
    online appendix · Online Appendix E
  • Exact-matched controls for survival estimation Sample definition and timing
    For each diagnosed individual, controls who in the year before diagnosis share age, marital status and gender and are in the same income ventile and years-of-education quintile. Up to ten controls with the smallest difference in total income are kept; unmatched observations are dropped.
    Registers: Population, income and education registers
    online appendix · Online Appendix E
  • Treatment/control (Fadlon-Nielsen DiD) Sample definition and timing
    Alternative design comparing individuals diagnosed in a given year with those diagnosed Delta years later (Delta from 3 to 8), with person, year-by-age, in-prison and cancer-recurrence fixed effects. The baseline sample keeps only the 10 years before cancer for pre-diagnosis observations.
    Registers: Cancer register, Crime registers
    online appendix · Online Appendix H; Appendix A
  • Change in municipal welfare generosity (2007 reform) Unemployment and benefits
    Percentage change in labour income plus transfers in post-diagnosis years relative to the five-year pre-diagnosis average, regressed on municipality fixed effects, age fixed effects, a cubic in pre-diagnosis income rank and year effects, separately pre-reform (1987-2006) and post-reform (2007-2018). People diagnosed 2004-2006 are excluded. The generosity change is the difference between post- and pre-reform municipality effects.
    Registers: Income registers (IND), Population register (municipality)
    online appendix · Online Appendix G, eq. (14)
  • Psychological distress Health care use
    Indicator for having received treatment by a psychologist or psychiatrist following the cancer diagnosis, from data on medical visits.
    Registers: Health insurance / medical visits data (name not given)
    online appendix · Online Appendix F; Table I.VI

Healthy at Work? Evidence from a Social Experimental Evaluation of a Firm-Based Wellness Program

Marianne Simonsen and Lars Skipper · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2025 · Individual + firm

A large social experiment across worksites, followed for up to twelve years in the registers, evaluates an employer-sponsored health programme. Employees at treated worksites see fewer GP visits and buy fewer prescription drugs for up to seven years, with no change in hospitalisations, absence or turnover and some spillovers within the family.

Data
Healthy-at-Work randomised experiment records (work-unit assignment, September 2008), Primary care physician consultation records (Statistics Denmark registers), Prescription drug purchase records, Hospital contact / hospitalisation records, Employment, sickness absence and turnover registers, Socio-economic background registers
Key variables
  • Treatment: work-unit randomised to the Healthy-at-Work wellness program
  • Outcome: primary care physician visits
  • Outcome: prescription drug purchases (any, months supply)
  • Outcome: hospitalisations (somatic, psychiatric)
  • Outcome: sickness absence and turnover
  • Spillover outcome: spouses' health care use
Period
Randomisation 2008; follow-up to 2020 (PCP visits and work outcomes), 2019 (prescriptions), 2018 (hospitalisations)
Sample
7,541 workers (3,735 treatment, 3,806 control) in 314 work-units Elderly-care health workers in 314 work-units of 110 employers across 11 Danish municipalities enrolled in the Healthy-at-Work experiment. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Treatment assignment and study population Sample definition and timing
    Work units (314 units of eldercare workers across 110 employers in 11 municipalities) were randomised in September 2008, with 144 units (46%) assigned to Healthy-at-Work. The population is individuals employed at participating work units in the month just before randomisation (7,541 of 7,660 linked to registers). Treatment status is fixed at the initial randomisation month, so post-randomisation moves are ignored and estimates are intention-to-treat.
    Registers: Healthy-at-Work experimental records, Statistics Denmark registers (CPR-linked)
    working paper · Sections 2.1, 3 and 4 (treatment assignment)
  • High-risk group Health care use
    Individuals with an above-median number of primary care physician consultations in the six months before randomisation; the low-risk group is at or below the median.
    Registers: Primary care physician consultation records (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Notes to Tables 2-5
  • Primary care physician consultations Health care use
    Number of consultations (and any consultation) with the primary care physician, from register data on fee-for-service payments to primary care physicians; follow-up to 2020. The paper does not give the register name or speciality codes.
    Registers: Primary care physician fee-for-service records (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 3; Section 4 results; cost-benefit section
  • Prescription drug purchases Health care use
    Any prescription drug purchase and months' supply per year (through 2019), covering drugs for hypertension, cholesterol, diabetes, severe pain relief and depression.
    Registers: Prescription drug purchase records (Statistics Denmark)
    Codes: ATC C9 (hypertension, as printed), C10, A10, N2, N05A, N05B, N05C, N06A
    working paper · Table 3 notes
  • Hospitalisations (psychiatric / somatic) Health care use
    Any hospital contact and number of days admitted to hospital, separately for contacts with a psychiatric diagnosis and with a somatic diagnosis; follow-up to 2018. Diagnosis code lists are not given.
    Registers: Hospital contact records (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Table 4 panels A-D
  • Sickness absence Employment and labour force status
    Any absence and yearly absence rate (share of scheduled hours missed), conditional on hours > 0. Absence data cover about 95% of the sample.
    Registers: Absence register (Statistics Denmark; name not given)
    working paper · Table 5 panels A-B; Table 1 notes
  • Hours, employer continuity and earnings Employment and labour force status
    Any hours worked, hours worked per year, continued employment with the same employer (turnover measure), and earnings per year.
    Registers: Employment registers (Statistics Denmark; names not given)
    working paper · Table 5 panels C-F
  • Spouses (spillover sample) Family links, fertility and household
    Individuals married to or cohabiting with individuals employed at participating work units in the month just prior to randomisation.
    Registers: Population register (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Table 6 notes (spillovers to spouses)

Background Matters, but Not Whether Parents Are Immigrants: Outcomes of Children Born in Denmark

Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen and Alan Manning · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2025 · Individual

Children born in Denmark to immigrant parents have lower earnings, more unemployment, less education, more transfers and more convictions than children of Danish-born parents. Conditional on parental socioeconomic characteristics, however, they do as well or slightly better, so the gaps reflect deprived backgrounds rather than immigrant parentage.

Data
Danish register data linking children to parents (Statistics Denmark, 1980–2017), Income and earnings registers (annual labour income incl. self-employment, transfers), Monthly employment register (hours, hourly wages, from 2008), Education registers (incl. survey-based registration of foreign education of immigrants), Criminal justice registers (convictions, prison sentences, dropped charges / not-guilty verdicts), Occupation codes (ISCO88)
Key variables
  • Group: number of parents born outside Denmark (0, 1, 2; Greenland/Faroe Islands)
  • Outcome: earnings and unemployment at age 30
  • Outcome: public transfers, completed education by age 30
  • Outcome: criminal convictions, prison sentences, dropped charges
  • Controls: parental income, unemployment years, occupation and education during childhood
Period
1980–2017
Sample
396,417 children (Table 1 total); 362,460 with two Danish-born parents, 10,399 with two immigrant parents, 20,908 with one immigrant parent, 2,650 with a parent from Greenland/Faroe Islands All children born in Denmark 1980–1987 with both parents known, followed to age 30. source
How variables are defined (11)
  • Child sample Sample definition and timing
    Everyone born in Denmark 1980-1987 with both parents known in BEF and known parental origin. Observed in the year they turn 30, kept only if fully liable to pay taxes in Denmark (AKM register) and resident in Denmark (BEF). Children missing any outcome or control are dropped (missing parental occupation and education allowed), as are children whose parents were not in the population at birth.
    Registers: BEF, AKM
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1
  • First-generation locals (parental birthplace groups) Immigration and origin
    Groups based on the parents' country of birth in BEF: two parents born in Denmark (reference), two parents born outside Denmark, one parent born in Denmark and one abroad, and at least one parent born in Greenland or the Faroe Islands. Origin regions: Middle East = MENAP+MENAT (incl. some North African countries, Israel, Turkey, Pakistan, Afghanistan); Europe split into Nordics, EU-15 ex. Nordic (incl. UK), EU-13 (incl. Cyprus) and non-EU (incl. Yugoslavia).
    Registers: BEF
    Codes: Country list per region in Online Appendix Table OA.1
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1 and Table OA.1; paper Section II.A fn. 4
  • Low-income origin Immigration and origin
    A first-generation local is 'low income origin' if at least one parent comes from a country whose 1980 GDP per capita (World Bank, supplemented with UN data) was below 4,000 USD at 2022 prices. Parents with only continent observed are assigned by the majority in that continent.
    Registers: BEF, World Bank WDI NY.GDP.PCAP.CD
    Codes: 1980 GDP per capita < 4,000 USD (2022 levels)
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1
  • Annual labour market income (earnings at 30) Earnings and income
    Aggregate labour market income including wage income and profits from self-employment in the year the child turns 30, in 2013 prices (CPI-deflated). Also used as an income rank, IHS and log.
    Registers: IND
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1; paper Section III
  • Hourly wage Earnings and income
    Hourly wage from monthly hours and monthly earnings for employees in the monthly register (available from 2008; self-employed excluded), in 2013 prices. Jobs are excluded if the hourly wage is above 5,000 or below 30 DKK, annual hours are above 3,500 or below 7.4, or total wages are above 10,000,000 or below 1,000 DKK.
    Registers: IDAN
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1
  • Unemployment Unemployment and benefits
    Not working for at least half of the year and not being retired (child at age 30; parents' years of unemployment counted over the child's first 21 years).
    Registers: AKM
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1; paper fn. 5
  • Transfers / public benefits Unemployment and benefits
    Yearly sum of all transfers primarily financed by government institutions, including all unemployment benefits, child benefits, housing support, student benefits and all public pensions, in 2013 prices.
    Registers: IND
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1; paper fn. 6
  • Prison sentence by 30 Crime
    Indicator equal to one if the child has ever been sentenced to prison, suspended or unsuspended, by the end of the year in which they turn 30.
    Registers: KRAF
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1
  • Guilty and dropped/not-guilty charges Crime
    Counts by end of the year turning 30 of guilty charges and of charges dropped without conditions or ending in a not-guilty verdict (following the Danish Institute for Human Rights 2022). Charges dropped with conditions (e.g. payment of a fine) count as guilty. Traffic Law (Faerdselsloven) offences are excluded. The share dropped/not guilty is computed among those with at least one charge.
    Registers: KRSI, KRKO, KRAF
    Codes: Excludes Faerdselsloven (traffic law) charges
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1
  • Parental background controls Family links, fertility and household
    For each parent: aggregate income (2013 prices) over the child's first 21 years; years of unemployment over those years; occupation as 2-digit ISCO88 of the primary job when the child is 21, with extra categories for retired, unemployed and unknown; and years of education when the child is 21 (UDDA, foreign education from the arrival survey, rounded to an integer).
    Registers: IND, AKM, UDDA, BEF
    Codes: ISCO88 2-digit
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1; paper Section II.C
  • Years of education by 30 Education and test scores
    Completed years of education by age 30 from the education register; foreign education of immigrants is registered on arrival via a survey, which causes missingness. Rounded to the nearest integer in regressions.
    Registers: UDDA
    online appendix · Online Appendix OA.1

Do Medical Treatments Work for Work? Evidence from Breast Cancer Patients

N. Meltem Daysal, William N. Evans, Mikkel Hasse Pedersen and Mircea Trandafir · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2025 · Individual

A Danish guideline change shifted which breast cancer patients received radiation therapy, giving quasi-experimental variation in treatment. Radiotherapy reproduces the survival gains found in trials and has economic returns: ten years after diagnosis it raises employment by 37 percent and earnings by 45 percent, undoing most of the post-diagnosis employment drop.

Data
Danish Breast Cancer Cooperative Group (DBCG) clinical Breast Cancer Database, Register of Causes of Death, Register-Based Labour Force Statistics (RAS), Income Statistics Register, DREAM weekly transfer register, Population Register (BEF), Education Register
Key variables
  • Treatment: receipt of radiotherapy
  • Instrument: January 1995 DBCG guideline change expanding radiotherapy eligibility (diagnosed after 1995 x eligible group)
  • Outcome: all-cause and breast cancer mortality
  • Outcome: employment, annual labour earnings, gross income
  • Outcome: sickness and disability benefit receipt
Period
1990–2008 (diagnoses 1990–1998)
Sample
2,823 observations (women) High-risk pre-menopausal women under 55 diagnosed with breast cancer in Denmark 1990–1998 and enrolled in the DBCG89 clinical trial. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Radiotherapy receipt Health care use
    Indicator for receiving adjuvant radiation therapy, from the DBCG clinical Breast Cancer Database, which records treatments administered and dates of diagnosis and major interventions.
    Registers: DBCG clinical Breast Cancer Database
    working paper · Section 3 (Data), Treatment Variable
  • T95 group and instrument Sample definition and timing
    T95 covers high-risk pre-menopausal women (risk classification not due to staging only) who had a mastectomy and were either older than 45 at diagnosis or younger than 45 with fewer than 4 positive lymph nodes. They became eligible for radiotherapy only from January 1995, when eligibility expanded to high-risk pre-menopausal women with at least 1 positive node or a tumour of at least 50mm. The instrument is T95 x diagnosed after January 1995. Comparison groups: always eligible (lumpectomy, or mastectomy under 45 with 4+ positive nodes) and never eligible (high-risk only through stage II/III ductal carcinoma, tumour under 50mm and no positive nodes).
    Registers: DBCG clinical Breast Cancer Database
    working paper · Sections 2.1 and 3 (Analysis Sample), Section 4 eq. (2); Appendix Figure A1
  • Analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    Female breast cancer patients diagnosed 1990-1998 (26,900), restricted to DBCG89 trial enrollees who are pre-menopausal and high-risk, excluding always-eligible patients whose radiotherapy intensity changed, patients missing radiotherapy, tumour size or micro-radical removal information, and women aged 55+ at diagnosis (final N = 2,823).
    Registers: DBCG clinical Breast Cancer Database
    working paper · Section 3 (Analysis Sample); Appendix Table A1
  • All-cause and breast cancer mortality Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicators for death from any cause and from breast cancer, using the exact date and ICD-coded cause of death in the Register of Causes of Death, measured for each year from the date of diagnosis up to 10 years after.
    Registers: Register of Causes of Death
    working paper · Section 3, Outcome Variables
  • Employed / unemployed / out of labour force Employment and labour force status
    Indicators of labour market status as of November from the Register-Based Labour Force Statistics, for each calendar year from diagnosis up to 10 years later. Non-survivors are assigned one for out of the labour force and zero for all other labour market outcomes.
    Registers: RAS
    working paper · Section 3, Outcome Variables
  • Labour earnings and gross income Earnings and income
    Annual labour earnings (zero for those not employed) and gross personal income including government transfers, from the Income Statistics Register, in 2015 DKK, for each calendar year from diagnosis up to 10 years later; zero for non-survivors.
    Registers: Income Statistics Register (IND)
    working paper · Section 3, Outcome Variables, fn. 8
  • Sickness and disability benefit receipt Unemployment and benefits
    From weekly DREAM records (a person is recorded if they receive a benefit for at least one day in the week; amounts not recorded): indicators for any benefit receipt and separately for sickness and disability benefits, plus number of weeks on benefits, cumulated over years 1-5 and 6-10 after diagnosis. Benefit types: sickness benefits, social assistance for uninsured unemployed, reduced-hours benefits due to health limitations (flex), and disability benefits.
    Registers: DREAM
    working paper · Section 3, Outcome Variables
  • Clinical eligibility controls Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicators and all their interactions for mastectomy, age under 45 at diagnosis, number of positive nodes (0, 1-3, 4+), tumour larger than 50mm and micro-radical removal, plus DBCG89 chemotherapy trial-arm indicators.
    Registers: DBCG clinical Breast Cancer Database
    working paper · Section 3, Control Variables

Attendance Boundary Policies and the Limits to Combating School Segregation

Andreas Bjerre-Nielsen and Mikkel Høst Gandil · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2024 · Individual

Uses address-level data on the universe of Danish children and changes in school attendance boundaries over time. Households defy reassignment to schools with lower socioeconomic status, resourceful households most of all, so redrawing boundaries toward highly disadvantaged schools barely changes those schools' composition.

Data
Register data on the universe of Danish children (Statistics Denmark), School attendance boundary data with boundary changes over time
Key variables
  • Treatment: reassignment of a residential area to a different school by an attendance boundary change
  • Outcome: enrolment in (or defiance of) the assigned school
  • Heterogeneity: household socioeconomic resources
  • Socioeconomic composition of the new school's students
Period
Not stated in the sources checked
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Danish children (universe) whose residential areas were affected by changes in school attendance boundaries. source (abstract)
How variables are defined (6)
  • Household SES index Family links, fertility and household
    Population rank (uniform on the unit interval) of the first principal component of four household variables: INC = highest market-income rank among adults in the household; LCE = any adult has completed a long-cycle education; NE = any adult has no education beyond primary school or no registered education; EMP = any adult is employed. With z-scored inputs, SES = 0.62 INC + 0.38 LCE - 0.44 NE + 0.53 EMP (47 percent of variance explained).
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers (income, education, employment)
    online appendix · Online Appendix A (Construction of SES index), equation (1)
  • School SES (average school SES) Education and test scores
    Mean of the household SES index among seven-year-old children enrolled in a school in a given school-year.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers
    online appendix · Online Appendix Figure B.2 notes
  • School non-Western share Immigration and origin
    Share of non-Western children in the school, used as an alternative school characteristic; it is interacted with a household non-Western dummy. The appendix does not state the exact origin coding.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers
    online appendix · Online Appendix Tables B.6-B.7 notes, Figure B.2
  • Compliance / enrolment in assigned school Education and test scores
    Binary indicator equal to one if the child is enrolled at age 7 in the district (attendance-zone) school that corresponds to the child's address at age 5. Control units are artificially assigned to nearby recipient schools. An alternative version uses enrolment in the assigned school at age 7 (see main text Section 5.4).
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers (school enrolment, addresses)
    online appendix · Online Appendix Tables B.2-B.4 notes, Figure B.4 notes
  • Margins of non-compliance (opt-out) Education and test scores
    Three binary outcomes measured at age 7 relative to the address at age 5: enrolled in another public school, enrolled in a private school, or moved out of the district between ages 5 and 7. Aggregate non-compliance is their sum.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers (school enrolment, addresses)
    online appendix · Online Appendix Figure B.3 notes
  • Population density categories Geography and neighbourhood
    Low density: less than 1,000 per sq. km; medium: 1,000-5,000 per sq. km; high: more than 5,000 per sq. km. Used to describe enrolment for all children aged 7 in 2008-2015.
    online appendix · Online Appendix Figure B.1 notes

Refugee Benefit Cuts

Christian Dustmann, Rasmus Landersø and Lars Højsgaard Andersen · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2024 · Individual

A 2002 reform cut welfare benefits for newly arrived refugees by roughly half. Employment rose modestly in the short run and then faded, while disposable income fell sharply. The cut raised crime among adults and harmed children's school enrolment and outcomes.

Data
Danish Immigration Service residence permit records, Income register from tax authority records (earnings, transfers, taxes), Hourly wage and occupation data, Labour market register (employment status), Population register (BEF), Crime registers: police and court records of charges and convictions, Job openings data from Jobindex.dk
Key variables
  • Treatment: residency granted after the July 2002 Start Aid benefit cut
  • Running variable: date residency was granted relative to the reform
  • Outcome: employment, labour earnings, transfer and disposable income
  • Outcome: crime convictions (property crime)
  • Heterogeneity: local labour demand in assignment municipality (low-skill job openings per unemployed)
Period
Residency granted 2001–2003; outcomes up to 10 years after residency
Sample
4,843 individuals Refugees and family-reunified refugees granted residency in Denmark between January 2001 and December 2003 aged 18–55, excluding Afghans, former Yugoslavs and re-migrants. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Refugee sample and reform treatment Immigration and origin
    Refugees and persons family-reunified with refugees granted residency 1 January 2001-31 December 2003 aged 18-55 (Danish Immigration Service permit records), excluding Afghans and former Yugoslavs and those re-migrating within 9 years (4,843 adults). Treatment: residency granted after 1 July 2002 (Start Aid); running variable is the exact residency date relative to the cutoff.
    Registers: Danish Immigration Service residence permit records
    working paper · Section 2.4; Appendix B.2
  • Income measures and public expenditure Earnings and income
    From the income register, from the first year post residency: pre-tax labor earnings (zero if none), pre-tax transfer income, pre-tax gross income (earnings plus transfers) and post-tax disposable income (gross income minus tax payments); public expenditure is transfers minus tax payments. All values in 2010 PPP USD (1 USD = 7.76 DKK).
    Registers: Income register (tax authority records)
    working paper · Section 2.5; Appendix B.2
  • Hourly wage rate Hours worked
    Register hourly wage rate estimated as annual labor earnings divided by annual hours worked.
    Registers: Hourly wage register (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Appendix B.2
  • Labor market status Employment and labour force status
    Three mutually exclusive ILO states from the first full year after residency: employed, unemployed (available to the labour market, participating in integration programs but not working), and not in the labor force (residual). For the 2012 repeal analysis, employment is non-zero labor earnings within the calendar year.
    Registers: Labour market register
    working paper · Section 2.5; Appendix B.2
  • Occupation skill categories Occupation and job hierarchy
    Occupations (ISCO-based) grouped into seven categories: high skill/manager; medium skill/office; sales/services; vocational medium/basic skill; construction/primary sector basic skill; unspecified self-employment; unskilled manual labor. Categories i-vi are 'jobs requiring some skills', vii is unskilled manual labor.
    Registers: Occupation register
    Codes: ISCO (ILO International Standard Classification of Occupations), grouped into 7 categories
    working paper · Appendix B.2
  • Crime convictions by offence date Crime
    Convictions (court rulings or pre-court settlements resulting in a fine, suspended sentence or imprisonment) for offenses against the criminal code, dated by the offence date; 'crime in year 1' is crime committed within 365 days after residency that leads to a conviction. Types include property crime, shoplifting from supermarkets (Central Police register label 'theft from supermarket'), violence, and a residual.
    Registers: Central Police register, Court/conviction records (Ministry of Justice, Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 2.5; Appendix B.2; Table A notes
  • Local labor demand: low/unskilled job openings per unemployed Geography and neighbourhood
    Jobindex.dk postings for low- and unskilled work aggregated from postal code to municipality, divided by the municipal stock of unemployed (population register residence plus labour market register unemployment), averaged over 2002-2003; predicted from 1999-2001 municipal employment conditions (average employment rate, non-Western immigrant and unskilled employment rates, immigrant earnings and interactions), ranked 0-1 and split at the unweighted median.
    Registers: Jobindex.dk, Population register, Labour market register
    working paper · Appendix B.2
  • Non-Western immigrant employment rate (municipality) Geography and neighbourhood
    Fraction of 20-60-year-old non-Western immigrants in the municipality who are employed in 1999-2001 (population register recorded 1 January, merged with labour market register), ranked 0-1 and split at the median.
    Registers: Population register, Labour market register
    working paper · Appendix B.2
  • 2012 repeal event-study cohorts Sample definition and timing
    Adults aged 18-55 granted residency 2008-2014; for year-1 outcomes the treatment group is those granted residency 2012-2014, for year-2 outcomes those granted residency 2011-2013; employment outcomes only for two years after residency.
    Registers: Danish Immigration Service records, Income register
    working paper · Appendix B.2

Unintended Consequences of Welfare Cuts on Children and Adolescents

Christian Dustmann, Rasmus Landersø and Lars Højsgaard Andersen · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2024 · Individual

The 2002 benefit cut for newly arrived refugees reduced family disposable income by 30 percent over five years. Children exposed at preschool or school age obtained lower grades, less education and lower adult earnings, and teenagers at exposure saw large increases in convictions for violent and property crime.

Data
Danish Immigration Service residence permit records, Historical Migrations database, Income register from tax authority records, Register on Completed Education, Daycare register, 9th-grade exam grades, 6th-grade national language test scores and school well-being survey (Ministry of Education), Crime registers: police and court records
Key variables
  • Treatment: parents granted residency after the 2002 Start Aid welfare cut
  • Running variable: residency date relative to the reform
  • Outcome: 9th-grade GPA, 6th-grade language test scores, completed education
  • Outcome: adult earnings and employment
  • Outcome: criminal convictions
Period
Residency granted January 2001–December 2003; income data through 2019
Sample
6,888 individuals (3,406 adults aged 18–45 with children and 3,482 children aged 0–18) Refugee families with children granted residency in Denmark within 18 months of the 2002 reform, excluding Afghans, former Yugoslavs and emigrants. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Refugee family sample and age at exposure Sample definition and timing
    Refugee and family-reunified families with children granted residency January 2001-December 2003 (18 months around the July 2002 Start Aid reform), excluding Afghanistan and former Yugoslavia and emigrants: 3,406 adults aged 18-45 with children and 3,482 children aged 0-18 whose residency date matches at least one parent's. Outcomes are analysed by age at exposure (e.g. 0-7 preschool age, 8-14 school age).
    Registers: Danish Immigration Service residence permit records
    working paper · Section 2.3; Table 2 notes
  • 9th-grade GPA (standardized) Education and test scores
    Average grade across all exams taken in 9th grade, standardized to mean 0 and SD 1 in the total population; population ranks and an indicator for being in the lowest population quartile are also used.
    Registers: Ministry of Education grade register
    working paper · Appendix B.3.3; Table 2 notes
  • 6th-grade Danish language test score Education and test scores
    Compulsory national Danish language test in grade 6 (from 2009), total score a composite of language comprehension, decoding and reading comprehension, standardized following Beuchert and Nandrup (2018).
    Registers: National tests (Ministry of Education)
    working paper · Appendix B.3.3
  • School well-being / self-esteem index Education and test scores
    Average of Likert responses (1-5: very often to never) to three national school well-being survey items (solve problems if trying hard enough; succeed in what you set out to do; how often stomach hurts), standardized to mean 0, SD 1 in the full population; available from 2015 (8th-9th grade responses for children under six at residency).
    Registers: National school well-being survey (Ministry of Education)
    working paper · Section 2.3 footnote 18; Appendix B.3.3
  • Completed education Education and test scores
    Years of completed schooling and highest level from the 2020 Register on Completed Education (status as of 1 October), collapsed into lower secondary (max ten years), academic high school, vocational degrees (vocational high school and short vocational college degrees), and college/university degrees.
    Registers: Register on Completed Education (2020)
    working paper · Appendix B.3.2
  • Daycare/preschool attendance Family links, fertility and household
    Attendance in daycare or preschool in the first year after residency, for children aged 0-5 at residency, from annual daycare register data.
    Registers: Daycare register
    working paper · Appendix B.3.3; Table 2 notes
  • Earnings, disposable income and employment Earnings and income
    Earnings = wage earnings plus self-employment income and business profits, pre-tax; disposable income = pre-tax earnings plus public transfers minus taxes (2020 PPP USD). Employment = positive earnings (Table 2 notes state wage earnings > 0), measured up to 15-16 years after residency (income data to 2019).
    Registers: Income register (tax authority records)
    working paper · Appendix B.2.1; Section 2.3; Table 2 notes
  • Criminal convictions by offence date Crime
    Convictions (court rulings resulting in a fine, suspended sentence or imprisonment) for offenses against the criminal code, labelled by the Central Police register (e.g. 'theft from supermarket'), dated by offence date; e.g. 'crime in year 1' is a crime committed within 365 days after residency. Separated into violent and property crime.
    Registers: Central Police register, Court records
    working paper · Appendix B.3.4

Public Pensions and Private Savings

Esteban García-Miralles and Jonathan M. Leganza · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2024 · Individual

A Danish reform raising the social security eligibility age, studied with a regression discontinuity in administrative data, increased contributions to personal and employer pension accounts when later eligibility kept people working longer. Inertia in previous savings behaviour and firms' default contribution rates are the key mechanisms.

Data
Population registers (date of birth, demographics), Labour-market and income/asset registers (tax-reported bank and stock balances, property values, pension contributions), Monthly earnings register (eIncome / eIndkomst), Voluntary early retirement pension (VERP) contribution and benefit records
Key variables
  • Running variable: birth date relative to 1 January 1954 cutoff
  • Treatment: higher pension eligibility ages from 2011 reform
  • Outcome: contributions to employer-sponsored and personal retirement accounts
  • Outcome: changes in bank and stock account balances and property values
  • Outcome: pre-tax earnings and monthly retirement age
Period
1985–2018 (annual); 2008–2017 (monthly)
Sample
40,042 individuals (analysis sample); 12,020 individuals (RD estimation sample) Non-self-employed Danes born within six months of 1 January 1954 who regularly contributed to the VERP early retirement scheme before the reform. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Reform treatment (birthdate cutoff) Retirement and pensions
    Those born on or after 1 January 1954 learned in 2011 that their early retirement age (ERA), incentivized retirement age and full retirement age (FRA) rose from 60, 62 and 65 to 60.5, 62.5 and 65.5; those born one day earlier were unaffected. Running variable is birth date relative to the cutoff; RD sample is those born within 56 days (8 weeks).
    Registers: Population register (exact date of birth)
    working paper · Sections 2.3 and 4.2
  • VERP participant analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    Danes born within six months of 1 January 1954 who made VERP participatory contributions in at least 70 percent of pre-announcement years 2001-2010, balanced over 2006-2018, excluding the self-employed (defined pre-announcement); 40,042 individuals (12,020 within 56 days for RD).
    Registers: Population registers, VERP contribution records
    working paper · Section 4.2
  • Contributions to employer-sponsored and personal retirement accounts Retirement and pensions
    Annual contribution flows to employer-sponsored DC accounts in levels (winsorized at the 95th percentile by year) and indicators for positive contributions to personal retirement accounts (also indicators for contributions of various sizes).
    Registers: Labour-market/income registers (tax-reported pension contributions)
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Changes in bank, stock and property values Wealth, debt and consumption
    Year-t minus year-(t-1) year-end values of bank account balances and stock market account balances (reported by financial institutions to tax authorities) and of property cash values as assessed by tax authorities; winsorized at the 5th and 95th percentiles each year (also 10th/90th).
    Registers: Tax-reported asset registers
    working paper · Section 4.1, footnote 20
  • Pre-tax earnings Earnings and income
    Income on which individuals pay the 8 percent labor market tax, winsorized by year at the 95th percentile; 2010 prices, 5.56 DKK per USD.
    Registers: Income register
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Monthly retirement age Retirement and pensions
    Absorbing-state measure from the monthly eIncome register (2008-2017): age in the last month with positive earnings before earnings permanently fall to zero.
    Registers: eIncome (eIndkomst) monthly earnings register
    working paper · Section 4.1, footnote 17
  • VERP benefit claiming Retirement and pensions
    Annual Voluntary Early Retirement Pension (VERP) benefit payments.
    Registers: VERP benefit records
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Firm default contribution rate Firm characteristics and productivity
    All individuals over 18 are assigned to workplaces in 2010; individual contribution rate = employer-sponsored plan contributions divided by earnings; the firm default rate is the median contribution rate among the firm's workers in 2010. Predicted contributions = current earnings times the 2010 firm default rate.
    Registers: Linked employer-employee data, Pension contribution records
    working paper · Section 6 (employer defaults), footnote 30

The Gender Application Gap: Do Men and Women Apply for the Same Jobs?

Jonas Fluchtmann, Anita M. Glenny, Nikolaj A. Harmon and Jonas Maibom · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2024 · Individual

Uses administrative records of the job applications made by every Danish unemployment insurance recipient. Men and women apply to very different job types even when observationally similar, and these differences in applications account for more than 70 percent of the residual gender wage gap.

Data
Joblog job application records from the public employment service platform (Jobnet), Unemployment insurance payment records / DREAM event-history data, Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Employment Statistics for Employees, monthly earnings and hours (BFL)
Key variables
  • Outcome: characteristics of applied-for jobs (occupation, industry, AKM firm wage premium, commute, hours)
  • Group: gender
  • Outcome: hourly wage in new job one month after hire
  • Predicted 'typical wage' of applied-for jobs
Period
September 2015–September 2017
Sample
105,879 individuals, 114,375 UI spells, 2,911,585 job applications Danish UI recipients entering new spells from September 2015 to September 2017 lasting at least 8 weeks, with at least 4 registered applications and finding a job within one year. source
How variables are defined (10)
  • New UI spell and analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    UI recipients of Danish nationality entering new UI spells September 2015-September 2017; a new spell is defined when an individual with no UI benefits in the previous 4 weeks is observed with at least 4 consecutive weeks of UI payouts. Restricted to spells lasting at least 8 weeks, with at least 4 registered Joblog applications, ending in a job within one year; applications made in the last four weeks before the job starts are dropped.
    Registers: DREAM, UI payment records, Joblog
    working paper · Section 2.1; Appendix A.1
  • Job applications (Joblog) Unemployment and benefits
    Applications registered by UI recipients in the Jobnet Joblog system during the UI spell; only applications actually sent are kept, using the first version of each entry. Mandatory fields include job title, part-/full-time hours and employer name, zip code and city.
    Registers: Joblog (Jobnet)
    working paper · Section 2; Appendix A.1
  • Occupation of applied-for job Occupation and job hierarchy
    Self-reported job titles matched to Danish ISCO (DISCO) codes: exact 1:1 occurrences of DISCO titles, then manual matches of acronyms, then fuzzy matching (SAS compget, speedist, soundex). 81.5 percent of applications are matched. Occupations are grouped at 1-, 2- and 3-digit levels (9, 55 or 153 groups).
    Registers: Joblog, IDA, BFL
    Codes: DISCO (Danish ISCO) 1-, 2-, 3-digit
    working paper · Section 2.2 fn. 15; Appendix A.2
  • Industry / firm of applied-for job Sector and industry
    Reported firm name and zip code matched to the CVR firm register (exact name+zip, then nearest sub-string matches, then fuzzy matching with Stata matchit and five scoring functions) and linked to firms in BFL; 86.4 percent of applications are matched. Industries follow NACE Rev. 2, grouped into 10, 21 or 38 industries.
    Registers: CVR, BFL
    Codes: NACE Rev. 2 (10/21/38 groupings)
    working paper · Section 2.2 fn. 15; Appendix A.2
  • Firm wage premium (AKM firm effect) Firm characteristics and productivity
    Firm fixed effects from an AKM log-wage regression with worker and firm fixed effects (plus month fixed effects) on a 2008-2015 monthly matched employer-employee panel from BFL, estimated on the connected set (290,108 of 306,900 firms). Effects are demeaned within industry, and the decile rankings are weighted by firm employment in August 2015.
    Registers: BFL
    working paper · Section 2.2; Appendix A.3
  • Hourly wage in new job Earnings and income
    Recorded monthly earnings divided by recorded monthly hours in the new job in the first full month of employment.
    Registers: BFL
    working paper · Section 2.2, footnote 17
  • Typical wage of a job Earnings and income
    Predicted log hourly wage from a Post-LASSO OLS model estimated on new jobs in the sample. Candidate regressors are 1-, 2- and 3-digit industry and occupation dummies, an AKM-availability dummy, the within-industry-demeaned AKM firm effect and all pairwise interactions (10,407 variables); Rigorous LASSO selects 233. Alternative models without firm or without occupation information fill in unmatched applications.
    Registers: BFL, IDA
    working paper · Section 2.2; Appendix A.4
  • Full-time vs part-time applied-for job Hours worked
    Mandatory Joblog field: full-time is 37 hours per week; part-time is less than full-time.
    Registers: Joblog
    working paper · Section 4 (non-wage job characteristics)
  • Implied commute Geography and neighbourhood
    Commuting distance or time from the applicant's municipality of residence to the job's postal code, computed with the Google Maps API (following Harmon 2015).
    Registers: Joblog, BEF/IDA residence
    working paper · Section 4, footnote 33
  • Firm family-friendliness Firm characteristics and productivity
    Firm-level average days of childbirth-related leave per birth, from benefit claims after 2011 where the worker returns to the same pre-birth employer, with leave demeaned by gender. Births are inferred from the start of a new parental-leave spell or a gap of more than half a year between payments. Firms with no employee births form a separate 'no birth' category.
    Registers: SGDP
    working paper · Appendix A.8.1

Credit Supply Shocks and Prices: Evidence from Danish Firms

Tobias Renkin and Gabriel Züllig · AEJ: Macroeconomics, 2024 · Firm

Combines loan-level data on Danish firm–bank relationships with survey producer prices and export unit values. Firms whose banks were exposed to the global financial crisis saw loans fall and rates rise, and they raised output prices by 3 to 5 percent to generate cash, with smaller increases where demand is more elastic.

Data
Bank account-level loan and deposit reports to the Danish Tax Authority (firm part), Bank balance sheets from the Danish FSA (Finanstilsynet) and Danmarks Nationalbank monetary and financial statistics, Producer Price Index survey microdata, Customs export data for export unit values, Firm register, Accounting statistics (regnskabsstatistik) and VAT sales data
Key variables
  • Treatment: firm exposure to banks with high pre-crisis loan-to-deposit ratios
  • Outcome: producer prices (PPI) and export unit values
  • Intermediate outcome: firm bank loans and average interest rate
  • Heterogeneity: product demand elasticity
Period
2005–2010
Sample
1,753 firms (213 linked to the PPI survey, 1,176 to export data) Danish manufacturing firms active 2005–2010 with at least ten employees and an active bank lending relationship in 2007. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Firm exposure to wholesale-funded banks Firm characteristics and productivity
    Share of a firm's total 2007 bank loans held with wholesale-funded banks. Banks are classified as wholesale-funded if their 2007 loan-to-deposit ratio (loans on the asset side over deposits on the liability side) exceeds the 2007 loans-weighted median of 1.37, and deposit-funded otherwise (following Jensen and Johannesen 2017).
    Registers: URTEVIRK, Finanstilsynet bank balance sheets, Danmarks Nationalbank MFI balance sheet statistics
    paper · Section II (Identification Strategy), equation (3)
  • Firm bank loans Wealth, debt and consumption
    Account balance as of December 31 summed over all of a firm's bank loan relationships reported by banks to the Danish Tax Authority, including regular and syndicated loans, credit card debt and variable-utilisation accounts (revolving loans, overdrafts). Mortgages are not included because they are provided by specialised mortgage institutions outside the banking system.
    Registers: URTEVIRK
    paper · Section I.A (Loan Data)
  • Average interest rate on bank loans Wealth, debt and consumption
    Firm-level average interest rate equal to total interest payments over the year divided by the mean of end-of-year loan balances in t-1 and t. Contractual rates and maturity are not used because most banks do not report them systematically; the measure fails to capture rates above 10 percent on short-run loans.
    Registers: URTEVIRK
    paper · Section I.A, equation (1)
  • Producer prices (PPI microdata) Firm characteristics and productivity
    Monthly transaction prices (DKK, incl. temporary sales and discounts) reported by firms in the PPI survey for products classified by eight-digit HS codes; baseline uses domestic prices only. Prices are quality-adjusted, monthly price changes winsorized at +/-1 log points, and the data converted to quarterly frequency by keeping the price in the first month of each quarter.
    Registers: Producer Price Index survey microdata (Statistics Denmark)
    Codes: 8-digit Harmonized System product codes
    paper · Section I.B (Price Data)
  • Export unit values Trade and offshoring
    Yearly unit value per firm and eight-digit CN product: export sales divided by quantity, after summing monthly customs data over destination countries and months. Unit value indices are then built per firm and two-digit CN category from consistent combinations of eight-digit CN codes (procedure in online Appendix A).
    Registers: UHDM
    Codes: Combined Nomenclature (CN) 8-digit, aggregated to CN2
    paper · Section I.B, equation (2)
  • Firm sample Sample definition and timing
    Active manufacturing firms in the 2007 firm register, excluding firms with fewer than ten employees or less than 1,000,000 DKK in sales, requiring continuous activity 2005-2010, and excluding firms with bank loans below 1 percent of sales in 2007 or below 100,000 DKK in 2006 or 2007 (1,753 firms; 213 linked to PPI, 1,176 to export data).
    Registers: FIRM, FIRE, FIKS, URTEVIRK
    paper · Section I.D (Sample); restrictions in online Appendix Table A.1
  • Product demand elasticity Other
    Price elasticity of demand from Broda and Weinstein (2006) estimated on US import data, at two product levels (958 and 13,972 categories), standardized by subtracting the median across goods and dividing by the standard deviation.
    Registers: Broda-Weinstein (2006) elasticities (external)
    paper · Section on heterogeneity, Table 3 discussion
  • Strategic complementarity Trade and offshoring
    Good-level responsiveness of prices to competitors' prices, estimated from exchange-rate pass-through into domestic-currency export unit values before the Great Recession at the two-digit CN level, following Amiti, Itskhoki and Konings (2014); details in online Appendix C.3.
    Registers: UHDM
    Codes: CN2
    paper · Section on heterogeneity, Table 3 discussion

How Do Households Respond to Job Loss? Lessons from Multiple High-Frequency Datasets

Asger Lau Andersen, Amalie Sofie Jensen, Niels Johannesen, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen and Adam Sheridan · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2023 · Individual

Combines bank transaction data with government registers to measure every margin of self-insurance after job loss. Over two years households cut spending by 30 percent of the income loss and cover about half of it by running down liquid balances; spousal labour supply, private transfers, home equity extraction and consumer credit contribute less.

Data
Danske Bank customer transaction and account records (spending, income inflows, balances, loans), Monthly payroll and income transfer records (BFL/eIndkomst) from the Danish Tax Agency, Population register (BEF) household structure and spouse links, End-of-year account-level bank loan and deposit records from the Danish Tax Agency, Loan-level mortgage data from mortgage banks (via Statistics Denmark), Mass layoff notifications to the Danish Agency for Labour Market and Recruitment, Annual income and wealth, education, home ownership and occupation registers
Key variables
  • Treatment: job loss event (main employer wage payments cease, followed by unemployment benefits)
  • Outcome: household spending (card, mobile, bills, ATM withdrawals)
  • Outcome: net saving in liquid assets, non-mortgage debt repayment, mortgage refinancing and equity extraction
  • Outcome: spousal labour income, private transfers, government transfers
  • Design: monthly event study from 18 months before to 24 months after job loss
  • Subsample: involuntary job loss from mass layoffs
Period
January 2009–December 2016 (job losses July 2010–December 2015)
Sample
10,002 individuals (baseline sample of active bank customers); gross sample of 66,844 job losers Danish individuals born 1950–1979 who lost their job between July 2010 and December 2015 after at least 18 months of stable earnings, in stable households that are active customers of Danske Bank. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Job loss event Unemployment and benefits
    Month in which wage payments from the individual's main employer cease and total gross wage income drops below DKr 1,000; the individual must receive unemployment benefits or social insurance in months -1 to 3 and no early retirement, sickness or parental leave benefits then, must have had gross wage income of at least DKr 10,000 for at least 18 consecutive months before, and must not return to the same employer within three months.
    Registers: Monthly payroll and income transfer records (Danish Tax Agency, via Statistics Denmark)
    paper · Section III
  • Analysis sample and event window Sample definition and timing
    Individuals born 1950-1979 with a job loss event July 2010-December 2015, observed from 18 months before to 24 months after; stable households (single throughout or same spouse), excluding those where the individual or spouse bought/sold real estate or worked at the same firm as the spouse before the job loss; restricted to active bank customers with at least five spending outflows in every month (both partners for couples).
    Registers: Payroll records, BEF, Danske Bank transaction data
    paper · Section III
  • Mass layoff subsample Unemployment and benefits
    Job losers whose employer reported a planned mass layoff to the Ministry of Employment (Danish Agency for Labour Market and Recruitment) within months -7 to -1 relative to the observed layoff month; reporting is required for firms with more than 20 employees, with 'large scale' ranging from 10 workers (firms with 20-100 employees) to 30 workers (more than 300 employees). Linked via firm ID to payroll data; 1,156 individuals.
    Registers: Mass layoff notifications (Danish Agency for Labour Market and Recruitment), Payroll records
    working paper · Appendix E
  • Household disposable income (bank inflows) and components Earnings and income
    Sum of monthly external inflows to accounts of the affected person and spouse: direct deposits, person-to-person transfers from outside the household, and cash deposits. Split into salary (inflows from a bank registration number mapped to the person's employer via payroll data, or salary type codes; joint-account salary attributed to spouse if from spouse's employer), government transfers (registration number linked to a paying agency, or the central-government number for non-central-government workers), and a residual of private transfers and other inflows.
    Registers: Danske Bank transaction data, Monthly payroll and transfer records
    working paper · Appendices A and C
  • Total spending (transaction based) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Sum of outgoing card (incl. in-store mobile), bill payments and ATM cash withdrawals from household accounts, excluding tax and debt payments and bank fees (identified by MCC); joint-account outflows split evenly between owners and summed over the affected person and spouse.
    Registers: Danske Bank transaction data
    working paper · Appendices A and B
  • Spending subcategories (MCC-based) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Utilities, restaurants/bars and groceries defined as subsets of total spending by recipient Merchant Category Code or bill-payment label.
    Registers: Danske Bank transaction data
    Codes: Utilities: MCC 4900, 4812, 4814, 4821, 4899 or bill labels utilities/elec/gas/water/heating/internet/cable TV/telephone/TV license; Restaurants and bars: MCC 5813, 5462, 5811, 5812, 5814; Groceries: MCC 5411, 5422, 5441, 5499, 5921 or bill label groceries
    working paper · Appendix A
  • Net saving in liquid assets Wealth, debt and consumption
    Change in end-of-month deposit balances at the bank owned by the affected person or spouse plus outflows minus inflows from transactions with type code 'securities trade' (net investment, excluding capital gains). Liquid assets are deposits plus financial securities.
    Registers: Danske Bank account and transaction data
    Codes: transaction type code 'securities trade'
    working paper · Appendix A; Section II
  • Net repayments on non-mortgage loans Wealth, debt and consumption
    Change in end-of-month balances on loan accounts (amounts owed coded negative) owned by the affected person or spouse; positive values are net repayment.
    Registers: Danske Bank account data
    working paper · Appendix A
  • Mortgage equity extraction and loan types (monthly) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Monthly mortgage portfolios built from end-of-year loan-level snapshots 2009-2015 using loan IDs and origination dates (terminated loans assumed to end at the new loan's origination). Equity extraction dummy = 1 if the household replaced an existing loan with a new one with principal exceeding (B + 20,000)/0.95, B being the outstanding balance in DKK; also dummies for having an interest-only and an adjustable-rate loan, and average monthly mortgage payments.
    Registers: Loan-level mortgage data from mortgage banks (via Statistics Denmark), Tax return mortgage interest
    working paper · Appendix D and Figure A8 notes

Household finance, saving and consumption Labour markets, wages and sorting

Consumption Heterogeneity: Micro Drivers and Macro Implications

Edmund Crawley and Andreas Kuchler · AEJ: Macroeconomics, 2023 · Individual

Estimates marginal propensities to consume across Danish households with a method that corrects biases in earlier register-based estimates. Liquid wealth is the dominant predictor of MPCs, and the estimated heterogeneity is used to quantify monetary policy transmission in Denmark and the United States.

Data
Tax-authority income records (household after-tax and transfer income), Tax-reported wealth data: bank deposits, loans, bond and stock holdings, mortgages (year-end balances), Private pension contribution records, Civil Registration System (CPR) family/household links, Mortgage reset data (amount resetting over the following year)
Key variables
  • Outcome: imputed household expenditure (income minus pension contributions minus change in non-housing net worth)
  • Shock: unexpected (residual) change in after-tax household income of the head
  • Heterogeneity: liquid wealth (bank deposits) quintiles
  • Heterogeneity: Unhedged Interest Rate Exposure (URE) and Net Nominal Position (NNP)
Period
2003–2015
Sample
7.7 million observations from 2004 to 2015 Danish households headed by an individual aged 30–55 in 2008, excluding business owners, households with housing transactions, and top/bottom 1% of income and income changes. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Household definition and head Family links, fertility and household
    Households have one or two adults; two cohabiting adults are one household if (i) married or in a registered partnership, (ii) have at least one common child in the Civil Registration System, or (iii) are of opposite sex, age difference of 15 years or less, not closely related and with no other adults present. Children under 25, never married and childless belong to the parents' family. The head is the highest earner over the 13-year sample period.
    Registers: Civil Registration System (CPR) family links
    working paper · Section 4.1, footnotes 26-27
  • Imputed household expenditure Wealth, debt and consumption
    C = Y - P - dNW: after-tax income (all labor and capital income, excluding capital gains) minus contributions to privately administered pension schemes minus the change in non-pension, non-housing net worth between 31 December of t-1 and t. Households in housing-transaction years and with more than trivial business income are excluded; equity holders are assumed to hold a diversified stock index; household-years with negative imputed expenditure (about 3 percent) are discarded.
    Registers: Tax-authority income records, Tax-reported wealth data, Private pension contribution records
    working paper · Section 4.2
  • Unexpected income change Earnings and income
    After dropping the top and bottom 1 percent of household after-tax-and-transfer income, income is normalized by average household income over the period and regressed on dummies for age, year, highest education, marital status, homeowner status and number of children plus age interactions with education, marital and homeowner status; the year-to-year change in the residual is the unexpected income change, trimming the top and bottom 1 percent. Expenditure residuals are constructed the same way.
    Registers: Tax-authority income records, Education register, Population register
    working paper · Sections 4.1 and 4.2
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Households headed by an individual aged 30-55 in 2008, observed 2004-2015 (registry data 2003-2015), excluding business owners and requiring no housing transaction within a five-year period; 7.7 million observations.
    Registers: Tax-authority income and wealth records, Population register
    working paper · Section 4.3
  • Liquid wealth quintiles Wealth, debt and consumption
    Liquid wealth is defined as bank deposits; households are divided into quintiles by mean household liquid wealth (and separately net wealth) over the entire sample period.
    Registers: Tax-reported wealth data
    working paper · Section 5, footnote 31
  • Unhedged Interest Rate Exposure (URE) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Difference between all maturing assets (including income) and maturing liabilities (including planned consumption), where maturing means due for an interest rate reset. All bank deposits and loans are treated as variable rate resetting instantly; for mortgages the amount resetting over the following year is observed and the new rate applies for half the year; all other assets and liabilities are assumed to have a five-year maturity. Scaled by mean expenditure.
    Registers: Tax-reported wealth data, Mortgage reset data
    working paper · Section 6.1, footnotes 36-38
  • Net Nominal Position (NNP) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Net value of a household's directly held nominal assets and liabilities, including bank deposits and loans, bond holdings and mortgages.
    Registers: Tax-reported wealth data
    working paper · Section 6.1
  • Nondurable consumption proxy Wealth, debt and consumption
    Imputed expenditure adjusted using registry data on household car purchases to proxy nondurable consumption (details in online appendix G, not in this file).
    Registers: Car purchase registry data

The Effects of DNA Databases on the Deterrence and Detection of Offenders

Anne Sofie Tegner Anker, Jennifer L. Doleac and Rasmus Landersø · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2021 · Individual

A large expansion of Denmark's DNA database cut recidivism within a year by up to 42 percent and raised the chance that re-offenders are caught, implying that a 1 percent higher detection probability lowers crime by more than 2 percent. Registered offenders also became more likely to work, study and live in stable families.

Data
Central Charge Register (crime date, charge date, crime type), Danish Central DNA Database person-specific section (DNA registration records), Conviction records (crime registers), Full-population registers on demographics, labour market and family links
Key variables
  • Treatment: offender registered in the DNA database
  • Instrument: charged after the May 2005 DNA database expansion (donut RD, excluding June–September 2005)
  • Running variable: months before May / after October 2005
  • Outcome: convictions within one, two and three years after the charge (all crime and by type)
  • Detection vs. deterrence: split by charges filed more vs. less than three weeks after the crime
  • Secondary outcomes: employment, education, marriage
Period
Charges June 2003–September 2007 (excluding June–September 2005), with follow-up outcomes
Sample
38,674 individuals with 66,911 charge observations Danish-resident males aged 18–30 charged with Penal Code or Weapons Act offenses who had at most 10 previous charges. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • DNA registration (treatment) Crime
    Indicator that the charged offender appears in the person-specific section of the Central DNA Database, merged to the charge register via personal identification and record numbers.
    Registers: Central DNA Database (person-specific section), Charge register
    working paper · Section 5.1
  • Post-reform charge instrument and donut window Sample definition and timing
    Indicator for being charged after the 24 May 2005 DNA database expansion; charges June-September 2005 are excluded because of lagged police implementation, with a 24-month window on each side (June 2003-May 2005 control, October 2005-September 2007 treatment) chosen by cross-validation; running variable is months before/after the excluded window.
    Registers: Charge register
    working paper · Sections 2.1 and 5.1, footnote 13
  • Charge-level analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    Charges for offenses against the Penal Code or Weapons Act (excluding traffic offenses, small-scale drug possession, Health Code and Tax Law violations) against Danish-resident males aged 18-30 at the charge with at most 10 previous charges; one charge per person per day; unit of observation is the charge.
    Registers: Charge register, Population register
    working paper · Section 5.1, footnotes 12 and 14
  • Recidivism: subsequent convictions Crime
    Convictions for crimes committed after the sample charge, counted from the day after the charge, within one, two and three years; coded as a binary (at least one conviction) and as a count top-coded at 10 convictions per follow-up year. Measured for all crime and separately for violence, property, sexual, other penal (incl. serious drug offenses) and Weapons Act violations.
    Registers: Conviction register, Charge register
    working paper · Section 5.2, footnote 16
  • Fast vs. slow charges (deterrence vs. detection) Crime
    Convictions split by whether the charge occurred three weeks or less after the crime date (fast: can only reflect deterrence, since DNA processing takes about four weeks) or more than three weeks after (slow: deterrence plus detection).
    Registers: Charge register, Conviction register
    working paper · Section 5.2
  • Crime categories Crime
    Penal Code subcategories mapped to Sexual (incest, rape, pedophilia, voyeurism/flashing, other sexual), Violence (violence against public servant, disturbance of public peace, murder/manslaughter incl. attempted, simple and major violence, threats, other assaults), Property (fraud, arson, theft, burglary, robbery, vandalism, other), Other (penal) (crimes against/as public servant, drug smuggling or sales, obstruction of justice, restraining orders, other); traffic and Drug Act possession excluded; Weapons Act separate.
    Registers: Charge register, Conviction register
    working paper · Table A-2
  • Labor market attachment Employment and labour force status
    Time during the first four years after the initial charge spent in each of three mutually exclusive states: employed (has a job), in education or training, and unemployed.
    Registers: Labour market register (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 5.2
  • Family stability outcomes Family links, fertility and household
    From timing of changes in marital status and home addresses: married; remaining with the same partner (marriage or cohabitation) held before the initial charge; and living with one's child and the child's mother, for children born before the initial charge (one observation per child and charge).
    Registers: Population register (BEF)
    working paper · Section 5.2, footnote 18

Family Labor Supply Responses to Severe Health Shocks: Evidence from Danish Administrative Records

Itzik Fadlon and Torben Heien Nielsen · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2021 · Individual

Compares households hit by a fatal versus a non-fatal health shock at the same time. After a spouse's death the surviving spouse raises labour supply to self-insure, while after a non-fatal shock spouses reduce labour supply to care for the patient. Children of the household adjust less.

Data
Cause of Death Registry, National Patient Registry (LPR) hospitalisation records with ICD diagnoses, Income and transfer registers (earnings, government transfers, pension and annuity payouts, capital income), 1980–2011, Third-party reported liquid wealth balances, 1984–2011, Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), incl. ATP-based full-/part-time employment, Household linkages of spouses and cohabiting partners (population registers)
Key variables
  • Treatment: spousal death (fatal health shock) or first non-fatal heart attack/stroke
  • Control group: households experiencing the same shock a few years later
  • Outcome: surviving/healthy spouse's labour force participation and earnings
  • Outcome: household income from transfers, pensions and insurance; liquid wealth
  • Heterogeneity: household liquidity, income loss, age
Period
1980–2011 (shocks 1985–2011)
Sample
310,720 treated and 409,190 control households (fatal shocks); 37,437 treated and 54,887 control households (non-fatal heart attacks and strokes) Danish married and cohabiting couples with both spouses aged 45–80 in the year of the (actual or placebo) shock; the non-fatal shock sample is limited to spouses under 60 surviving at least three years. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Fatal health shock (spousal death) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Death of one spouse in a married or cohabiting couple, identified from death dates in the Cause of Death Registry, for shocks occurring 1985-2011 with both spouses aged 45-80 in the (actual or placebo) shock year; a sub-sample uses spouses who had a first heart attack or stroke and died within the same calendar year.
    Registers: Cause of Death Registry, National Patient Registry, Population register household linkages
    working paper · Sections 3.2 and 4.2
  • Non-fatal severe health shock Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    First-time heart attack or stroke (from ICD-coded hospitalization records in the National Patient Registry) of one spouse, who survives at least three years; sample restricted to households with both spouses under 60. Specific ICD codes are not listed in this version.
    Registers: National Patient Registry (LPR)
    working paper · Sections 3.2 and 4.2
  • Control group: same shock five years later Sample definition and timing
    Each treatment group of households shocked in year tau is matched to households from the same cohorts that experience the same shock in year tau + 5 (Delta = 5), who are assigned a placebo shock at t = 0 with t = year - tau; effects are identified up to four years after the shock via difference-in-differences relative to a baseline period (t = -2 in summary statistics).
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Labor force participation Employment and labour force status
    Indicator for having any positive level of annual earnings.
    Registers: Income registers
    working paper · Section 5
  • Full-time and part-time employment (ATP-based) Hours worked
    From IDA, constructed from employee ATP pension contributions (available for individuals under 60): full-time means working at least 30 hours per week all 12 months of the calendar year (full-time full-year); part-time means working at some point in the year but fewer than 30 hours per week or fewer than 12 months.
    Registers: IDA, ATP contributions
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Household income from all sources Earnings and income
    Sum of earnings, government transfers from any program (old-age pensions, disability insurance, welfare, housing assistance, unemployment benefits), payouts from retirement savings accounts, annuity payouts from insurance companies, and capital income, 1980-2011, deflated to 2000 DKK.
    Registers: Income and transfer registers
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Liquid wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Third-party reported liquid wealth balances measured annually on 31 December, 1984-2011, including bank-account balances and lump-sum transfers from insurance companies; used in robustness checks to account for life insurance payouts.
    Registers: Tax-reported wealth data
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Potential income loss from spousal death Earnings and income
    Household income from any source in t = 1 holding the surviving spouse's earnings and social benefits (labor income, Social DI and Social Security) at their t = -1 level, divided by household income in t = -1, then normalized for treated households by the corresponding control-group mean.
    Registers: Income and transfer registers
    working paper · Section 5.2, footnote 22
  • Municipal survivors-benefit instrument Unemployment and benefits
    For each municipality and year, the leave-one-out mean of survivors benefits received through Social Disability Insurance by non-working surviving spouses, assigned to a widow according to her municipality of residence before the shock.
    Registers: Transfer registers, Population register (municipality)
    working paper · Section 5.2, eq. (5)

Do People Respond to the Mortgage Interest Deduction? Quasi-Experimental Evidence from Denmark

Jonathan Gruber, Amalie Sofie Jensen and Henrik Kleven · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2021 · Individual

A major reform that scaled back the mortgage interest deduction for middle- and high-income households had a precisely estimated zero effect on home ownership. It did reduce the size and price of houses bought, lowered household indebtedness and pushed down equilibrium house prices.

Data
Income tax records (incomes, taxes, deductible interest expenses), Housing register (homeownership, property characteristics, home size), Tax authority property value appraisals (for imputed rent and wealth tax), Population registers with spouse/cohabitant and child links
Key variables
  • Policy: 1987 tax reform reducing the value of the mortgage interest deduction for top-rate taxpayers
  • Treatment: top-bracket taxpayers vs. below-top/middle/bottom groups (difference-in-differences)
  • Outcome: homeownership
  • Outcome: home size (square metres) and home value
  • Outcome: total deductible interest expenses (debt)
  • Elasticity with respect to the net-of-tax rate (1−τ)
Period
1980–2011 (main panel 1980–1996)
Sample
about 40 million individual-year observations; 34,440,869 observations in the main homeownership regression (below-top controls) Semi-balanced panel of Danish individuals aged 20–80 observed in every year 1980–1996, excluding children living with parents. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Homeownership (household-based) Wealth, debt and consumption
    From the housing register's owner-occupancy indicator matched via home address: children living with parents are dropped; everyone in a home not occupied by the owner is a renter; in owner-occupied homes a single resident or a married/cohabiting couple are owners. For other multi-person addresses, a person living there in 1987 who owns property in the 1987+ tax files (and his/her spouse) is the owner; remaining residents are renters; unassignable individuals are dropped.
    Registers: Housing register, Income tax files (from 1987), Population register spouse links
    working paper · Section 3.2, Figure A.I
  • Home size Wealth, debt and consumption
    Area of the house in square metres used for habitation, from the housing register.
    Registers: Housing register
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Home value Wealth, debt and consumption
    Appraisal of the property by the Danish Tax Authorities made for assessing imputed rental income and taxable wealth.
    Registers: Tax authority property appraisals
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Total deductible interest expenses Wealth, debt and consumption
    Interest paid on mortgage debt, consumer debt and other loans (all deductible), for homeowners; mortgage interest cannot be separated over the whole period.
    Registers: Income tax records
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Household tax bracket / treatment status Taxes and tax rates
    A taxpayer is assigned to the top bracket if she or her spouse is in the top bracket, to the middle bracket if either is in the middle and neither in the top, and to the bottom bracket if both are in the bottom. Treated are those in the top bracket in every year 1984-1986; controls are in the middle or bottom bracket in every year 1984-1986.
    Registers: Income tax records, Population register spouse links
    working paper · Section 4
  • Net-of-tax interest rate Taxes and tax rates
    (1 - tau) R, where tau is the marginal tax rate on negative capital income; the 1987 reform set this rate to 51 percent in all brackets (pre-reform top about 73, middle 62, bottom 48 percent in the average municipality), raising the net-of-tax rate by 81 percent for the top group, 29 percent for the middle and reducing it 6 percent for the bottom.
    working paper · Section 3.1, Figure 1
  • Semi-balanced panel 1980-1996 Sample definition and timing
    Individuals observed in every year 1980-1996 while aged 20-80 (entering at 20, leaving after 80), giving 7 pre-reform and 10 post-reform years; about 40 million person-years.
    Registers: Population register
    working paper · Sections 3.2 and 4
