What Is the Added Value of Preschool for Poor Children? Long-Term and Intergenerational Impacts and Interactions with an Infant Health Intervention

Maya Rossin-Slater and Miriam Wüst · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2020 · Individual

Access to preschool targeted at low-income children between 1933 and 1960 raised adult education, earnings and survival past 65, and the children of exposed women obtained more education by 25. Exposure to the nurse home visiting programme in infancy reduces preschool's added value, so the two programmes are partial substitutes.

Data
Archival data on all approved Danish preschools 1933–1960 (establishment and approval year, slots), Nurse Home Visiting program implementation dates by municipality, Statistical Commune Data Archive (elections and censuses) for municipality controls, Municipal live births and infant deaths, DigDag historical administrative geography (parish-municipality mapping), Administrative population register data 1980–2012 (education, earnings, survival, hospital admissions, diagnoses), Mother-child links (Danish Civil Registration System)
Key variables
  • Treatment: approved preschool in municipality of birth at age 3
  • Interaction: exposure to the infant Nurse Home Visiting program
  • Outcome: education and earnings around age 50
  • Outcome: survival past age 65, hospital admissions, diagnoses
  • Intergenerational outcome: oldest child's educational attainment by age 25
  • Controls: municipality and birth-year fixed effects, county-by-year trends, municipality characteristics
Period
Cohorts born 1930–1957; outcomes 1980–2012; children born 1955–1987
Sample
1,640,214 observations (Danish-born with valid parish codes); 880,708 observations in municipalities with an approved preschool by 1960, collapsed to 3,862 municipality × birth-year cells Danish-born individuals born 1930–1957 with a valid parish of birth who are observed after 1980, focusing on the 138 municipalities that ever had an approved preschool. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Preschool exposure at age 3 Sample definition and timing
    Indicator equal to one for birth cohorts that had at least one government-approved preschool in their municipality of birth at age 3, using the year of government approval from archival lists of all approved preschools (Skjernbaek, nine editions 1921-1960); municipality of birth is assumed to be the early-childhood municipality.
    Registers: Archival preschool lists (Skjernbaek), Parish of birth (population register), DigDag
    working paper · Sections 2 (Data on preschools) and 3, eq. (1)
  • Nurse Home Visiting (NHV) exposure in birth year Sample definition and timing
    Indicator for an approved NHV program in the municipality in the birth year, based on DNBH approval dates 1937-1949 from the Danish National Archives (approval required sufficient nurse coverage). For 28 municipalities without an NHV program by 1949, treatment year is assigned from Skjernbaek lists (year of previous publication if listed, otherwise never treated).
    Registers: Danish National Board of Health (DNBH) archival records, Skjernbaek lists
    working paper · Section 2 (NHV data)
  • Municipality of birth from parish of birth Geography and neighbourhood
    Births are registered at parish level; parish of birth is mapped to 1930-1960 municipalities using DigDag. Individuals with invalid or undocumented parish codes, post-1970 municipality coding, registration by religious minorities, or hospital births are dropped (about 90 percent of Danish-born have a valid parish of birth).
    Registers: Population register (parish of birth), DigDag
    working paper · Section 2, Sample construction and selection, footnote 15
  • Years of schooling and more than compulsory schooling at age 50 Education and test scores
    Years of schooling at age 50 adding up schooling across educational programs, and an indicator for having more than nine years of compulsory schooling at age 50.
    Registers: Education register (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Log average wage income ages 30-60 Earnings and income
    Natural log of average wage income (in 2012 prices) over all ages between 30 and 60 observable in the 1980-2012 register data.
    Registers: Income register (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Human capital index Education and test scores
    Equally weighted average of years of schooling at 50, more-than-compulsory indicator and log average wage income 30-60, each standardized by the mean and SD of the control group (municipality-by-cohort cells without an approved preschool by age 3 in the 138 ever-implementing municipalities).
    Registers: Education register, Income register
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Survival beyond age 65 Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicator for surviving past age 65, with data left-censored so that all individuals enter the risk period at age 50 (outcome data start in 1980). Supplementary outcomes include hospital care utilization (e.g. nights in hospital ages 55-64) and diagnoses of cardiovascular disease, heart disease, diabetes and cancer; specific diagnosis codes are not given in the main text.
    Registers: Population/death registers, National Patient Register
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Second-generation education by age 25 Family links, fertility and household
    For women born 1935-1957 linked to their oldest child (child cohorts 1955-1987), the child's completed years of schooling, an indicator for more than compulsory education, and an indicator for graduating gymnasium, all by age 25.
    Registers: Civil Registration System mother-child links, Education register

Liquidity Constraint Tightness and Consumer Responses to Fiscal Stimulus Policy

Claus Thustrup Kreiner, David Dreyer Lassen and Søren Leth-Petersen · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2019 · Individual

The 2009 payout of Special Pension savings worked as a fiscal stimulus. Measuring constraint tightness by the marginal interest rate households pay, the spending response is highest for households facing high marginal rates and otherwise small, which supports targeting stimulus at the credit constrained.

Data
Telephone survey of SP account holders on spending of the 2009 SP payout (Epinion, January 2010), ATP register of Special Pension (SP) savings accounts (balances on 1 May 2009), Income tax register with incomes, assets and liabilities, 1998–2009, Account-level deposit and loan records with interest payments from the Danish Tax Agency (SKAT), 2007–2009, Demographic registers (Statistics Denmark)
Key variables
  • Outcome: self-reported share of the SP payout spent
  • Key regressor: household marginal interest rate in 2008 (from account-level loan and deposit data)
  • Policy: 2009 early release of Special Pension (SP) savings
  • Controls: payout size, income, liquid wealth, demographics
  • Validation: register-based measures of net savings and pension savings
Period
1998–2009 registers; account-level data 2007–2009; survey January 2010
Sample
5,037 completed interviews with respondents who took out the SP balance Random sample of Danish Special Pension account holders who withdrew their SP savings in 2009, linked to administrative registers. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Household marginal interest rate (2008) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Computed at household level (respondent linked to spouse/partner) from SKAT account-level deposit and loan files: account-specific rate = 2008 interest payments on account l divided by the average of end-2007 and end-2008 balances. Only loans with balance of at least 1,000 DKK are included; if the household has at least one loan account the highest loan rate is used, otherwise the smallest deposit rate. Mortgage loans are excluded in reported results.
    Registers: SKAT account-level deposit and loan records 2007-2009
    working paper · Section 4.2
  • Propensity to spend the SP payout (survey) Wealth, debt and consumption
    From the Epinion telephone survey (weeks 4-7 of 2010) asking how the increase in funds from the SP payout was allocated across spending, free savings, debt reduction and pension savings; the amount allocated to spending is put in proportion to the total payout.
    Registers: Epinion telephone survey of SP account holders
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • SP payout / SP account balance Retirement and pensions
    Balance on the Special Pension (SP) account administered by ATP on 1 May 2009 (from the ATP SP register, also used to draw the survey sample); the payout could be withdrawn 1 June to 31 December 2009 and was taxed at 35 percent for the first 15,000 DKK and 50 percent beyond; net-of-tax payout is used.
    Registers: ATP Special Pension (SP) account register
    working paper · Sections 2 and 4.2
  • Register net savings Wealth, debt and consumption
    Change in net bank assets (bank deposits minus bank debt, including credit card debt, recorded on the last day of the year) between t and t-1 from the income-tax/wealth register; used to validate survey answers for 2005-2011.
    Registers: Income tax register (SKAT wealth data)
    working paper · Section 5.1
  • Imputed spending Wealth, debt and consumption
    Disposable income minus net savings (change in net bank assets) minus private pension contributions, c = y - dW - p, following Browning and Leth-Petersen (2003).
    Registers: Income tax register
    working paper · Section 5.1
  • Low liquid assets dummy Wealth, debt and consumption
    Indicator equal to one if the individual holds liquid assets worth less than one month's disposable income (threshold chosen for highest predictive power); a continuous liquid-assets-to-disposable-income ratio is also used.
    Registers: Income tax register
    working paper · Section 5.3.2
  • High debt service dummy Wealth, debt and consumption
    Indicator equal to one if debt service is 15 percent or more of disposable income; also used as a continuous debt-service-to-disposable-income ratio.
    Registers: Income tax register, SKAT account-level loan records
    working paper · Section 5.3.2
  • Holding a deposit balance Wealth, debt and consumption
    Individuals with total deposit-account balances exceeding one month's disposable income are labelled as having a balance (to net out salary accounts credited just before 31 December); used to define the group holding both assets and debt.
    Registers: SKAT account-level deposit records
    working paper · Section 5.3.1

Children and Gender Inequality: Evidence from Denmark

Henrik Kleven, Camille Landais and Jakob Egholt Søgaard · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2019 · Individual

Event studies around the birth of the first child show mothers' earnings fall about 20 percent relative to fathers' in the long run, through hours, participation and wage rates. These child penalties now account for most of the remaining gender earnings gap and are transmitted across generations through mothers' own upbringing.

Data
Full-population Danish administrative registers linked by personal ID (earnings, labour supply, occupation, firm, education), 1980–2013, Family and generational links (population register), ATP pension contributions as third-party measure of hours worked, Additional administrative data back to 1964 for intergenerational analysis, Matched employer-employee data (firm family-friendliness), International Social Survey Program (ISSP) 2002 for gender attitudes
Key variables
  • Treatment/event: birth of first child (event time relative to first birth)
  • Outcome: earnings, labour force participation, hours worked (ATP), wage rates
  • Outcome: occupation rank, sector, firm family-friendliness
  • Child penalty: percentage drop of women's relative to men's earnings
  • Intergenerational: maternal grandparents' labour supply
Period
1980–2013 (with data back to 1964 for intergenerational transmission); first births 1985–2003
Sample
around 470,000 births or 15,040,000 individual-year observations Danish parents with a first child born 1985–2003 who are observed alive and resident in Denmark from 5 years before to 10 years after the birth. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • ATP hours worked Hours worked
    Annual hours inferred from mandatory employer contributions to the ATP pension scheme (since 1964), which depend on hours in discrete steps: weekly bins 0-8, 9-17, 18-26, 27+ for weekly paid, or monthly bins 0-38, 39-77, 78-116, 117+ for monthly paid; summing 12 monthly steps gives an annual hours measure with 37 steps, capped at the top bin. Self-employed contribute on their own behalf.
    Registers: ATP pension contributions
    working paper · Section 2 (Data), footnote 8
  • Wage rate Earnings and income
    Earnings divided by the ATP hours measure, for those who are working (conditional on participation).
    Registers: ATP pension contributions, Income registers
    working paper · Section 2; Section 3.2 footnote 9
  • Child penalty Family links, fertility and household
    Event study around year of first birth (t=0), event time -5 to +10 with t=-1 omitted, separately by gender with age and year dummies, estimated in levels; penalty P_t = (alpha_men_t - alpha_women_t) / E[counterfactual women's outcome | t], the percentage by which women fall behind men due to children.
    Registers: Population register (family links)
    working paper · Section 3.1, eqs. (1)-(2)
  • Event-study sample Sample definition and timing
    First child births 1985-2003 whose parents are known, alive and reside in Denmark in every year from 5 years before to 10 years after the birth (balanced panel), regardless of relationship status; about 470,000 births / 15.04 million person-years. Long-run version follows parents up to 20 years after birth.
    Registers: Population register
    working paper · Section 2; Section 3.1
  • Never-parent control group with placebo births Family links, fertility and household
    Childless individuals assigned placebo first-birth ages drawn from a log-normal distribution of age at first child within birth cohort x education cells (with linear drift in the mean for cohorts born after 1973); for truncated post-1973 cohorts, individuals predicted most likely to have zero lifetime fertility (linear probability model estimated on 1955-1973 cohorts, age 40 as latest first-birth age) are selected.
    Registers: Population register, Education register
    working paper · Section 3.4; Appendix A.1
  • Occupational rank and top manager Occupation and job hierarchy
    Occupation ranked in five levels: unskilled labour, skilled labour, white-collar work (low level), white-collar work (high level) and top manager, an ordering consistent with average earnings or wage rates by occupation; separate indicator for being top manager.
    Registers: Occupation (matched employer-employee data)
    working paper · Section 3.3, Figure 5 Panels A-B
  • Firm family friendliness Firm characteristics and productivity
    Share of women with children below age 15 in the firm's workforce (excluding the woman's own first child when it arrives); outcome is the percentile rank in the distribution of firm family friendliness.
    Registers: Matched employer-employee data
    working paper · Section 3.3, Figure 5 Panel D
  • Public-sector employment Sector and industry
    Indicator for working in the Danish public sector (no register code given).
    Registers: Matched employer-employee data
    working paper · Section 3.3, Figure 5 Panel C
  • Grandparental relative labour supply rank Family links, fertility and household
    Cumulated ATP labour supply 1964-1979 of the maternal grandmother minus that of the maternal grandfather (analogously paternal), ranked in quantiles within the grandparents' cohort distribution; controls include 22 education dummies per grandparent, quantiles of the grandfather's within-cohort average net wealth 1980-90 and grandparents' birth-cohort dummies.
    Registers: ATP pension contributions, Population register (generational links), Wealth register
    working paper · Section 5.2

How variables are defined (7)
  • Treatment: born after municipal program implementation Sample definition and timing

    paper · Section III.A, footnote 34; Section II footnote 17
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Danish-born individuals of cohorts 1935-1949 residing in Denmark at least one year after 1980 who survive to age 45 (conditioning to equalize left-censoring since deaths are only observed from 1980), with a valid parish code, non-missing municipality observables, excluding hospital births; 876,912 individuals collapsed to 20,078 municipality x birth cohort x treatment cells.
    Registers: Population registers
    paper · Section III.A, footnotes 35, 38
  • Age-specific survival Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicators for survival beyond each age 46-64, from the Danish Death Register 1980-2012.
    Registers: Danish Death Register
    paper · Section III.B
  • Hospital nights ages 45-64 Health care use
    Total number of nights spent in hospital between ages 45 and 64 from the Danish Inpatient Register 1980-2012; robustness winsorizes at the 99th percentile (about 190 nights).
    Registers: Danish Inpatient Register (LPR)
    paper · Section III.B, footnote 39
  • Disease diagnoses (heart, cardiovascular, diabetes, cancer) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicators for being diagnosed with heart disease, cardiovascular disease, diabetes or cancer in middle age (45-64), including those diagnosed at death (dying from the condition); plus an indicator for more than one of heart disease, cardiovascular disease and diabetes. Diagnosis coding is described in online Appendix A.1 (not accessed).
    Registers: Danish Inpatient Register (LPR), Danish Death Register
    paper · Section III.B; online Appendix A.1 referenced
  • Cause-specific death Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicators for death between ages 45-64 from the four biggest cause groups: cancer, heart disease and other cardiovascular disease, digestive system and respiratory disease, plus an indicator for missing cause of death (about 7 percent); uses first and second causes on the death certificate (up to three recorded).
    Registers: Danish Death Register
    paper · Section III.B, footnote 40; online Appendix Table B.3
  • Pre-1937 municipality characteristics Geography and neighbourhood
    From the Statistical Commune Data Archive: party vote shares in three elections, population and urbanization in 1935, percent female 1930, percent workers in agriculture/industry 1930, percent on public aid 1936, percent income/property taxpayers 1936, aggregate taxable income and assessed property value 1936; plus 1936 infant mortality and enteritis deaths per 1,000 births by medical district (Medical Reports) and distance to Copenhagen; used as controls interacted with cohort and for propensity-score matching (caliper 0.05, one control without replacement).
    Registers: Danish Commune Archive, Medical Reports for the Kingdom of Denmark, DigDag
    paper · Section III.A; Section II matching, footnote 26

Health Children, intergenerational mobility and skills

Tax Reforms and Intertemporal Shifting of Wage Income: Evidence from Danish Monthly Payroll Records

Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen and Peer Ebbesen Skov · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2016 · Individual + firm

The 2010 cut in the top marginal tax rate was announced in advance, and monthly payroll data show top earners shifting wage income from December 2009 into January 2010. Shifting is concentrated among managers and employees of small firms, and it inflates short-run elasticity estimates.

Data
Monthly payroll records (eIndkomst / eIncome register) from the tax agency SKAT, Background registers on individuals and firms at Statistics Denmark (incl. firm size, liquid assets), Telephone survey on awareness of income-shifting opportunity (January 2011), merged to eIncome register
Key variables
  • Outcome: percentage change in monthly gross wage relative to 2008 average
  • Treatment: private-sector employees with 2008 monthly earnings above DKK 35,000 (top-tax incentive from 2010 reform)
  • Control group: monthly earnings DKK 30,000–35,000
  • Heterogeneity: firm size, liquid assets, earnings percentile
  • Elasticity of taxable income with and without shifting component
Period
January 2008–December 2011 (monthly)
Sample
328,679 individuals, of which 219,179 in the treatment group; survey sample of 878 taxpayers Private-sector employees with a wage record in every month of 2008 and positive income in all years, earning above DKK 30,000 per month in 2008. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Monthly wage change relative to 2008 Earnings and income
    Percentage change in individual monthly gross wage income (year t, month m) relative to the individual's average monthly gross earnings in 2008; percentage changes are used instead of logs because monthly earnings may be zero or near zero.
    Registers: eIncome register (SKAT)
    working paper · Section II, eq. (1)
  • Treatment and control groups (top-tax incentive) Taxes and tax rates
    Treatment group: private-sector employees with average monthly gross earnings above DKK 35,000 in 2008 (about the 75th percentile); control group: monthly income DKK 30,000-35,000 in 2008. Assignment based on 2008 income, before the reform could affect income (328,679 individuals, 219,179 treated).
    Registers: eIncome register (SKAT)
    working paper · Section II
  • Analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    Individuals employed throughout 2008 (a wage record in every month of 2008) with positive income in all years, observed January 2008 - December 2011; includes people who are both wage earners and self-employed. Sensitivity: excluding employees with any exit to unemployment during 2009-2010.
    Registers: eIncome register (SKAT)
    working paper · Section II, footnote 5; footnote 6
  • Income-shifting indicator Earnings and income
    Equals one if income in a month is high (more than 50 percent above) relative to its level in the same month of 2008 and income in the preceding month is low (more than 50 percent below) relative to its 2008 level; zero otherwise. Robustness with 25%-25% and 75%-75% cutoffs; a stricter version also requires November 2009 income to be unusually low.
    Registers: eIncome register (SKAT)
    working paper · Section III.A, eq. (3) and footnote 6
  • Financial capacity (liquidity) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Financial assets (money in bank accounts and value of shares and bonds) at end of 2008 relative to 2008 annual disposable income; groups below one month, between one and two months, and above two months of disposable income.
    Registers: Background registers at Statistics Denmark
    working paper · Section III.B, Figure 8
  • Firm size groups and top-five paid Firm characteristics and productivity
    Firm size groups: fewer than 25, 25-99, 100-499 and 500+ employees; large firms defined as more than 100 employees (top decile by number of employees); top-five paid employees within each firm used to isolate top management.
    Registers: eIncome register (SKAT), Firm registers
    working paper · Section III.B, Figures 6-7
  • Awareness of shifting opportunity Other
    From a January 2011 telephone survey of a random adult sample merged to the eIncome register (878 taxpayers): aware if the respondent answered both that extra income is taxed lower 'after 1 January' and that postponing payout from 2009 to 2010 is 'legal'.
    Registers: Telephone survey, eIncome register (SKAT)
    working paper · Section III.C, Table 4

Do Employer Pension Contributions Reflect Employee Preferences? Evidence from a Retirement Savings Reform in Denmark

Itzik Fadlon, Jessica Laird and Torben Heien Nielsen · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2016 · Individual + firm

A reform that cut the subsidy to capital pension accounts for top-bracket workers led employers to reduce contributions to those accounts immediately, by more the larger the share of affected employees, and to shift the money to annuity accounts. Employer contributions track employees' savings preferences.

Data
Income tax register (incl. third-party reported pension contributions), Population register (BEF), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA)
Key variables
  • Outcome: employer contribution rate to capital and annuity pension accounts (median within workplace)
  • Treatment: share of workplace employees above the top income tax threshold
  • Policy variation: 1999 reform cutting the deduction for capital pension contributions for top-bracket taxpayers
  • Unit: workplace = 2-digit occupation × firm cell
  • Comparison: individual private (IRA-type) pension contributions
Period
1996–2001
Sample
2,020,705 worker-year observations; 84,764 workplace-year observations (26,775 unique workplaces) Private-sector white-collar wage earners aged 20–60 without self-employment income, in occupation-firm cells with at least five employees. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Workplace (occupation-firm cell) Firm characteristics and productivity
    All employees with the same 2-digit occupation code in the same firm in a given year; cells with fewer than five employees are excluded.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: Statistics Denmark 2-digit occupation codes (Online Appendix E list)
    working paper · Section 2.2; footnote 14; Online Appendix E
  • Employer contribution rate (default) Retirement and pensions
    Employer-sponsored pension contributions divided by taxable labor income, computed separately for capital (lump-sum) and annuity pension accounts; the workplace-level measure is the median contribution rate within the occupation-firm cell in a year (modes used as robustness). Main outcome is the change from t-1 to t.
    Registers: Income tax register (third-party reported pension contributions)
    working paper · Section 2.2; Section 3 eq. setup; Appendix A
  • Share of workplace above top tax threshold Taxes and tax rates
    Fraction of employees in the occupation-firm cell with labor income above the top income tax threshold (about 49 percent of workers on average), interacted with year dummies with 1998 as baseline; the 1999 reform cut the deduction value for capital pension contributions from 59 to 45 cents per DKr for top-bracket taxpayers.
    Registers: Income tax register
    working paper · Section 2.1; Section 2.3; Section 3
  • White-collar occupation Occupation and job hierarchy
    Occupations whose 2-digit Statistics Denmark occupation code has first digit 1-5 (management, high-level knowledge work, intermediate-level work, office jobs, retail sales/service/care); first digits 6-9 treated as blue-collar and excluded.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: occupation code first digit 1-5 = white-collar
    working paper · Online Appendix E
  • Analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    Private-sector white-collar wage earners aged 20-60 in 1996-2001, excluding public-sector and blue-collar workers (likely under collective agreements), workers with self-employment income, and occupation-firm cells with fewer than five employees (2,020,705 worker-years; 26,775 workplaces).
    Registers: Income tax register, Population register, IDA
    working paper · Section 2.2-2.3
  • Individual private (IRA-type) pension contributions Retirement and pensions
    Individual contributions to private capital and annuity pension accounts outside the employer plan, as contribution rates relative to taxable labor income, used as the comparison to employer responses.
    Registers: Income tax register
    working paper · Section 2.3; Section 4

Immigrants' Effect on Native Workers: New Analysis on Longitudinal Data

Mette Foged and Giovanni Peri · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2016 · Individual

Refugee-country immigration into Danish municipalities from 1991 to 2008 pushed less-educated native workers toward more complex, less manual occupations. Native wages and employment rose rather than fell, and effects were positive even for low-skilled natives who moved across firms.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Occupation codes linked to O*NET task intensities (manual, communication, cognitive), Full population registers for municipality immigrant shares, Refugee spatial dispersal policy 1986–1998 (initial refugee allocation by municipality)
Key variables
  • Treatment: share of refugee-country immigrants in the municipality of work
  • Instrument: immigrant inflow predicted from the 1986–1998 refugee dispersal policy
  • Outcome: occupational complexity index (O*NET-based)
  • Outcome: log hourly wage (incl. mandatory pension contributions)
  • Outcome: fraction of year worked; occupational mobility
  • Controls: age, experience, tenure, education, marital status, region, industry
Period
1991–2008
Sample
1,864,027 observations of employed low-skilled natives, 1995–2008, in the fixed-effects panel (20 percent random sample of natives); balanced-panel difference-in-differences regressions use 71,053 natives employed in 1994 Danish-born individuals aged 18–65, not in school or permanently disabled, focusing on low-skilled (non-college) natives, across 97 municipalities. source
How variables are defined (10)
  • Refugee-country immigrants Immigration and origin
    Immigrants (foreign-born) from eight refugee-sending countries that generated substantial refugee inflows 1994-2008: Yugoslavia, Somalia, Afghanistan, Iraq, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Iran and Lebanon (Bosnia included in actual inflow but not in the instrument).
    Registers: IDA, Population registers
    working paper · Section 2, footnote 12; footnote 26
  • Refugee-country immigrant employment share Immigration and origin
    S_mt = F_mt / P_mt, the stock of employed refugee-country immigrants divided by total employment in municipality of work m in year t; computed on the full population (outcomes use a 20 percent random sample of natives).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 4.1; footnote 16
  • Dispersal-policy imputed refugee share (instrument) Immigration and origin
    For t > 1994, imputed working-age population from refugee country c in municipality m = s_cm x F_ct, where s_cm is the share of new immigrants from c first settling in m during 1986-1998 under the dispersal policy and F_ct is the national working-age population from c; summed over refugee countries and divided by municipality working-age population in 1988. Also used to define top and bottom quartile exposure municipalities for the difference-in-differences.
    Registers: Population registers
    working paper · Section 4.3
  • Occupational complexity index Occupation and job hierarchy
    ln((Communication + Cognitive)/Manual), using O*NET task intensities of occupations following Ottaviano, Peri and Wright (2013), linked to Danish 4-digit ISCO occupations; observed only for those employed at end of November.
    Registers: IDA, O*NET
    Codes: ISCO-88 4-digit (2-digit groups are population-weighted averages)
    working paper · Section 3.1; Figure 3 notes
  • Occupational mobility Occupation and job hierarchy
    Dummy equal to one if the individual changed 4-digit ISCO-88 occupation between year t-1 and t.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: ISCO-88 4-digit
    working paper · Section 3.1; Section 5
  • Hourly wage Earnings and income
    Log hourly wage of native worker including mandatory pension contributions, deflated by the Danish CPI; since pension payments are available only from 1995, wages net of pension contributions are used when pre-1995 data are included. Observed only for those employed at end of November.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1, footnote 15
  • Fraction of year worked Employment and labour force status
    Equals one for a full-time employee throughout the year; for part-time and/or part-year employment, the share of the regular working year spent at work.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1
  • Working-age native samples Sample definition and timing
    Working-age population: aged 18-65, not in school and not permanently disabled. Panel regressions use Danish-born individuals employed in November (IDA recorded last week of November); DiD uses a balanced panel of natives aged 21-51 in 1994, followed 1991-2008 unless disabled, emigrated or died. Low skilled = without college education.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1
  • Local labour market Geography and neighbourhood
    97 municipalities identifiable consistently 1988-2008, merging Frederiksberg and Copenhagen; exposure measured by municipality of work (DiD exposure by 1994 municipality of residence).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.2; Introduction
  • Experience and tenure Employment and labour force status
    Labour market experience = cumulative employment in years since first joining the labour force; tenure = time elapsed since hiring in the current establishment; low tenure = below sample average of 4.35 years in the establishment as of 1994.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1; Section 5 heterogeneity

When the Floodgates Open: Northern Firms' Response to Removal of Trade Quotas on Chinese Goods

Hale Utar · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2014 · Individual + firm

The dismantling of Multi-Fibre Arrangement quotas on Chinese textiles at WTO accession exposed Danish textile firms to low-wage competition. Within firms, employment, value added and intangible assets fell and the workforce shifted toward skilled workers, while firms refocused away from products where China's advantage grew.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Firm accounting statistics (Regnskabsdata / FIRE), International trade data from customs records (Udenrigshandel / UHDI), Domestic production/sales by product (Varestatistik / VARES), 1995–2005, EU SIGL textile and clothing quota licence database
Key variables
  • Treatment: firm produced 2005 MFA-quota goods for China in 1999 (exposure to quota removal)
  • Outcome: firm employment, value added, intangible assets, capital intensity
  • Outcome: workforce skill composition by occupation and education
  • Outcome: product scope / product innovation from transaction-level data
  • Firm fixed effects, year effects
Period
1995–2007
Sample
1,090 unique textile and clothing firms (875 firms, 1995–2005, for the product-portfolio analysis) All Danish textile and clothing firms with at least 0.5 full-time-equivalent employees, 1995–2007, matched to their employees and product transactions. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • MFA quota goods (MFAQ2, MFAQ5) Trade and offshoring
    Products subject to EU MFA quotas on China, from the EU SIGL licence database's 163 quota categories mapped to CN-1999 codes: 88 CN/HS 6-digit plus 45 CN 8-digit products abolished in 2002 (phases I-III) and 210 HS6 plus 47 CN8 products abolished in 2005; categories re-quotaed in the 2005 EU-China agreement ('Bra War') are excluded from MFAQ5.
    Registers: SIGL (EU), Udenrigshandel (customs trade)
    Codes: CN-1999 8-digit / HS 6-digit codes linked across years via Eurostat CN correspondence tables
    working paper · Section 2 (Data) and footnotes 8, 12
  • Treatment: produced MFA quota goods in 1999 Trade and offshoring
    MFAQProd99 = 1 if the T&C manufacturing firm is found to have produced any MFA quota good in 1999 (before China's WTO accession), identified from domestic sales (Varestatistik, firms with 10+ employees) and export data; MFAQShare99 is the share of 1999 firm sales from MFA quota goods. Interacted with a post-2002 dummy (Dum02) in firm and year fixed-effects regressions.
    Registers: Varestatistik, Udenrigshandel
    working paper · Section 4, eqs. (3)-(4) and footnotes 14-15
  • Value added Firm characteristics and productivity
    Turnover + work performed for own purposes and capitalized + (end-of-year minus beginning-of-year inventory) - (purchases of raw materials + energy + subcontracting expenses), deflated to constant 2000 DKK; production fragmentation measured as the logit of value added over gross output.
    Registers: Regnskabsdata (firm accounts)
    working paper · Appendix B.1; Section 5
  • Intangible assets Firm characteristics and productivity
    Assets intended for long-term ownership or use, including licences, trademarks, copyrights, exclusive distribution rights, software and goodwill, from the accounting statistics; outcomes are log intangible assets and the logit of intangibles over total assets. Physical capital: plants, machinery, technical installations, land, buildings, furniture and office equipment.
    Registers: Regnskabsdata (firm accounts)
    working paper · Section 5, footnote 26; Appendix B.1
  • Occupational skill groups Occupation and job hierarchy
    From IDA occupational status variable pstill2 (from 1996, DISCO-88 based; analysis starts 1996): professional and technical employees = executives, top-level and intermediate-level professional/technical employees; basic-skill jobs; no-skill jobs (cleaning, delivery, guard, transport); unclassified jobs excluded. Inactive people (retirees, employees on leave, owners' spouses) dropped before aggregating to firm counts.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: pstill2 31, 32, 34 = professional/technical; 35 = basic skill; 36 = no skill; 37 = unclassified
    working paper · Appendix B.2; footnote 17
  • Employee education groups Education and test scores
    From the 8-digit highest completed education code hffsp (not available for 2007): at most high school diploma = first two digits <= 25; at least some college = first two digits >= 40; T&C production (skill) training = hffsp 355880, 355890; college-level T&C technical design education = hffsp 405985. Outcomes are log(1 + number of such employees) per firm.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: hffsp first two digits <=25 (high school or less), >=40 (some college); 355880, 355890 (T&C production training); 405985 (T&C technical design)
    working paper · Appendix B.2; footnotes 18-20
  • New and dropped products Trade and offshoring
    Products defined at HS 6-digit from merged export (1993-2007) and domestic sales (1995-2005) data; a new product is one a firm starts to sell/export in the current year and was not observed produced by the firm in previous years; a dropped product is one the firm stops selling in the current year and is not observed sold in subsequent years. Export records include only shipments of DKK 10,000 or more.
    Registers: Udenrigshandel, Varestatistik
    Codes: HS 6-digit; CN 8-digit; 10-digit domestic product codes
    working paper · Appendix B, B.3; Table A-4 notes
  • Firm employment (FTE and head-count) Employment and labour force status
    Full-time equivalent employment from firm accounts (firms with at least 0.5 FTE are covered) and head-count of employees from IDA matched via the unique firm identifier.
    Registers: Regnskabsdata, IDA
    working paper · Section 2; Appendix B, B.2

Estimating Taxable Income Responses Using Danish Tax Reforms

Henrik Jacobsen Kleven and Esben Anton Schultz · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2014 · Individual

Uses a series of Danish tax reforms between 1984 and 2005 and full-population tax records to estimate the elasticity of taxable income. Elasticities are small for labour income (around 0.05) and larger for capital income and for top earners, and they are larger for big reforms than small ones.

Data
Income Tax Register (tax return information), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Authors' own tax simulator of the Danish tax system, 1984–2005
Key variables
  • Outcome: three-year changes in taxable labour income and capital income (positive and negative)
  • Treatment: change in simulated marginal net-of-tax rate
  • Instrument: mechanical (predicted) change in marginal tax rate from tax reforms
  • Controls: pre-reform (base year s−1) income levels
  • Key reforms: 1987 and 1994 Danish tax reforms
Period
Data since 1980; tax simulator and estimation 1984–2005 (three-year intervals 1984–1987 to 2002–2005)
Sample
about 37 million observations (stacked three-year differences; about 49 million before sample restrictions) Full Danish population aged 15–70 who are fully tax liable and whose base-year income is not primarily welfare benefits, 1984–2005. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Labor income (LI) Earnings and income
    Tax-code labor income: salary, wages, honoraria, fees, bonuses, fringe benefits and business earnings. Main outcome is the three-year growth rate (s to s+3) in real labor/wage earnings; regressions weighted by labor income and restricted to positive labor income.
    Registers: Income Tax Register, IDA
    paper · Table 1; Section II; Table notes for labor income elasticity tables
  • Capital income (CI), positive and negative Earnings and income
    Interest income, rental income and business capital income minus interest on debt (mortgage, bank loans, credit cards, student loans), excluding stock income; analysed separately as positive and negative capital income because they are taxed very differently.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    paper · Table 1; Section I; footnote 6
  • Personal, stock and taxable income (PI, SI, TI) Earnings and income
    Personal income PI = LI + transfers, grants, awards, gifts, received alimony minus labour market contribution and certain pension contributions; stock income SI = dividends and realized capital gains on shares; deductions D = commuting, union fees, UI contributions, other work expenses, charity, paid alimony; taxable income TI = PI + CI + SI - D (differs from the tax-code label, which excludes SI).
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    paper · Table 1
  • Simulated marginal tax rate Taxes and tax rates
    Marginal tax rate on income component j computed with the authors' own Danish tax simulator (1984-2005) as [T(z_j + 100) - T(z)]/100, i.e. by raising that component by DKK 100; accounts for spousal jointness of exemptions and the marginal tax ceiling.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    paper · Section II; footnote 9
  • Mechanical change in net-of-tax rate (instrument) Taxes and tax rates
    log(1 - tau_{s+3}(z_s)) - log(1 - tau_s(z_s)): change in the marginal net-of-tax rate simulated by applying year s+3 tax law to base-year s incomes; analogous mechanical change in virtual income instruments for the change in log virtual income.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    paper · Section III.B
  • Stacked three-year difference sample Sample definition and timing
    Stacked three-year intervals 1984-1987 to 2002-2005, keeping taxpayers also observed in year s-1 (used for pre-reform income controls: splines of log s-1 income and the log deviation between s-1 and s incomes); restricted to ages 15-70, fully tax liable in Denmark, excluding those whose base-year income comes primarily from welfare benefits (about 37 million observations).
    Registers: Income Tax Register, IDA
    paper · Section II; Section V table notes
  • Taxpayers close to kink points Taxes and tax rates
    Taxpayers with income within DKK 5,000 of the top kink, DKK 3,000 of the middle kink or DKK 2,000 of the bottom kink (excluded in robustness checks).
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    paper · Notes to labor income elasticity table (Section V)
  • 1987 reform DD treatment/control groups Sample definition and timing
    Treatment group: taxpayers experiencing an increase in the marginal net-of-tax rate on labor income (or on positive capital income) due to the 1987 reform over 1986-1989; control group: those experiencing a reduction; large-treatment group has net-of-tax rate increases of at least 15 percent.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    paper · Section IV, Figure 4 discussion

Productivity Spillovers Across Firms through Worker Mobility

Andrey Stoyanov and Nikolay Zubanov · AEJ: Applied Economics, 2012 · Individual + firm

Tracks firm-to-firm worker moves in Danish manufacturing. Firms that hire workers from more productive firms see productivity gains of about 0.35 percent a year for an average firm, rising with the education, tenure and skill of the new hires and persisting for several years, consistent with knowledge spillovers carried by workers.

Data
Matched employer-employee data from Statistics Denmark (worker records from 1983, ages 15–65), Manufacturing firm-level accounts data with sales, value added, materials, capital and investment, 1995–2007
Key variables
  • Outcome: receiving firm's log value added per worker normalised by 4-digit industry-year mean
  • Treatment: productivity gap between sending and receiving firms of newly hired workers, weighted by hires' employment share
  • Positive and negative productivity gaps (hires from more vs. less productive firms)
  • Worker characteristics: education, occupation/skill level, experience, wage
  • Firm characteristics: size, industry
Period
1995–2007
Sample
173,929 firm-year observations (about 5.8 million worker-year observations, 668,034 job changers); benchmark regressions use 74,507 and 61,112 firm-year observations All Danish manufacturing firms and their employees with positive annual salary, 1995–2007. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Normalized labour productivity Firm characteristics and productivity
    Natural log of firm value added per worker normalized by the 4-digit NACE industry-year average; manufacturing firms 1995-2007, with firm accounts from annual surveys (all firms with 50+ workers) and interpolated values for less frequently surveyed small firms.
    Registers: Firm-level accounts (Statistics Denmark)
    Codes: NACE 4-digit
    paper · Section I.A
  • Productivity gap of new hires Firm characteristics and productivity
    For receiving firm j hiring in year t: average over new workers of (normalized productivity of sending firm minus that of receiving firm, both in t-1), multiplied by new hires' share of total employment H/N. Positive and negative gaps computed separately for hires from more and less productive sending firms, each weighted by that group's employment share.
    Registers: Matched employer-employee data (Statistics Denmark)
    paper · Section I.A eqs. (1)-(3)
  • Job mover / new hire Employment and labour force status
    Worker observed at a different firm than in the previous year; employment record is as of end of calendar year, so only the year of the move is observed. Sample restricted to manufacturing firms and employees aged 15-65 with positive annual salary; multiple jobs treated as different.
    Registers: Matched employer-employee data (Statistics Denmark)
    paper · Section I.A
  • Skill level / occupation category Occupation and job hierarchy
    Occupation grouped into four categories: low-skilled, mid-skilled, high-skilled workers and managers.
    Registers: Matched employer-employee data (Statistics Denmark)
    paper · Section I.A
  • Educational attainment Education and test scores
    Highest completed education measured in three levels: high school, college and university.
    Registers: Matched employer-employee data (Statistics Denmark)
    paper · Section I.A
  • Labour market experience Hours worked
    Work experience recorded in thousands of hours in the individual-level data.
    Registers: Matched employer-employee data (Statistics Denmark)
    paper · Section I.A
  • Firm human capital of workers (AKM-based) Earnings and income
    Firm average of worker wage net of the AKM firm effect, h = (1/N) sum (w - lambda - psi_j), from a wage equation with person and firm fixed effects (Abowd, Kramarz and Margolis 1999); new workers' human capital measured in t-1, their last full year in the previous firm.
    Registers: Matched employer-employee data (Statistics Denmark)
    paper · Section I.B eq. (5)

Estimating the Effect of Student Aid on College Enrollment: Evidence from a Government Grant Policy Reform

Helena Skyt Nielsen, Torben Sørensen and Christopher Taber · AEJ: Economic Policy, 2010 · Individual

A 1988 reform raised Danish student grants for students from higher-income families. Roughly 1,000 dollars of extra aid raised enrolment by about 1.35 percentage points, a response that is consistent with modest credit constraints rather than binding ones.

Data
Register-based dataset covering the entire Danish population, 1983–2005 (Statistics Denmark), Educational event histories (education registers), 1973–2005, High school GPA records, Parental income used for student-aid means-testing (tax records), Parental liquid assets from wealth/tax records
Key variables
  • Outcome: college enrollment within one year of high school graduation
  • Treatment: stipend (fraction of full student grant) the individual is eligible for
  • Variation: 1988 Danish student grant reform and kinked means-tested aid schedule
  • Running/ranking variable: parental (social) income percentile
  • Borrowing-constraint proxy: low parental liquid assets
  • Controls: high school GPA, sex, age, region, parents' education
Period
1983–2005 (population register data); high school graduation cohorts 1983–1990, estimation on cohorts 1985 and 1988–1990
Sample
108,933 high school graduates in the final selected sample; 54,843 observations in the main probit estimates (cohorts 1985, 1988–1990) Danish graduates of the ordinary academic high school track who graduated at ages 19–20 in 1983–1990, with observed GPA and parental information. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • College enrollment within one year Education and test scores
    Indicator for accumulated enrollment in any college (short-, medium- or long-cycle higher education) by one year after high school graduation, taken from educational event histories 1973-2005; one-year horizon chosen so pre-reform cohorts decided before the reform was announced.
    Registers: Educational event histories (education registers)
    paper · Section II; Section V.B and Table 3
  • Social income (means-test income X) Earnings and income
    Pre-reform means-testing measure X = mother's taxable income + father's taxable income - a x number of siblings below the age limit + f(parents' wealth); in 1985 a = 16,600 DKK and f(W) = 0.1(W-447,700)1[W>447,700] + 0.15(W-895,400)1[W>895,400] + 0.25(W-1,492,100)1[W>1,492,100]. Since social income no longer exists in the registers after 1988, a best post-reform analogue is computed accounting for wealth and number of siblings; analyses use the social income percentile within cohort.
    Registers: Tax/income registers
    paper · Section II eq. (1) and footnotes 6, 12; Section IV end
  • Counterfactual pre-reform stipend (S_pre) Unemployment and benefits
    Stipend the individual would be eligible for under the 1985 rule: compute X, find its quantile within the current cohort, take the corresponding quantile of X in the pre-reform cohort, and apply the 1985 grant schedule (maximum stipend if X < DKK 156,400, none if X > DKK 256,200 in 1985). Stipend measured as four years of grant.
    Registers: Tax/income registers
    paper · Section II footnote 6; Section II procedure steps (1)-(4) and footnote 13
  • Low parental liquid assets indicator Wealth, debt and consumption
    Basic indicator D1 = 1 if parents' liquid assets at time of high school graduation fall short of one month's income; extreme indicator D2 = 1 if below two months' income. Liquid assets are all non-housing assets: cash, shares, bonds, mortgage deeds and other assets; children of self-employed parents (liquid assets not registered) are set to D1 = D2 = 0.
    Registers: Wealth/tax records
    paper · Section V.B, Tables 4-6
  • Analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    High school graduates from the ordinary (academic) high school track in 1985-1990 (assets not observed before 1985) who graduate at 'normal' ages 19-20, with observed GPA, non-missing parental income and education, excluding those with divorced parents at graduation; the 1986 and 1987 cohorts are dropped because of anticipation of the reform and an earlier change in the means-testing age limit. Final sample 108,933.
    Registers: Population register, Education registers
    paper · Section V.A, Table 2; Section V.B
  • High school GPA Education and test scores
    High school grade point average on the Danish 13-point scale (grades 0, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 13; 6 and above passed); only observed for the traditional academic high school track.
    Registers: High school GPA records
    paper · Section V.A footnote 18; footnote 21

Review of Economics and Statistics

Managing Inequality: Manager-Specific Wage Premiums and Selection in the Managerial Labor Market

Alex Xi He and Daniel le Maire · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2025 · Individual + firm

Builds a manager-firm-worker matched dataset for the whole Danish population to estimate manager effects on wages. Manager-specific premiums are almost as important as firm premiums for between-firm wage inequality, are unrelated to productivity, and high-paying managers are more likely to be replaced after acquisitions.

Data
Matched employer-employee data covering all Danish workers and firms (IDA), Occupation codes used to identify managers, Firm balance sheet data for private-sector firms (FIRE), Mergers and acquisitions identified from firm and establishment identifiers
Key variables
  • Outcome: worker log wages
  • Key estimate: manager-specific wage premiums (manager fixed effects identified from worker and manager mobility)
  • Comparison: firm-specific wage premiums
  • Event: firm acquisition and manager replacement
  • Heterogeneity: industry concentration (HHI)
Period
1995–2011 (per 2019 working-paper slides)
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Manager-firm-worker matched panel covering the entire Danish population; acquisitions sample of about 3,700 private-sector acquisitions in the 2019 working-paper version. source (abstract)
How variables are defined (8)
  • Manager identification Occupation and job hierarchy
    A worker is a manager if their ISCO-88 occupation is 1200-1399 or their job position code is top management (pstill 31); a manager status is carried forward within an establishment in years where it has no identified manager. If no manager is found, the top earner (or anyone in the top 5% of earners) is flagged when not in a non-managerial ISCO>=2000 occupation, earns at least 1.6 times the average of co-workers, or earns more than 1.5 times the second-highest earner; further fallbacks assign the top earner with a unique occupation/position earning >1.3 times the second highest.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: isco 1200-1399; PSTILL==31 (top manager), PSTILL 32 exception; ratio = lonind*(n-1)/(wagebill-lonind) >= 1.6; lonind/second-highest > 1.5
    replication code · clean_manager.do
  • Top manager per firm-year Occupation and job hierarchy
    Among identified managers, one manager per establishment-year is kept by successively preferring ISCO 1210 (CEOs), then pstill 31, managers with longer tenure in the establishment, and higher within-establishment earnings rank; only managers observed in at least two firms are retained (mobility needed for identification), establishments that were acquisition targets are excluded, and at the firm (CVR) level the manager of the largest establishment is used.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: isco==1210; pstill==31; target_cumu>=1 dropped
    replication code · clean_manager.do
  • Log hourly wage (AKM outcome) Earnings and income
    Log of the IDA hourly wage, deflated to constant prices; when the hourly wage is zero it is replaced by annual labour income divided by 1800. Observations with missing firm ID, labour income <=1, missing education or experience, or unemployment degree above 500 are dropped; firms whose maximum employment is 5 or fewer are excluded.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: timelon; lonind; replace timelon=lonind/1800 if timelon==0; arledgr (unemployment degree) >500 dropped; maxemp<=5 dropped
    replication code · AKM_merger_cvrnr.do
  • Mergers and acquisitions Firm characteristics and productivity
    M&As are identified from establishment (workplace) IDs changing firm (CVR) IDs: a firm-year is a merger if its establishments were owned by more than one distinct firm in the previous year (ignoring spurious ownership changes where an establishment's firm ID reverts); the acquirer is the establishment whose firm ID is unchanged, and targets are establishments whose previous-year firm ID differs when the firm also has an acquirer.
    Registers: IDA, IDAS
    Codes: lbnr (establishment), cvrnr (firm); merger = nvals(cvrnr_prevyear)>1 within cvrnr-year; acquirer: cvrnr==cvrnr_prevyear; target: cvrnr!=cvrnr_prevyear & nacquirer>0
    replication code · clean_merger.do
  • Firm spinouts and exits Firm characteristics and productivity
    Share of a firm's workers in establishments that move to a different firm ID next year (spinout) or disappear next year before 2011 (exit).
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: spinout = cvrnr_nextyear!=cvrnr; exit = cvrnr_nextyear missing & year<2011
    replication code · clean_merger.do
  • Education groups Education and test scores
    Four education groups from the first two digits of the highest completed education code: basic (<=25), vocational (35), short/medium higher (40-50), long higher (>=60).
    Registers: IDA, UDDA
    Codes: max_educ = int(HFFSP/1e6): <=25 basic; 35 vocational; 40-50; >=60
    replication code · AKM_merger_cvrnr.do; clean_merger.do
  • Firm industry Sector and industry
    Establishment industry is the modal worker industry code if held by more than 50% of workers; firm industry (127- and 36-group) is assigned only if at least 70% of the firm's workers share it, otherwise missing.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: persbrc mapped to pb07, ind127, ind36; thresholds 0.5 (establishment) and 0.7 (firm)
    replication code · clean_merger.do
  • Hiring and firing rates Firm characteristics and productivity
    Hiring rate = workers whose firm ID differs from the previous year divided by lagged firm employment; firing rate = workers whose firm ID differs next year divided by current employment.
    Registers: IDA
    replication code · AKM_merger_cvrnr.do

  • Treatment: assignment to a low-SES (parental education) physician after clinic closure

  • Outcome: detection/treatment of chronic conditions (CVC, cancer, diabetes, COPD)

1995–2019 (clinic closures 1999–2016)
Sample
over 352,000 adult patients affected by 894 clinic closures; 1,019,005 observations in the main mortality regression Danish adults aged 40–70 whose primary care clinic closed between 1999 and 2016, observed at least four years before the closure. source

Do Export Support Programs Affect Prices, Quality, Markups, and Marginal Costs? Evidence From a Natural Policy Experiment

Magnus T. Buus, Jakob R. Munch, Joel Rodrigue and Georg Schaur · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2025 · Firm

Uses a quasi-natural experiment in the Danish Trade Council's export support to firms. Support raises firm-level exports within destination markets but leaves prices, quality, markups and marginal costs unchanged, consistent with firms growing abroad by shifting demand rather than changing products.

Data
Trade Council export promotion records: firm purchases and Trade Council approaches by destination, International Trade in Goods statistics: Intrastat and Extrastat firm exports by CN8 product and destination (UHDI), Manufacturers' Sales of Goods (VARES/Prodcom): firm sales by product, value and quantity, Firm Statistics Register (FirmStat) and Firm Accounts Statistics (FIRE)
Key variables
  • Treatment: purchase of export promotion services for a destination in year t or t-1
  • Instrument: whether the Trade Council approached the firm
  • Outcome: firm-product-destination export sales
  • Outcome: export unit values (prices), quality, markups and marginal costs
Period
2002–2015
Sample
18,181 firm-years (manufacturing exporters in Prodcom data, 77 destinations) Danish manufacturing exporters with at least 10 employees present in the production data, exporting to the 77 destinations served by the Trade Council, 2002–2015. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Export support treatment Trade and offshoring
    Dummy equal to 1 if the firm purchased an export promotion service from the Danish Trade Council for a given destination (or, at firm level, any destination) in year t or year t-1; multiple purchases within a year are not distinguished (collapsed with max). Trade Council records restricted to 2002-2015 with non-missing destination.
    Registers: Trade Council export promotion records (promodata.dta)
    Codes: treated=1 for all promodata cases, 0 for turned-down cases (tdc.dta); treated_2 = (treated_1==1 | L.treated_1==1)
    replication code · BMRS_restat/4_reg_variables/code/4_4_promotion.do; 1_data/code/1_5_promotion.do; 2_prepare/code/2_2_variables.do
  • Trade Council initiative (instrument) Trade and offshoring
    Dummy equal to 1 if the firm was contacted (approached) by the Trade Council for a destination, defined over both purchased cases and turned-down cases where contact was established but no support was bought; used as of year t or t-1 like the treatment.
    Registers: Trade Council export promotion records (promodata.dta, tdc.dta)
    Codes: tdcinitiative=1 if firm contacted by the TC; tdcinitiative_2 = (tdcinitiative_1==1 | L.tdcinitiative_1==1)
    replication code · BMRS_restat/1_data/code/1_5_promotion.do; 4_reg_variables/code/4_4_promotion.do
  • Firm-product-destination exports and quantity Trade and offshoring
    Export value (1000 DKK) by firm, CN8+ product, destination and year from the trade-in-goods statistics, exports only. Quantity is weight in kg unless the supplementary unit is not kg, is unique within the product, and the value of observations with non-missing amounts is at least that with non-missing weights, in which case the supplementary amount is used; observations with zero/missing value or quantity are dropped. A variant keeps only flows above 7.5 (1000 DKK).
    Registers: UHDI
    Codes: ie=="2" (exports); value vrd, weight vgt, amount mgd, unit enhedskode ("00" = kg); vrd_exp_exsmall if vrd_exp>7.5
    replication code · BMRS_restat/1_data/code/1_3_export_import.do; 4_reg_variables/code/4_3_export.do
  • Product classification (CN8+) Trade and offshoring
    CN8 product codes are made consistent over 2002-2015 by aggregating to CN8+ categories using the Van Beveren et al. (2012) algorithm; each CN8+ code is assigned the CN6 category with the largest Prodcom sales value.
    Registers: UHDI, VARS
    Codes: cn8_cn8plus_2002_2015 concordance; Prodcom vnr>100, cn8=floor(varenr/100)

    Firm-years present in the Prodcom (manufacturers' sales) data from 2002, matched to FIRM and FIRE, in manufacturing with at least 10 employees year by year (employees >= 9.5), observed in FIRM in the previous year, and with positive sales, wage bill, capital and material expenditures.

Understanding the Rise in Life Expectancy Inequality

Gordon B. Dahl, Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Torben Heien Nielsen and Benjamin Ly Serena · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2024 · Individual

Decomposes widening life expectancy gaps between rich and poor into changes in age-specific mortality and differences in survivability to each age. Lower survivability of the poor explains the entire rise in Danish life expectancy inequality; cardiovascular gains helped everyone, but lifestyle-related survivability diverged.

Data
Population registers (BEF, FAIN): sex and age, Income register (IND): household income net of universal transfers, Death registers (DODAARS, DODAASG) with cause of death, US mortality by income from Chetty et al. (2016), IRS tax data
Key variables
  • Outcome: period life expectancy by income group
  • Income rank: household income measured two years before mortality
  • Decomposition: mortality changes vs. survivability
  • Cause of death: cardiovascular, cancer, lifestyle-related, other
Period
2001–2014
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Universe of Danish residents 2001–2014, compared with US tax-return-based mortality data. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • Household income (net of transfers tied to age/pension) Earnings and income
    Individual income = total personal income PERINDKIALT minus public pensions (QPENSNY), cash assistance (KONTHJ/KONT_GL) and other transfers (ANDOVERFORSEL), with negative business income, negative capital income (after removing surplus from owner-occupied housing OVSKEJD02_NY/OVSKEJD07) and negative wage components added back; household income is the mean of own and spouse/cohabiting partner income (rowmean of inc and partner inc).
    Registers: IND (INDUPD), BEF, FAIN
    Codes: PERINDKIALT, QPENSNY, KONTHJ/KONT_GL, ANDOVERFORSEL, NETOVSKUD_GL, FORMUEINDK_NY, OVSKEJD02_NY, OVSKEJD07, LOENMV, ERHVERVSINDK_GL, OVERFORSINDK, RESUINK_GL; partner via EFALLE (from 1986) / C_FAELLE_ID (before 1986)
    replication code · Replication files/DKRepCode/CollectData.sas (income block) and CreateData_DK.do lines ~13-69
  • Income rank (two-year lag) Earnings and income
    Percentile rank (1-100, ties broken randomly) of household income measured two years earlier (t-2), computed within gender x birth cohort x year cells; mortality sample ages 40-100, years 2001-2014, collapsed to income tertiles for trends.
    Registers: IND, BEF
    Codes: laginc = hhinc[t-2]; incrank by gender birthyear year
    replication code · CreateData_DK.do lines ~108-130, 195-200
  • Cause of death categories Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Underlying cause of death (ICD-10) from the cause-of-death registers: cardiovascular = I00-I78; cancer = C00-C97 and D00-D09; lifestyle-related = alcohol (K70, K74, K86.0, F10), smoking (COPD J40-J44) and obesity (E66, diabetes E10-E14); other = all remaining deaths. A Case-Deaton 'behavioural' grouping (diabetes E10-E14, suicide X60-X84/Y87.0, poisoning X40-X45/Y10-Y15/Y45/Y47/Y49, chronic liver K70/K73/K74, lung cancer C34) is also built.
    Registers: DODSAASG, DODSAARS
    Codes: C_DODTILGRUNDL_ACME (DODSAASG), C_DOD1 (DODSAARS); ICD-10 I00-I78; C00-C97, D00-D09; K70,K74,K860,F10; J40-J44; E66,E10-E14
    replication code · CreateData_DK.do lines ~132-192
  • Mortality sample and estate correction Sample definition and timing
    Population from BEF (1986+) and FAIN (before 1986), years 1998-2014, ages 37+ (mortality analyses ages 40-100, 2001-2014); person-years after the death year are dropped (unresolved estates). Age-specific mortality by income tertile and gender is linearly trended across 2001-2014 to predict 2001 and 2014 rates.
    Registers: BEF, FAIN, DODSAASG, DODSAARS
    replication code · CreateData_DK.do lines ~7-9, 94-98, 195-215

The Long-Run Effects of Individual Debt Relief

Gustaf Bruze, Alexander Kjær Hilsløv and Jonas Maibom · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2024 · Individual

Links court records on the Danish debt relief programme to the registers and uses quasi-random assignment of applicants to court trustees with different admission rates. Debt relief raises earned income, employment, assets, home ownership and wealth for more than 25 years, with the move into employment accounting for two thirds of the income gain.

Data
Hand-collected debt relief announcements from the official gazette Statstidende (court records), 1984–2005, Central Person Register (CPR) for linkage, Income Tax Register: earned income, taxable assets and debt, real estate ownership, Labour market status registers (employment status in November), Hourly wage measure from Statistics Denmark
Key variables
  • Treatment: being granted court-ordered debt relief
  • Instrument: court trustee admission rate (judge/trustee leniency design)
  • Outcome: earned income and employment
  • Outcome: taxable assets, secured and unsecured debt, home ownership, wealth
Period
Applications 1984–2003; register outcomes 1980–2019
Sample
46,571 individuals (final sample); 32,794 observations in the IV sample with 515 trustee identifiers All applicants for debt relief in Danish City Courts from 1984 to 2003, linked to national registers. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Granted debt relief (treatment) Other
    Applicants identified from Statstidende announcements (decision types P = proklama, K = kendelse/ruling, T = tilbagekaldelse/revocation, I); granted = the person's sequence of announcements contains a Kendelse (court ruling granting debt relief); alternative definition requires no subsequent revocation.
    Registers: Statstidende (hand-collected), CPR
    Codes: granted = 1 if any decision 'K'; granted_not_revoked = granted & no 'T' after 'K'
    replication code · 01classify_rep.sas, section 'Classify individuals into those who receive debt relief and those who don't'
  • Trustee leniency instrument Other
    Leave-one-out mean grant rate of the applicant's court-appointed trustee (lawyer ID unique within court), net of the leave-one-out court grant rate; sample restricted to trustees with at least 20 cases; regressions include court x year fixed effects, SEs clustered by trustee.
    Registers: Statstidende (hand-collected)
    Codes: iv_lawyer2 = (mean_lawyer_leniency*n_lawyer - granted)/(n_lawyer-1) - (iv_court*obs_court - granted)/(obs_court-1); keep if n_lawyer >= 20
    replication code · 05IV_regressions_rep.do, lines ~19-35
  • Employment status Employment and labour force status
    Through 2012: employed if IDA occupational status PSTILL < 38 or in 71-77; unemployed if PSTILL = 40; out of labour force if PSTILL 41-57 or 90-98. From 2013: employed if JOB_P_SOCIO_KODE 110, 120, 131-136; unemployed if 200; out of labour force if 311-517. Alternative: employed if wage income LOENMV_13 > 0.
    Registers: IDAP, IDA
    Codes: PSTILL <38 or 71-77 (employed), 40 (unemployed), 41-57/90-98 (OLF); SOCIO 110,120,131-136 / 200 / 311-517
    replication code · 03panel_rep.sas, 'Employment' block
  • Earned income and hourly wage Earnings and income
    Earned income ERHVERVSINDK_13 from the income register and hourly wage TIMELON from IDA, CPI-deflated and winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles by year.

    Registers: IND, INDK
    Codes: QAKTIVF, QAKTIVF_NY05, QPASSIV, QPASSIVN, PRIGALD, OBLGAELD, KOEJD, BANKGAELD, PANTGAELD, GALDIO

Spending Response to a Predictable Increase in Mortgage Repayments: Evidence from Expiring Interest-Only Loans

Henrik Yde Andersen, Stine Ludvig Bech and Alessia De Stefani · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2024 · Individual

Matches the universe of Danish mortgages to borrower registers and studies the fully anticipated start of amortisation on interest-only loans. When instalments rise by 9 percent of income, consumption falls by 3 percent of income and stays down, with the failure to smooth concentrated among highly leveraged borrowers likely to be refused a new interest-only loan.

Data
Mortgage registry: loan-level data on the universe of Danish mortgages reported by mortgage institutions to Danmarks Nationalbank (from 2009), Income and wealth registers (IND/FORMUE): household income, bank deposits, stocks, bonds, pensions, debts, Population/household registers (BEF): family composition, residence, Imputed household consumption from income and wealth registers
Key variables
  • Treatment: expiry of the interest-only period (start of amortisation)
  • Outcome: imputed household consumption relative to income
  • Installment increase relative to income
  • Heterogeneity: loan-to-value ratio and liquid savings
Period
Mortgage registry 2009–2018; IO loans originated 2003–2007 expiring 2013–2017
Sample
46,025 household-year observations (baseline regressions); 8,813 households beginning amortization Danish households with an interest-only mortgage originated 2003–2007 whose IO period expires in 2013–2017 and who keep the original loan, excluding self-employed and house buyers/sellers. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • Expiring interest-only loan sample / treatment year Sample definition and timing
    Households with a mortgage loan taken in year t-10 that started with an interest-only (IO) period lasting at least 9 years (IO length = years between IO start and end dates in REAL) and that survives from t-1 to t; treatment year is when the IO period expires; event time = year - treatment year. Households with any self-employed member, non-tax-liable members, or a property purchase/sale/ownership change in event years -1 to 1 are dropped.
    Registers: REAL, BEF, EJER
    Codes: y_laanoptag = t-10 & l_afdragsfrihed_aar >= 9; drop if selvst, ikkeskattepligtig, or koebt/solgt/ejerskift in t_count -1..1
    replication code · 1_Extractdata.sas macro 'sample' lines ~119-135; 4_VarDefinition.do section 1
  • Imputed household consumption Wealth, debt and consumption
    Family disposable income (excluding imputed rent of own home) plus one-off pension payouts (ATP, SP, LD, withdrawn pensions) net of their tax, minus savings in bank deposits, minus stock savings corrected for price changes (change in stock holdings less lagged holdings x stock index return), minus foreign asset savings, minus repayments (afdrag) on mortgage, bank, mortgage-deed and foreign debt, minus private pension contributions. From 2010 the mortgage repayment uses loan-level REAL repayments (version 3).
    Registers: IND, FORMUE, REAL
    Codes: famforbrug1a / famforbrug3 = famdispindk + (famatp_engang+famsp_pension+famld_udbetal+famhaevpen) - taxes on these - op_famindestpi - (op_famkursakt - famkursakt_lag*makro_aktie/100) - op_famudlakt - af_famoblgaeld (or af_famrealgaeld) - af_fambankgaeld - af_fampantgaeld - af_famudprigael - fampripensindbetal
    replication code · 0c_Familydata.sas lines ~1586-1695
  • Outcomes scaled by lagged disposable income Wealth, debt and consumption
    Annual changes in household consumption, bank deposits, financial assets, bank debt and mortgage debt, and levels of installments and interest payments, divided by previous-year family disposable income (DISPON_13); all censored at the 1st and 99th percentile by year.
    Registers: IND, FORMUE, REAL
    Codes: rdiffconsump = (famforbrug - L.famforbrug) / L.famdispon_13; rfamafdrag_for = famafdrag_for / L.famdispon_13
    replication code · 4_VarDefinition.do section 4
  • Liquid assets, debt-to-income, mortgage payment Wealth, debt and consumption
    Liquid assets = bank deposits + bonds + stocks (market value); total assets add housing value; liabilities = bank debt + mortgage outstanding; debt-to-income = total liabilities (QPASSIVN) / gross income (PERINDKIALT_13); total mortgage payment (ydelse) = installments + interest paid + administration fee (bidrag).
    Registers: FORMUE, IND, REAL
    Codes: liq_assets = fambankakt + famoblakt + famkursakt; dti = famqpassivn/famperindkialt_13; ydelse = famafdrag_for + famrente_bet_nu + fambidrag
    replication code · 4_VarDefinition.do section 2
  • Refinancing behaviour at IO expiry Wealth, debt and consumption
    At the expiry year: loan stays (survives, no new loan in t-1, t, t+1); new IO loan taken in t-1, t or t+1; new amortising loan (no IO); or pays out the loan (none of the above).

Language Training and Refugees' Integration

Mette Foged, Linea Hasager, Giovanni Peri, Jacob Nielsen Arendt and Iben Bolvig · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2024 · Individual

A 1999 reform improved language training for newly recognised refugees. A regression discontinuity around the cut-off date shows a permanent, positive effect on earnings that emerges after classes are completed, together with more schooling and a higher probability of working in complex jobs.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Income register (IND), Education enrollment and completion registers, Crime register: charges and convictions, Population register (BEF), Admission/residence permit register (OPHG), Migration register (VNDS) and internal mobility register (FLYT), Register for Labour Market Policy Measures (AMFORA), Danish language training database (Danskuddannelsesdatabasen), O*NET task intensities
Key variables
  • Running variable: date refugee status granted relative to January 1, 1999
  • Treatment: 1999 reform expanding Danish language training
  • Outcome: annual earnings and employment
  • Outcome: education, occupation task complexity, crime
  • Outcome (children): lower secondary completion and crime
Period
Admissions 1997–2000; followed until 2016 (children's outcomes until 2018)
Sample
8,558 individuals; children sample of 9,730 Refugees and reunified family members aged 18–49 granted asylum in Denmark between January 1, 1997 and December 31, 2000. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Running variable: days from 1 January 1999 Sample definition and timing
    Number of days between the date the residence permit (refugee status) was granted (tilladelsesdato) and 1 January 1999; RD with triangular kernel, local linear, cutoff 0. Sample: refugees and family-reunified to refugees admitted from 1997, aged 18-64, restricted to age < 50 so they can be followed 18 years post-reform; Somalis excluded in main sample.
    Registers: OPHG, BEF
    Codes: day_nr = dofd(tilladelsesdato) - date('01011999'); keep if age < 50; keep if somalia == 0
    replication code · 9. Sample selection.do, lines ~37-60, 122
  • Annual employment rate Employment and labour force status
    Annual first difference in cumulative labour market experience (ERHVER/1000 + ERHVER79) from IDAP, bounded to [0,1] and set to 0 if missing; first observed year uses the level. Separately, 'employed in November' = has a workplace ID (LBNR) in IDA.
    Registers: IDAP
    Codes: ERHVER, ERHVER79; emp = exper - exper_lag, truncated to 0-1; employment_nov = (LBNR ne ' ')
    replication code · 8. Controls and outcomes.sas, lines ~5016-5050, 5442, 5452-5474
  • Gross earnings and welfare benefits Earnings and income
    Gross earnings = LOENMV_13 from the income register; welfare benefits = sum of cash assistance (KONTHJ), refugee introduction allowance (KHFLYGT), other assistance (ANDBISTANDYD) and integration allowance (INTGRAYD); all deflated by the CPI (PRIS112 from Statistikbanken) and converted to 1000 USD at 6.6 DKK/USD.
    Registers: IND (INDUPD01)
    Codes: LOENMV_13; UA_sum = KONTHJ + KHFLYGT + ANDBISTANDYD + INTGRAYD; DISPON_13

Olivier B. Bargain and Anders B. Jonassen · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2024 · Individual

Maximum social assistance for childless unmarried Danes rose by 55 percent at age 25 between 2000 and 2006. Only the low-skilled respond: employment falls by 2 to 3 percent and benefit take-up rises by 10 to 14 percent, two thirds through moves from work to welfare, and crime shows no discontinuity.

Data
Danish administrative panel data on welfare benefit take-up, employment, earnings and crime (registers not named in abstract)
Key variables
  • Running variable: age relative to 25th birthday
  • Treatment: 55% increase in maximum social assistance at age 25 for childless unmarried individuals
  • Outcome: employment
  • Outcome: welfare benefit take-up
  • Outcome: criminal activity
Period
2000–2006
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Childless unmarried young people in Denmark around age 25, with effects concentrated among the low-skilled. source (abstract)
