  • Baseline sample (childless, single, low-educated natives) Sample definition and timing
    Individuals aged 20-29 (age measured in months, weekly panel 2000-2006) who are of Danish origin, have only basic education at the start and end of the year, live alone (not in a couple), have no children and are unmarried at both start and end of year; running variable is age relative to the 25th birthday.

    Codes: IE_TYPE == 1; edu (AUDD2015_L1L5_K from HFAUDD) == '10'; FM_MARK == 6; d_child == 0; CIVST == 'U'

    replication code · baseline.do, 'Defining weekly ordinary employment (wage), earnings (wage2), social assistance (sa)'
  • Ordinary employment (weekly) Employment and labour force status

Onur Altındağ, Jane Greve and Erdal Tekin · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2024 · Individual

A nationwide campaign against sudden infant death syndrome, delivered mainly through universal nurse home visits, cut infant mortality by 17 percent in a regression discontinuity on population birth data. Effects were 11 to 14 times larger for low-birthweight and preterm infants and concentrated among low-SES families.

Data
Medical Birth Register (MFR): birth weight, gestational age, parity, maternal age, immigrant status, Register of Causes of Death (exact date and cause of death), Education register (parental education)
Key variables
  • Running variable: birth month relative to December 1991
  • Treatment: birth after the 1991 change in infant sleep-position guidelines
  • Outcome: SIDS mortality per 10,000 births
  • Outcome: infant and child mortality per 10,000 births
  • Heterogeneity: low birth weight, preterm, maternal education
Period
Live births 1973–2006
Sample
568,106 births (SIDS outcome, MSE-optimal bandwidth of 52 months); 632,449 births for infant mortality (58 months) All live births in Denmark within the RD bandwidth around the December 1991 guideline change. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • Running variable / post-campaign treatment Sample definition and timing
    Days between the child's birth date and 31 December 1991 (main tables), with treatment = born after the cutoff; local linear specification with separate slopes, SEs clustered by birthday. The setup file also defines a birth-month distance to January 1992. Births up to 2006 retained.
    Registers: MFR
    Codes: dif = birthday - mdy(12,31,1991); setup: dif = ym(byear,bmonth) - ym(1992,1), treat = dif >= 0

  • Infant and child mortality per 10,000 births Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    mor1 = 10,000 if the child died (death register date) before the first birthday, 0 otherwise; mor5 = 10,000 if died before the fifth birthday. Deaths taken from DOD and linked to birth-register children.

    replication code · 01 Set up RD data.do, lines ~45-60; 01_mortality_no_cause.do

Other groups: infectious, neoplasms, nervous system, respiratory, perinatal, congenital malformations, unknown.
    Registers: DODSAARS, DODSAASG

Trade Shocks, Firm Hierarchies, and Wage Inequality

Benjamin U. Friedrich · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2022 · Individual + firm

Shows that trade shocks change within-firm wage inequality by changing firm hierarchies, using both firm-level foreign demand shocks and the Muslim boycott of Danish exports after the 2006 cartoon crisis. Adding a hierarchy layer widens pay gaps throughout the firm, and delayering after the boycott compresses wages through cuts, demotions and turnover.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) with DISCO occupation codes, Firm-Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (FIDA), Danish Business Register / firm statistics (GF): sales, value added, industry, Foreign Trade Statistics Register: firm-level exports by CN8 product and destination (UHDI), UN Comtrade bilateral trade flows (HS6), U.S. Imports of Merchandise, Penn World Tables distances, Brent oil prices (transport cost estimation)
Key variables
  • Outcome: within-firm wage inequality (std. dev. of log wages, 90-10 gap)
  • Treatment: number of hierarchy layers based on occupations
  • Instrument: firm-specific world import demand and transport-cost shocks
  • Natural experiment: 2006 Muslim boycott of Danish exports (Cartoon crisis)
Period
1999–2008
Sample
68,090 firm-year observations on 12,470 firms (within-firm inequality regressions) Universe of pre-existing private-sector exporting firms in Denmark, 1999–2008. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Occupational layer Occupation and job hierarchy
    Workers' DISCO occupation code (DISCOALLE_INDK) harmonised to 3 digits and mapped to four hierarchical layers following Caliendo et al. via a DISCO3-to-PCS layer correspondence; missing layers imputed from the same worker-firm's adjacent years (up to 2 years), then from the layer whose average hourly wage is closest; firm-years with more than 20% of hours requiring imputation are set to missing.
    Registers: IDAP, FIDA
    Codes: DISCOALLE_INDK; military code 0110/011000 recoded to 900; file correspondence_DISCO3_pcslayer
    replication code · Setup_Workerdata.do
  • Number of hierarchy layers Occupation and job hierarchy
    Number of distinct occupational layers present in the firm-year (layers renumbered consecutively from the lowest present), missing if more than 20% of firm hours had imputed layers; alternative 3-layer versions collapse layers 1-2 or use DISCO 3-digit <200 for layer 3.
    Registers: IDAP, FIDA
    Codes: layers = max(layerN); managers: first DISCO digit = 1
    replication code · Setup_Firm_Outcomes.do, lines ~72-185
  • Hourly wage and within-firm wage inequality Earnings and income
    Hourly wage TIMELON (job earnings JOBLON / hours) for active November jobs (JOBLON and TIMELON > 0), CPI-deflated to 2000; observations below the 0.25th or above the 99.75th percentile of the yearly hourly wage distribution dropped; firm-year inequality is the s.d. of log hourly wages and percentile gaps 90-10, 75-25, 90-50, 50-10.
    Registers: IDAP
    Codes: TIMELON, JOBLON; hours = JOBLON/TIMELON
    replication code · Setup_Firm_Outcomes.do, lines ~60-218; Setup_Workerdata.do
  • Private-sector sample Sector and industry
    Worker-level data restricted to IDA sector code 2 (private sector) before building firm outcomes.
    Registers: IDAP
    Codes: SEKTOR == "2"
    replication code · Setup_Firm_Outcomes.do, line 14
  • Firm sales, value added, industry Firm characteristics and productivity
    Sales (GF_OMS), value added (GF_BAV) and full-time equivalent employment (GF_AARSV) from firm statistics, CPI-deflated; industry from DB93/DB03 9-, 27- and 53-group aggregations, 2007 industry carried forward to 2008 if missing; firm age = year - start year + 1.
    Registers: FIRM (GF), FIRE
    Codes: GF_OMS, GF_BAV, GF_AARSV, GF_gr009_DB93/DB03, GF_gr027_DB93/DB03, GF_gr053_DB93/DB03
    replication code · Prepare_firmdata.do
  • Firm-level world import demand shock Trade and offshoring
    Firm-level Bartik shock: sum over HS6 product-destination pairs of the firm's pre-sample (first year exported, from 1998) export share times log world import demand, where world import demand is the destination country's total HS6 imports from the world excluding Denmark (Comtrade 1999-2008), aggregated to HS4/HS2 when HS6 unavailable.
    Registers: UHDI, UN Comtrade
    Codes: UHDI ie == 2 (exports); vrd (value), vgt (weight); HS1988/92 concordance
    replication code · Setup_Tradedata_Bartik.do, sections 'Main Setup' and '(A) WID'
  • Transport cost shock Trade and offshoring
    Predicted transport costs per product-destination from US Imports of Merchandise estimates, combining HS2 group coefficients, log Brent oil price, log distance, their interaction and (for one version) new-EU-member accession after 2003, weighted by the firm's pre-sample export shares.
    Registers: UHDI, US Imports of Merchandise, Brent oil prices
    Codes: neweumember = CY,CZ,EE,HU,LV,MT,PL,SI,SK & year > 2003
    replication code · Setup_Tradedata_Bartik.do, section '(B) Transport Costs'
  • Cartoon-crisis exposure (treatment) Trade and offshoring
    Treated firms exported to Muslim-majority countries (>50% Muslim population) in 2003-2005 and had more than 0.5% of 2005 exports going to those countries; control firms had no such exports in 2003-2005.
    Registers: UHDI
    Codes: treatment = 1 if Arabpre == 1 & Arabshare > 0.005; 0 if Arabpre == 0; country list by ISO2 (AE, AF, AL, AZ, BD, ...)
    replication code · Main_Sample_Cartoon.do, lines ~127-300
  • Offshoring indicator Trade and offshoring
    Firm imports (ie == 1) a product at HS4 or HS6 level that it also exports in the same year.
    Registers: UHDI
    Codes: offshoring_hs4, offshoring_hs6

Long-Run Saving Dynamics: Evidence from Unexpected Inheritances

Jeppe Druedahl and Alessandro Martinello · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2022 · Individual

Sudden parental deaths deliver unexpected inheritances. Heirs' wealth jumps and then declines over roughly a decade back toward its pre-inheritance path, which implies a moderate marginal propensity to consume out of wealth and informs the calibration of buffer-stock saving models.

Data
Wealth data from yearly third-party financial institution reports in the income/wealth registers (IND/FORMUE: BANKAKT, KURSANP, etc.), Individual tax returns / Income register (IND) for disposable income, Housing and land registers (property values, number of housing units), Birth registers / parent-child links (BEF), Mortality register / Register of Causes of Death (ICD-10 cause of death)
Key variables
  • Outcome: net worth normalized by permanent income
  • Outcome: liquid assets, housing equity, financial investments, uncollateralized debt
  • Treatment: timing of sudden parental death (ICD-10 I21–I22, V, X, Y, R96)
  • Potential inheritance: deceased parent's net worth split among children, net of inheritance tax
  • Permanent income: weighted average of past five years' disposable income
Period
1995–2012
Sample
6,286 heirs Heirs aged 25–50 at inheritance whose unmarried parent died suddenly between 1995 and 2012, with potential inheritance exceeding one year of permanent income, excluding the wealthiest 1 percent. source
How variables are defined (10)
  • Net worth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Sum of housing equity, liquid assets and financial wealth minus uncollateralized (bank) debt, at year end, CPI-deflated (2010=100) and divided by permanent income; pension funds and durables (cars, boats) excluded. Each component floored at 0 in code; individuals with net worth outside the 1st-99th percentile in any year are dropped.
    Registers: IND/FORMUE (GRUND files)
    Codes: totassets = stocks(KURSANP+KURSAKT) + bonds(PANTAKT+OBLAKT) + KOEJD + BANKAKT; totdebts = mortgage(OBLGAELD+PANTGAELD) + BANKGAELD; networth = totassets - totdebts
    replication code · data/server/rawbuild.do ('Wealth' block, 'SAMPLE SELECTION'); CEBI WP 02-17 Table D.1
  • Liquid assets Wealth, debt and consumption
    Sum of cash and savings accounts held in Danish banks (BANKAKT), floored at 0, normalized by permanent income.
    Registers: IND/FORMUE
    Codes: BANKAKT
    replication code · rawbuild.do; WP Table D.1
  • Housing equity Wealth, debt and consumption
    Value of owned real estate (KOEJD) minus collateralized debt (mortgage bonds OBLGAELD + other mortgage debt PANTGAELD, at market value of associated bonds at year end), normalized by permanent income.
    Registers: IND/FORMUE
    Codes: hequity = KOEJD - (OBLGAELD + PANTGAELD)
    replication code · rawbuild.do; WP Table D.1
  • Financial wealth and uncollateralized debt Wealth, debt and consumption
    Financial wealth = market value of directly held stocks, bonds and mutual funds (KURSANP+KURSAKT plus PANTAKT+OBLAKT in code; WP lists KURSANP+KURSAKT+OBLAKT); uncollateralized debt = bank debts not associated with a bond (BANKGAELD). Both normalized by permanent income.
    Registers: IND/FORMUE
    Codes: finw = max(0, KURSANP+KURSAKT + PANTAKT+OBLAKT); liqdebts = BANKGAELD
    replication code · rawbuild.do; WP Table D.1
  • Permanent income Earnings and income
    Weighted average of current and four lagged years of disposable income: 0.45, 0.25, 0.15, 0.10, 0.05 for t to t-4; disposable income = BRUTTO + SKATFRIYD + AKTIEINDK - SKATMVIALT_NY, CPI-deflated; floored at DKK 60,000 in code. Inheritance is normalized by permanent income in the year before parental death.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: dispinc = brutto + skatfriyd + aktieindk - skatmvialt_ny; perminc = filter(dispinc), coef(45 25 15 10 5) lags(0/4) normalise
    replication code · rawbuild.do ('Income'); WP Appendix D
  • Sudden parental death Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Parental death (1996-2012) is sudden if the primary cause of death has the listed ICD-10 codes. The WP states I21*-I22*, V*, X*, Y*, R96*; the replication code additionally includes I23, I24 and I46.
    Registers: Register of Causes of Death (doedsaars1), FTDB (parent-child links)
    Codes: WP: ICD-10 I21-I22, V*, X*, Y*, R96; code: substr(doedsaars1,1,3) in I21,I22,I23,I24,I46,R96 or first letter V, X, Y
    replication code · rawbuild.do ('DEATHS AND INHERITANCE'); CEBI WP 02-17 fn. 7 and Appendix D
  • Potential inheritance Wealth, debt and consumption
    Deceased parent's gross bequest (max(0,housing equity) + financial wealth + liquid assets - uncollateralized debt, floored at 0, in the last observed year) split equally among all children (from FTDB), net of inheritance tax: if estate exceeds the exemption bundfr, net = (0.85*(estate - bundfr) + bundfr)/n_heirs. Where both parents die, the largest inheritance is kept. Normalized by heir's permanent income; main sample has potential inheritance > 1 year of permanent income.
    Registers: IND/FORMUE, FTDB2012, Register of Causes of Death
    Codes: gross_bequest; n_heirs; bundfr (yearly exemption, e.g. 264,100 DKK in 2010); inhgroup==2 if inheritance>1
    replication code · rawbuild.do ('Remove taxes from inheritance'); main_analysis.do line ~96; WP Appendix D, Table D.3
  • Heir sample Sample definition and timing
    Heirs aged 25-59 in observed years, aged under 50 at the parental death (alder_atshock<50), with non-missing inheritance; net-worth outliers (outside p1-p99 in any year) dropped. WP: parents die unmarried between 1995 and 2012.
    Registers: BEF/GRUND, FTDB
    Codes: inrange(alder,25,59); alder_atshock<50
    replication code · rawbuild.do ('SAMPLE SELECTION'); main_analysis.do lines 14-29; WP Section I
  • Labour income, salary and pension contributions Earnings and income
    Labour income = ERHVERVSINDK (labour-market income incl. bonuses, compensations and self-employment income); salary = LOENMV (salary only); pension contributions = private (qpripen) plus labour-market (qarbpen) pension contributions.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: erhv (labor_income), loenmv (salary), pencontr = qarbpen + qpripen
    replication code · rawbuild.do ('INCOME UPDATE'); WP Table D.2
  • Number of housing units owned Wealth, debt and consumption
    Count of distinct properties (ejendom number x municipality) owned by the individual in the ownership register (EJER), plus total ownership share.
    Registers: EJER
    Codes: bnr = group(ejdnr komnr); n_owned; pct_owned = total(ejerpct)

The Impact of Immigration on Firm-Level Offshoring

William W. Olney and Dario Pozzoli · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2021 · Individual + firm

Uses the Danish refugee dispersal policy as a natural experiment and matched data on all firms and workers from 1995 to 2011. An exogenous inflow of immigrants into a municipality reduces firm-level offshoring on both margins, while immigrants' ties to their origin countries raise offshoring to those particular countries.

Data
Firm Statistics Register (FirmStat), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Firm-Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (FIDA), Foreign Trade Statistics Register: Intrastat and Extrastat firm-level imports (UHDI), Central Business Register (foreign ownership)
Key variables
  • Outcome: extensive margin of offshoring (firm imports in same HS4 as own production)
  • Outcome: log volume of narrow offshoring
  • Treatment: non-EU immigrant share of municipality workforce
  • Instrument: refugee placement under the 1986–1998 Spatial Dispersal Policy (shift-share)
Period
1995–2011
Sample
approximately 35,000 firms and 1 million workers Unbalanced panel of Danish private-sector firms with more than one employee in 97 municipalities, 1995–2011. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Narrow offshoring (volume and extensive margin) Trade and offshoring
    Sum of a firm's imports (Foreign Trade Statistics, Intrastat/Extrastat, 1995-2011) in the same product category as the firm's production (paper: same HS4 category; code: import product code equals the firm's export product code or domestic-production product code). Extensive margin = 1 if narrow offshoring > 0; intensive margin = log of narrow offshoring volume. Broad offshoring = all imports.
    Registers: UHDI (Foreign Trade Statistics: Intrastat/Extrastat), VARES (vars, firm product sales), FirmStat
    Codes: uhdi ie=='1' imports, ie=='2' exports; product vare (8-digit CN) -> HS4_imp=int(vare/100), HS4_exp=int(vare/100); vars varenr -> HS4_dom_1=int(varenr/10000); narrow=(HS6_imp==HS6_exp | HS6_imp==HS6_dom_1); ext_narrow_off=(narrow_off>0); int_narrow_off=ln(narrow_off)
    replication code · Trade_data.sas; offshoring_project_will_dario.do (narrow offshoring block); working paper Section 3 and fn. 23
  • Non-EU immigrant share of municipality workforce Immigration and origin
    Share of workers in a municipality-year (IDA, workplace municipality akom) who are not natives, where natives are ie_type=='1' (Danish origin) or born in an EU15 country; lagged one year in regressions. 97 municipalities (Copenhagen and Frederiksberg combined; pre-2007 municipalities recoded to post-reform codes).
    Registers: IDA, ie_type (immigrant type/origin from BEF)
    Codes: ie_type=='1' native; opr_land (ieland) EU15 codes 5126,5130,5180,5134,5142,5150,5108,5140,5156,5164,5170,5182,5104,5120 treated as natives; foreigner_nonEU=(natives!=1)

  • Shift-share instrument (predicted non-EU immigrant share) Immigration and origin
    For each origin country d, the national number of immigrants in year t is allocated to municipalities using the municipality's 1990 share of immigrants from d, summed over non-EU origins and normalized by municipality total employment in 1990.
    Registers: IDA (1990 extract idapall_eer_1990)
    Codes: F_hat_cmt=s_cm88*F_ct; s_hat=F_hat_no_eu/P_m88

  • Managers, middle managers and blue-collar workers Occupation and job hierarchy

Correlation of Brothers' Earnings and Intergenerational Transmission

Paul Bingley and Lorenzo Cappellari · Review of Economics and Statistics, 2019 · Individual

Decomposes the earnings correlation between Danish brothers into the part explained by fathers' earnings and the part due to other shared family and community factors. Intergenerational transmission accounts for a larger share of sibling similarity than simple father-son elasticities suggest, once permanent earnings and life-cycle bias are handled.

Data
Civil registration system / population register with parent-child links (BEF), Income Statistics Register (IND): annual pre-tax labour earnings from tax returns
Key variables
  • Outcome: annual pre-tax labour earnings (sum over all employments), ages 25–60
  • Family structure: father/first-son/second-son triads
  • Life-cycle: 3-year birth cohort groups and age
Period
1980–2014
Sample
303,231 men in 101,077 families; 5,488,445 earnings observations Danish fathers born 1935–1961 and their first and second sons (born 1959–1985) with the same mother, with at least five consecutive positive earnings observations. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Annual labour earnings Earnings and income
    Annual pre-tax labour earnings from income tax returns, summed over all employments in the year, 1980-2014, deflated to 2012 DKK with a year-specific index (earn/R*6768). In code: IDA person variable lonind for 1980-2009, corloen for 2010-2011 and from the IND register for 2012-2014; negative values recoded to 0.
    Registers: IDA (idaperson), IND, Income Statistics Register
    Codes: lonind (IDA person 1980-2009); corloen (2010-2014)
    replication code · triplet-data-creation-20160706.do ('collect earnings histories'); IZA DP10761 Section III
  • Earnings sample trimming and age window Sample definition and timing
    Person-year observations kept at (cohort-central) ages 25-60; missing and non-positive earnings dropped; the lower and upper 0.5% of earnings dropped by family member type (father, son 1, son 2) and year; individuals must have at least 5 consecutive years of earnings observations.
    Registers: IDA, IND
    replication code · inspection.do ('EARNINGS TRIMMINGS', consecutive-observation block)
  • Father/first-son/second-son triads Family links, fertility and household
    Fathers born 1935-1961 (code frame 1935-1969) with two sons by the same mother, linked through the fertility database (ftdb2010, father pnrf and mother pnrm) restricted to madopt=='1'; twins/multiple births dropped; only sons of the same mother-father match as the father's first son kept; sons who are themselves fathers in the sample are dropped; families whose triplet birth order is inconsistent with population birth order are purged; fathers younger than 18 (216 months) at first son's birth dropped; brother spacing must be 12-144 months; first sons born 1959-1985, second sons 1962-1985.
    Registers: BEF/fodselsdata, Fertility database (ftdb2010)
    Codes: koen=='1' (male); madopt=='1'; birth order border 0=father,1=son1,2=son2
    replication code · triplet-data-creation-20160706.do; inspection.do; IZA DP10761 Section III
  • 3-year birth cohort groups Sample definition and timing
    Individuals are grouped into 3-year birth cohorts (central years 1936, 1939, ..., 1984), with the cohort's central birth year used to compute age (ageco = year - cohort).
    Registers: BEF
    replication code · inspection.do
  • Years of schooling (own and father's) Education and test scores
    Years of completed education computed as int(HFPRIA/12) from the latest available education register record (1980-2009), recoding 0-7 to 7 and 18-21 to 18; father's schooling linked through the fertility database father identifier.
    Registers: UDDA, Fertility database (ftdb2010)
    Codes: hfpria; educ=int(hfpria/12), recode 0/7=7, 18/21=18
    replication code · data-creation-triplet-education.do
  • Sibling birth-order counts Family links, fertility and household
    Numbers of older/younger brothers and sisters with the same father and with the same father-mother pair, computed over all children of the father (twins ordered randomly), for robustness to sibling composition.
    Registers: fodselsdata, Fertility database (ftdb2010)
    Codes: nobsf, nybsf, nobsfm, nybsfm, nossf, nyssf, nossfm, nyssfm
    replication code · triplet-data-creation-20160706.do ('find all siblings')

Follows Danish textile and clothing workers for a decade after the removal of quotas on Chinese imports, using within-industry and within-occupation differences in exposure. 1999–2010

10,521 workers All workers with primary employment in the Danish textile and clothing sector in 1999, born 1943–1982 (aged 20–67 over 2002–2010). source

    Worker is treated if his/her 1999 primary employer domestically produced in 1999 (at the 8-digit CN level, per VARES) any good subject to the MFA quota removal for China; SIGL quota categories are mapped to CN 8-digit products (CN 1999) and firm ids are linked to workers through FIDA. Universal Daycare and Mothers' Working Lifetime

Sarah Sander · Economic Journal, 2026 · Individual

Exploits the roll-out of daycare centres across Danish municipalities to follow mothers over their working lives. Daycare availability raises participation, hours and earnings sixteen years after the first birth, with effects driven by low-educated mothers and mediated partly through fertility and separation.

Data
1970 Census (FT70) with parish of residence, Historical daycare institution yearbooks digitised (1964–1975) and daycare institutions in registers from 1976, Population register with parent-child links and fertility histories (BEF), Earnings from tax records (income registers), 1980–2015, Supplementary Pension Fund register (ATP) contributions for hours and participation, Education registers (UDDA)
Key variables
  • Treatment: daycare availability in the mother's 1970 parish after first birth
  • Outcome: labour force participation by age of first child
  • Outcome: log annual earnings
  • Outcome: weekly hours and full-time employment from ATP contributions
  • Mediators: fertility and separation from child's father
Period
First births 1964–1975; earnings 1980–2015
Sample
370,602 mothers Non-immigrant women resident in Denmark in the 1970 census who had their first child between 1964 and 1975 and stayed in Denmark until the child turned 16. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Daycare availability in 1970 parish (treatment) Geography and neighbourhood
    Mothers are placed in their parish of residence in the 1970 Census. vg = 1 if a daycare institution for ages 0-2 (nursery or integrated institution, from digitised institution data) existed in the parish in the year of first birth; bh = same for ages 3-6 (kindergarten); availability is also tracked for each year from child age 0 to 6 (all/some/no years).
    Registers: FT70 (1970 Census, parish), Daycare institution yearbooks/registers
    Codes: institution number NUMMER < 120000 = nursery (vuggestue), > 250000 = integrated; parish (SOGNNR) x year; vg, bh, daycare0-daycare6
    replication code · dofiles/createfirst.do, 'FOLKETÆLLING 1970', 'DAYCARE 0-2', 'DAYCARE 3-6'
  • Mother sample and timing of first birth Sample definition and timing
    Native (IE_TYPE 1) women born 1920-1959 with a first child born 1964-1975, aged at least 13 at first birth, with a 1970 parish observed and surviving until the first child is 16. First-birth year is the earliest birth year among children linked through MOR_ID (supplemented by family-register child counts).
    Registers: BEF, Fødselsdata (birth data), FAMILIE, FT70
    Codes: IE_TYPE == 1; MOR_ID; yrfirst in 1964-1975
    replication code · dofiles/createfirst.do, 'SAMLING AF BEF...' block
  • Hours (ATP-based) and full-time employment Hours worked
    Annual ATP pension contributions (sum of orer/100 per person-year) are divided by the full-time contribution amount for the year (194.4 up to 1964, 259.2 up to 1971, 302 in 1972, 432 in 1973-1981, 1166.4 from 1982) and capped at 1. Full-time = ratio of 1; for workers the ratio is converted to weekly hours as 9 + 26 x ratio. Measured for child ages 0-35; missing set to 0 if the mother is alive.
    Registers: ATP
    Codes: ATP field ORER; divisors 194.4/259.2/302/432/1166.4 by year; full = hours>=1
    replication code · dofiles/createfirst.do, '*ATP' block and final forvalues x=0/35 loop
  • Labour force participation by child age Employment and labour force status
    For child ages 0-15, participation = positive ATP contributions in the year (hours > 0); for ages 16-40, participation = positive wage earnings (non-missing log earnings), set to 0 if missing and the mother is alive.
    Registers: ATP, IND
    Codes: work = hours>0; xwork = learn (loglon non-missing) for ages 16-40
    replication code · dofiles/createfirst.do, final loops
  • Log annual earnings Earnings and income
    Wage income (LONIND, replaced with corrected wage income CORLOEN in 2010-2015) converted to 2016 DKK with fixed year factors and to US dollars (6.7327), negative values set to 0, top-coded at 400,000, and logged (also inverse hyperbolic sine); measured child ages 5-40. Gross income (BRUTTO) is treated the same way for 1976 onward.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: LONIND, CORLOEN, BRUTTO
    replication code · dofiles/createfirst.do, 'LØN INDKOMST' and 'BRUTTO INDKOMST'
  • Mother's education before first birth Education and test scores
    Years of education (normed months/12) completed by the year of first birth, taken from the highest, vocational or general education fields with completion dates before the first birth (or inferred from age 5 + length), with self-reported sources dropped and minimum 7 years; grouped into basic (main level 10), medium (20, 25, 35) and high.
    Registers: UDDA
    Codes: HFPRIA, EKPRIA, ALMPRIA; HFAUDD, ERHAUDD, ALMAUDD; HF_VFRA, ERH_VFRA, ALM_VFRA; drop HF_KILDE in 3, 9, 10, 17, 18; H1 10 = basic, 20/25/35 = medium
    replication code · dofiles/createfirst.do, 'UDDANNELSE FØR FØRSTE BARN'
  • Separation from the first child's father Family links, fertility and household
    divor = 1 if the mother's partner ID (C_FAELLE_ID) in the population register when the first child is 16 differs from the first child's father ID (FAR_ID); missing if father unknown.
    Registers: BEF
    Codes: C_FAELLE_ID at age 16 of first child vs FAR_ID
    replication code · dofiles/createfirst.do, 'DIVORSE' block and divor definition
  • Fertility and birth spacing Family links, fertility and household
    Number of children (more1-more4 indicators for at least 2-5 children) and time from first to second birth (space1-space3: second birth within 1, 2, 3 years).
    Registers: BEF, FAMILIE
    Codes: numkid; yrnext - yrfirst
    replication code · dofiles/createfirst.do; resfirst_final_EJ.do, Table 7
  • Early retirement / pension Retirement and pensions
    From IDA labour market position, early retirement pension = PSTILL 50, 55 or 56 and old-age pension = PSTILL 92, 93 or 94; first year observed used to compute pension age.

Genetic and Socioeconomic Achievement Gaps in Elementary School

Mikkel Aagaard Houmark, Victor Ronda, Esben Agerbo, Preben Bo Mortensen and Michael Rosholm · Economic Journal, 2025 · Individual

Shows that the achievement gap by polygenic score for educational attainment is as large as the gap by socioeconomic status and widens during elementary school, but only among low-SES children. Selection into neighbourhoods and schools explains part of the SES gap but none of the genetic gap, which instead relates to conscientiousness and the learning environment.

Data
iPSYCH2015 case-cohort genotype sample (neonatal blood spots from the Danish National Biobank), Danish national tests (reading and mathematics, grades 2–8), Population registers with parent-child links (BEF), Parental income registers (IND), Parental education registers (UDDA), Psychiatric diagnoses of parents (patient registers), School and neighbourhood identifiers
Key variables
  • Outcome: standardised national reading test scores (grades 2, 4, 6, 8); mathematics tests (grades 3, 6, 8)
  • Key regressor: polygenic score for educational attainment (EA PGS)
  • Key regressor: SES index from parental income and education
  • Sibling fixed effects: within-family variation in the PGS
  • Mediators: neighbourhood and school sorting
Period
Births 1994–2008; national tests from 2010
Sample
40,136 individuals with 87,917 reading test outcomes (24,062 psychiatric cases, 16,074 random controls); sibling sample 2,705 individuals Genotyped iPSYCH children of European descent born 1994–2008 who completed at least one national test between 2nd and 8th grade. source
How variables are defined (11)
  • National reading test score Education and test scores
    Danish national (adaptive, Rasch-scored) reading tests in grades 2, 4, 6 and 8: each of the three profile areas (text comprehension, language comprehension, decoding) is standardised by school year, averaged, and the average re-standardised to mean 0, SD 1. Repeated tests of the same subject-grade are dropped (first test kept by test time).
    Registers: Danish national tests
    Codes: FAGID 0102, 0104, 0106, 0108 = reading grades 2, 4, 6, 8; outcome variable ztheta
    working paper · Section 3.2; Results (for replication).do
  • National mathematics test score Education and test scores
    Mathematics national tests in grades 3 and 6 and, from 2018, grade 8, constructed in a similar fashion to the reading score.
    Registers: Danish national tests
    Codes: FAGID 0203, 0206, 0208 = mathematics grades 3, 6, 8
    replication code · Results (for replication).do; IZA DP 15418 Section 3.2
  • Parental years of education Education and test scores
    Mother's and father's highest education category converted to years of schooling.
    Registers: UDDA
    Codes: mhighestedu/fhighestedu: 10,15 -> 10 years; 20,25,30,35 -> 13; 40 -> 15; 50,60 -> 16; 65 -> 18; 70 -> 21
    replication code · Results (for replication).do, 'Prepare covariates'
  • Family disposable income in early childhood Earnings and income
    Mother's and father's disposable income deflated by CPI (2015=100), averaged over child ages 1-7, summed across parents and logged (set to 0 if negative).
    Registers: IND
    Codes: disp_income_m_1..7, disp_income_f_1..7; famdinc18 = momdispinc18 + daddispinc18
    replication code · Results (for replication).do
  • SES rank / SES index Earnings and income
    Families are ranked in percentiles (one observation per child) on the sum of parents' years of education and on log family disposable income; the two percentile ranks are summed and re-ranked into percentiles scaled to 0-0.99 (ses_rank), and the SES index is this rank standardised to mean 0, SD 1 within the sample.
    Registers: IND, UDDA
    Codes: xtile famedu_rank, faminc_rank nq(100); famses_rank; ses_std = std(ses_rank)
    replication code · Results (for replication).do; IZA DP 15418 Section 3.4
  • Parental psychiatric diagnosis Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicators for the mother and father ever having received a psychiatric diagnosis (based on the date of the parent's first psychiatric diagnosis in the parental psychiatry file); an additional indicator flags a diagnosis by the child's birth year.
    Registers: Psychiatric patient registers (parentalpsych file)
    Codes: mpsych_date, fpsych_date -> mmh_ever, fmh_ever, mmh_age0, fmh_age0
    replication code · Results (for replication).do
  • Risk index / low-SES indicator Family links, fertility and household
    Sum of four risk indicators: both parents with 10 years of education; family disposable income in the bottom birth-cohort quintile; either parent ever with a psychiatric diagnosis; family not intact. ses2 groups risk 0-1 vs 2-4.
    Registers: IND, UDDA, BEF
    Codes: risk1..risk4; fdinc2 = xtile(famdinc18, n(5)) by yearborn
    replication code · Results (for replication).do
  • Sibling sample / family fixed effect Sample definition and timing
    Families defined by the mother-father ID pair (full siblings); the sibling sample includes children with at least one full sibling observed on the same test.
    Registers: BEF
    Codes: fef = group(pnrm pnrf)
    replication code · Results (for replication).do
  • European descent sample restriction Immigration and origin
    Keeps children of European genetic ancestry (non_european==0) or, if missing, those whose own and both parents' region of birth is Denmark or Europe; required because the EA GWAS uses European-descent samples.
    Registers: BEF, iPSYCH2015
    Codes: non_european; region_birth, region_birth_m, region_birth_f in {Denmark, Europe}
    replication code · Results (for replication).do, top
  • School quality (teacher-based) Education and test scores
    Following Gensowski et al. (2020), teachers are linked to schools; school-by-year averages of teacher high-school GPA, age, experience, tenure, sick-leave share and share of the previous ten years unemployed are used to predict school national test scores, and the predictions are used to rank schools by teacher quality.
    Registers: Population, institution and workplace registers, Danish national tests
    Codes: schoolqlt3 (merged by INSTNR, skoleaar)
    working paper · Section 3.6
  • School absence Education and test scores
    Total fraction of school days absent, including all absence regardless of reason, from the absence registries.
    Registers: School absence register (fravaer)
    working paper · Section 3.6

Neighbourhood Gangs, Crime Spillovers and Teenage Motherhood

Christian Dustmann, Mikkel Mertz and Anna Okatenko · Economic Journal, 2023 · Individual

Uses the random assignment of refugees to municipalities between 1986 and 1998. Gang crime in the assignment neighbourhood raises boys' probability of offending before 19 and girls' probability of teenage motherhood, with lasting consequences: more inactivity for men and lower earnings and more benefit claims for women at ages 19 to 28.

Data
Immigration register, Annual population registers (BEF), Central Police Register (criminal charges and convictions), Education registers (including survey-based register of immigrants' education), Income registers and register-based labour force statistics (RAS), National Patient Register (abortions)
Key variables
  • Outcome: teenage motherhood (child born while aged 15–18); youth crime convictions for boys
  • Treatment: municipal group (gang) crime conviction rate of males 15–25 in assignment year
  • Identification: quasi-random assignment of refugees to municipalities under the 1986–1998 dispersal policy
  • Long-run outcomes: earnings, employment, education
Period
Refugee assignment 1986–1998; population registers 1980–2019
Sample
8,172 assigned refugee children; 3,792 girls in teenage motherhood estimation sample Refugee children from eight refugee-sending countries assigned to Danish municipalities at age 0–14 between 1986 and 1998, observed every year until age 19. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Convictions (guilty cases) Crime
    Judicial decisions 1980-2018 from the conviction register; for each person-case (journr) the final decision is kept (appeals), and a case counts as guilty unless the decision type is acquittal or dismissal. Offences are classified by 7-digit offence code into violent/sexual, property, drug, other and traffic, and traffic offences are dropped; the date of the offence comes from the charge register.
    Registers: KRAF (conviction register), KRSI (charge register)
    Codes: AFG_AFGTYP3 in 514, 411, 412, 413, 414 = acquitted/dismissed (else guilty); AFG_GER7: sexual and violent 1110505-1180705 and 1210501-1292520; property 1304505-1398590; drug 1435505-1440505 and 3210505-3210510; other 1410303-1430740, 1445705-1485720, 3410505-3410509, 3610105-3870505 (residual non-missing also other); traffic 2110005-2610180 (dropped)
    replication code · do/build/clean/convictions.do
  • Group (gang) crime conviction Crime
    A conviction for a gang-type offence in a case where more than one person is convicted (gang_crime_3 requires at least three). Gang-type offences are non-sexual violence, arson/robbery-type property offences, drug offences and weapons offences; a case is gang-type if anyone in the case is convicted of a gang-type offence.
    Registers: KRAF
    Codes: gang type: 2-digit AFG_GER7 (floor(ger7/100000)) == 12; 4-digit (floor(ger7/1000)) in 1312, 1339, 1380, 1390, 1435, 1440, 3410; 7-digit in 1366505, 1445750, 1445777-1445782, 3210510; gang_crime = N convicted in journr > 1 & gang type
    replication code · do/build/clean/convictions.do
  • Municipal youth (gang) crime conviction rate Crime
    Per municipality and year: number of male residents aged 15-25 (calendar year minus birth year between 15 and 26) with at least one conviction (resp. gang-crime conviction) for an offence committed that year at age above 14 and below 27, divided by the number of such male residents, times 100. Offences from 2017 onward or before 1980 are dropped.
    Registers: KRAF, KRSI, BEF
    Codes: sh_g (gang), sh_nc (overall); KOEN==1 for men; KOM municipality
    replication code · do/build/prepare/kom_year_n_criminals.do
  • Assigned refugee (dispersal-policy sample) Immigration and origin
    Immigrants arriving 1986-1998 from refugee-sending countries (Balkan origins excluded as covered by a different placement policy), with some countries restricted by arrival year; the household head at immigration is identified via father, mother (if under 18) or spouse links, and individuals arriving more than a year after the household head, or with a gap of more than one year between immigration and first appearance in the registers, are dropped.
    Registers: BEF, Immigration register (date of immigration)
    Codes: IELAND: Iraq 5436; Iran 5438 (arrival>=1980); Vietnam 5468, 5488; Sri Lanka 5418 (>=1984); stateless Lebanon 5103, 5456, 5473; Ethiopia 5214 (<1991); Afghanistan 5404; Somalia 5289 (>=1989); keep refugee_ieland<=8
    replication code · do/build/prepare/assigned_refugees.do
  • Assignment municipality Geography and neighbourhood
    The first municipality (KOM) in which the household head at assignment is observed in the population registers after immigration; children assigned to a different municipality than their household head are dropped, and Copenhagen assignment is KOM 101.
    Registers: BEF
    Codes: first_kom = kom[1]; copenhagen = KOM 101
    replication code · do/build/prepare/assigned_refugees.do; sample_girls_15_20_at_assignment.do
  • Teenage motherhood Family links, fertility and household
    Date of first birth is the earliest birth date among children linked to the woman through the mother ID (PNRM) in the population registers; teenage motherhood (mother_1518) equals 1 if the first birth occurs at age at least 14 and below 19 (commented 'had a child by age 19'). For girls aged 15-20 at assignment, motherhood within 4 years of assignment is used, dropping those whose first birth is within 280 days of immigration.
    Registers: BEF
    Codes: PNRM (mother ID); mother_1518 = (date_first_birth - date_birth)/365.25 in [14,19)
    replication code · do/build/clean/pnr_date_first_two_births.do; do/build/prepare/kids_by_age.do; sample_girls_15_20_at_assignment.do
  • Abortion Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicator for an abortion diagnosis in the National Patient Register 1980-2014 (medical, other, unspecified and failed attempted abortion), attached to refugee girls.
    Registers: LPR
    Codes: ICD-10 (DIAG first 4 chars) DO04, DO05, DO06, DO07
    replication code · do/build/prepare/abortion.do
  • Labour market status (employed / unemployed / not in labour force) Employment and labour force status
    Primary labour market status in the last week of November from RAS, with code schemes varying by year.
    Registers: RAS
    Codes: 1981-1993 ARBSTIL: employed 11-39, unemployed 40, NILF 50-92 (1990+ keep NOVPRIO==1); 1994-1995 NYARB: employed 11-39, unemployed 40, NILF 41-400; 1996-2007 SOCSTIL_KODE: employed 115-199, unemployed 200, NILF 201-400; 2008-2015 SOC_STATUS_KODE (PRIMAER_STATUS_KODE==1): employed 110-138, 611, 612, unemployed 200, NILF 311-517
    replication code · do/build/clean/pool_ras_for_lm_status.do

    For assigned refugee children 1987-2018, income outcomes are taken from the income register over the full year and education from the education registers (measured in October of the year prior), with employment taken from RAS for November of the previous year.

Education, Birth Order and Family Size

Jesper Bagger, Javier A. Birchenall, Hani Mansour and Sergio Urzúa · Economic Journal, 2021 · Individual

Develops a model of parental investment with birth order preferences and human capital cost differences that delivers a generalised quantity–quality trade-off. Danish administrative data confirm its predictions: at any given parity, children in smaller families have more education, and the average child's education falls with family size even after accounting for birth order.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), 1980–2006, with mother-child links, Precise date of birth from Statistics Denmark (to identify twin/multiple births)
Key variables
  • Outcome: years of education (measured in 2006)
  • Key regressors: birth order and family size
  • Instrument: twin birth at last birth (twins at 2nd, 3rd or 4th birth)
  • Controls: parental education, gender, age
Period
1980–2006 (outcomes measured in 2006)
Sample
1,256,031 children in 581,159 families (excluding single-child families) Individuals aged 25–41 in 2006 whose mother was alive and present in IDA during 1980–2006, in families with completed fertility, siblings defined by common mother. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Years of education Education and test scores
    Highest completed education in 2006 from the IDA person files (8-digit HFFSP code), mapped to years of education using the first two digits per Table A.1 (e.g. 10 = primary: 7 years if born 1958 or earlier, 9 years if born 1959 or later; 20/25 = high school 12; 35 = vocational 12; 40 = short further 14; 50 = medium-length further 16; 60 = Bachelor 15; 65 = Master 18; 70 = PhD 20; 90 = unknown, missing).
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: HFFSP 2-digit: 10->7/9, 15,17->10, 20->12, 25->12, 30->10, 35->12, 40->14, 50->16, 60->15, 65->18, 70->20, 90->missing
    working paper · Appendix C and Table A.1
  • Family size and siblings Family links, fertility and household
    Siblings are children born to the same mother (families defined by mother's identity, via the IDA pointer to mother's person ID); family size is the number of siblings born to the same mother, recorded before individual-level selection. Families with children born after 1991 (any child aged 0-14 residing at mother's address in 2006) are excluded so family size reflects completed fertility.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 4 and Appendix C (fn. 29)
  • Birth order Family links, fertility and household
    Order of birth of each child within the mother's family, identified using precise date of birth obtained from Statistics Denmark and merged onto IDA (69.4% of IDA individuals matched, unmatched mostly older cohorts).
    Registers: IDA, Date-of-birth data (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Appendix C and footnote 22
  • Twin (multiple) birth instrument Family links, fertility and household
    Multiple births identified from precise dates of birth (24,186 twin sets, 217 triplets, 5 quadruplets); twin observations themselves are dropped, retaining an indicator for a twin birth in the family and its order. Family size is instrumented with twins at the second, third or fourth birth in respective samples, and with twins at last birth.
    Registers: IDA, Date-of-birth data (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Appendix C (fn. 25) and Section 5
  • Analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    Individuals aged 25-41 in 2006 linked to a mother alive, aged 15-70 and present in IDA during 1980-2006. Excludes families with mother younger than 17 or older than 49 at birth, missing education for any member, non-twin siblings born less than seven months apart, unknown or different fathers, children born after 1991, and single-child families; 1,256,031 individuals in 581,159 families.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 4 (fn. 15) and Appendix C
  • Parental income measures Earnings and income
    Parental income measures are trimmed by recoding observations in the 1st and 99th percentiles as missing; mother's education measured in the last year she appears in the data.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Appendix C

Children, intergenerational mobility and skills Education Family responses and insurance

Family, Community and Long-Term Socio-Economic Inequality: Evidence from Siblings and Youth Peers

Paul Bingley, Lorenzo Cappellari and Konstantinos Tatsiramos · Economic Journal, 2021 · Individual

Decomposes sibling correlations in permanent earnings, education and unemployment for the Danish population into family and community components, allowing for life-cycle dynamics. Family is the dominant factor; community background shapes earnings and unemployment correlations early in working life but fades quickly.

Data
Civil registration system / population register with parent links (BEF), Central person register address histories (parish of residence), Education register / national pupil database (school at age 15), Annual earnings from tax-based income registers
Key variables
  • Outcome: pre-tax annual labour earnings (residual log earnings), 1984–2011
  • Grouping: brothers (family), schoolmates at age 15, parish neighbours at age 15
  • Parameters: sibling, school-peer and neighbour correlations over the life cycle
Period
Men born 1960–1983; earnings 1984–2011
Sample
695,960 men; 10,930,859 earnings observations (122,652 brother pairs, 380,948 singletons) Danish men born 1960–1983 (first and second sons sharing both legal parents, plus singletons and same-age peers), linked to schoolmates and parish neighbours at age 15. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • Residual log annual earnings Earnings and income
    Pre-tax annual labour earnings 1984-2011 in 2005 prices; zero-earnings observations excluded, a quarter of a percentile trimmed from each tail of the annual distribution, and at least three consecutive earnings observations required. Residuals from regressing log real gross annual earnings on year dummies and a quadratic age trend by two-year birth cohort group.
    Registers: Tax-based income registers (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 2 (Eq. 1) and Section 3.1
  • Brother pairs Family links, fertility and household
    First and second sons (born 1960-1983) of sampled fathers who share both legal parents from registration at birth and are not adopted; son birth order determined irrespective of daughters. Excludes sons also observed as fathers and brothers born less than 12 months or more than 12 years apart (122,652 pairs); singletons kept.
    Registers: Civil registration system (CPR) / population register
    working paper · Section 3.1 and footnote 10
  • Schoolmates at age 15 Education and test scores
    Males born in the same calendar year enrolled in the same school on 31 October of the calendar year they turn 15 (normally 9th grade), from the national pupil database (covers grade 8 and above from August 1973). Pupils at schools exclusively for special educational needs are excluded.
    Registers: Education register / national pupil database
    working paper · Section 3.1 and footnotes 11, 13, 14
  • Parish neighbours at age 15 Geography and neighbourhood
    Neighbourhood defined as parish of residence (available from 1973) from the central person register address data on 31 October of the calendar year the male turns 15; neighbours are males born in the same year living in the same parish (2,123 parishes).
    Registers: Central person register (CPR addresses)
    working paper · Section 3.1 and footnote 12
  • Cohort grouping Sample definition and timing
    Data grouped into two-year birth cohorts (1960-61 to 1982-83) with age imputed from the first year of birth; each cohort observed from age 24 for at least 6 years and up to 28 years.
    Registers: Population register, Income registers
    working paper · Section 3.1, Table 1

Sibling Spillovers

Sandra E. Black, Sanni Breining, David N. Figlio, Jonathan Guryan, Krzysztof Karbownik, Helena Skyt Nielsen, Jeffrey Roth and Marianne Simonsen · Economic Journal, 2021 · Individual

Identifies spillovers within the family from having a disabled younger sibling using administrative data from both Denmark and Florida. Comparing first- and second-born children in families with three or more children, the second child, who spends more early childhood with the younger sibling, is differentially affected when the third child is disabled.

Data
Medical Birth Register (MFR), National Patient Register (LPR) for disability diagnoses, 9th grade exit exam grades (school/education registers), Parental education, labour market, earnings and leave registers, Florida birth records linked to Florida public school records (FCAT)
Key variables
  • Outcome: cohort-standardised 9th grade exit exam GPA (Denmark); FCAT test scores (Florida)
  • Treatment: third-born sibling has a disability (diagnosed in medical registers) observed by age five
  • Comparison: second-born vs first-born child (difference-in-differences)
  • Controls: parental age, education, labour market status, earnings, immigrant status
Period
Danish births 1990–2001; Florida births 1994–2002
Sample
Denmark: 134,277 families with first two children observed, 28,581 families with first three children (4,430 with a disabled third child by age five); Florida: 80,879 and 9,987 families Families in Denmark (births 1990–2001) and Florida (births 1994–2002) with at least three children where the first two children have the same father. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • Third-born sibling disability (treatment) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicator D = 1 if the third-born child is observed disabled, in Denmark from disabilities recorded in the medical (patient) registries, with the main treatment being disability first observed by age five (alternatively between ages five and ten). Most common Danish by-age-five disabilities: asthma (41%), congenital malformations of the musculoskeletal system (20%), congenital malformations of the circulatory system (10%); diagnosis code lists are not given.
    Registers: Danish medical patient register
    working paper · Section 2 (Data) and Eq. (1)
  • 9th grade exit exam GPA Education and test scores
    Cohort-standardised 9th grade exit exam grades (GPA), based on assessments by the student's teacher and an external reviewer, normalised to mean zero and standard deviation one.
    Registers: School records / grade register
    working paper · Sections 1-2 and Eq. (1)
  • Birth order / exposure (second vs first born) Family links, fertility and household
    M = 1 if the child is second born ('more exposed'), 0 if first born; birth order measured from exact dates of birth in the Birth Register with parent-child links. Sample restricted to families with at least three children where the first two children have the same father; Danish births 1990-2001.
    Registers: Danish Birth Register (MFR)
    working paper · Sections 2-3, Eq. (1)
  • Disability type and severity Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Disabilities grouped into physical, cognitive and behavioral; severity checked using hospitalisation records (inpatient, outpatient and emergency room admissions).
    Registers: Danish medical patient register
    working paper · Section 4, footnotes 11-12
  • Parental background controls Family links, fertility and household
    Parental age, educational attainment, labour market status, earnings, leave taking and immigrant status from administrative registers linked via the unique identification number; regression covariates include year and month of birth and child gender with family fixed effects.
    Registers: Administrative registers (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 2 and Section 3

Gender Differences in Negotiation: Evidence from Real Estate Transactions

Steffen Andersen, Julie Marx, Kasper Meisner Nielsen and Lise Vesterlund · Economic Journal, 2021 · Individual

Men appear to secure better prices than women in Danish real estate transactions, but the gap shrinks with better controls for property value and disappears in repeat-sales and inherited-property samples. The price differences reflect men and women demanding different properties, not differences in negotiation.

Data
Property transactions from the Danish Tax and Customs Administration (SKAT), Housing register (BBR), Civil Registration System (CPR), Income and tax-assessed property values from SKAT, Education registers (Ministry of Education), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) employment status, Cause-of-Death Register (Danish National Board of Health)
Key variables
  • Outcome: realised transaction price of house or apartment
  • Key regressor: gender of single buyer/seller
  • Controls: tax-assessed property value, BBR property characteristics, property fixed effects (repeated sales)
  • Death sales: properties inherited by an only child from a deceased parent
Period
1994–2013
Sample
337,685 real estate transactions (97,216 in repeated-sales sample; 13,953 inherited houses and apartments in death-sales sample) Arm's-length transactions of Danish houses and apartments involving single female or single male buyers and sellers, 1994–2013. source
How variables are defined (10)
  • Buyer and seller identification Sample definition and timing
    Buyers are the owners of the property (per BBR owner records) on January 1 in the year after the transaction; sellers are the owners on January 1 in the year of the transaction. If the sales agreement is signed in year t but ownership is transferred in t+1, buyers are the owners on January 1 of t+2, conditional on no registered trades during t+1.
    Registers: BBR, SKAT property transactions (Statstidende), CPR
    online appendix · Appendix A, Data sources (and footnote 1)
  • Transaction sample restrictions Sample definition and timing
    All property transactions 1994-2013 restricted to single-family houses and apartments bought and sold by individuals; drops transactions flagged by Statistics Denmark as involving price clauses or extreme prices, rented-out properties, properties traded more than once within a year, transactions within a household or between parents and children, households buying or selling more than three properties in a year, and agents outside ages 18-65. Cottages, farms and cooperative housing are excluded.
    Registers: SKAT property transactions, BBR, CPR
    online appendix · Appendix A, Sample selection; paper Section 2
  • Stable household / single man / single woman Family links, fertility and household
    Households use the Statistics Denmark household ID: one or two adults plus children under 25 living with them; three types are couples (married, registered and cohabiting partners), single women and single men. A household must be stable: constant number of adults in the transaction year and the year after, no divorce from two years before to one year after the transaction, and no adult member lost to death within one year before or after.
    Registers: CPR, BEF (Statistics Denmark household ID)
    online appendix · Appendix A, Sample selection and Variable definition
  • Transaction price (outcome) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Log of the realised transaction price in thousand year-2015 DKK, from property transactions announced in the Danish Gazette (Statstidende) as received by SKAT.
    Registers: SKAT property transactions (Statstidende)
    online appendix · Appendix A, Variable definition
  • Tax-assessed property value Wealth, debt and consumption
    SKAT's assessment of the property's value if sold (basis for property value tax and municipal land tax), carried out every other year and regulated by local house price growth in non-assessment years; the paper uses the assessed value in the year prior to the transaction, entered as log of thousand year-2015 DKK.
    Registers: SKAT
    online appendix · Appendix A, Data sources and Variable definition; paper Section 2
  • Employment status (employed / self-employed / retired / unemployed) Employment and labour force status
    IDA status classified at end of November each year: employed if the majority of personal income is from paid employment, self-employed if the majority is from self-employment, retired if outside the labour market with the majority of income from private or public pensions, and unemployed otherwise. Household variables are shares of adult members (0, 0.5 or 1), measured in November of the year before the transaction.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 2 (data source 6); Appendix A Variable definition
  • Household income and net wealth Earnings and income
    Household totals of total income and net wealth (third-party reported to SKAT) in million year-2015 DKK, measured December 31 of the year before the transaction and winsorised at the 1st and 99th percentiles.
    Registers: SKAT income and wealth records
    working paper · Table 1 note; Appendix A Variable definition
  • First-time buyer / out-of-town buyer Wealth, debt and consumption
    First-time buyer: no member of the buyer household has previously owned real estate. Out-of-town buyer: the household buys property in a municipality it did not previously live in.
    Registers: BBR, CPR
    online appendix · Appendix A, Variable definition
  • Death sales Sample definition and timing
    Household terminations (death of the only member of a one-person household: single, widowed or divorced) of individuals owning real estate at death, identified by linking the Cause-of-Death Register to CPR; restricted to decedents with exactly one child (the beneficiary, linked via CPR) and to sales of the property within 1.5 years of the death, applying all full-sample selection criteria (13,953 death sales).
    Registers: Cause-of-Death Register, CPR, SKAT property transactions
    online appendix · Appendix A, Death data; paper Section 4
  • School-age children Family links, fertility and household
    Indicator for having children aged 5 to 15 (not necessarily living in the household), interacted with the transaction quarter following Harding, Rosenthal and Sirmans (2003).
    Registers: CPR
    online appendix · Appendix A, Variable definition

Financial Trouble Across Generations: Evidence from the Universe of Personal Loans in Denmark

Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen and Louise Charlotte Willerslev-Olsen · Economic Journal, 2020 · Individual

Loan-level records on all personal loans show strong intergenerational persistence in financial trouble: children of parents who default are far more likely to default themselves, and the correlation is present already in early adulthood and is not explained by income or education.

Data
Loan register from the Danish Tax Agency (SKAT): all personal loan accounts with default status (60+ days late), Population register (BEF) for parent-child links, Income-tax register and other administrative registers on labour market history, income and wealth, Credit bureau bad-payer files (Experian, Debitor Registret), 2009 snapshot, Survey of 1,748 individuals on risk willingness, patience and impulsivity (2014)
Key variables
  • Outcome: child default on personal loans (60+ days late)
  • Key regressor: parental default status
  • Preference measures from survey (risk willingness, patience, impulsivity)
  • Controls: income, wealth, education, GPA
Period
2004–2011
Sample
28,027,610 parent-child-year observations on 2,501,088 individuals All Danes aged 18–45 in 2004–2011 with at least one living parent, organized as parent-child-year cells. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Loan default (financial trouble) Wealth, debt and consumption
    An individual is in default if at least one interest-bearing personal loan is at least 60 days late with payments at the end of the year, as reported by banks and other financial intermediaries to the Danish Tax Agency (SKAT); annual data 2004-2011 covering all loan accounts. Mortgage loans are supplied in separate files; loan type is otherwise not observed.
    Registers: SKAT loan register
    working paper · Section 3.1 and footnote 2; Figure 1 notes
  • Default by loan size Wealth, debt and consumption
    Alternative severity measures defining default at defaulted loan levels exceeding DKK 0, 10,000, 50,000 and 100,000 (the defaulted amount may reflect several smaller loans).
    Registers: SKAT loan register
    working paper · Figure notes (Panel B, defaulting at loan levels)
  • Bad-payer file registration Wealth, debt and consumption
    Recorded in the bad-payer files of credit bureaus Experian or Debitor Registret (snapshot of persons registered in 2009); people can be recorded after at least three reminders and a warning letter, for at most five years per missing payment.
    Registers: Experian bad-payer file, Debitor Registret
    working paper · Section 3.1 and footnote 3
  • Parent-child sample Sample definition and timing
    All individuals aged 18-45 in 2004-2011 with at least one living parent, linked via CPR to parents in the population register; unit of observation is the parent-child-year cell (separate child-mother and child-father observations; new partners of divorced parents ignored).
    Registers: Population register, SKAT loan register
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Unemployment shock (event study) Unemployment and benefits
    Unemployment spell of at least three months in event year 2007, 2008 or 2009 for individuals employed with no unemployment spells in the five preceding years, aged 18-38 at t-5; controls are similar individuals without a shock in t. Amounts index-adjusted to 2009-DKK within cohort.
    Registers: Income register, Unemployment histories (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 4 (Unemployment event analysis)
  • Liquidity constraint indicator / financial wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Financial wealth = stocks + bonds + bank deposits; indicator for having financial assets at end of year below one month's worth of average disposable income over the five years preceding the shock year.
    Registers: Income and wealth registers (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Figure 8 notes
  • Historical parental asset path (instrument) Wealth, debt and consumption
    Ratio of parental financial assets to average disposable income for each year 1987-1996; parents are assigned to behavioural types by within-cohort decile of the average asset-income ratio over the ten years, used to instrument parental default in 2011.
    Registers: Income and wealth registers (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 4 (Historical financial behavior of parents)
  • Middle-school GPA decile Education and test scores
    Within-cohort deciles of grade point average from the 9th grade graduation exam in Danish and Mathematics, available for those completing 9th grade in 2001/2002 or later.
    Registers: Education registers (grades)
    working paper · Section 3.2 and Figure on GPA deciles
  • Survey preference measures Other
    January 2014 telephone survey of 1,748 individuals asking respondents to place themselves and both parents on a 1-10 scale for risk willingness, patience and impulsivity; linked to register data.
    Registers: 2014 survey linked to registers
    working paper · Section 4 (survey), Figure 11

Human Capital and Career Success: Evidence from Linked Employer-Employee Data

Anders Frederiksen and Takao Kato · Economic Journal, 2018 · Individual + firm

Uses complete Danish career histories to study who reaches top management, through internal promotion or external recruitment. Formal schooling and breadth of experience across occupations both help, they are complementary, and breadth acquired within the firm matters more than breadth acquired outside it, consistent with human capital theories of corporate leadership.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA) with DISCO occupation codes, Education registers
Key variables
  • Outcome: appointment to top management (DISCO 12/13) in firm with 100+ employees
  • Key regressor: breadth of occupational experience over prior 8 years (TOCC)
  • Formal schooling
  • Tenure, general work experience, age, gender
Period
1992–2002 (appointments in 2000 and 2001)
Sample
773,094 observations (3,813 appointed to top management) Private-sector employees in Denmark with complete 8-year occupational histories forming the contestant pool for top management positions. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Top management appointment (career success) Occupation and job hierarchy
    APPOINTMENT = 1 if the worker is appointed to a top management position, defined as DISCO 12 (Corporate Managers) or DISCO 13 (General Managers), in a firm with 100 or more employees between year t and t+1 (appointments in 2000 and 2001); robust to a 50-employee cut-off. CEO-only definitions were not used because 4-digit codes are inconsistently assigned.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: DISCO (2-digit) 12, 13; firm size >= 100 employees
    working paper · Section 2 and footnotes 3, 6; Eq. (1)
  • Breadth of occupational experience (TOCC) Occupation and job hierarchy
    Number of distinct 2-digit DISCO occupations held prior to the current occupation over years t-8 to t-1; alternatives are dummies OCC1-OCC7 for number of prior occupations differing from current one.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: DISCO 2-digit
    working paper · Section 3, Eq. (1) and Table 3
  • Internal vs total occupational experience (INT_OCC, INT_EXT_OCC) Occupation and job hierarchy
    INT_OCC = number of occupations experienced within the present firm excluding the current one; INT_EXT_OCC = total number of all occupations experienced excluding the present one, counting the same occupation in two different firms as two occupations. Internal promotion vs external recruitment distinguished by whether the appointment occurs without switching firm.
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: DISCO 2-digit
    working paper · Section 4, Tables 5-6
  • Contestant pool Sample definition and timing
    Private-sector employees in year t with complete occupational histories (DISCO codes) for t-8 to t-1 whose primary occupation in t-1 is one of the 2-digit DISCO occupations from which any top manager appointed in year t came in t-1. DISCO data used for 1992-2002 (before the 2003 switch from 4-digit to 6-digit DISCO).
    Registers: IDA
    Codes: DISCO 2-digit
    working paper · Section 2
  • Firm tenure and general work experience Employment and labour force status
    Constructed by matching the linked employer-employee data with pension contribution data dating back to 1964.
    Registers: IDA, Pension contribution data (ATP)
    working paper · Section 2
  • Formal schooling (SCH) Education and test scores
    Five levels of highest educational attainment: less than high school (reference), regular high-school diploma, vocational, college degree (3-year Bachelor), graduate (Master's and PhD combined).
    Registers: Education registers
    working paper · Section 3 and footnote 8

Labour markets, wages and sorting

Born with a Silver Spoon? Danish Evidence on Wealth Inequality in Childhood

Simon Halphen Boserup, Wojciech Kopczuk and Claus Thustrup Kreiner · Economic Journal, 2018 · Individual

Third-party reported wealth records of children show that wealth inequality is as high in childhood as among adults, with top shares driven by transfers from parents and grandparents. Wealth at age 18 predicts wealth in adulthood, and intergenerational wealth correlations are present from early ages.

Data
Individual wealth data from tax return records (Danish Tax Agency SKAT, via Statistics Denmark), Population register with parent identifiers (BEF), Education and income registers
Key variables
  • Outcome: child wealth and wealth rank in adulthood (age 45)
  • Key regressor: childhood wealth (age 18) and parental wealth rank
  • Inferred inter vivos transfers and bequests (bunching at gift-tax allowance)
  • Portfolio components (deposits, securities, real estate, debt)
Period
1983–2011
Sample
Pooled cross-section: on average close to 650 thousand observations per one-year age group; panel regressions: 36,102 observations All individuals aged 1–40 in 2000–2011 with living parents (pooled cross-section), plus a panel of the 1965 birth cohort with both parents alive in 2011, followed 1983–2011. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Net wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Value of assets minus liabilities measured on the last day of the year from administrative tax return records (SKAT), 1983-2011; mostly third-party reported by banks and financial institutions. Assets include deposits, stocks, bonds, real estate and deposited mortgages; liabilities include bank debt, mortgage credit debt, card debt, student debt, debt to municipalities, unpaid taxes, etc. Pension funds are not included; self-reported items (cars, boats, etc.) are excluded after the 1996 abolition of the wealth tax.
    Registers: SKAT wealth records (via Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 2 (Data)
  • Real estate valuation Wealth, debt and consumption
    Public (tax-assessed) values of real estate are adjusted upwards each year using the average relative difference between selling price and public value of real estate traded that year, following Leth-Petersen (2010).
    Registers: SKAT wealth records
    working paper · Section 2, footnote 6
  • Portfolio components Wealth, debt and consumption
    From 1995 onwards complete portfolio information on bonds, stocks, cash in banks, real estate, mortgage loans and the sum of other loans; childhood holdings summarised as bank deposits, securities and real estate.
    Registers: SKAT wealth records
    working paper · Sections 2 and 3.1
  • Wealth percentile rank Wealth, debt and consumption
    Percentile rank computed within child age-year specific wealth distributions (parents ranked on total parental wealth observed at the same time); ties, notably zero wealth among young children, are randomly broken. Adult outcome is the child's rank at age 45 (27 years after age 18).
    Registers: SKAT wealth records, Population register (parent links)
    working paper · Section 3.3, footnote 11; Section 3.4
  • Inferred wealth transfers (residual) Wealth, debt and consumption
    For each child, wealth at a given age minus the present value of earnings up to that age (real interest rates 0%, 3%, 6%), censored at zero, as a lower bound on transfers received.
    Registers: SKAT wealth records, Income registers
    working paper · Section 3.2, Table 1
  • Gift-tax bunching measure Taxes and tax rates
    First time an individual (ages 1-12) has positive wealth, wealth at that point treated as the transfer; distance to the gift-tax basic allowance (DKK 58,700 in 2011) and to twice that amount (two donors) is plotted to look for bunching.
    Registers: SKAT wealth records
    working paper · Section 3.2, Figure 6
  • PCD and PD samples Sample definition and timing
    PCD: pooled cross-section of all individuals aged 1-40 in 2000-2011 with parents alive (parent IDs registered for Danes born from 1960). PD: panel of the 1965 birth cohort with both parents alive in 2011, followed 1983-2011 (ages 18-46). Monetary values deflated by CPI (2011 prices).
    Registers: Population register (parent links), SKAT wealth records
    working paper · Section 2; Tables A1-A2

School Starting Age and the Crime-Age Profile

Rasmus Landersø, Helena Skyt Nielsen and Marianne Simonsen · Economic Journal, 2017 · Individual

Children born just after the school start cut-off begin school almost a year later. Starting school older lowers crime at young ages, especially for boys, by shifting the crime-age profile rather than permanently reducing crime, consistent with an incapacitation and maturity channel.

Data
Population register with exact birth dates and parent links (BEF), Criminal charge register (charges for property, violence and other crimes, with dates), Birth records: birth weight, gestational length, APGAR score (likely Medical Birth Register, MFR; not named in paper), Education registers (age in 8th grade as proxy for school starting age), Parental education and labour market registers
Key variables
  • Outcome: criminal charge at a given age / at or before a given age (from age 15)
  • Treatment: school starting age (7.6 vs 6.6)
  • Instrument/running variable: birth date relative to January 1 cut-off (±30 days)
  • Heterogeneity: gender; crime type (property, violence, other)
Period
Children born mid-1981 to mid-1993
Sample
48,546 and 50,383 children (the two gender groups) at age 15, born in December or January (Table 1) Danish children born in December or January between December 1981 and January 1993 (main bandwidth ±30 days around January 1). source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Crime at a given age Crime
    Indicator for being charged with a crime between one birthday and the next (memoryless measure), from age 15 onwards. Charges rather than convictions are used to gain three additional years of data; results are robust to using convictions.
    Registers: Danish crime registers (charges)
    working paper · Section 3.1 and footnote 17
  • Crime at or before a given age Crime
    Accumulated indicator for having been charged with a crime at or before a given age (from age 15), keeping track of earlier incidences; also number of crimes for the intensive margin. Outcomes aligned by age are measured exactly at the birthday.
    Registers: Danish crime registers (charges)
    working paper · Sections 3.1 and 3.3
  • Crime type (property, violence, other) Crime
    Three broad categories: property crime (most frequently shoplifting, burglary, vandalism), violent crime (ordinary and aggravated assault, threats, violence towards public servants) and residual other crime (dominated by traffic-related crime such as driving without a licence, then drug or weapon crime).
    Registers: Danish crime registers (charges)
    working paper · Section 3.1, Table 1 and footnote 19
  • School starting age (old-for-grade) Education and test scores
    Timing of school start is not observed for these cohorts, so age in 8th grade is used as an approximation; SSA is modelled as a binary indicator for school starting age 7.6 versus 6.6 (old-for-grade), with robustness to a continuous measure. Validated with exact ages at all grade levels observed from 2007 onwards.
    Registers: Education registers
    working paper · Sections 2 and 3.2; Table A2
  • Birth-date discontinuity instrument and bandwidth Sample definition and timing
    Instrument is being born after the January 1 cut-off (January=1); main sample uses children born within +/-30 days of January 1, cohorts born mid-1981 to mid-1993, controlling for a flexible function of distance in days to the cut-off and cohort fixed effects. Covariates are centred on cut-off dates, comparing January year t with December year t-1.
    Registers: Population register (exact birth dates)
    working paper · Sections 2 and 3, Section 3.3
  • Birth outcomes (APGAR, birth weight, gestation) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Child birth weight, gestational length and APGAR score (0-10, based on appearance, pulse, grimace, activity, respiration) used as background controls; register not named in the paper.
    Registers: Birth records (register not named)
    working paper · Section 3.3 and footnote 21
  • Parental background Family links, fertility and household
    Parents' education and labour market outcomes measured one year prior to the child's birth, aligned to cut-off (e.g. children born Dec 1981 or Jan 1982 use parental characteristics from 1980); also mother's age at first birth.
    Registers: Parental education and labour market registers
    working paper · Section 3.3 and footnotes 16, 22
