Mathematics and Gender: Heterogeneity in Causes and Consequences

Juanna Schrøter Joensen and Helena Skyt Nielsen · Economic Journal, 2016 · Individual

A pilot scheme in Danish high schools that let students combine advanced mathematics with chemistry increased advanced maths take-up, especially among girls. The induced maths qualification raised later earnings, with the gains concentrated among students who would otherwise have taken less maths and operating through higher education choices.

Data
Education registers: detailed educational histories, high school branch choice and GPA (Statistics Denmark), Labour market registers: earnings, occupation, industry, self-employment, part-time work
Key variables
  • Outcome: log earnings (measured 18 years after high school graduation)
  • Outcomes: college graduation, field of major, occupation/top corporate jobs, sector
  • Treatment: choice of advanced high school math

Period
High school entrants 1984–1986, followed into the labour market
Sample
about 25,658 females and 19,406 males from about 140 high schools Danish high school entrants of 1984–86 who graduated in three years and have at least one year of employment. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Advanced high school math (treatment) Education and test scores
    Indicator MathA for choosing the advanced math course in the branch-based high school; because the instrument works through the option to combine advanced math with advanced chemistry, the treatment is effectively the combined advanced math and advanced chemistry package.
    Registers: Education registers (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Sections 2 and 4.1
  • Pilot scheme instrument (PilotIntro) Education and test scores
    PilotIntro equals one if the individual enrolled in a high school which afterwards decided to introduce the experimental (math-chemistry) curriculum for the first time, i.e. unexpectedly exposed before choosing math level; zero otherwise.   • Log earnings Earnings and income

  • High school GPA Education and test scores

  • College graduation and field of major Education and test scores
    Graduation from 2- or 4-year college, Master's education, and PhD measured 8-18 years after leaving high school, excluding those who already graduated at a higher level; field of major (e.g. Humanities, Health Sciences, Technical Sciences) from detailed education codes.

    working paper · Section 5; Tables 4-5
  • CEO / Top CEO Occupation and job hierarchy
    CEO = high-level managers as defined by raw occupation codes (7% of males, 2% of females); Top CEO = top-level managers in public and private enterprises regardless of number of employees using the Danish version of ISCO (D-ISCO) (1% of males, 0.2% of females); also Manager, Managerial Employee, Vice-Director, Middle Manager categories. Measured 18 years after graduation.

    Codes: D-ISCO (specific codes not stated)

  • Private-sector employment and industry Sector and industry
    Indicator for being employed in the private sector 18 years after high school graduation; also nine industry indicators (e.g. transportation, mail and communication).
    Registers: Labour market registers (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 5; Table 6
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Population of high school entrants 1984-86 who graduated in three years and have at least one year of employment (25,658 females, 19,406 males from about 140 high schools). Controls: county, entry cohort, high school controls, parental highest education and parental income at end of year before high school start.
    Registers: Education registers (Statistics Denmark)

Housing Wealth and Consumption: A Micro Panel Study

Martin Browning, Mette Gørtz and Søren Leth-Petersen · Economic Journal, 2013 · Individual

Uses register-based imputed consumption and house price changes over the 1987 to 1996 boom and bust to test whether housing wealth drives spending. For most households consumption does not respond to unanticipated house price changes; the response is confined to young households, consistent with a collateral rather than a wealth effect.

Data
Administrative income and wealth (tax) registers for a 10% random sample of the Danish population aged 16+, House price / housing wealth information from registers
Key variables
  • Outcome: imputed household total expenditure (disposable income minus change in net wealth)
  • Key regressor: unexpected changes in house prices / housing wealth
  • Heterogeneity: age, owners vs renters, credit constraints (1992–93 mortgage reform allowing home-equity borrowing)
  • Disposable household income
Period
1987–1996
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Married or cohabiting stable couples from a 10% random sample of the Danish population aged 16+, who were either homeowners or renters throughout the period. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Imputed household total expenditure Wealth, debt and consumption
    Household disposable after-tax income minus the change in net financial wealth from t-1 to t, following Browning and Leth-Petersen (2003); deflated to 1990 prices. Possible only up to 1996 because wealth-tax register data end after the wealth tax was abolished in 1997.
    Registers: Income and wealth tax registers (10% sample)
    working paper · Section 4 (Expenditure imputation), eq. (1), footnote 1
  • Household disposable income Earnings and income
    Gross income including interest income, housing transfers and dividends, minus taxes on income, taxes on shares, surplus on owner-occupied housing and tax-exempted interest expenses (labour, transfer and capital income net of personal taxes).
    Registers: Income tax registers
    working paper · Section 4 (Expenditure imputation)
  • Net wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Financial assets (market value of shares, bank deposits, market value of bonds and securities) minus debt (mortgage debt, bank debt etc.).
    Registers: Wealth tax registers
    working paper · Section 4 (Expenditure imputation)
  • Municipal house prices and house price innovations Geography and neighbourhood
    Average sales prices of traded single-family houses by municipality (275 municipalities), 1985-2001, collected by the tax authorities. Log municipal price modelled as an AR process with municipality effects, average house size (square metres, rooms) and year effects, estimated by system GMM; the predicted change is the expected price change and the residual is the house price innovation.
    Registers: Tax authority house sales statistics (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section 4 (House prices); Section 5 (house price process); Appendix 1
  • Analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    10% random sample of the Danish population aged 16+, 1987-1996; married or cohabiting stable couples who were either home owners or renters throughout; split before and after the 1992-93 mortgage/collateral and tax reforms.
    Registers: Income and wealth tax registers (10% sample)
    working paper · Section 4 (Data); Abstract
  • Liquidity constraint Wealth, debt and consumption
    Liquidity-constrained households have liquid funds (cash and bonds) below 1.5 months of disposable income; high-liquidity households have liquid funds above half a year's disposable income. Mortgage sensitivity measured by mortgage debt / house value.
    Registers: Income and wealth tax registers
    working paper · Section 6 (credit constraints) and robustness section

Is Business Failure Due to Lack of Effort? Empirical Evidence from a Large Administrative Sample

Mette Ejrnæs and Stefan Hochguertel · Economic Journal, 2013 · Individual

Danish self-employed can voluntarily buy unemployment insurance, which creates a moral hazard test. Using a large administrative panel, insured entrepreneurs are more likely to close their businesses and enter unemployment, with effects that strengthen as the eligibility date approaches, consistent with reduced effort rather than selection alone.

Data
CAM 10% Sample: 10% random sample of the Danish population aged 16+ (linked administrative registers incl. tax and benefit records), Unemployment insurance fund membership records
Key variables
  • Outcome: transition from self-employment to unemployment (registered unemployed >10% of year)
  • Treatment: UI fund membership (insurance status)
  • Instrument: eligibility for early retirement scheme (VERP) available only to UI members
  • Estimator: bivariate random effects probit
Period
1981–1998
Sample
13,434 individuals and 86,092 observations (estimation sample) Denmark-born male Danish citizens aged 25–59 who were self-employed in their first three observed years, excluding agriculture, from the CAM 10% sample. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • CAM 10% sample Sample definition and timing
    10% random sample of the Danish population aged 16 and above from the Danish National Register, followed annually from 1981; waves up to and including 1998 are used. Unbalanced: new residents turning 16 or immigrating enter, people leave through death or emigration.
    Registers: CAM 10% Sample
    working paper · Section 4.1 (Register Data)
  • Self-employment / labour market status Employment and labour force status
    Labour market status is recorded in calendar week 48 (late November) of each year; individuals are classified as self-employed according to their main economic activity in that week. Persons originally classified as 'on leave' (possible for UI fund members from 1994) are re-classified to their state of origin.
    Registers: CAM 10% Sample
    working paper · Section 4.1 and footnote 22
  • Unemployment (outcome) Unemployment and benefits
    Indicator equal to one if the individual was registered unemployed in excess of 10% of the year according to the annual 'unemployment degree' (fraction of the year UI benefits are received), zero otherwise. 'Unemployed' means registered as such with the job centre, which also covers non-UI-members on social assistance; an alternative measure is the week-48 unemployment stock.
    Registers: CAM 10% Sample
    working paper · Sections 4.1 and 5.1
  • UI fund membership (insured) Unemployment and benefits
    Membership in an unemployment insurance fund, as recorded in the administrative data; 'insured' and UI fund member are used interchangeably. Treatment enters the unemployment equation lagged one year (status in t-1).
    Registers: CAM 10% Sample
    working paper · Section 4.1 (fn. 16) and Section 5.1
  • Early retirement (VERP) eligibility instrument Retirement and pensions
    Institutional-rule indicator of eligibility for the UI-fund-linked early retirement (ER) scheme (retirement from age 60). Before 1992 members qualified with 10 years of UI membership before age 60 ('10-year rule'); the 1992 reform required at least 20 years ('20-year rule', latest joining age 40), with those aged 40-50 in 1992 required to join in 1992 and stay until 60. Identification comes from changes over year and cohort in this rule.
    Registers: CAM 10% Sample
    working paper · Section 2 (institutions) and Sections 5.1-5.2
  • Analysis sample restrictions Sample definition and timing
    Denmark-born males with Danish citizenship aged 25-59; excludes students, retirees, persons out of the labour force in every year, persons receiving public pensions, and anyone who worked as wage earner or self-employed in agriculture 1981-1998; requires at least one employment spell. Estimation sample: persons self-employed in their first three observed years and not unemployed (>10% measure) in any of those years (13,434 individuals, 86,092 obs).
    Registers: CAM 10% Sample
    working paper · Sections 4.1 and 5.1
  • Health proxy (sickness benefits) Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Receipt of sickness benefits is used as the health or illness measure because of data limitations.
    Registers: CAM 10% Sample
    working paper · Section 5.2
  • Self-employment income Earnings and income
    Income from self-employment (surplus or profit of business), entered linearly with a dummy for negative values; income and wealth measured in constant 1981 million DKK. Controls also include receipt of start-up allowance (for entrants from unemployment via active labour market programmes) and regional unemployment calculated from the micro data.
    Registers: CAM 10% Sample
    working paper · Section 5.2

Unemployment Insurance, Wage Dynamics and Inequality Over the Life Cycle

Paul Bingley, Lorenzo Cappellari and Niels Westergård-Nielsen · Economic Journal, 2013 · Individual

Models permanent and transitory wage dynamics over the life cycle for Danish men, allowing dynamics to differ by unemployment insurance membership. Insurance is associated with lower wage inequality and less persistence of shocks, and the paper quantifies how much of life-cycle wage inequality UI members avoid relative to non-members.

Data
Administrative register data on the Danish labour force (Statistics Denmark): annual labour earnings and hours-derived hourly wages, UI fund membership contributions reported to tax authorities, Mandatory pension contributions (ATP) for year of labour market entry
Key variables
  • Outcome: log gross hourly wage (permanent and transitory components)
  • Key regressor: UI fund membership
  • Potential labour market experience
  • Birth cohort (1943–1973, 31 cohorts)
Period
1980–2003
Sample
roughly 810,000 individuals, about 12.5 million person-year observations Danish men aged 21–55, full-time private-sector employees, born 1943–1973, with at least five consecutive valid wage observations. source
How variables are defined (4)
  • Gross hourly wage Earnings and income
    Calculated by Statistics Denmark as annual labour earnings (reported by employers to the tax authorities) divided by hours worked, where hours are an annual average derived by Statistics Denmark from mandatory pension (ATP) contributions adjusted for contribution rates by sector and collective agreement. Zero wages dropped, bottom and top 0.5% trimmed per year, observations below minimum wage dropped.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark administrative registers, ATP
    working paper · Section 4 and footnote 13
  • UI fund membership Unemployment and benefits
    Annual dummy for UI fund membership, observed from tax-deductible UI fund membership contributions reported annually by the funds to the tax authorities.
    Registers: Tax records
    working paper · Section 4
  • Potential labour market experience Employment and labour force status
    Years since entering the labour market, where year of entry is observed from the first mandatory pension (ATP) contribution; ATP was introduced in 1964, so entry is censored at 1964.
    Registers: ATP
    working paper · Section 4
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Men aged 21-55, full-time private-sector employees, 1980-2003, birth cohorts 1943-1973 (31 single-year cohorts; each observed at least ten years). Individuals must have valid wage observations for at least five consecutive years.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark administrative registers
    working paper · Section 4

Estimating Class-size Effects using Within-school Variation in Subject-specific Classes

Eskil Heinesen · Economic Journal, 2010 · Individual

Uses within-school variation over time in the size of French classes, which Danish seventh graders choose between French and German, as quasi-random variation in class size. Larger classes lower French exam marks, especially for weaker students and boys, and marks in subjects taught in the regular class serve as a check on selection.

Data
Administrative registers on 9th-grade marks and exam results, school attended, merged via personal and school ID numbers, Family background registers (parents' education, income, labour market status, family structure)
Key variables
  • Outcome: French examination marks at end of 9th grade
  • Treatment: French class size (school/year cell)
  • Identification: within-school year-to-year variation in subject-specific class size
  • Placebo/control: marks in other subjects taught in basic classes
Period
School years 2001/2002–2003/2004
Sample
6,507 students in 782 school/year cells and 375 schools 9th-grade students in 2002–2004 studying French at schools offering both German and French from 7th grade, with at most 20 French students per grade. source
How variables are defined (4)
  • French class size Education and test scores
    Number of students with marks for the year's work in French in 9th grade, measured per school/year cell; sample restricted to schools offering French from 7th grade where at most 20 students attend French (so only one French class) and where some students attend German.
    Registers: Administrative registers on 9th-grade marks and school attended
    working paper · Section 3 (Data and descriptive statistics); footnote 4
  • French examination mark Education and test scores
    Examination mark in French at the end of 9th grade on the Danish 13-scale (values 0-13 excluding 1, 2, 4 and 12; pass at 6); marks for the year's work are not analysed. Cohorts finishing 9th grade in 2001/02-2003/04.
    Registers: Administrative registers on 9th-grade marks
    Codes: 13-scale (0,3,5,6,7,8,9,10,11,13)
    working paper · Section 3
  • Marks in other subjects (placebo and ability) Education and test scores
    Examination marks in English, Danish (oral, written, spelling), math (oral, written) and science; average mark computed over each student's non-missing marks. Academic ability dummy = average marks in other subjects at least 9.
    Registers: Administrative registers on 9th-grade marks
    working paper · Section 5 (Table 3); Section 6 (Table 6)
  • Family background controls Family links, fertility and household
    32 variables for siblings, family structure, parents' education, age, labour-market status, income, unemployment and housing conditions, all measured in the calendar year the child turned 12; parental high education = at least one parent with long further or higher education.
    Registers: Family background registers (parents' education, income, labour market status)
    working paper · Section 3; Section 6

Job Satisfaction and Co-worker Wages: Status or Signal?

Andrew E. Clark, Nicolai Kristensen and Niels Westergård-Nielsen · Economic Journal, 2009 · Individual + firm

Links survey measures of job satisfaction to register wages of all co-workers at the same establishment. Satisfaction is higher when co-workers earn more, the opposite of the usual income comparison result, which the authors interpret as co-worker pay signalling one's own future earnings; the effect is stronger for men and in the private sector.

Data
Danish sample of the European Community Household Panel (ECHP), eight waves, Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), matched via CPR number
Key variables
  • Outcome: overall job satisfaction (1–6 scale)
  • Key regressor: co-workers' wages within the same establishment
  • Own wage (gross annual income from IDA)
  • Wage deficit relative to establishment wage distribution
Period
1994–2001
Sample
about 16,000 observations on around 4,100 individuals Employees in the Danish ECHP 1994–2001 matched to IDA, in establishments with at least 5 colleagues. source
How variables are defined (4)
  • Overall job satisfaction Other
    ECHP question 'How satisfied are you with your work or other main activity?', ordered scale from 1 (not at all satisfied) to 6 (fully satisfied); Danish ECHP waves 1994-2001, employees only.
    Registers: ECHP (Danish sample)
    working paper · Section 3.1; Figure 1 note
  • Own wage Earnings and income
    Individual's gross annual income from IDA, matched to ECHP respondents via CPR number; entered as ln(own wage) together with a Mundlak term (individual mean wage over waves); summary statistics in 1994 DKK real terms.
    Registers: IDA, ECHP
    working paper · Section 3.1-3.2; Appendix Table B1
  • Co-worker (establishment) wage Firm characteristics and productivity
    Average wage of all other employees at the same establishment (IDA establishment identifier); alternatives are the 75th (and 90th) percentile of the establishment wage distribution and mean wage by three occupation categories (managers, middle-ranking, lower-level). Sample restricted to establishments with at least 5 colleagues (robustness 4 and 6).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1-3.2; Section 4 (Tables 3-4); footnotes 7, 11, 12
  • Wage surplus / wage deficit Earnings and income
    Following Ferrer-i-Carbonell (2005): if own wage > establishment average wage, wage surplus = ln(own) - ln(average) and deficit = 0; if own < average, wage deficit = ln(average) - ln(own) and surplus = 0; both zero if equal.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.2

Are Homeowners Really More Unemployed?

Jakob Roland Munch, Michael Rosholm and Michael Svarer · Economic Journal, 2006 · Individual

Tests the Oswald hypothesis that home ownership raises unemployment. Danish homeowners are less geographically mobile, but they find local jobs faster, so their unemployment spells are shorter overall. Ownership does not raise aggregate unemployment.

Data
Administrative register data on unemployment spells for a 2.5% random sample of the Danish population, Regional unemployment measure from the Institute for Local Government Studies (1987–2000)
Key variables
  • Outcome: unemployment duration in weeks
  • Outcome: exit destination (new job locally, job in another commuting area, other states)
  • Key regressor: home ownership indicator
  • Controls: age, gender, children, household type, immigrant status, education, UI fund membership and replacement rate
Period
1997–2000
Sample
18,992 persons with 52,738 unemployment spells Flow sample of all unemployment spells in 1997–2000 for individuals aged 19–66 in a 2.5% random sample of the Danish population. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Unemployment spell inflow sample Sample definition and timing
    Flow sample of all unemployment spells in 1997-2000 for individuals in a 2.5% random sample of the Danish population, restricted to inflow into unemployment of workers aged 19-66; spell duration measured in weeks (18,992 persons, 52,738 spells).
    Registers: Administrative registers (2.5% random population sample)
    working paper · Section 3 (Data and the Danish labour and housing markets), pp. 9-10
  • Exit destination Unemployment and benefits
    Destination after an unemployment spell: new job in the local labour market, new job in another commuting area, or other states than employment and unemployment. A worker is geographically mobile if he or she gets a job and moves to another commuting area up to 8 weeks before and 52 weeks after the start of the job spell (exact moving dates known).
    Registers: Administrative registers
    working paper · Section 3, p. 9
  • Commuting areas (local labour markets) Geography and neighbourhood
    Local labour markets are commuting areas built from geographically connected municipalities such that the internal migration rate is 50% higher than the external migration rate (Andersen 2000); the 275 municipalities are merged into 51 commuting areas.
    Registers: Administrative registers
    working paper · Section 3, p. 9
  • Regional unemployment rate Geography and neighbourhood
    Measure constructed by the Institute for Local Government Studies (AKF): unemployment rate in an area around each municipality, defined by how far a resident can commute without a daily commuting cost exceeding DKK 60 (1987 prices); available 1987-2000.
    Registers: Institute for Local Government Studies regional unemployment data
    working paper · Section 3.1, p. 10
  • Home ownership Wealth, debt and consumption
    Indicator for being a home owner (living in owner-occupied housing) versus renting (private rental, social or cooperative housing).
    Registers: Administrative registers
    working paper · Section 2-3, pp. 8-10
  • UI fund membership and replacement rate Unemployment and benefits
    Indicator for membership of an unemployment insurance fund and, for members, the UI replacement rate; other controls are age, gender, number of dependent children aged 0-17, two-adult household, immigrant from a non-OECD country, municipality size and education.
    Registers: Administrative registers
    working paper · Section 3, p. 10

Is there a Threat Effect of Labour Market Programmes? A Study of ALMP in the Danish UI System

Lars Pico Geerdsen · Economic Journal, 2006 · Individual

Exploits the timing rules for compulsory activation in the Danish unemployment insurance system to test whether the prospect of being activated speeds up exit from unemployment. Exit rates rise markedly as the activation deadline approaches, which identifies a sizeable threat effect of active labour market programmes.

Data
Danish UI system administrative data (not specified in abstract)
Key variables
  • Outcome: exit from unemployment to employment before programme participation
  • Identification: legislative changes to the length of the UI benefit period before compulsory activation
  • Treatment: approach of compulsory ALMP participation (threat effect)
Period
Not stated in the sources checked
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Unemployed UI recipients in Denmark subject to compulsory labour market programmes after the benefit period. source (abstract)
How variables are defined (5)
  • UI spell Unemployment and benefits
    Unemployment spell = at least 15 days of unemployment within a given month; a spell is broken if the individual receives no UI for more than 2 weeks in a month or regains the right to a new UI period mid-spell. Exit is any departure from UI (employment, leave, social benefits, early retirement, disability pension, education) in the thesis version. UI days per month come from SSHS, built from CRAM (unemployment fund records).
    Registers: SSHS, CRAM
    working paper · PhD thesis (SFI 2003), Paper II, Sections 5.1-5.2, pp. 113-116
  • Activation participation Unemployment and benefits
    Days in activation per month after 1994 from the Register on Labour Market Measures (AMFORA), based on the Labour Market Agency's Labour Market Policy Register (AMPO) reports of activation start and end; before 1994 from the Job Offer Data Set (ATB), 1980-1994.
    Registers: AMFORA, AMPO, ATB
    working paper · PhD thesis (SFI 2003), Paper II, Section 5.1, pp. 113-114
  • Time remaining to activation period Unemployment and benefits
    Months of passive UI left before the compulsory activation period, constructed by replicating the 1994 departmental order that placed each unemployed person in the new UI system (entitlement depends on prior activation, UI use and employment before 1994). Passive period cut from 4 years (1994) to 3 years (July 1996) to 2 years (January 1998); three expectation models (perfect foresight, system foresight, no foresight) for how individuals perceive the remaining months.
    Registers: CRAM, SSHS, AMFORA, IDA
    working paper · PhD thesis (SFI 2003), Paper II, Sections 2.2, 4.1, 5.2 and Appendix A
  • Monthly employment Employment and labour force status
    IDA gives employment status in November and the number of months employed in the year; monthly employment is located in the residual months not covered by other monthly/weekly states (leave schemes, UI, activation, early retirement, social benefits).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · PhD thesis (SFI 2003), Paper II, Section 5.1, p. 114
  • Analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    10% sample of the Danish population aged 17-67, panel 1980-1998, topped up each year with 10% of new 17-year-olds and immigrants; leavers at age 68, emigration or death drop out. Restricted to UI spells beginning between January 1994 and January 1998.
    Registers: IDA, CPR
    working paper · PhD thesis (SFI 2003), Paper II, Section 5.2, pp. 114-115

Martin Browning and Søren Leth-Petersen · Economic Journal, 2003 · Individual

Tests whether consumption can be imputed from register data as income minus the change in wealth, by comparing the imputation with expenditure survey responses for the same households. The imputation works well for most households but is noisy for those with housing transactions or large stock holdings.

Danish Expenditure Survey 1994–96, Administrative income and wealth (tax) records: disposable income and year-end asset holdings
Key variables

1994–1996 survey years, linked to register years around the survey year

Not stated in the sources checked Households in the 1994–96 Danish Expenditure Survey linked to their administrative income and wealth records. source (abstract)
How variables are defined (3)
  • Imputed total household expenditure Wealth, debt and consumption
    Total expenditure imputed at the household level as disposable after-tax income minus the change in net wealth between end of year t-1 and end of year t (c = y - dW). Relies on wealth-tax register information, which ends after the wealth tax was abolished in 1997.
    Registers: Income and wealth tax registers (Statistics Denmark), Danish Expenditure Survey 1994-96

    Firm sales (oms_firm) and total exports (eksport_ialt) from the IDA firm file; exporter = 1 if exports > 0. Merged by CVR number.
    Registers: FIRM
    Codes: oms_firm, eksport_ialt > 0
    replication code · 3 Produce regression data.do, 'EXPORT AND SALES FROM FIRM'
  • Partner and children Family links, fertility and household
    Partner = 1 if civil status CIVST is 'G' (married) or 'P' (registered partnership); number of children and age of youngest/oldest child from the IDA family file (c_antboernf, c_aldyngst, c_aldaeldst), with dummies for youngest/oldest child aged 0-2, 3-4, 5+.
    Registers: IDA personer, IDA familie
    Codes: CIVST in G, P; c_antboernf, c_aldyngst, c_aldaeldst

Instrumental Variables with Unordered Treatments: Theory and Evidence from Returns to Fields of Study

Eskil Heinesen, Christian Hvid, Lars Kirkebøen, Edwin Leuven and Magne Mogstad · Journal of Labor Economics, 2026 · Individual

Shows that the assumptions needed to identify returns to unordered treatments, such as fields of study, have testable implications, and characterises the bias when they fail. Using admission cut-offs and applicants' ranked choices in Denmark and Norway, payoffs to fields are strongly correlated across the two countries once fields violating the assumptions are dropped.

Data
Danish administrative data on all applications to post-secondary education 1994–2002 (coordinated admission system), Population register and other registers (background, completed field of study, annual earnings), Norwegian post-secondary application data 1998–2004 linked to registers (comparison country)
Key variables
  • Outcome: annual earnings eight years after application (wages, self-employment and income-replacing transfers)
  • Treatment: completed field of study (nine broad fields)
  • Instrument: application score just above vs below the admission cutoff of the preferred field
  • Preferred and next-best field from applicants' rankings
Period
Applications 1994–2002 (Denmark), outcomes eight years after application
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked First-time applicants to Danish post-secondary education without a prior post-secondary degree who applied to at least two broad fields, with the preferred field having an admission cutoff, and who completed a field within eight years (paralleled with Norwegian applicants). source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Annual earnings eight years after application Earnings and income
    Annual earnings eight years after the first observed application: wage income, self-employment income and transfers replacing such income (short-term sickness pay, paid parental leave), excluding unemployment benefits; deflated by CPI (base 2011) and converted to 1,000s of USD at 2010-2016 average rates (5.9 DKK per USD).
    Registers: Income registers
    working paper · Section 5.2 'Data and descriptive statistics'
  • Completed field of study (nine broad fields) Education and test scores
    Field of the post-secondary degree completed within eight years of application, aggregating detailed fields into nine broad fields (Medicine, Law, Technology, Other Health, Humanities, Teaching, Social Science, Business, Science) following Kirkeboen et al. (2016), except that Technology covers integrated, vocational/professional short- and long-cycle degrees (mostly computer science and engineering) and Science covers open-ended bachelor programmes in sciences plus agriculture, forestry and aquaculture.
    Registers: Education register
    working paper · Section 5.2; Figure 3
  • Admission-cutoff instrument (Denmark) Education and test scores
    z = 1[GPA > Q1] + 1[Std <= GPA <= Q1] x Offer, where Q1 and Std are the Quota 1 and standby GPA thresholds of the preferred field; at GPA exactly equal to a threshold the offer is treated as random conditional on age (and on applying for standby). Applicants rank up to 8 programmes; where several programmes in the preferred broad field are listed, the lowest cutoff is used.
    Registers: Coordinated admission system (KOT) applications
    working paper · Appendix E 'Specification of instrument'; Section 5.2
  • Preferred and next-best field Education and test scores
    Defined from the local ranking on the application list around the admission cutoff: the preferred field is the one ranked just above the next-best field, where the applicant's score is near the preferred field's cutoff; fixed effects for preferred-field x next-best-field combinations are included.
    Registers: Coordinated admission system (KOT) applications
    working paper · Section 5.1 and Section 6
  • Applicant sample Sample definition and timing
    All applications to post-secondary education 1994-2002 (Denmark; Norway 1998-2004); first observed application kept; those already holding a post-secondary degree excluded; restricted to those who completed a field within eight years and who applied to at least two broad fields with the most-preferred field having an admission cutoff.
    Registers: Coordinated admission system (KOT) applications, BEF
    working paper · Section 5.2
  • Application score (high-school GPA) Education and test scores
    High-school GPA over all subjects of the study programme, recorded to one decimal on the 13-point scale (0-13, omitting 1, 2, 4, 12); used as the running variable, controlled linearly on each side of the cutoff.
    Registers: Coordinated admission system (KOT) applications
    working paper · Appendix E 'Danish admission institutions'; Section 6

Education Measurement and methods

Educational Ambition, Marital Sorting, and Inequality

Frederik Almar, Benjamin Friedrich, Ana Reynoso, Bastian Schulz and Rune Vejlin · Journal of Labor Economics, 2026 · Individual

Classifies detailed Danish education programmes into ambition types by their graduates' starting wages and wage growth. Assortative matching by educational ambition has risen sharply even though sorting by conventional education levels looks flat, and the marriage market accounts for more than 40 percent of the rise in household income inequality since 1980.

Data
Population register with partner links (BEF), Education register with four-digit ISCED programme codes (UDDA), Employment register with hourly wages (IDAN), Income register (IND), Danish Labour Force Survey (LFS/AKU), 2000–2018, Employment register for hours, part-time/full-time (RAS)
Key variables
  • Classification: educational 'ambition types' from programme-level starting wages and wage growth (about 1,800 programmes)
  • Outcome: marital sorting by ambition type (assortative matching)
  • Outcome: household labour income inequality
  • Wage measure: residualised log hourly wages by programme
  • LFS job attributes: hours, evening/weekend/home work
Period
1980–2018
Sample
on average 3,031,511 individuals per year aged 19–60; 1,800,866 individuals in couples per year All individuals living in Denmark aged 19–60 in 1980–2018, with couples defined as married or cohabiting opposite-sex partners. source
How variables are defined (12)
  • Residualised log hourly wage Earnings and income
    Hourly wage in the primary job held in the last week of November (IDAN), ranking job types H, 3, A, S, M and keeping the highest; variable TIMELON before 2008 and SMAL_TIMELOEN from 2008. Log hourly wages are regressed on year dummies (base 2000) and education-specific experience profiles, and the year coefficients are subtracted. Hours underlying the wage are contractual (pre-2008 in four bins).
    Registers: IDAN, IND, IDAP
    Codes: TIMELON (<2008), SMAL_TIMELOEN (>=2008); JOB_TYPE rank H,3,A,S,M; reg log_wage ib2000.aar i.educ_eika#c.erhverv_akk_new
    replication code · Data/Gen_sample1_new/Make analysis sample 1.do; IZA DP 17814 Online Appendix A.1 fn. 35 and A.2
  • Final educational programme Education and test scores
    Highest completed education (HFAUDD, four-digit Danish ISCED/audd code, about 1,800 programmes) measured at age 35, or at the oldest observed age if the person is not observed at 35; graduation year from HF_VFRA. Grades 7-9 pooled as 9th grade; 9th grade (1109) and 10th grade (1110) split into 5 sub-programmes by region of graduation (regions 81-85); old pre-1980 high-school code mapped to the new one.
    Registers: UDDA
    Codes: HFAUDD, HF_VFRA; 1109 and 1110 split by region 81-85; 1097 mapped to 1198
    replication code · Make analysis sample 1.do ('final education'); kmeans ambition types.do; Online Appendix A.2 'Education', 'Educational programs'
  • Programme starting wage (w0) and wage growth (g) Education and test scores
    For each individual graduating in 1980 or later: w0 = mean residualised log hourly wage in years 1-5 after graduation; w1 = mean in years 9-11. Programme-level values average across graduates observed in both windows, excluding those with individual wage growth exp(w1-w0)-1 at or above the 99th percentile; programme growth g = exp(mean w1 - mean w0) - 1.
    Registers: IDAN, UDDA
    replication code · Make analysis sample 1.do ('peer wage growth'); Online Appendix A.2 'Starting wages and growth'
  • Educational ambition type Education and test scores
    Programmes are clustered by k-means on (programme starting wage, programme wage growth), with k = 3, 4 or 5 (seed 1234), both in raw and standardised versions; the four-type classification gives the (low/high w0) x (low/high g) ambition types.
    Registers: IDAN, UDDA
    Codes: cluster kmeans wage_start_mean_ambition wage_growth_ambition, k(4) s(kr(1234))
    replication code · Data/Gen_kmeans ambition types/kmeans ambition types.do
  • Couples (married and cohabiting) Family links, fertility and household
    Relationship = married (CIVST = 'G') or with a cohabitation partner id (FAELLE_NR non-missing); couple id is the man's PNR, linked through AEGTE_NR (spouse) or FAELLE_NR (cohabitant). Only couples where both partners are observed and both are aged 19-60 are kept.
    Registers: BEF, PERSONER
    Codes: CIVST == "G"; AEGTE_NR; FAELLE_NR
    replication code · kmeans ambition types.do, 'Define marital status' and 'Make couple ID'
  • Programme-outcome estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    All persons living in Denmark at end of year 1980-2018 aged 19-60, irrespective of marital status (about 3.0 million per year); persons with missing education (2.6%) excluded.
    Registers: BEF, PERSONER, UDDA
    Codes: keep if age>=19 & age<=60
    replication code · Make analysis sample 1.do; paper Section 2 (IZA DP 17814)
  • Region of graduation Geography and neighbourhood
    Residence municipality (BOPAEL_KOM_KODE) mapped from pre-2007 to post-2007 municipalities using each person's modal 2005-to-2006 transition, then grouped into the five regions 81-85 by municipality code lists; region in the graduation year (or first observed year) is used.
    Registers: BEF
    Codes: BOPAEL_KOM_KODE; region 81 (Nordjylland) ... 85 (Sjaelland) via inlist() of municipality codes
    replication code · Data/Gen_regions/region codes.do; Make analysis sample 1.do
  • Full-time / part-time and part-time penalty Hours worked
    Full-time from RAS: at least 32 hours per week (threshold 30 hours in 1980-1992 and 27 hours in 1993-2007). Part-time penalty = ratio of w1 (wage in years 9-11 after graduation) of full-time workers to that of part-time workers, by programme.
    Registers: RAS
    working paper · Section 3 (Table 1 description) and footnotes 14-15
  • LFS 'super full-time' and irregular hours Hours worked
    From LFS (AKU, 2000-2018): sft = 1 if usual weekly hours >= 38, or = 37 combined with evening, night, Saturday, Sunday or home work (answer 1 or 2) or overtime as reason (hourreas = 16); evening/night/weekend defined only when shiftwk = 3. Programme averages use yfactor weights for programmes with >= 50 (or 100) LFS observations; hwactual = 99 dropped.
    Registers: AKU, RAS
    Codes: hwusual >= 38; evenwk/nightwk/satwk/sunwk/homewk in 1,2; shiftwk == 3; hourreas == 16
    replication code · Results/fig_A1/LFS_clustering_prep_BF_dropmissing.do
  • Lifetime earnings Earnings and income
    Sum over 30 years after graduation of deflated log annual earned income ERHVERVSINDK_13 (employment plus self-employment income), year effects (base 2000) removed, for graduates observed for all 30 years; averaged by programme.
    Registers: IND
    Codes: ERHVERVSINDK_13
    replication code · Data/Gen_life_earnings_ambition_final/Get life-time earnings.do; Online Appendix A.2 'Income measure'
  • Wealth at age 50 Wealth, debt and consumption
    Average net wealth at age 50 by programme, excluding pension assets, deflated to 2000 prices.
    Registers: IND
    working paper · Section 3, footnote 16
  • Ever manager Occupation and job hierarchy
    Fraction of a programme's graduates who reach a managerial position, i.e. hold a corresponding occupational code for at least two consecutive years.
    Registers: RAS, AKM
    working paper · Section 3 (Table 1 description)

Permanent Residency and Refugee Immigrants' Skill Investment

Jacob Nielsen Arendt, Christian Dustmann and Hyejin Ku · Journal of Labor Economics, 2025 · Individual

A Danish reform tightened the employment and language requirements refugees must meet to obtain permanent residency. Rather than encouraging investment, it lowered overall employment and barely moved language proficiency, because refugees with weak pre-reform prospects reduced effort when the requirements looked out of reach.

Data
Population, income, education and immigration registers linked via the Central Person Registry, Danish language test results, Employment in annual full-time equivalents (register data)
Key variables
  • Outcome: annual employment in full-time equivalents
  • Outcome: passing the Danish language test at intermediate or higher level
  • Treatment: temporary residency in Jan–Oct 2004 (exposed to the 2007 permanent-residency reform) vs Jan–Oct 2003
  • Heterogeneity: pre-reform employment or language performance type
  • Time: years since temporary residency (YSR 1–7)
Period
Residency cohorts 2003–2004, followed seven years since temporary residency (to 2011)
Sample
767 unique individuals; 5,122 person-year observations Refugees aged 18–64 who applied for asylum after 28 February 2002 and received temporary residency in Jan–Oct 2003 (control) or Jan–Oct 2004 (treatment). source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Annual employment in full-time equivalents Employment and labour force status
    Employment in annual full-time equivalents (FTE = 1 for a full year of work), from a register variable recording cumulative employment in a calendar year, observed for everyone in Denmark on 1 January. For YSR = 1 only, FTE can exceed 1 because the cumulative variable includes work in the year residency was granted.
    Registers: Income registers, CPR
    paper · Section 5 'Data on Refugee Immigrants' and footnote 17
  • Danish language proficiency Education and test scores
    Indicator for having passed the standard Danish language test at the intermediate or higher level (test levels: basic, intermediate, high); observed from YSR = 1; passing is treated as absorbing, so the person counts as proficient at that level in all later periods.
    Registers: Danish language test results
    paper · Section 4, footnote 13; Section 5
  • Treatment and control cohorts Sample definition and timing
    Refugees who applied for asylum after 28 February 2002 and were aged 18-64 when granted temporary residency; treatment = temporary residency granted January-October 2004 (exposed to the 1 May 2007 permanent-residency reform), control = January-October 2003.
    Registers: Immigration registers, BEF
    paper · Sections 2, 4 and 5
  • Years since residency (YSR) Sample definition and timing
    For persons granted temporary residency during year y, YSR = 1 is year y+1 (first full calendar year with employment observed as of 1 January), followed for seven years (YSR 1-7).
    Registers: Immigration registers
    paper · Section 4 and Section 5
  • Pre-reform employment performance type Employment and labour force status
    HIGH if cumulative employment by YSR = 2 is above 0.75 FTE, otherwise LOW (20% HIGH, 80% LOW). The reform's requirement is 2.5 FTE of cumulative employment.
    Registers: Income registers
    paper · Section 5, 'Classifying workers into performance types'
  • Pre-reform language performance type Education and test scores
    HIGH if the person had passed the Danish language test at the intermediate level or higher by YSR = 2 (about 16%), otherwise LOW; combined with employment type into LOW/LOW, LOW/HIGH, etc.
    Registers: Danish language test results
    paper · Section 5, 'Classifying workers into performance types'
  • Matched native comparison group Sample definition and timing
    Danish natives selected by propensity-score matching to treated (control) refugees on YSR = 1 employment (2005 for treated, 2004 for control), age, gender, being single, having any children and county of residence (initial assignment county for refugees), used in a triple-difference check for the 2009 recession.
    Registers: BEF, Income registers
    paper · Section 6.3 'Comparison with natives'

The Impact of the Level and Timing of Parental Resources on Child Development and Intergenerational Mobility

Sadegh Eshaghnia, James J. Heckman and Rasmus Landersø · Journal of Labor Economics, 2025 · Individual

Uses Danish registers covering parents' full income histories to separate the level of parents' lifetime resources from their timing during childhood. Lifetime resources matter far more than when income arrives, and conventional intergenerational elasticities based on short income windows give a misleading picture of mobility.

Data
Population register with family links (BEF), Education register (UDDA), Income, assets and transfers register (IND), Sentencing register (KRAF), Incarceration register (KRIN), Danish Household Expenditure Survey, Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (DALSC), 9th-grade national leaving exam scores
Key variables
  • Outcome: child income at ages 30–35 (IGE)
  • Outcome: years of education by age 35
  • Outcome: any criminal conviction by age 35
  • Outcome: math test score at age 16 and language test at age 11
  • Explanatory: level and timing of parental income/resources by child age (lifetime vs snapshot)
Period
1980–2019
Sample
around 100,000 children and their families (105,953 individuals; 98,686 in the IGE log-log sample) Children born in 1981 and 1982 linked to their parents, non-migrants with non-migrant parents; plus the 1995–1997 birth cohorts for exam scores and DALSC children born 1995. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Parental wage income Earnings and income
    Pre-tax taxable wage earnings plus other wage-type income such as fringe benefits and stock options; parental resources are the sum of mother's and father's amounts irrespective of marital status, measured at each age of the child.
    Registers: IND
    working paper · Section 3.2, measure 1
  • Disposable income Earnings and income
    Total personal income (wage income, business and self-employment income, capital income, public transfer income, property income and other non-classifiable personal income) plus the rental value of own home for owner-occupiers, minus taxes and interest expenses. Spouses' or cohabitees' resources pooled where appropriate.
    Registers: IND
    working paper · Section 3.2, measure 2 and footnote 18
  • Expected lifetime wealth Wealth, debt and consumption
    Expected present value at age t of future disposable income (adjusted for unrealized housing capital gains) discounted with a subjective stochastic discount factor (beta = 0.96), where expectations condition on an estimated information set (gender, education level, employment status, cohabitation, number of children, quartiles of mean income, mean consumption, consumption growth and consumption SD, homeownership, and interactions).
    Registers: IND, UDDA, BEF, Danish Household Expenditure Survey
    working paper · Sections 2.1, 3.2 measure 3 and 3.3
  • Imputed household consumption Wealth, debt and consumption
    Household consumption predicted from register disposable income and assets and liabilities in t and t-1 by a random forest (number of trees by 5-fold cross-validation) trained on the Danish Household Expenditure Survey (1997+); adult-equivalent using the OECD equivalence scale.
    Registers: IND, Danish Household Expenditure Survey
    working paper · Appendix A.1, 'Danish Household Expenditure Survey'
  • Years of education by age 35 Education and test scores
    Minimum number of years it takes to complete the highest degree obtained by age 35.
    Registers: UDDA
    working paper · Section 3.1
  • Participation in crime by age 35 Crime
    Indicator for appearing in the crime registers (criminal convictions from the sentencing register KRAF) by age 35, regardless of offence type. Appendix D.2 splits into violent, property (e.g. forgery, arson, burglary, theft, shoplifting, embezzlement, fraud, extortion, robbery, tax fraud, vandalism) and other crimes (all except violent, property and traffic), measured by ages 20, 25 and 30.
    Registers: KRAF, KRIN
    working paper · Section 3.1, footnote 17; Appendix A.1; Appendix D.2
  • Math test score at age 16 Education and test scores
    Mathematics grade at the 9th-grade national leaving exam for all children born 1995-1997, standardised to mean 0 and SD 1.
    Registers: UDFK
    working paper · Section 3.1; Appendix A.1-A.2
  • Language test score at age 11 Education and test scores
    Language development test at age 11 from the Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (children born 15 Sept-31 Oct 1995, 2007 wave), standardised to mean 0 and SD 1.
    Registers: DALSC
    working paper · Section 3.1; Appendix A.1 'DALSC'
  • IGE sample (1981-1982 cohorts) Sample definition and timing
    Children born 1981-1982 linked to parents, with neither child nor parents having migrated (105,953); child resources averaged over ages 30-35; for log-log IGE, zero/negative average income and incomes more than 4 SD from the mean dropped (100,344) and children with fewer than three observations dropped (98,686).
    Registers: BEF, IND
    working paper · Section 3.1; Appendix A.2

Is Parental Leave Costly for Firms and Coworkers?

Anne Ardila Brenøe, Serena Canaan, Nikolaj A. Harmon and Heather N. Royer · Journal of Labor Economics, 2024 · Individual + firm

Compares small Danish firms where a female employee is about to give birth with similar firms without an impending birth. There is little evidence of negative effects on firm output or coworkers: most firms cover the absence by hiring temporary workers and raising other employees' hours, and only firms unable to reallocate work show losses.

Data
Central Person Registry with parent-child links (CPR/BEF), Parental leave benefit payouts and employer leave reimbursements, Central education register (UDDA), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Annual employer wage payment records (CON and RAS), Mandatory pension contributions for approximate hours (ATP), Value-added tax (VAT) firm sales and purchases data
Key variables
  • Treatment: a female employee at a small private firm giving birth (event year)
  • Outcome: firm employment, FTE hours, wage bill (total and excluding leave), sales, gross profit proxy, survival
  • Outcome: coworker hours, earnings, employment and sick days
  • Mechanism: parental leave days at the firm
  • Design: dynamic difference-in-differences with matched control events
Period
2001–2013 (births 2003–2012)
Sample
24,829 treatment events (births) and 162,151 control events covering 45,940 unique firms; 9,934 treatment events in 16,080 firms after trimming Births to prime-age (21–35) women employed in small private-sector Danish firms, compared with matched control firms without such births. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Treatment and control events Sample definition and timing
    Potential event = a woman's main job at a firm in a baseline year; event year = baseline + 2. Treatment event: woman gives birth in the event year but not in the year before or after; control event: no birth in the event year, the year before or the year after. Woman aged 19-33 at baseline, at least one year tenure at the baseline firm and not a student.
    Registers: CPR, IDA
    working paper · Sections 5.1-5.2; Appendix C.2
  • Small private firm sample Firm characteristics and productivity
    Private-sector firm (CVR) with 3-30 employees in November of the baseline year and fewer than 60 employment relationships during the baseline year; active at baseline (hours at least one FTE, positive sales and wage payments in baseline, positive sales or wages the year before); sales per employee 10,000 DKK-100 million DKK and wages per worker 10,000 DKK-1 million DKK.
    Registers: IDA, VAT, CON, RAS
    working paper · Section 5.2; Appendix C.2
  • Firm employees (November stock) Employment and labour force status
    Standard IDA main November employment relationship: worker counted at the firm if their main job was there in the last week of November; includes workers on leave. Main job = job with most hours, ties broken by highest earnings.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 4.2; Appendix C.1
  • FTE hours from ATP contributions Hours worked
    Approximate yearly hours from mandatory ATP pension contributions (step schedule for 0-9, 9-17, 18-26 and 27+ weekly hours, topping out at full time, 37 hours), scaled to full-time equivalents (Lund and Vejlin 2016); share of year on paid parental leave subtracted since ATP continues during paid leave. Misses overtime.
    Registers: ATP
    working paper · Section 4.2; Appendix C.1
  • Wage bill and wage bill ex. leave Earnings and income
    Total wage bill = sum of all pre-tax payments to workers in the year (from CON and RAS), including payments to workers on paid leave. Wage bill ex. leave: each worker's wage = payments / ATP hours incl. paid leave, multiplied by hours excluding paid leave; the gap (paid leave covered by the firm) is subtracted from the total wage bill.
    Registers: CON, RAS, ATP
    working paper · Section 4.2; Appendix C.1
  • Sales, gross profit proxy and survival Firm characteristics and productivity
    Total sales and purchases from VAT data (corrected to include exports; negative values recoded to zero). Gross profit proxy = sales minus purchases minus wage bill ex. leave (purchases include capital equipment). Total variable costs = purchases + wage bill ex. leave. Exiting firms kept with zero employees/hours/sales; shutdown proxied by zero sales.
    Registers: VAT
    working paper · Section 4.3; Appendix C.1
  • Parental leave days Family links, fertility and household
    Total days of paid and unpaid leave from payouts of parental leave benefits to individuals and leave reimbursements to firms, incl. pregnancy-related extensions; prenatal and postnatal days allocated around the birth; truncated at 38 weeks any prenatal, 6 weeks paid prenatal, 52 weeks paid postnatal, 104 weeks any postnatal.
    Registers: Parental leave benefit payouts, Employer leave reimbursements
    working paper · Section 4.1; Appendix C.1
  • Coworker sample Sample definition and timing
    Male and female coworkers of event women in the baseline year whose job at the baseline firm is their main labour market attachment, with hours at least half an FTE and earnings above 75,000 DKK in the baseline year; followed even if they leave the firm.
    Registers: IDA, ATP
    working paper · Section 5.4; Appendix C.2
  • Coworker sick days Health care use
    Take-up of publicly paid sick days (any sick days); eligibility for public sickness funds starts after two weeks of sickness, so the measure captures longer sickness spells.
    working paper · Section 6, footnote 18; Figure 7(d)

Grades and Employer Learning

Anne Toft Hansen, Ulrik Hvidman and Hans Henrik Sievertsen · Journal of Labor Economics, 2024 · Individual

Uses a nationwide rescaling of Danish university grades to identify the return to GPA that is unrelated to ability. A reform-induced higher GPA raises earnings right after graduation, especially for graduates with fewer other signals, but the effect fades within a few years, consistent with employers learning quickly about productivity.

Data
University student records (Aarhus University and University of Copenhagen) with grades before and after the 2007 recoding, Administrative registers from Statistics Denmark (background, parental income and education, earnings)
Key variables
  • Outcome: log total gross earnings in each of the first five calendar years after graduation
  • Treatment: reform-induced change in GPA from the 1 August 2007 recoding to the new grading scale
  • Outcome: indicator for positive earnings
  • Controls: gender, age at graduation, high school GPA, parental income, employment and education
Period
Students enrolled on 1 August 2007 who graduated before 2011; earnings for the first five years after graduation
Sample
3,813 students Master's students at Aarhus University or University of Copenhagen enrolled on 1 August 2007 with at most 40 ECTS remaining who graduated before 2011. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Reform-induced GPA (treatment) Education and test scores
    Deviation of a student's recoded (post-1 August 2007, 7-point scale) GPA from a cubic fit of post-recoding GPA on pre-recoding (13-scale) GPA; grades were recoded per the Ministry of Education mapping. Final GPA is a weighted average of recoded grades and grades from exams after the recoding.
    Registers: University student records (Aarhus University, University of Copenhagen)
    Codes: 13-scale to 7-point scale mapping (paper Table 1)
    working paper · Sections 2 and 3.4; Table 1; Figure 3
  • Master's student sample Sample definition and timing
    Students enrolled in a master's program on 1 August 2007 at Aarhus University (incl. Aarhus School of Business) or University of Copenhagen with at most 40 ECTS points remaining on the recoding date, who graduated before 2011 (3,813 students).
    Registers: University student records
    working paper · Section 3.1
  • Log total gross earnings after graduation Earnings and income
    Log total gross earnings in each of the first five calendar years after graduation; individuals with zero earnings excluded. A separate extensive-margin outcome is an indicator for positive earnings. Monetary values in 2015 prices (CPI).
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers
    working paper · Section 3.2; Table 2 notes
  • Other labour market outcomes Earnings and income
    Log disposable income (after transfers and taxes), unemployment, public-sector employment, job changes, annual earnings growth, and earnings growth with the same employer, in each of the first five years after graduation.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers
    working paper · Section 5; Table 7
  • Parental background controls Family links, fertility and household
    Parental income (mean total disposable income across observed parents, calendar year before graduation/reform), parental unemployment (mean annual unemployment), indicator for at least one parent with a university degree, and parental origin (non-Western vs Western per Statistics Denmark); missing values set to zero with missing dummies.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers
    working paper · Sections 3.2 and 4; Table 2 notes
  • Earnings while studying (heterogeneity) Earnings and income
    Low earnings while studying used as a proxy for little relevant labour-market experience; Aarhus University attendance used as a further proxy.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers
    working paper · Section 6; Table 8 panels E-F

Unemployed Job Search across People and over Time: Evidence from Applied-For Jobs

Jonas Fluchtmann, Anita M. Glenny, Nikolaj A. Harmon and Jonas Maibom · Journal of Labor Economics, 2024 · Individual

Uses the logs of job applications made by Danish unemployment insurance recipients to document how the jobs people apply for differ across job seekers and change over an unemployment spell, and what these patterns imply for models of directed search.

Data
Joblog applied-for job records (Danish Agency for Labour Market and Recruitment), DREAM event-history register of public transfers, Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Employment statistics for employees with hours and earnings (BFL), Firm purchases data (FIKS), Auxiliary survey of UI recipients on application coverage, O*NET Related Occupation Matrix
Key variables
  • Outcome: predicted log wage of applied-for jobs (occupation and AKM firm effect)
  • Outcome: share of applied-for jobs that are full-time
  • Outcome: scope of search index (commute time, related occupation, related industry)
  • Outcome: share of applications to publicly posted vacancies
  • Time variable: month of unemployment spell
Period
September 2015–September 2017
Sample
127,695 individuals (spells) and over 4 million applied-for jobs Individuals of Danish origin starting UI spells between September 2015 and September 2017, eligible for the full two years of benefits, with spells of at least 8 weeks and at least one registered application. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • UI spell (start and end) Unemployment and benefits
    New UI spell: at least 4 consecutive weeks of UI benefit payments with no UI payout in the 4 weeks before spell start (DREAM). Spell ends with 4 consecutive weeks without UI paid out; followed for a year or until exit.
    Registers: DREAM
    working paper · Section 3.2; Online Appendix B.2, footnote 38
  • Analysis sample of UI recipients Sample definition and timing
    Individuals of Danish origin (immigrants excluded) starting UI spells September 2015-September 2017 with full two-year UI eligibility; spell lasts at least 8 weeks; applications in the last 4 weeks of a spell dropped; at least one Joblog application registered; first spell only. 127,695 spells.
    Registers: DREAM, Joblog, IDA
    working paper · Section 3.2; Online Appendix B.2
  • Predicted (typical) wage of applied-for jobs Unemployment and benefits
    Log wage predicted for each applied-for job from re-employment wages of new hires: post-LASSO OLS (Rigorous-LASSO selects 233 of 10,407 regressors) on 1-, 2- and 3-digit industry and occupation dummies, an AKM-availability dummy, the within-industry-demeaned AKM firm effect, and all pairwise interactions; averaged per recipient-month. Robustness uses the AKM firm effect directly.
    Registers: BFL, Joblog
    Codes: DISCO-08 and NACE Rev. 2 at 1-3 digits
    working paper · Section 3.3; Online Appendix B.4, footnote 42
  • AKM firm fixed effect Firm characteristics and productivity
    Firm fixed effects from an AKM log-wage model estimated on BFL matched employer-employee data 2008-2015 (290,108 connected firms) with year-month fixed effects; worker-weighted industry means removed after estimation.
    Registers: BFL
    working paper · Online Appendix B.4
  • Share of full-time applications Hours worked
    Share of a recipient's applied-for jobs in a month reported as full-time by the UI recipient in Joblog (full-time in Denmark is 37 hours per week).
    Registers: Joblog
    working paper · Section 3.3; Online Appendix B.2 footnote 36
  • Scope of search index Occupation and job hierarchy
    Standardized combination of average commute time to applied-for jobs (Google Maps driving times from residence municipality to firm address, Harmon 2013), share in an occupation unrelated to the previous job (not among the O*NET top-10 related occupations, mapped to 3-digit DISCO), and share in an unrelated industry (not among the 10 most skill-related 3-digit NACE Rev. 2 industries, Neffke and Henning 2013); restandardized by first-month mean and SD.
    Registers: Joblog, BFL
    Codes: DISCO 3-digit; NACE Rev. 2 3-digit
    working paper · Section 3.3; Online Appendix B.5
  • Share of applications to publicly posted vacancies Unemployment and benefits
    Monthly share of applied-for jobs that the job seeker reports in Joblog as found via a publicly posted vacancy (other channels: network, contacted by firm/headhunter, cold contact).
    Registers: Joblog
    working paper · Section 3.3
  • Firm purchases and employment (validity checks) Firm characteristics and productivity
    Firm purchases from FIKS, built from mandatory VAT reports; firm employment computed from BFL.
    Registers: FIKS, BFL
    working paper · Online Appendix B.6.4, footnote 50

Mette Foged, Linea Hasager and Giovanni Peri · Journal of Labor Economics, 2024 · Individual

Uses quasi-experimental variation from several Danish reforms to compare, in a common framework, the long-run employment and earnings effects of language training, active labour market programmes and benefit cuts for refugees, and ranks the policies by their effects and costs.

Data
Admission Register (OPHG), Migration register (VNDS), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Income register (IND), Population register (BEF), Education register (UDDA), Family register (FAM)
Key variables
  • Outcome: employment (any employment in the year)
  • Outcome: annual gross labour earnings (2015 USD)
  • Policy 1: initial dispersal across municipalities (conditional random assignment)
  • Policy 2: 1999 language training reform (RD at 1 January 1999 admission)
  • Policy 3: Start Aid welfare benefit cut (RD at 1 July 2002 admission)
  • Policy 4: 'Industry Packages' ALMP rolled out across municipalities 2015–2018
Period
1986–2008 refugee arrivals (outcomes followed up to 15 years; ALMP analysis January 2008–April 2019)
Sample
56,192 adult refugees Refugees and family-reunified refugees aged 18–55 on arrival who settled in a Danish municipality 1986–2008, split into policy-specific arrival cohorts. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Refugee identification and settlement date Immigration and origin
    Refugees and family members reunified with refugees identified from admission category in the Admission Register (OPHG) from 1997 onward; refugee status before 1997 imputed from year of arrival and country of origin. Date of first settlement in Denmark and later out-migration from the migration register (VNDS); refugees followed from first settlement in a municipality (within two months of being granted status), 1986-2008 arrivals.
    Registers: OPHG, VNDS
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Employment (any in year) Employment and labour force status
    Indicator equal to one if the individual was employed at some point in the year (IDA). Appendix alternative: employment as a fraction of a full working year. For the ALMP analysis, monthly any-employment.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 4.1, footnote 9
  • Annual gross labour earnings Earnings and income
    Annual gross labour market income from the income register (IND), converted to US dollars at 2015 prices; short/medium/long-run outcomes are individual averages over years 1-5, 6-10 and 11-15 since asylum. Monthly version (ALMP) multiplied by 12.
    Registers: IND
    working paper · Section 4.1, footnote 9; Section 5.2
  • Initial placement: municipal labour market strength and co-nationals Geography and neighbourhood
    For the conditionally random dispersal (refugees granted status 1987-1998): employment rate of non-Western immigrants in the municipality of first placement in the placement year, and share of co-nationals in that municipality's population; both divided by their SD.
    Registers: VNDS, BEF, IDA
    working paper · Sections 4.2 and 6.3, equation (4)
  • 1999 language training reform RD Sample definition and timing
    Refugees granted status 1997-2000 (Somalis excluded); treatment = recognized after 1 January 1999, giving eligibility to 430 additional hours of language training in the first 3 years. RD on days between grant date and cutoff, triangular kernel, 548-day bandwidth.
    Registers: OPHG
    working paper · Sections 4.2 and 6.2, footnote 22
  • Start Aid welfare cut RD Unemployment and benefits
    Refugees arriving 2001-2003 (Bosnians and Afghans omitted); treatment = admitted after 1 July 2002, when Start Aid reduced welfare benefits (cut reversed in 2012). RD with triangular kernel and 548-day bandwidth around the admission-date cutoff.
    Registers: OPHG
    working paper · Sections 4.2 and 6.2
  • Industry Packages ALMP exposure Unemployment and benefits
    Exposure = share of a refugee's first year in the municipality during which the Industry Packages program was available; monthly refugee-arrival cohorts January 2008-April 2019 observed one year after placement; Vejle implemented August 2013, other municipalities 2015 to early 2018.
    working paper · Section 6.1
  • Linguistically close vs far origin Immigration and origin
    Linguistically far = refugees from countries with non-Latin-based languages; close = Latin-based (country-based because mother tongue is only available around 1999).
    working paper · Section 6.2, footnote 23

Constraints on Hours within the Firm

Claudio Labanca and Dario Pozzoli · Journal of Labor Economics, 2022 · Individual + firm

Uses Danish linked employer-employee data with hours and tax-rate variation from the 2010 Danish tax reform. Employees in firms with tight constraints on working hours do not adjust their hours when their taxes change, while employees in more flexible firms respond both directly and through spillovers from their coworkers.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Wage statistics with annual regular and overtime hours (Lønstatistikken, LON), Firm Statistics Register (Firmstat), Danish Foreign Trade Statistics Register, Firm-Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (FIDA), Danish Tax Register (income tax records), O*NET occupational data
Key variables
  • Outcome: annual hours worked (regular plus overtime)
  • Treatment: change in simulated marginal tax rate from the 2010 Danish tax reform (2008–2011 interval)
  • Moderator: firm-level hours constraints/coordination measured by within-firm dispersion of hours
  • Hourly wage: annual earnings over total hours
  • Spillovers: tax changes of coworkers
Period
2003–2011
Sample
more than 400,000 employees and approximately 8,300 firms (787,683 individual-year observations) Full-time employees aged 15–65 in private firms where hours are reported for at least 95% of the workforce, 2003–2011 (working-paper version 'Coordination of Hours within the Firm', IZA DP 12062). source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Annual hours worked Hours worked
    Annual hours of regular plus overtime work from Lønstatistikken (LON), reported by employers whose pension contributions depend on hours. Only firms where hours are observed for at least 95 percent of the workforce are kept; for spells in week 48 shorter than a year, hours and earnings are annualized.
    Registers: LON, IDA, FIDA
    working paper · Section 3 (The data)
  • Hourly wage Earnings and income
    Annual earnings divided by the sum of regular and overtime hours.
    Registers: IDA, LON
    working paper · Section 3
  • Employer link and full-time sample Sample definition and timing
    Each employee is matched to the highest-paying employer in the employment spell of week 48 (FIDA). Sample: full-time employees aged 15-65 in 2003-2011, full-time defined (official definition) as working more than an average of 26 weekly hours over a year, in private firms covered by Firmstat.
    Registers: FIDA, Firmstat, IDA
    working paper · Section 3
  • Hours coordination (dispersion of hours across skill groups) Hours worked
    Standard deviation across skill groups in a firm-year of the average annual (regular plus overtime) hours of each skill group; firm measure is its average over 2003-2011. Lower dispersion means greater coordination. Skill groups are deciles of the sum of the fixed and time-varying individual components of an AKM hourly-wage model; alternative: education (primary/secondary/tertiary) x occupation (manager/middle manager/blue collar) cells.
    Registers: LON, IDA
    working paper · Section 4.3, equation (9)
  • Simulated marginal tax rate Taxes and tax rates
    Marginal tax rate on labour income simulated from the Danish Tax Register with an extension of the Kleven-Schultz (2014) tax simulator to 2006-2011: increase in tax liability from raising labour income by 100 DKK, holding other income components fixed. Changes are taken over the 2008-2011 interval.
    Registers: Danish Tax Register
    working paper · Section 5.2
  • Mechanical net-of-tax rate change (instrument) Taxes and tax rates
    Post-reform (2011) marginal tax rate simulated using pre-reform (2008) income adjusted for inflation; the log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate from this mechanical rate instruments the observed change. For spillovers, the firm average of mechanical changes among high-income workers instruments the change in their average hours.
    Registers: Danish Tax Register
    working paper · Section 5.5
  • High- vs low-income workers Taxes and tax rates
    Low-income: tax-exempt or in the bottom tax bracket in 2008. High-income: in the middle or top bracket in 2008, excluding a residual group in the top bracket in 2008 predicted (from 2008 real income and the post-reform schedule) to fall into the bottom bracket in 2011.
    Registers: Danish Tax Register
    working paper · Section 5.1
  • Firm productivity Firm characteristics and productivity
    Value added per employee and TFP from Firmstat accounting data; in some specifications value added per employee is instrumented with TFP. Construction details are in an online appendix not included in the WP.
    Registers: Firmstat
    working paper · Section 4.1, footnote 15; Figure notes

Exploits idiosyncratic variation in the share of female peers across cohorts within Danish high schools. A higher share of female peers lowers women's probability of enrolling in and graduating from STEM programmes and raises men's, widening the gender gap in STEM.

Student/education registers with high school, track and cohort identifiers (UDDA), Population register with parental links (BEF), Parental income and education registers (IND, UDDA), Earnings and employment registers, Occupation codes (STEM occupations), Fertility from population/birth registers
Key variables

Period
High school entry 1980–1994; outcomes followed up to 20 years after entry
Sample
182,211 students in 127 schools (1,877 school-cohort observations) All students entering the math track of Danish academic high schools between 1980 and 1994, excluding schools with tiny or atypical cohorts. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • STEM enrolment and completion Education and test scores
    Enrolment: indicator for ever having been enrolled in a STEM study at college level or higher. Completion: field of the highest obtained degree is STEM. STEM = ISCED fields Natural Sciences, Mathematics and Statistics (05), ICT (06), and Engineering, Manufacturing and Construction (07); split into subfields Biology, Math and Physics, ICT and Engineering, and a fourth group.

  • Proportion of female peers Education and test scores
    Share of female students in the student's high school math-track cohort at high school entry, constructed at the cohort-school-track level and excluding the student (leave-one-out).

    working paper · Section II.C
  • Math-track high school sample Sample definition and timing
    All students entering the math track of general (academic) high school 1980-1994; excludes students missing gender/age, students not aged 14-19 at entry, schools where under 95 percent of a cohort is aged 14-19, school-cohorts with fewer than 10 students, and schools not admitting students for at least four consecutive years.
    Registers: Student registers
    working paper · Section II.B
  • STEM occupation Occupation and job hierarchy
    Indicator for working in a high-skilled STEM occupation for at least half the years observed in 11-15 and 16-20 years after high school entry.
    Codes: DISCO (Danish ISCO) codes 21, 25, 31, 35
    working paper · Footnote 22; Table 7 notes
  • Earnings percentile rank Earnings and income
    Average of the individual's annual labour earnings percentile over a five-year period (11-15 and 16-20 years after high school entry), with percentiles computed by year of birth and age using the entire Danish population as reference; earnings in 2015 DKK.

  • Fertility by age 36 Family links, fertility and household
    Number of children by age 36, and timing of first child.
    working paper · Section V; Table 8

Paul Bingley, Petter Lundborg and Stéphanie Vincent Lyk-Jensen · Journal of Labor Economics, 2020 · Individual

Uses the Danish draft lottery to estimate the effect of conscription on later outcomes. Military service delays education and labour market entry, and the paper quantifies the resulting losses in schooling and earnings for those who serve.

Data
Danish Defence military register (Armed Forces Day draft records: IQ test, eligibility, height, lottery number), Earnings from employer reports to tax authorities (income registers), Education registers (UDDA), Central Crime Register, National hospital discharge register (LPR), Medical Birth Register (MFR) birth weight, Population register (BEF)
Key variables
  • Outcome: annual labour income at ages 25–35
  • Treatment: military service
  • Instrument: draft lottery number below the threshold
  • Heterogeneity: cognitive ability (draft board IQ test)

Period
Birth cohorts 1976–1983; earnings at ages 25–35
Sample
152,269 men without missing earnings (military register covers 155,570 fit-for-service conscripts) Danish men born 1976–1983 declared fit for military service who drew a draft lottery number at the Armed Forces Day. source
How variables are defined (11)
  • Annual labour income Earnings and income
    Annual labour income from employment and self-employment, including sickness benefits and paternity leave benefits, from employer reports to the tax authorities (sum over all employments in the calendar year); excludes occupational pension contributions and study grants/loans. Measured at ages 25-35 and used in logs (zeros drop out); sensitivity measure excludes sickness and leave benefits.
