  • Drafted (lottery instrument) Sample definition and timing

    working paper · Sections II-III
  • Military service (served) Sample definition and timing
    Men who start military service aged 18-24, regardless of whether drafted; those who serve without being drafted are volunteers.
    Registers: Danish Defence military register
    working paper · Section II
  • Cognitive ability (draft board IQ test) Education and test scores
    Armed Forces Day IQ test score: number of correct answers out of 78 items; used to split the sample into ability quartiles.
    Registers: Danish Defence military register
    working paper · Section II, footnote 10
  • Years of schooling Education and test scores
    Years of schooling imputed from Statistics Denmark's highest completed education, based on enrolment and qualifications reported by educational institutions.

    working paper · Section III
  • Unemployment (UI receipt share) Unemployment and benefits
    Proportion of the year during which unemployment insurance benefits were received, at age 26; social assistance recipients are not counted as unemployed.

  • Bank holdings Wealth, debt and consumption
    Bank assets minus bank debt at age 26 from financial institution reports to the tax authorities; mortgage debt and stocks/bonds excluded.

    working paper · Section V, Table 9 panel B, footnote 19
  • Criminal conviction from age 25 Crime
    Indicator for having been convicted of any type of crime, excluding traffic offences, from age 25, from the Central Crime Register; pre-conscription values used as controls.

    working paper · Section V, Table 9 panel C
  • Hospitalization, psychiatric diagnosis, psychiatric medication, addiction treatment Health care use
    Any admission to somatic or psychiatric hospitals including same-day patients (national hospital discharge register); psychiatric diagnoses and addiction treatment from the hospital discharge register; purchase of GP-prescribed mental-health medicine from the Danish Medicines Agency.

  • Immigrant / native Dane Immigration and origin
    Statistics Denmark classification: native Danes are born in Denmark with at least one parent born in Denmark; others are first- or second-generation immigrants.

  • Out-of-home care / single-parent family Family links, fertility and household
    Out-of-home care: placed in out-of-home care (foster care or residential care homes) before age 18. Single-parent family: 0 if living with both legal parents on the 17th birthday according to the central person register.

Sanni Breining, Joseph Doyle, David N. Figlio, Krzysztof Karbownik and Jeffrey Roth · Journal of Labor Economics, 2020 · Individual

In both Denmark and Florida, second-born boys are substantially more likely than their first-born brothers to be disciplined in school and to enter the criminal justice system. Data
Medical Birth Register (MFR), Population register with parent and sibling links (BEF), Central Crime Register (convictions, sentences, incarceration), School registers (9th grade exit exam grades), Register of Daycare Institutions, National Patient Register (LPR) and Psychiatric Central Register, Parental education, employment, earnings and maternity leave registers, Florida birth records linked to school and juvenile justice records

Period
Danish birth cohorts 1981–1990; Florida births 1994–2002
Sample
Denmark: 121,100 children in 60,550 families (first- and second-born boys); 448,979 singleton births 1981–1990 in the full Danish population Danish families with two or more children with the same father, comparing first-born and second-born boys born 1981–1990 (plus Florida comparison samples). source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Criminal conviction by age 16 / 21 Crime
    Indicator (x100) for having any criminal conviction by age 16, and by age 21, from the Criminal Registers; convictions observable from age 15 (age of criminal responsibility). Traffic offences are excluded; crime outcomes cover convictions for violent, property and special offences.

    working paper · Section 3.1; footnote 20; Table 3 notes
  • Prison sentence / incarceration by age 16 / 21 Crime

    Registers: Danish Criminal Registers
    working paper · Section 3.1; footnote 20; Figure 1 notes
  • Violent, property and special crime convictions Crime
    Convictions by age 21 split by crime type: violent (e.g. manslaughter, rape, death threats), property (e.g. forgery, arson, burglary) and special offences (e.g. drug offences, illegal weapon possession, human trafficking). Denmark birth cohorts 1981-1990.

  • 9th grade exit exam grades Education and test scores
    Ninth grade exit exam grades in reading and math from the School Registers, based on assessments by the student's teacher and an external reviewer; standardized to mean zero and unit SD within each cohort.
    Registers: School Registers

  • Psychiatric diagnoses by age 10 Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicator for having received, by age 10, a diagnosis at a Danish hospital of a disorder of psychological development, or a behavioural and emotional disorder (e.g. ADHD), from the National Patient Registry and Psychiatric Central Registry.
    Registers: LPR, Psychiatric Central Register
    Codes: ICD-10 F80-F89 (psychological development); ICD-10 F90-F98 (behavioural and emotional)
    working paper · Section 3.1, footnote 5
  • Daycare enrolment ages 1-3 Family links, fertility and household
    Enrolment in out-of-home daycare at ages 1, 2 and 3, from the Register of Daycare Institutions (type and place of daycare observed yearly 1995-2008).

  • Maternal employment after birth Employment and labour force status

  • Birth order sample (second-born boys) Family links, fertility and household
    Birth order from the Birth Register (1960-2010 births) using exact birth dates and parent links; twins excluded; sample is the first two children of families with two or more children, restricted to full biological siblings (same mother and father) with a second-born boy (boy-boy and girl-boy families). Main crime sample is birth cohorts 1981-1990.

  • Parental controls measured before birth Earnings and income
    Maternal and paternal employment and family income are measured in the year before birth; missing parental education/employment (about 9-10 percent) are mean-imputed with a missing indicator.

Estimating Equilibrium Effects of Job Search Assistance

Pieter Gautier, Paul Muller, Bas van der Klaauw, Michael Rosholm and Michael Svarer · Journal of Labor Economics, 2018 · Individual

A randomised activation experiment in two Danish counties helped treated job seekers find work faster, but untreated job seekers in the same counties found work more slowly than in comparison counties. An equilibrium search model fitted to the data shows that these displacement effects make a large-scale rollout far less beneficial than the partial estimates suggest.

Data
National Labour Market Board administrative data on unemployment benefit spells (all Danish counties), Randomised activation experiment assignment (Storstrøm and South Jutland, birth date 1st–15th of month), Income transfer data (exit destinations), National Labour Market Board monthly stock of open vacancies by county (from local job centres)
Key variables
  • Outcome: unemployment duration / exit rate from benefits (weeks)
  • Treatment: assignment to intensive activation programme (born 1st–15th of month)
  • Spillover comparison: non-participants in experiment counties vs comparison counties (difference-in-differences)
  • Outcome: log stock of open vacancies by county and month
  • Structural equilibrium search model parameters
Period
Benefit inflows November 2004–February 2005 (pre-experiment) and November 2005–February 2006 (experiment), followed up to two years; vacancies January 2004–November 2007
Sample
40,403 benefit claimants in experiment period (3,751 experiment participants: 1,814 treated, 1,937 controls); 49,063 in pre-experiment sample All individuals in Denmark who started collecting regular unemployment benefits between November 2005 and February 2006, plus a pre-experiment inflow cohort one year earlier. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • Unemployment duration / exit from benefits Unemployment and benefits
    Duration (in weeks) of collecting regular unemployment benefits from the week benefits start, followed for at most two years; exits treated as exits from unemployment (linked income-transfer data show almost all exits in the first two years are to employment); durations censored otherwise.
    Registers: National Labour Market Board benefit spell data, Income transfer data
    working paper · Section 3 (Data)
  • Activation programme treatment Unemployment and benefits
    All individuals starting to collect unemployment benefits November 2005-February 2006 in Storstrom and South Jutland counties took part; those born on the 1st-15th of the month were assigned to the intensive activation programme (letter after ~1.5 weeks, 2-week JSA course after 5-6 weeks, weekly/biweekly caseworker meetings, new programme after 4 months); those born 16th-31st are controls.
    Registers: National Labour Market Board benefit spell data
    working paper · Sections 2.1 and 3
  • Experiment, comparison and pre-experiment samples Sample definition and timing
    All 41,801 individuals applying for regular benefits November 2005-February 2006 in all Danish counties, minus 1,398 with inconsistent county of residence; non-experiment counties form the comparison group; a pre-experiment sample of 49,063 individuals starting benefits November 2004-February 2005 controls for county differences (difference-in-differences in a stratified proportional hazard model).
    Registers: National Labour Market Board benefit spell data
    working paper · Sections 3 and 4.1.1
  • Stock of open vacancies Other
    Monthly average number of open vacancies per day by county, January 2004-November 2007, collected by the National Labour Market Board from local job centres; used in logs.
    Registers: National Labour Market Board vacancy data
    working paper · Section 3
  • Benefit history covariates Unemployment and benefits
    Weeks of benefit receipt in the previous year and in the past two years, plus gender, nationality and an indicator for entering unemployment in November or December.
    Registers: National Labour Market Board benefit spell data
    working paper · Section 4.1.1; Table 1

Not stated in the sources checked

Measurement and methods Education

The Dynamics of Marriage and Divorce

Gustaf Bruze, Michael Svarer and Yoram Weiss · Journal of Labor Economics, 2015 · Individual

Estimates a dynamic model of marriage, divorce and remarriage with learning about match quality on long register histories of Danish cohorts. Spousal education is complementary in generating marital surplus, education stabilises marriages, education raises men's share of the surplus, and divorce costs are high both early and late in a marriage.

Data
Population register with marital and cohabitation histories (BEF), Education registers (UDDA), completed education at age 46
Key variables
  • Outcome: transitions into and out of marriage, divorce and remarriage
  • Key variable: completed education group at 46 (high school or less, vocational, college)
  • Assortative matching by education of spouses
  • Structural model parameters: match quality, gains from marriage, divorce costs
Period
1980–2006 (ages 20 to 46)
Sample
61,780 individuals (31,835 men and 29,945 women) All men and women born in Denmark in 1960 with complete residence records 1980–2006 and not married at age 20. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • 1960 birth cohort panel Sample definition and timing
    All men and women born in 1960 followed annually 1980-2006 (ages 20-46); individuals must have a Danish address in every year (complete marital history), and those already married at age 20 are excluded, leaving 61,780 individuals.
    Registers: BEF
    working paper · Section 2 (The sample)
  • Completed education at age 46 Education and test scores
    Three groups based on completed education at age 46: high school or less, vocational education, and college (some college or more).
    Registers: UDDA
    working paper · Section 2.1
  • Cohabitation (Statistics Denmark definition) Family links, fertility and household
    Classified as cohabiting if sharing an address with an opposite-sex person who is not family-related and is no more than 15 years older or younger. The paper uses two alternative partnership definitions: legal marriage only, and partnerships including legal marriage and cohabitation.
    Registers: BEF
    working paper · Section 2.2.1
  • Marital states and transitions Family links, fertility and household
    Yearly states: single never married, single previously married, or married (characterised by own and spouse's marital history, spouse's education and type, and marriage duration). Divorced persons are assumed single for at least one year before remarrying; direct marriage-to-marriage moves (2.3%) have the first year of the new marriage recoded as singlehood.
    Registers: BEF
    working paper · Sections 4.2 (Likelihood function)
  • Marriage duration (divorce cost) Family links, fertility and household
    Fixed cost of divorce parameterised with ten dummies for marital duration of 1, 2, ..., 9 and 10 or more years.
    Registers: BEF
    working paper · Section 4.1/4.2

Family responses and insurance Gender and the family Education

Wage Dispersion and Decentralization of Wage Bargaining

Christian M. Dahl, Daniel le Maire and Jakob R. Munch · Journal of Labor Economics, 2013 · Individual + firm

Exploits the shift in Denmark during the 1990s from centralised to firm-level wage bargaining. Workers covered by firm-level bargaining earn a wage premium, returns to skills are higher, and wage dispersion is greater than under sector-level bargaining.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), matched employer-employee data, Income register (tax files), Supplementary Pension Fund (ATP) contributions for hours worked, DA/LO bargaining-segment classification by NACE industry and DISCO occupation (Confederation of Danish Employers)
Key variables
  • Outcome: log hourly wage (labour income plus mandatory pension payments over hours)
  • Treatment: wage-setting system (standard-rate, minimum-wage, minimum-pay, firm-level bargaining)
  • Outcome: wage dispersion (quantile regressions) and returns to skills
  • Controls: gender, children, marriage, immigrant status, education, experience, plant size, industry-by-year dummies
  • Worker fixed effects; changes in wage-setting system over time
Period
1992–2001
Sample
about 1.14 million worker-year observations (1,137,367) 30% random sample of full-time private-sector workers aged 25–65 in 36 DA/LO bargaining segments, in plants with at least five employees. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Hourly wage rate Earnings and income
    Sum of total labour income (from tax files in the Income Register) and mandatory pension fund payments, divided by the total number of hours worked in the year (ATP-imputed); observations with unobserved wage, wage flagged by Statistics Denmark as low precision, or in the top or bottom half percentile are discarded.
    Registers: IND, IDA, ATP
    working paper · Section 4 (pp. 13-14)
  • Annual hours (ATP-based) Hours worked
    Imputed from the worker's ATP contribution group: no payment for 0-9 weekly hours, 1/3 of full-time payment for 9-18, 2/3 for 18-27, and full payment for 27+; workers paying full-time ATP are assigned hours corresponding to the standard 37-hour week. Overtime not captured.
    Registers: ATP
    working paper · Section 4 (p. 13)
  • Bargaining segment / wage-setting system Sector and industry
    Workers are allocated to 36 DA/LO bargaining segments using six-digit NACE industry and four-digit DISCO (ISCO-88) occupation codes, as DA and LO do (about 85% of DA/LO employment); each segment's yearly system is classified as standard-rate (normallønssystemet), minimum-wage (minimallønssystemet), minimum-pay (mindstebetalingssystemet) or firm-level bargaining (uden lønsats).
    Registers: IDA, DA/LO bargaining segment classification
    Codes: NACE 6-digit x DISCO 4-digit (segment list not given)
    working paper · Section 2 (p. 10) and Section 4 (p. 12)
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Full-time workers aged 25-65 employed in one of the DA/LO bargaining segments, 1992-2001, excluding scholarship recipients in ordinary education, plants with fewer than five employees, and observations with unreliable/extreme wages; a 30% random sample is drawn (about 1.14 million worker-years).
    Registers: IDA, IND
    working paper · Section 4 (p. 14)
  • Education groups Education and test scores
    Unskilled (high school or equivalent or less), vocational education (final stage of secondary education preparing for direct labour market entry), short-term higher education and long-term higher education, from the Danish education code corresponding to ISCED (higher education = ISCED 5 and 6).
    Registers: UDDA
    Codes: ISCED 5-6 = higher education
    working paper · Section 4 and footnote 4
  • Labour market experience Employment and labour force status
    Actual labour market experience accumulated since 1964.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 4 (p. 13)
  • Plant size and workforce composition Firm characteristics and productivity
    Plant size defined as the number of employees, plus variables measuring the labour force composition at plant level; regressions also include 25 industry dummies interacted with year dummies.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 4 (p. 13)

Ethnic Enclaves and Immigrant Labor Market Outcomes: Quasi-Experimental Evidence

Anna Piil Damm · Journal of Labor Economics, 2009 · Individual

Uses the quasi-random dispersal of refugees across Danish municipalities between 1986 and 1998 to separate the effect of living in an ethnic enclave from self-selection. Larger enclaves raise refugee men's annual earnings without changing their employment rates, and the gains are larger where more co-nationals are employed, pointing to job information networks.

Data
Longitudinal administrative registers on the immigrant population (Statistics Denmark), 1984–2000, Population register (BEF) incl. country of origin, year of immigration and municipality, Survey-based register on immigrants' pre-immigration education and integrated pupil register, Municipality statistics: unemployment register, election statistics, register-based labour force statistics, housing statistics, Danish Refugee Council administrative statistics on temporary housing (to identify assignment municipality)
Key variables
  • Outcome: employment probability
  • Outcome: real annual labour earnings
  • Key regressor: ethnic enclave (co-national group) size in municipality
  • Instrument / identification: initial assignment municipality under the 1986–1998 spatial dispersal policy
  • Controls: gender, age, marital status, children, education, country of origin, year of immigration
Period
Registers 1984–2000; refugee immigration cohorts 1986–1993
Sample
13,927 individuals (balanced panel observed annually for seven years after immigration) Adult refugees from 11 main refugee-sending countries assigned to Danish municipalities under the dispersal policy, observed annually from receipt of residence permit to seven years after. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Employment Employment and labour force status
    Based on labour market status in November of each year: employed if main occupation is wage-employment with at least 9 hours of weekly work, or self-employment (includes part-time of at least 9 weekly hours and full-time). Outcome measured seven years after immigration.
    Registers: Immigrant population registers (Statistics Denmark), RAS
    working paper · Section III.D
  • Real annual earnings Earnings and income
    Sum of wage earnings, profits from own company and sickness benefits, deflated by the consumer price index (base year 1980); analysed for refugees with positive earnings seven years after immigration.
    Registers: Income register (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section III.D; Table I notes
  • Ethnic group (enclave) size Immigration and origin
    Number of first- and second-generation immigrants (immigrants and descendants) from individual i's source country living in i's municipality of residence; ethnicity proxied by country of origin.
    Registers: BEF (100 per cent sample of immigrants)
    working paper · Section III.B (p. 13); Table A.I Part B
  • Refugee sample identification Immigration and origin
    Individuals from 11 main refugee-sending countries extracted by an algorithm based on country of origin and first year of residence permit (built from official asylum permit counts), immigrating under the 1986-1998 dispersal policy, aged 18-59, observed annually up to seven years after immigration (balanced panel of 13,927). Excludes those married at immigration to a Dane, an immigrant from a non-refugee-sending country, or an immigrant from a refugee-sending country who immigrated at least one year earlier (family reunification).
    Registers: Immigrant population registers (Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Section III.D and footnote 12
  • Municipality of assignment Geography and neighbourhood
    The first municipality of residence observed in the registers is classified as temporary housing if the person relocates to another municipality within the same county within one year after receipt of the first residence permit; otherwise the first municipality is the municipality of assignment (algorithm based on the Danish Refugee Council's statistics on temporary housing).
    Registers: BEF, Danish Refugee Council administrative statistics
    working paper · Section III.D
  • Instrument: number of placed co-nationals Immigration and origin
    Number of immigrants from the individual's source country placed by the authorities in the individual's municipality of assignment in year t, for t = -7, ..., 0 (0 = year of immigration), i.e. initial and past inflows of placed co-nationals.
    Registers: BEF (100 per cent sample of immigrants)
    working paper · Table A.I Part B
  • Education attained (pre-immigration) Education and test scores
    Dummies from the education code of highest degree attained: no degree = 0-9 years, high school = 10-12 years, professional = 13+ years, plus unknown education.
    Registers: Survey-based register on immigrants' pre-immigration education, Integrated pupil register
    working paper · Table A.I Part A
  • Local unemployment rate Unemployment and benefits
    Unemployment rate within a radius of DKK 60 (approx. USD 10) of transport cost around the largest post office in the municipality, constructed by Local Government Studies.
    Registers: Unemployment register (Statistics Denmark), Ministry of Transport cost statistics
    working paper · Table A.I Part B
  • Municipality characteristics (right-wing votes, county jobs, social housing) Geography and neighbourhood
    % right-wing votes: Liberal plus Conservative votes as a share of Liberal, Conservative, Social Democratic and Socialist People's Party votes at the latest municipal election; % county jobs: persons employed in the municipality as a share of county employment; % social housing: social housing dwellings for all-year residence as a share of all such dwellings.
    Registers: Election statistics, RAS, Buildings and housing statistics
    working paper · Table A.I Part B

Migration, neighbourhoods and refugees Labour markets, wages and sorting

On-the-Job Search and the Wage Distribution

Bent Jesper Christensen, Rasmus Lentz, Dale T. Mortensen, George R. Neumann and Axel Werwatz · Journal of Labor Economics, 2005 · Individual + firm

Estimates an on-the-job search model on the Danish Integrated Database for Labour Market Research, splitting each firm's separation rate into an exogenous part and a job-to-job part that falls with the firm's wage. Workers search less intensely the higher their wage, and the estimated model accounts for the gap between the distribution of wages earned and the distribution of wage offers.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), matched employer-employee data
Key variables
  • Outcome: job separations (stayers one year later) by establishment
  • Establishment average hourly wage (Statistics Denmark hourly wage estimate)
  • Wage offer distribution weighted by hires from non-employment
  • Wage earned distribution weighted by establishment employment
  • Sub-samples by occupation: skilled, unskilled, managers, salaried
Period
November 1994–November 1995
Sample
113,332 private-sector establishments All establishments in the Danish private sector, with workers aged 18–65, split by occupational category. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Stayers (job separations) Sample definition and timing
    For each establishment, the number of employees in November 1994 and the number of 'stayers', defined as workers who were employees both initially (November 1994) and in the following November (1995); separations are modelled as stayers out of initial employment.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1 (p. 8)
  • Establishment average hourly wage Firm characteristics and productivity
    For each private-sector establishment and occupational sub-sample, the average of the Statistics Denmark estimate of the hourly wage of each worker of that occupational type employed during November 1994 to November 1995, in 1994 DKK; only workers aged 18-65 included, and wage rates below 69 DKK per hour (taken as the effective legal minimum wage) and in the top 1 percent are excluded from the average (but such workers are kept in employment and stayer counts).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.2 and Table 1 (pp. 9-10)
  • Wage offer distribution F Earnings and income
    Distribution of establishment average hourly wages, each weighted by the fraction of all non-employed workers hired by the establishment during the year (only hires from non-employment are used, to avoid selection among job-to-job movers).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Sections 3.1-3.2 (pp. 8-10)
  • Wage earned distribution G Earnings and income
    Distribution of the same establishment average hourly wages weighted by the establishment's relative employment size in November 1994.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.2 (p. 10)
  • Occupational sub-samples Occupation and job hierarchy
    Pooled private-sector establishment sample partitioned by worker occupation into skilled and unskilled workers ('blue collar') and managers and salaried workers ('white collar'); distributions and counts are built separately per sub-sample.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.2 (p. 9)
  • Private sector establishments Sector and industry
    All establishments in the Danish private sector are included (overall 'private sector sample', 113,332 establishments).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.2 and Table 1

Sick of Your Poor Neighborhood? Quasi-Experimental Evidence on Neighborhood Effects on Health

Linea Hasager and Mia Jørgensen · Journal of Public Economics, 2026 · Individual

Uses the quasi-random dispersal of refugees across Danish neighbourhoods from 1986 to 1998. Refugees placed in low-income neighbourhoods had a 12 percent higher risk of developing a lifestyle-related disease 8 to 15 years later, driven by neighbours and the local environment rather than health care access, ethnic networks or labour market outcomes.

Data
National Patient Register (LPR), Health Insurance Register (SYSI, SSSY), Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Income register (IND), Population register (BEF) and address/mobility registers (BEFBOP, BEFADR), Migration register (VNDS), Criminal convictions register (KRAF), O*NET occupational data merged via occupation codes
Key variables
  • Treatment: assignment to a bottom- vs top-income-third parish (neighbourhood median household disposable income) under the 1986–1998 Refugee Spatial Dispersal Policy
  • Outcome: lifestyle-related disease diagnosis (circulatory, nutritional/metabolic, COPD, hip arthrosis, alcohol-related) 2–15 and 8–15 years after immigration
  • Outcome: mental disorder diagnoses
  • Mechanisms: health care access, employment and earnings, neighbour characteristics
Period
1985–2017 (refugees arriving 1986–1998)
Sample
21,965 refugees Refugees aged 18–64 at arrival from nine refugee-sending countries who arrived in Denmark in 1986–1998 and were assigned a municipality under the dispersal policy (excluding family-reunified spouses). source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Lifestyle-related disease diagnosis Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicator for any primary or secondary hospital diagnosis (inpatient or outpatient, National Patient Register; ICD-8 before 1994, ICD-10 after) within 2-15 years, or within 8-15 years, after immigration in one of: circulatory diseases (hypertension, ischaemic heart diseases, pulmonary diseases, other heart disease, cerebrovascular and arterial diseases), nutritional/endocrine/metabolic diseases (diabetes type I and II, obesity, elevated cholesterol), COPD, hip arthrosis, and alcohol-related diseases. Exact code grouping is in Online Appendix Section B (not accessed).
    Registers: LPR
    working paper · Section I (data), footnotes 17-19
  • Mental disorder diagnosis Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Indicator for a hospital diagnosis 2-15 or 8-15 years after immigration of mental and behavioural disorders due to psychoactive substance use; schizophrenia, schizotypal and delusional disorders; mood (affective) disorders; neurotic, stress-related and somatoform disorders; behavioural syndromes associated with physiological disturbances; and disorders of adult personality and behaviour.
    Registers: LPR
    working paper · Section I, footnote 20
  • Neighbourhood income group (parish) Geography and neighbourhood
    Neighbourhood = parish (alternatives: municipality, apartment building). Each year, neighbourhoods are ranked by median household disposable income per adult household member (Income Register, CPI-deflated to 2000) and split into thirds: bottom (below 33rd percentile), middle (34th-66th), top (67th-100th); groups are recomputed every year for all neighbourhoods.
    Registers: IND, BEF
    working paper · Section I, footnote 25
  • Assignment neighbourhood Geography and neighbourhood
    Neighbourhood of the refugee's address on 1 January in the year after immigration, to capture permanent resettlement rather than temporary accommodation.
    Registers: BEFBOP, BEFADR
    working paper · Section II (identification), p. ~14
  • Refugee (dispersal policy) sample Immigration and origin
    Immigrants arriving 1986-1998 from Afghanistan, Ethiopia, Iran, Iraq, Lebanon, Palestine (stateless), Sri Lanka and Vietnam (1986-1998) or Somalia (1989-1998), aged 18-64 at arrival; former Yugoslavs excluded; excludes those married at arrival to a non-refugee partner or to a refugee partner who arrived earlier (family reunification).
    Registers: VNDS, BEF
    working paper · Section I, footnotes 14-16
  • Employment as fraction of full working year Employment and labour force status
    Fraction of a full-time working year employed: 1 if full-time employee during the whole year, less than one for part-time or part-year employment.
    Registers: IDA, IND
    working paper · Section I (labour market outcomes)
  • Annual gross earnings Earnings and income
    Annual gross earnings from tax returns in the Income Register, CPI-deflated to 2000 and converted to USD at the 27 March 2020 exchange rate.
    Registers: IND
    working paper · Section I
  • Occupational task content Occupation and job hierarchy
    Ratio of communication and cognitive tasks to manual tasks from O*NET, merged via ISCO occupation codes, for those employed at the end of November each year.
    Registers: IDA, O*NET
    working paper · Section I
  • GP and psychologist visits Health care use
    Number of visits to general practitioners and psychologists (no diagnosis codes available in these data).
    Registers: SYSI, SSSY
    working paper · Section I, footnote 23

Joint Retirement of Couples: Evidence from Discontinuities in Denmark

Esteban García-Miralles and Jonathan M. Leganza · Journal of Public Economics, 2024 · Individual

Uses age discontinuities in eligibility for Danish early retirement and public pensions to show that when one spouse becomes eligible and retires, the other spouse is substantially more likely to retire as well, quantifying spillovers that matter for evaluating retirement reforms.

Data
Danish administrative registers for the full population 1986–2014 (labour market outcomes, pension benefits, socio-demographics, family/couple links), Annual taxable earnings registers, Monthly earnings records for all employees (eIndkomst/BFL) and monthly pension benefit records, from 2008, Voluntary early retirement pension (VERP) contribution records
Key variables
  • Outcome: spouse's retirement (ceasing to earn labour income)
  • Outcome: pension claiming (VERP or OAP) and annual labour earnings
  • Running variable (age-based design): reference individual's age relative to early pension eligibility age 60
  • Running variable (reform-based design): birth date relative to 1 January 1954 cutoff of the 2011 reform raising VERP eligibility age by 6 months
Period
1986–2014 (age-based design 1991–2013; reform-based design 2008–2014)
Sample
367,585 couples and 2,206,044 couple-year observations (age-based sample); 10,321 couples and 73,395 couple-year observations (reform-based sample) Dual-earner Danish couples (married, registered partners or cohabiting) up to 8 years apart in age, with the reference individual aged 57–60, excluding self-employed and disability recipients. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Retirement (age-based design) Retirement and pensions
    Retirement is ceasing to earn labour market income: the year in which the individual earned labour income for the last time, treated as an absorbing state (1 thereafter). Small positive income up to the equivalent of one month of average earnings is allowed after retirement (holiday pay, delayed wages). A flow definition allowing multiple retirements is used as robustness.
    Registers: Annual labour market/income registers
    working paper · Section 3.2 (Key Variables), footnote 10
  • Working past July 1 (reform-based design) Retirement and pensions
    Using monthly earnings records (eIncome, from 2008), a dummy equal to one if the individual works past the first half of the year (past July 1) in a given year.
    Registers: eIndkomst (monthly earnings)
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Pension claiming Retirement and pensions
    Receiving pension income, either voluntary early retirement pension (VERP) or old-age pension (OAP): annual indicator for any pension income in the year (age-based design), or indicator for receiving pension income before July 1 using monthly pension benefit records (reform-based design).
    Registers: Annual pension benefit registers, Monthly pension benefit records (from 2008)
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Annual labour earnings Earnings and income
    Taxable annual labour market earnings from the annual registers, winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles, deflated to 2010 prices and converted at 1 USD = 5.56 DKK.
    Registers: Annual income registers
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Couples Family links, fertility and household
    Married, registered-partnership or cohabiting couples residing in Denmark 1991-2014, identified when both partners are below age 60 and followed while they remain together; age difference within couple at most 8 years.
    Registers: Population/family registers
    working paper · Section 3.3
  • Dual-earner couple restrictions Sample definition and timing
    Reference individual (partner reaching own eligibility age) earned labour income at least once at ages 55-59 and was never self-employed or on disability benefits at ages 50-59; spouse earned labour income at least once at ages 50-59. Age-based sample: 1991-2013, reference individual aged 57-60 (eligibility age 60). Reform-based sample: 2008-2014, reference individuals with qualifying VERP contributions at least once at ages 50-59, born within 3 months either side of 1 January 1954, balanced panel.
    Registers: Annual registers, VERP contribution records
    working paper · Section 3.3, footnote 11

Does Granting Refugee Status to Family-Reunified Women Improve Their Integration?

Linea Hasager · Journal of Public Economics, 2024 · Individual

Women who enter Denmark through family reunification usually hold permits that depend on staying married. Granting them independent refugee status improves their economic integration, raises divorce rates and lowers the risk of violence against them, consistent with reduced residency uncertainty and greater bargaining power.

Data
Admission register on immigrant status and residence permit application/approval dates (Danish Immigration Service data via Statistics Denmark), Labour market data from the Danish tax authorities (employment; hours and earnings from 2008), Police registers on victimisation and criminal convictions, Hospital admissions data (National Patient Register) for assault injuries, Central population register (BEF) for demographics, spouse links and divorce
Key variables
  • Treatment: family-reunified woman granted her own refugee status (asylum), staggered timing
  • Outcome: quarterly employment, hours of work and earnings
  • Outcome: victimisation of violence (police records or assault-related hospitalisation)
  • Outcome: divorce
  • Design: staggered difference-in-differences with not-yet-treated women as controls
Period
2001–2019 (hours and earnings from 2008)
Sample
1,349 adult women Women aged 18+ who were family-reunified to a refugee spouse in Denmark between 2001 and 2017 and later applied for and obtained their own refugee status. source
How variables are defined (4)
  • Treatment: change from family reunification to own refugee status Immigration and origin
    Adult women (18+) admitted 2001-2017 as family-reunified to a refugee spouse who later apply for and obtain their own asylum (UN Convention, de facto/B-status or temporary protection), identified from application and approval dates of residence permits in the admission register; event time is the quarter of asylum recognition. Controls are not-yet-treated women recognized at most three years later; women followed from 3 years before to 1.5 years after recognition.
    Registers: Admission register (Danish Immigration Service, via Statistics Denmark)
    working paper · Sections 3.1 and 4
  • Violent victimization Crime
    Quarterly indicator equal to one if police records show the woman was a victim of violence or sexual assault, or if she was hospitalized due to assault based on physician classification of injury (following Aizer 2010); captures mainly severe cases and also non-partner violence.
    Registers: Police registers on victimization, National Patient Register (hospital admissions)
    working paper · Section 3.2, footnote 12
  • Quarterly employment, hours and earnings Employment and labour force status
    Quarterly employment indicator (available 2001-2019) and quarterly hours of work and earnings (from 2008) from tax-authority labour market data; earnings CPI-deflated to 2015 and converted to 1,000 USD at the 27 March 2019 exchange rate.
    Registers: Labour market data from Danish tax authorities
    working paper · Section 3.2, footnote 11
  • Divorce Family links, fertility and household
    Indicator equal to one if the woman is divorced (quarterly), from the central population register with spouse links.
    Registers: BEF
    working paper · Section 3.2

Income Effects and Labour Supply: Evidence from a Child Benefits Reform

Mathias Fjællegaard Jensen and Jack Blundell · Journal of Public Economics, 2024 · Individual

A 2011 Danish cap on child benefits cut payments to families with several young children and left smaller families unaffected. Mothers' labour supply rises substantially after the cut, mainly on the extensive margin, and sterilisation records are used to control for differences in preferences for more children.

Data
Population register (BEF) for family composition, marital status and cohabitation, Monthly payroll records with hours worked (BFL/eIndkomst), Child benefit payment records (BOBO/BOTI), Register OF (monthly demographics and parental leave status), Sterilisation consultations from the National Patient Register (LPRADM) and health insurance service registers (SYSI, SSSY), Annual income register (IND) for self-employment robustness
Key variables
  • Treatment: 2011 cap on child benefits (DKK 35,000) reducing unearned income for larger families with young children
  • Outcome: monthly hours worked (intensive and extensive margins)
  • Outcome: annual earnings (robustness incl. self-employed)
  • Control/restriction: family sterilisation consultation before the reform
  • Design: difference-in-differences, treated vs unaffected families
Period
September 2008–December 2014 (monthly)
Sample
28,968 treated women and 22,477 treated men Native Danish married or cohabiting parents aged 25–59 over the window with 2–4 children (at least two under 18) in January 2011, not self-employed, observed in a balanced monthly panel. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Monthly hours worked Hours worked
    Total hours worked per month from employer reports to the tax authorities (BFL, from 2008), summed over all jobs held in the month; for employees on parental leave with fixed contractual hours not adjusted in BFL, hours are adjusted using observed days of leave.
    Registers: BFL, OF
    paper · Section 5.1 and footnote 4
  • Employment indicator (extensive margin) Employment and labour force status
    Indicator for working non-zero hours in the month in BFL.
    Registers: BFL
    paper · Fig. 10 and Table notes (employment indicator), Section 6
  • Treatment group (child benefit cap) Family links, fertility and household
    Family experienced a strictly positive reduction in child benefits due to the DKK 35,000 cap in the first and/or second quarter of 2011 (benefits based on number and ages of children in the previous quarter; simulated from population registers and validated with Q4 BOBO/BOTI payments); control group = families not affected in Q1-Q2 2011. Continuous treatment = reduction in child benefits in 2011 in thousand DKK for treated families, zero otherwise.
    Registers: BEF, BOBO/BOTI
    paper · Sections 3.1, 5.2, 6.2
  • Family sterilisation consultation Health care use
    Monthly indicator equal to one if the individual has ever (from 1994 onwards) consulted a doctor regarding sterilisation; a family-level version equals one if either partner in the couple has done so.
    Registers: LPRADM, SYSI, SSSY
    paper · Section 5.1
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Balanced monthly panel September 2008-December 2014 of individuals aged at least 25 in September 2008 and under 60 in December 2014; excludes immigrants and children of immigrants, parents of children with irregular child benefit payments, and (main analysis) anyone self-employed at any point; in January 2011 must have at least 2 children under 18, no more than 4 children in total, and be married or cohabiting.
    Registers: BEF, OF, BFL, BOBO/BOTI
    paper · Sections 5.1-5.2, footnotes 5-6
  • Annual earnings incl. self-employment (robustness) Earnings and income
    Annual income measures from the income register IND, used in a robustness check that includes the self-employed because self-employment income is not measured monthly.
    Registers: IND
    paper · Section 5.1

The Division of Parental Leave: Empirical Evidence and Policy Design

Thomas Høgholm Jørgensen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard · Journal of Public Economics, 2024 · Individual

Uses sharp incentives in the Danish parental leave benefit system for about 190,000 births to estimate parents' willingness to pay for leave. Parents bunch at kinks and are willing to pay for a traditional split with little leave for fathers, and simulations show that earmarked leave works much better when combined with high replacement rates.

Data
Parental leave benefit spell data (parents of children born 2008–2015), incl. benefits paid to parent or employer, Monthly earnings records for all employees (BFL/eIndkomst), from 2008, Danish administrative registers on demographics, family links and firm links (population and labour market registers)
Key variables
  • Outcome: weeks of parental leave taken by mother and father within three years of birth
  • Incentive: individual benefit replacement rates and benefit cap creating kinks in the household budget set
  • Incentive: employer-provided full wage compensation (from benefits paid to employer)
  • Policy: earmarked (father quota) leave and replacement rate counterfactuals in a structural model
Period
Births 2008–2015
Sample
189,974 births Births 2008–2015 to parents in stable employment and not on non-birth public benefits in the three months before birth, excluding births followed by another child within 15 months. source
How variables are defined (5)
  • Weeks of parental leave Family links, fertility and household
    Total number of parental leave weeks computed from start and end dates of benefit spells in the parental leave spell data (children born 2008-2015); includes all full-time leave taken at most three years after childbirth, separately for mother and father.
    Registers: Parental leave benefit spell data, BFL/eIndkomst
    working paper · Section 3.2 (Data)
  • Individual benefit replacement rate Unemployment and benefits
    Computed from total parental leave benefits paid out per parent-child spell relative to weeks of leave; statutory benefits replace 100% of pre-birth earnings for a full-time (37 hours/week) employee up to a cap of EUR 580 per week (2019 level), scaled down proportionally for part-time.
    Registers: Parental leave benefit spell data
    working paper · Sections 2 and 3.2, footnote 11
  • Weeks with full wage compensation Unemployment and benefits
    Weeks of leave with employer-provided full wage compensation, computed from the amount of parental leave benefits paid to the employer (benefits are paid to the employer as reimbursement when it pays full wage) using the individual replacement rate.
    Registers: Parental leave benefit spell data
    working paper · Section 3.2
  • Imputed individual right to wage compensation Unemployment and benefits
    Public sector: imputed from collective-agreement rules (6-6-6 model, Apr 2008-Apr 2015: 6 weeks each parent plus 6 shared weeks if both parents work in the same public sub-sector, otherwise the shared 6 accrue to the public-sector parent) using both parents' employment sector. Private sector: equals observed compensated weeks for parents who also take uncompensated leave (exhausters); otherwise the mode of compensated weeks among exhausting co-workers with weakly higher compensation, with co-worker groups defined as firm-year cells, or 6-digit then 5-digit industry-year cells when fewer than two exhausting co-workers exist.
    Registers: Parental leave benefit spell data, employer-employee links
    working paper · Section 3.3, eq. (11), Table 3
  • Birth sample Sample definition and timing
    Births 2008-2015; parents must be continuously employed in the same firm in the 3 months before birth and not on non-birth-related public benefits during those 3 months; births are excluded if parents have a subsequent child within 15 months; parents must appear in the parental leave data (final sample 189,974 births).
    Registers: BEF, BFL/eIndkomst, Parental leave benefit spell data
    working paper · Section 3.2, Table 1 and notes

Estimating Labor Supply Responses to Danish Tax Reforms

Hans Schytte Sigaard · Journal of Public Economics, 2023 · Individual

Applies taxable income elasticity methods to register data on hours actually worked. The intensive-margin labour supply elasticity is about 0.08, close to the labour income and taxable income elasticities, and it comes from changes in contract hours, paid absence and switches between main and secondary jobs.

Data
Wage Statistics Register (Lønstatistikken, LON) for performed hours of work, Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDAN) for workplace controls, Income registers (IND, INDK, INPI) for marginal tax rate simulation, Population register (BEF) and family income register (FAIN), Family register (FAMILIE), Education register (UDDA), Danish tax simulation programs (Kleven and Schultz 2014, extended by the Ministry of Finance)
Key variables
  • Outcome: three-year log change in annual performed hours of work
  • Treatment: three-year log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate on labour income
  • Instrument: mechanical (simulated) change in marginal tax rate from tax reforms, using lagged income
  • Secondary outcomes: labour income and taxable income
  • Controls: income splines, socio-economic and municipality controls
Period
2002–2016
Sample
10,755,733 observations Employed wage earners aged 25–65 covered by the Wage Statistics Register with positive hours in both years of each three-year difference and base-year labour income above DKK 250,000. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Performed hours of work Hours worked
    Contract hours plus paid overtime, minus paid absence, vacation and weekday holiday hours, summed over all employments in a year per individual (including secondary jobs). Contract hours are available from 2002, so the sample covers 2002-2016. LON covers all public firms and private firms with 100+ employees, plus a sample of private firms with 10-99 employees (about 50% of main employments).
    Registers: LON (Lønstatistikken)
    paper · Section 4 (Data), eq. (5); Appendix A.1
  • Three-year log change in performed hours Hours worked
    Main outcome: log change in annual performed hours between base year t and t+3. Strictly positive hours are required in both years. Decompositions condition on staying in the same job versus switching jobs between t and t+3.
    Registers: LON
    paper · Section 3, eq. (1); Section 5.1, Tables 3-4
  • Marginal tax rate on labour income Taxes and tax rates
    Simulated using tax programs from Kleven and Schultz (2014), extended by the Danish Ministry of Finance (available 1984-2016), as [T_t(z+100) - T_t(z)]/100, with income information mainly from IND, INDK and INPI. The treatment is the three-year log change in the marginal net-of-tax rate.
    Registers: IND, INDK, INPI
    paper · Section 4 (Data)
  • Predicted (mechanical) change in net-of-tax rate instrument Taxes and tax rates
    ln(1 - T'_{t+s}(z_{i,t-k})) - ln(1 - T'_t(z_{i,t-k})): marginal rates under the period t+s and t tax systems evaluated at income lagged k periods, following Weber (2014). The main specification uses k = 2, with lags 2-4 used for overidentification tests.
    Registers: IND, INDK, INPI
    paper · Section 3.1.1, eq. (2); Section 3.2
  • Lagged income controls Earnings and income
    Ten-piece spline with breakpoints at the deciles of log labour income lagged twice, to control for mean reversion and heterogeneous income trends.
    Registers: IND, INDK
    paper · Section 3.1
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Individuals aged 25-65 with all information needed to simulate marginal taxes, who are neither jobless nor outside the labour force as primary occupation at end of November in year t, and have strictly positive hours at t and t+3. Base-year labour income must exceed DKK 250,000 (2015 prices, CPI-deflated) and all controls must be non-missing.
    Registers: LON, IDAN, BEF, IND
    paper · Section 4 (Data), Table A.1
  • Workplace, socioeconomic and family controls Firm characteristics and productivity
    Workplace controls from IDAN, socioeconomic and municipal controls from BEF and FAIN, children from FAMILIE, and education from UDDA; industry groups follow Statistics Denmark's standard groupings.
    Registers: IDAN, BEF, FAIN, FAMILIE, UDDA
    paper · Section 4 (Data); Section 3.1 footnote 6

How variables are defined (7)
  • Treatment / running variable: parent's admission date Immigration and origin

Sofie Cairo and Robert Mahlstedt · Journal of Public Economics, 2023 · Individual

A field experiment in Denmark informed welfare recipients about a minimum work requirement, either with personalised running counts of their hours or with generic rules. Personalised information raised employment among those below the required hours, while generic notices reduced labour supply among those at low near-term risk of sanctions.

Data
Field experiment assignment and messaging data (Danish public employment service, jobnet.dk online tool), Population registers (socio-demographic background), Benefit payment records (DREAM), Monthly income and employment records (eIndkomst/BFL), Public employment service data on sanctions, exemptions, collected working hours, click data and registered job applications
Key variables
  • Treatment: random assignment to personalised online information tool about benefit-reduction risk under the work requirement (three arms)
  • Outcome: employment and earnings
  • Outcome: welfare benefit receipt and exit to alternative income support
  • Outcome: working hours collected toward the requirement and job applications
  • Heterogeneity: job search activity and sanction risk
Period
Intervention from 15 August 2018 with up to five monthly reminders
Sample
47,294 individuals All Danish welfare benefit recipients on 15 August 2018 subject to the 225-hour work requirement who had received the official notification letter. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • 225-hour work requirement / sanction Unemployment and benefits
    After 12 months on welfare benefits within the last three years, recipients keep the full benefit only if they worked at least 225 hours in regular non-subsidised jobs in the previous 12 months. Otherwise the benefit is reduced by about DKK 500-1,000 per month depending on family status; after a sanction the hour count resets to zero. Caseworkers may grant exemptions to those unable to work at least five hours a week.
    Registers: Public employment service data (sanctions, exemptions, collected hours)
    working paper · Section 2
  • Experimental sample and treatment arms Sample definition and timing
    All welfare benefit recipients in stock on 15 August 2018 who were subject to the work requirement and had received the official notification letter (N = 47,294), randomised into three arms. Treated: up to six monthly messages plus access to the personalised online tool on jobnet.dk. Control I: general reminders only. Control II: neither.
    Registers: Experimental data (jobnet.dk)
    working paper · Sections 3.1-3.2, Table 1 notes
  • Cumulated job finding rate, hours and earnings Employment and labour force status
    Cumulated job finding rates by month since the intervention (extensive margin), and total working hours and labour earnings accumulated over the first 12 months after the start (intensive margin), from monthly income and employment records.
    Registers: E-income (eIndkomst)
    working paper · Section 4.2, Figure 3, Table 3
  • Full-time vs part-time job Hours worked
    Full-time jobs have average weekly working hours at or above 90% of the full-time equivalent (37 hours per week); part-time jobs are below that.
    Registers: E-income (eIndkomst)
    working paper · Section 4.2, Table 3 note (a)
  • Entering other transfer program Unemployment and benefits
    Indicator that the individual receives any other benefit not subject to the work requirement, such as educational support, sickness or disability benefits.
    Registers: DREAM
    working paper · Section 4.3
  • Active vs inactive job seeker Unemployment and benefits
    Active job seekers have a positive number of collected working hours at the onset of the intervention, or at least one job application registered in the public employment service portal in the last four weeks; all others are inactive.
    Registers: Public employment service data (collected hours, job applications)
    working paper · Section 4.4
  • Local counselling intensity Geography and neighbourhood

Identifying Behavioral Responses to Tax Reforms: New Insights and a New Approach

Katrine Jakobsen and Jakob Egholt Søgaard · Journal of Public Economics, 2022 · Individual

Shows that standard estimates of taxable income elasticities from tax reforms are biased by mean reversion and diverging income trends across the distribution, and proposes an approach that exploits reform timing to separate behavioural responses from these trends, applied to Danish tax reforms.

Data
Danish administrative registers for the full population since 1980 (labour market history, education, earnings, demographics), Third-party reported income tax records, Simulated marginal tax rates from an extended Danish tax simulator (Kleven and Schultz 2014 model)
Key variables
  • Outcome: changes in taxable income (broad, personal, labour income) over four-year periods
  • Treatment: predicted change in log net-of-tax rate from the 2004 and 2009–10 Danish tax reforms
  • Income-bin dummies capturing trend differentials across the income distribution
  • Validation: income trends in parts of the distribution unaffected by the reform
Period
Data since 1980; main analyses 1999–2012 (2004 reform: 1999–2003 pre-period, 2003–2007 reform period; 2009–10 reform: 2004–2008 pre-period, 2008–2012 reform period); 1987 and 1994 reforms in appendix
Sample
over 2,000,000 individuals per period (2,240,332 and 2,295,922 for the 2004 reform pre-reform and reform periods; 2,097,862 and 2,240,833 for the 2009–10 reform) Individuals present in the tax data with positive income over each four-year period and initial personal income above DKK 200,000 (2004 reform) or DKK 250,000 (2009–10 reform), about half the Danish adult population. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Labour market income (LI) Earnings and income
    Salary, wages, honoraria, fees, bonuses, fringe benefits and business earnings, as defined in the Danish income tax system.
    Registers: Danish tax records
    paper · Section 3.1, Table 1
  • Broad income (BI) Earnings and income
    Labour market income plus transfers, certain pension payouts and received alimony; it equals personal income before deductions.
    Registers: Danish tax records
    paper · Table 1; Fig. 3 notes
  • Personal income (PI) Earnings and income
    Broad income minus the labour market contribution and certain pension contributions (employer-administered annuity pension contributions were fully deductible until 2010, then capped at DKK 100,000 for expiring annuities). PI is the main outcome and initial-income concept, and responses are also shown with and without pension contributions.
    Registers: Danish tax records
    paper · Table 1; Section 3.1; footnote 21
  • Taxable income (TI) Earnings and income
    Personal income plus capital income (interest, rental and business capital income minus interest on debt) minus itemized deductions (commuting, union fees, unemployment insurance contributions, other work expenses, charitable donations, paid alimony). Stock income is taxed separately.
    Registers: Danish tax records
    paper · Table 1
  • Simulated marginal tax rate / predicted change in log net-of-tax rate Taxes and tax rates
    Marginal tax rates are imputed with an extension of the Kleven and Schultz (2014) Danish tax simulator, as the increase in total household taxes from an incremental increase in labour income. The predicted change compares rates under the period-t and t-1 tax systems, holding income and characteristics fixed at their t-k levels (k = 1 baseline).
    Registers: Danish tax records
    paper · Section 2 (eq. 5); Section 3.3
  • Reform and pre-reform period samples Sample definition and timing
    Four-year periods: 2004-08 (pre) and 2008-12 (reform) for the 2009-10 reform; initial years 1999 and 2003 for the 2004 reform. Individuals present in tax data with positive income over the period, and initial personal income above DKK 250,000 (2009-10 reform) or DKK 200,000 (2004 reform) at 2019 levels deflated by tax-code wage indexes.
    Registers: Danish tax records
    paper · Section 3.3, Table 3
  • Initial income bin dummies Earnings and income
    Fifty dummies for initial personal income measured at the start of each period (e.g. 2004 or 2008). The DKK 300,000 bin is omitted, so coefficients measure income-growth trend differentials relative to that bin.
    Registers: Danish tax records
    paper · Section 4, eq. (11)

Spot Price Biases in Non-Linear Health Insurance Contracts

Marianne Simonsen, Lars Skipper, Niels Skipper and Anne Illemann Christensen · Journal of Public Economics, 2021 · Individual

The Danish prescription drug reimbursement scheme has coverage that rises with annual spending and resets each year. Consumers look forward-looking around the reset but react too strongly to current prices within the year, and liquidity constraints rather than plan literacy or cognitive decline explain the spot-price bias.

Data
Population-wide individual data on prescription drug purchases and reimbursement under the Danish non-linear drug insurance scheme (registers not named in the abstract)
Key variables
  • Incentive: spot price of drugs as a non-linear function of year-to-date spending
  • Incentive: end-of-year reset of the coverage (deductible) year
  • Outcome: timing and amount of prescription drug purchases
  • Heterogeneity: liquidity constraints, plan literacy, cognitive decline
Period
Not stated in the sources checked
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Population-wide data on Danish consumers of prescription drugs covered by the non-linear reimbursement scheme (details not available from the abstract). source (abstract)
How variables are defined (8)
  • Prescription drug spending and purchases Health care use
    The full history of prescription drug purchases from the Danish Prescription Drug Register (Laegemiddelstatistikregisteret), covering 1995-2014: date, shelf price, government coverage, type of coverage and type of drug. It is aggregated to daily (descriptive) or monthly (estimation) spending within coverage years. Outcomes include spending, number of pharmacy visits, and days until next purchase truncated at 365.
    Registers: Laegemiddelstatistikregisteret (Danish Prescription Drug Register)
    paper · Section 3; Section 4 (outcomes before reset)
  • Coverage year and synthetic pre-reform coverage year Health care use
    Post-reform coverage years start with the first purchase after the March 2000 reform and reset 365 days after the first purchase, with the next year starting at the next purchase. Synthetic pre-reform coverage years apply the same rule from the first observed purchase, keeping only years that end by December 1999.
    Registers: Laegemiddelstatistikregisteret
    paper · Section 2; Section 3
  • Spot price Health care use
    Coinsurance rate at the start of coverage month m given year-to-date spending, taking values 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.15 or 0. Under the 2000 contract: a DKK 500 deductible, 50% coinsurance to DKK 1,200, 25% to DKK 2,800, 15% beyond, and a stop-loss at DKK 18,500 capping out-of-pocket costs at DKK 3,600. The spot price is 1 for the purchase that starts a coverage year.
    Registers: Laegemiddelstatistikregisteret
    paper · Section 2, Figure 1; Section 5 (price definition a)
  • Expected end-of-year (shadow) price Health care use
    Average realised end-of-year price within cells of 5 age groups x 6 sextiles of predicted health spending x 100 percentiles of year-to-date spending, for each coverage month. Pre-reform counterfactual prices for 1998 are imputed by matching percentiles to pooled coverage years starting in 2000-2001.
    Registers: Laegemiddelstatistikregisteret
    paper · Section 5 (price definitions b-c, steps i-iii)
  • Predicted pharmaceutical spending (health index) Health care use
    Following Handel (2013), year-t drug spending is regressed on year t-1 gender, age and age squared, number of GP office visits, fee-for-service payments to the physician, drug spending and its square, ATC level-3 drug-type indicators (88 categories), and hospital ICD-10 level-2 diagnosis indicators (215 categories). The model is then used to predict next year's spending; for coverage-reset analyses, covariates are measured in the 365 days before the coverage year starts.
    Registers: Laegemiddelstatistikregisteret, National Patient Register (hospital diagnoses), Health insurance (GP) records
    Codes: ATC level 3 (88 categories); ICD-10 level 2 (215 categories)
    paper · Appendix D
  • Chronic drug Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality
    Following Alpert (2016), a drug at ATC level 3 (pharmacological subgroup) is chronic if its median consumer buys it in at least three calendar months of a year (more than twice).
    Registers: Laegemiddelstatistikregisteret
    Codes: ATC level 3
    paper · Section 3 footnote 5; Appendix C
  • Self-reported liquidity constraint Wealth, debt and consumption
    From the 2000 Danish National Health Interview Survey (DNHIS) question 'During the last 12 months, how often have you had trouble paying your bills'. Respondents answering at least 'some months' are coded as liquidity constrained (12%).
    Registers: DNHIS 2000 (survey linked by personal ID)
    paper · Section 6 (mechanisms), Table 5
  • Plan literacy groups Education and test scores
    'Economic literates' are individuals with a master-level degree in economics or business (ISCED level 7); medical professionals hold a university degree in medicine or pharmacology (ISCED levels 7-8). Cognitive decline is proxied by age 65 and above versus below 65.
    Registers: Education register
    Codes: ISCED 7 (economics/business); ISCED 7-8 (medicine/pharmacology)
    paper · Section 6, Table 5 notes

N. Meltem Daysal, Michael Lovenheim, Nikolaj Siersbæk and David N. Wasser · Journal of Public Economics, 2021 · Individual

Medical Birth Register (MFR), National Patient Register (LPR), State's Sales and Valuation Registry (public property valuations and sales prices), Population register (BEF) and other registers for demographics, education, household income and partner status

1992–2011 (fertility analysis 1995–2006)
Sample
1,105,559 observations on 198,435 women (125,903 births) Women aged 20–44 who became first-time homeowners between 1993 and 2004, purchasing between ages 18 and 42. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Estimated home value Wealth, debt and consumption
    The public valuation of the home times the owner's share, multiplied by the mean ratio of sale price to public valuation among homes sold in the same year, municipality, housing type and valuation-quartile cluster (a SPAR-type index); woman's and partner's shares are summed.     working paper · Section 3 and 3.1, footnote 13
  • Housing sample restrictions Sample definition and timing
    Residential houses and apartments in clusters with at least five sales; only normal sales between individuals (no intra-family sales). Excluded: negative valuations or sale prices, multiple addresses at the same location, and sales above 300% or below 40% of the public valuation.

  • Potential first-time homeowner women Sample definition and timing
    Women not homeowners at the beginning of 1992-1993 who became homeowners between 1993 and 2004 at ages 18-42; owning means the woman, her partner or both own the home. Women whose partner bought before the couple formed, who moved out of the new home within the year, or who have incomplete income or home data are dropped, leaving women aged 20-44 observed 1995-2006.

    working paper · Section 1 footnote 2; Section 3.1
  • Low / very low birth weight, prematurity Health outcomes, diagnoses and mortality

Danish students lose part of their study grant when annual earnings exceed a threshold. Register data show bunching below the threshold that grows as students gain experience with the rule, so optimisation frictions hide a structural elasticity well above the observed response.

Data
Danish administrative registers for the full population (education, earnings, benefits, demographics), Annual income tax returns, Monthly student benefit (SU) take-up records from the Student Benefit Administration, Monthly payroll records of earnings and hours (BFL/eIndkomst), from 2008
Key variables

  • Incentive: kink/notch from phase-out (payback) of student grants above the individual income limit

Period
2006–2011 (monthly earnings from 2008)
Sample
around 75,000 observations per year (core sample 75,500 individuals per year on average) Individuals aged 18–35 enrolled in tertiary education, fully eligible for student benefits and with positive labour earnings (above DKK 8,000 per year). source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Core student sample Sample definition and timing
    Individuals aged 18-35 enrolled in tertiary education, fully eligible for student benefits (SU), and with positive labour earnings, defined as earned income above DKK 8,000 per year. This gives about 75,500 observations per year, 2006-2011.

  • Income counted against the SU income limit Earnings and income

  • Individual income limit Unemployment and benefits

  • Effective marginal tax / phase-out rate Taxes and tax rates
    Marginal income tax of 42% above a personal allowance of DKK 49,900. Benefits are phased out at 50% for the first DKK 11,600 above the individual income limit and at 100% beyond that, so the effective marginal rate jumps from 42% to 72% at the baseline limit under optimal take-up. If the payback exceeds DKK 9,200, the whole payback rises by 7% (a notch). The 2009 reform raised the baseline limit by 24% and the phase-out rate from 52% to 62%.
    working paper · Section 3.1, footnotes 5 and 11, Figure 2
  • Excess income and predicted payback Earnings and income
    Total earned income from tax records minus the individual income limit; positive amounts translate into payback of benefits. Predicted end-of-year benefits (initial payout minus predicted payback) match reported benefits within DKK 2 for 97.9% of the core sample.
    Registers: Tax returns, Student Benefit Administration records
    working paper · Section 4.3; Appendix C, Table C.I
  • Study-related job Sector and industry
    All jobs not in wholesale (NACE 46), retail (47), postal service (53), hotels and restaurants (55, 56), cleaning (81), elderly, social and childcare (87, 88), or sports and amusement facilities (93).
    Registers: Monthly earnings records (employer/firm link)
    Codes: NACE 46, 47, 53, 55, 56, 81, 87, 88, 93 = not study-related
    working paper · Table 3, note e
  • Monthly earnings and hours Hours worked
    Monthly records of earnings and hours worked for all wage earners, available from 2008 and used for average weekly hours and the within-person variability of monthly earnings.
    Registers: Monthly payroll records (from 2008)
    working paper · Section 3.2, Table 3, Appendix Figure A.II
  • Student experience Education and test scores
    Number of years enrolled in tertiary education between 2004 and 2007 (that is, over the previous four years).
    Registers: Education registers
    working paper · Table 3 note a; Appendix Figure A.VI

Spillovers in Education Choice

Juanna Schrøter Joensen and Helena Skyt Nielsen · Journal of Public Economics, 2018 · Individual

Exploits the Danish high school pilot that made advanced mathematics cheaper to take for some cohorts. An older sibling's advanced maths choice raises the probability that the younger sibling also chooses advanced maths, with spillovers that depend on the siblings' gender composition.

Data
Danish administrative registers on high school enrolment, course packages and completion (Statistics Denmark education registers), Parent and sibling links from population registers, Parental education and income registers, Earnings registers (younger siblings' earnings at ages 30–35)
Key variables
  • Outcome: younger sibling chooses advanced math-science course package in high school
  • Endogenous regressor: older sibling's advanced math-science choice
  • Instrument: older sibling enrolled in a high school that unexpectedly introduced the pilot scheme (PilotIntro)
  • Outcomes: younger sibling's college/STEM education at age 30 and log earnings at ages 30–35
  • Controls: parental education and income, county and entry-cohort fixed effects
Period
High school entry cohorts 1984–1987 (older siblings) and 1988–1991 (younger siblings, main sample); register data from 1980 onwards
Sample
7,786 sibling pairs (main closely spaced sample); 17,691 sibling pairs in the wider sample with age gap < 10 years Older siblings entering academic high school 1984–1987 who graduated in three years, paired with younger siblings entering high school 1988–1991 with an age gap of at most 4 years. source
How variables are defined (7)
  • Advanced math-science choice (MathScience) Education and test scores
    Indicator that the student chose a high-school course package combining advanced math and advanced science. In traditional schools the only such package was advanced math, advanced physics and intermediate chemistry; pilot schools also offered advanced math, advanced chemistry and intermediate physics. The choice is made at the end of the first high-school year.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark education registers
    working paper · Section 2
  • PilotIntro / PilotSchool instrument Education and test scores
    PilotIntro = 1 if the (older sibling) enrolled in a high school that unexpectedly introduced the pilot scheme after the student's enrolment but before the advanced-course choice (cohorts entering 1984-87). PilotSchool = 1 if the school had adopted the pilot before the student's enrolment.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark education registers
    working paper · Section 2, Table 1
  • Sibling-pair sample Sample definition and timing
    Older siblings entering academic high school 1984-87 who graduated in three years, paired with a younger sibling who entered after 1987 and graduated in three years. The main sample has younger-sibling cohorts 1988-91 and an age gap of at most 4 years; the wider sample has cohorts 1988-97 and a gap of at most 10 years.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark population and education registers
    working paper · Section 3.1; Appendix Table B1
  • Parental education and income controls Family links, fertility and household
    Mutually exclusive indicators for the mother's and father's highest completed education, plus their gross income as observed at the end of the year before the child started high school (when the child was 15).
    Registers: Statistics Denmark administrative registers
    working paper · Section 3.1-3.2
  • STEM field education Education and test scores
    Indicator that the highest completed education is in a STEM field, following the National Science Foundation definition (math, engineering, natural and technical sciences, and some social and life sciences). It is used for parents and for younger siblings' education at age 30.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark education registers
    working paper · Section 3.2; notes to Tables 6-7
  • Long college degree at age 30 Education and test scores
    Indicator that the younger sibling's highest completed education at age 30 is more than a 4-year college degree (also interacted with STEM field).
    Registers: Statistics Denmark education registers
    working paper · Table 7
  • Earnings at ages 30-35 Earnings and income
    Log annual earnings of the younger sibling at ages 30-35, in real 1989 DKK.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark income registers
    working paper · Section 5 (Table 7); Appendix A Figure A1 note
