Parental Responses to Child Support Obligations: Evidence from Administrative Data

Maya Rossin-Slater and Miriam Wüst · Journal of Public Economics, 2018 · Individual

Uses discontinuities in the Danish child support schedule by fathers' income to estimate how higher obligations affect separated parents. The paper documents responses in fathers' income, subsequent family formation and the parents' living arrangements.

Data
Danish administrative registers on children born 1985–2008 linked to parents and siblings (population/family registers), Income and tax records including tax-deductible child support payments, Labour market registers (employment, earnings, disability insurance, early retirement), Birth records (fertility through 2010), Education registers, Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children (DALSC) and Children and Youth in Denmark (CYD) survey (descriptive, supplementary)
Key variables
  • Treatment: father's average child support obligation (from Danish child support guideline schedule)
  • Identifying variation: income thresholds in the child support guidelines (simulated instrument)
  • Outcome: father's annual child support payment
  • Outcome: father–child co-residence (physical custody)
  • Outcomes: post-separation fertility and labour supply of both parents
Period
1998–2010 (separation years 1999–2008)
Sample
73,303 fathers (71,575 unique mothers) Fathers observed every year 1998–2010 who separated from their oldest child's mother (or had a first child while not cohabiting) in 1999–2008, with one or two children under 18 and separation-year income near the first three guideline thresholds. source
How variables are defined (8)
  • Separation year Family links, fertility and household
    The year in which the father no longer resides with his oldest child's mother, or the year he has a first child while not living with the child's mother. The sample is restricted to separation years 1999-2008.
    Registers: Danish administrative population/family registers
    working paper · Section 4 (Analysis Sample)
  • Analysis sample of fathers Sample definition and timing
    Fathers observed in the registers every year 1998-2010 who either were married to or cohabiting with their oldest child's mother at childbirth (or in 1998 for children born earlier), or had a first child 1999-2008 while not married to or cohabiting with the mother. Also required: separation in 1999-2008, one or two children under 18 at separation, and separation-year income in a 100,000 DKK window around the first three schedule thresholds (175,000-505,000 DKK). The result is 73,303 fathers, one observation each.
    Registers: Danish administrative registers
    working paper · Section 4 (Analysis Sample), footnotes 17-18
  • Child support obligation (actual average) Taxes and tax rates
    The father's annual obligation from the Danish child support guideline (normal amount plus extra amount per child, plus a supplement of 25-300% of the normal amount above income thresholds). It is a step function of current gross income and the number of biological children under 18, including new children. It is averaged over all post-separation years and expressed in thousands of real 2000 DKK.
    Registers: Danish income registers
    working paper · Section 2; Section 5, equation (2)
  • Predicted (simulated) child support obligation Taxes and tax rates
    Instrument: the obligation in each post-separation year computed from the father's separation-year gross income and his 'original' children still under 18, so children ageing out are counted but new children and post-separation income changes are ignored. It is averaged over the post-separation period.
    Registers: Danish income registers
    working paper · Section 5 (Simulated IV Method), equation (3)
  • Child support payment Earnings and income
    Tax-deductible annual child support payments by non-custodial fathers as reported to the tax authorities, so only payments above the non-deductible extra amount are observed. Formal and voluntary payments cannot be distinguished.
    Registers: Danish income/tax registers
    working paper · Section 4 (Outcomes)
  • Father-child co-residence Family links, fertility and household
    Indicator that the father shares a residence address with the child in any year after separation, based on one address per person per year. It captures sole-father and some joint physical custody but understates joint custody.
    Registers: Danish population register (addresses)
    working paper · Section 4 (Outcomes)
  • Post-separation fertility Family links, fertility and household
    Whether the mother or father has an additional child after separation, measured from the universe of birth records through 2010 and split by birth within or outside a new partnership.
    Registers: Birth records
    working paper · Section 4 (Outcomes); Section 6.3
  • Labour force participation / NILF Employment and labour force status
    Fraction of post-separation years in which the father has any positive labour income, and the proportion of years not in the labour force. NILF is split by disability leave (Social Disability Pension), retirement including early retirement (Post-Employment Wage program, ages 60-64), and means-tested welfare.
    Registers: Danish labour market registers
    working paper · Section 6.4, Table 6, footnote 29

Taxation and the Long Run Allocation of Labor: Theory and Danish Evidence

Claus Thustrup Kreiner, Jakob Roland Munch and Hans Jørgen Whitta-Jacobsen · Journal of Public Economics, 2015 · Individual + firm

Estimates a search model with non-linear taxation, in which workers keep looking for better-paid jobs, on employer-employee register data for all Danish workers and workplaces in 2004 to 2006. Danish taxes reduce total income by about 12 percent through the allocation of labour across jobs, and moving to low-tax OECD levels would recover four fifths of the loss.

Data
Integrated Database for Labour Market Research (IDA), Wage Statistics Register (Lønstatistikken) for hours-adjusted wages (robustness), Empirical effective marginal tax rate schedule for 2006 from Kleven and Kreiner (2006)
Key variables
  • Workplace average hourly wage rate (annual labour income / annual hours)
  • Workplace size, number of stayers and new hires (job-to-job flows)
  • New hires from non-employment
  • Effective marginal tax rates by income level (used to estimate structural search model and efficiency loss)
Period
2004–2006 (base year 2005)
Sample
126,400 workplaces employing 1.4 million workers Full population of private-sector workplaces in Denmark in 2005 and their workers aged 18–65, with wages between DKK 90 and DKK 714 per hour. source
How variables are defined (9)
  • Estimation sample Sample definition and timing
    Workers aged 18-65 employed in private-sector workplaces in 2005, drawn from IDA for 2004-2006; employment at each workplace is observed in a specific week in each year. Workers with hourly wage rates in the top percentile (above DKK 714) or below DKK 90 are excluded.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1 (Data)
  • Workplace Firm characteristics and productivity
    A workplace is an IDA establishment defined by a geographical location; most firms have one workplace but some larger firms have several.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1, footnote 9
  • Hourly wage rate (IDA) Earnings and income
    Annual labour income (including mandatory pension fund payments) divided by annual hours; annual hours are based on the mandatory ATP pension contributions, so overtime is not counted and part-time hours are imprecise.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1; Section 5 (robustness)
  • Workplace average wage Earnings and income
    Each worker is assigned the average hourly wage rate of employees at his/her workplace in 2005 (following Christensen et al. 2005), after trimming wages below DKK 90 and above DKK 714.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1
  • Workplace size and stayers Firm characteristics and productivity
    Size is the number of employees at the workplace in 2005; stayers are workers employed at the workplace in 2005 who are still employed there in 2006.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1, Table 1
  • New hires / new hires from non-employment Employment and labour force status
    New hires are workers employed at the workplace in 2005 who were not employed there in 2004; new hires from non-employment are workers employed at the workplace in 2005 who were not employed at any workplace in 2004 (non-employment or non-participation).
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1
  • Wage offer distribution Earnings and income
    Distribution of firm-specific average wages for persons entering firms in 2005 from non-employment in 2004, weighting each firm's wage by its share of all hires from non-employment.
    Registers: IDA
    working paper · Section 3.1
  • Effective marginal tax rate Taxes and tax rates
    Effective marginal tax rates by annual labour income from the Kleven and Kreiner (2006) empirical tax function for 2006 (income taxes, indirect taxes and benefit claw-back), deflated to 2005 by average labour income growth; hourly wages are converted to annual income using median annual hours of 1,660. The participation tax rate m0 is 0.59 at baseline (0.82 in a robustness check).
    working paper · Section 3.1, Figure 1; Section 5
  • Hours-adjusted wage rate (WSR imputation) Earnings and income
    Robustness check: the employer-reported hourly wage from the Wage Statistics Register (Lønstatistikken) is regressed on the IDA wage rate after dropping the top and bottom 1% and IDA wages flagged as low quality by Statistics Denmark. The fitted relationship is then used to impute an overtime- and part-time-adjusted wage for all workers.
    Registers: IDA, Lønstatistikken (WSR)
    working paper · Section 5 (robustness), Figure 5

Tax Bunching, Income Shifting and Self-Employment

Daniel le Maire and Bertel Schjerning · Journal of Public Economics, 2013 · Individual

Self-employed Danes bunch sharply at the top tax kink, but much of the bunching reflects intertemporal shifting of income through retained earnings in the business rather than real changes in effort. Accounting for shifting implies a much smaller elasticity of real income.

Data
Tax records of Danish self-employed individuals (taxable income, retained earnings)
Key variables
  • Outcome: bunching of taxable income at kinks of the tax schedule
  • Mechanism: intertemporal income shifting via retained earnings in the business tax schemes
  • Estimate: taxable income elasticity (0.43–0.53 ignoring shifting; structural 0.14–0.20)
Period
Not stated in the sources checked
Sample
Not stated in the sources checked Danish self-employed taxpayers. source (abstract)
How variables are defined (8)
  • Self-employed (main occupation) Employment and labour force status
    Persons whose primary occupation is self-employment, classified with the Statistics Denmark occupation variables pstill2 (primary) and sstill2 (secondary); narrower than Chetty et al. (2011), excluding wage earners with self-employment as secondary occupation.
    Registers: IDA, Income Tax Register
    Codes: pstill2, sstill2
    working paper · Section 2.1, Table 1 notes
  • Analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    Entire population panel 1994-2009, aged 25-59, main occupation self-employment; restricted to self-employed whose spouse's primary or secondary occupation is not self-employment (because transfers to assisting spouses are only observed 1994-2001).
    Registers: Income Tax Register, IDA
    working paper · Section 2 'Data and Institutional Background'
  • Personal income Earnings and income
    Sum of wage earnings, declared firm profits (net of retained earnings), remunerations, provisions, alimony etc. minus deductions; interest income is capital income and not part of personal income.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    working paper · Figure 1 notes; Section 2.1
  • Taxable income relative to the effective kink Taxes and tax rates
    For each individual, the difference between actual taxable income and the taxable income needed to reach the middle or top tax bracket, computed with the authors' own tax simulator accounting for special deductions and joint taxation of couples (simulated tax within +/-5 DKK of actual for 95% of the sample); distributions plotted in 1,000 DKK bins.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    working paper · Section 2 and Figure 2
  • Tax schedule kinks Taxes and tax rates
    Piecewise-linear personal income tax with five brackets before 1996 and four from 1996; e.g. 2001: about 8% below 33,400 DKK, about 44% up to 179,900 DKK (bottom tax), 49% above (middle tax) and 63% above 279,900 DKK (top tax). Top-tax base is mainly individual; middle-tax base depends on household income; middle cutoff raised to the top cutoff in 2009.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    working paper · Section 2
  • Business tax scheme and retained earnings Firm characteristics and productivity
    Self-employed choose the personal income tax scheme, the capital returns scheme (from 1993) or the firm tax scheme (from 1987); the latter two are treated as one and allow retaining profits in the firm, taxed provisionally at the firm tax rate (34% in 1994 falling to 25% in 2009), with withdrawals taxed as personal income. Retained earnings = profits retained under these schemes.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    working paper · Section 2.1 'Three Tax Schemes for the Self-employed'; Table 2
  • Earned income Earnings and income
    Income before shifting: personal income plus retained earnings plus income shifted along other margins such as pension contributions and transfers to assisting spouses; used (adjusted for income shocks) to estimate the real bunching response.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    working paper · Section 4 discussion of Figures 11-12
  • Excess mass at kink (bunching) Taxes and tax rates
    Excess mass at the tax cutoff estimated following Saez (2010) within a bandwidth around the kink, applied to taxable income and to adjusted earned income; the dynamic extension separates bunching from intertemporal shifting via retained earnings.
    Registers: Income Tax Register
    working paper · Section 3-4, equation (3)

Links the Danish Longitudinal Survey of Children to the registers to compare non-cognitive outcomes at age seven for children in universal preschool, family day care and home care at age three. 1994–2003 (children born 1995; care measured 1999, outcomes 2003)

How variables are defined (8)

  • Mother's education level Education and test scores

    Registers: Statistics Denmark education register

  • Mother's degree of employment after birth Employment and labour force status

  • Early public care enrolment (nursery / family day care 1997-1998) Family links, fertility and household

How to Help Unemployed Find Jobs Quickly: Experimental Evidence from a Mandatory Activation Program

Brian Krogh Graversen and Jan C. van Ours · Journal of Public Economics, 2008 · Individual

A randomised experiment in two Danish counties assigned newly unemployed workers to an intensive activation programme with early job search courses, frequent meetings and mandatory activation. Treated workers found jobs substantially faster, with the threat of mandatory activation an important part of the effect.

Data
Public Employment Service (PES) administrative registers (treatment status, demographics, meetings with caseworkers), DREAM weekly register of public income transfers (Danish National Labour Market Authority)
Key variables
  • Outcome: unemployment duration in weeks / job finding rate
  • Treatment: random assignment to mandatory activation programme by birth date (born 1st–15th of month)
  • Mechanism: meetings with caseworkers, job search programmes, training programmes
  • Exit states: employment, other benefits, right-censoring
Period
November 2005–mid September 2006
Sample
4,520 unemployment spells (2,229 treatment, 2,291 control) Newly unemployed UI benefit recipients registering at the PES in Storstrøm and South Jutland counties between November 2005 and February 2006, first spell only. source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Unemployment spell duration Unemployment and benefits
    From weekly DREAM transfer data: the spell starts in the week the person became unemployed and continues until the person has not received UI benefits (or participated in ALMPs) for four consecutive weeks; switching to sickness benefits counts as still unemployed. Only the first spell is used; data run to mid-September 2006, so spells are censored after 26-43 weeks depending on assignment week.
    Registers: DREAM, PES registers
    working paper · Section 2.3 'Available data' and footnote 11
  • Exit to employment and other exit states Unemployment and benefits
    A worker is assumed to find a job as soon as he or she no longer receives benefit payments (after the 4-week rule); other exit states (e.g. early retirement pay, other benefits) and right-censoring are distinguished using the DREAM event history.
    Registers: DREAM
    working paper · Section 2.3 footnote 11; Appendix A Table A2
  • Random assignment by birth date Sample definition and timing
    Newly unemployed UI benefit recipients (clean seniority record, i.e. eligible for the full 4-year UI period) registering at the PES in Storstrom and South Jutland counties between week 43 of 2005 and week 8 of 2006 and still unemployed on the Friday of the registration week; treatment if born on the 1st-15th of a month, control if born on the 16th or later. Bad-weather and work-sharing unemployment excluded.
    Registers: PES registers, CPR
    working paper · Section 2.2 and Appendix A
  • Net analysis sample Sample definition and timing
    From 5,180 assigned: drop 27 incorrectly assigned by birth date, 43 bad-weather/work-sharing cases, 37 who died or moved abroad, and 553 who did not receive UI benefits within 6 weeks of PES registration, leaving 4,520 (2,229 treatment, 2,291 control).
    Registers: PES registers, DREAM
    working paper · Appendix A, Table A1
  • Treatment programme components (meetings, job search and training programmes) Unemployment and benefits
    Meetings with caseworkers (type and date, from PES registers, including private contractors); job search programmes (2-week courses); training programmes grouping short work experience (up to 4 weeks), employment subsidy and training/education programmes.
    Registers: PES registers
    working paper · Sections 2.3-2.4
  • Previous occupation Occupation and job hierarchy
    Occupational classification based on the name of the UI fund that pays the individual's UI benefits.
    Registers: PES registers
    working paper · Section 2.3, footnote 9

Rent Control and Unemployment Duration

Michael Svarer, Michael Rosholm and Jakob Roland Munch · Journal of Public Economics, 2005 · Individual

Uses Danish register data on unemployment spells and housing to study whether living in rent-controlled housing affects job finding. Unemployed workers in rent-controlled dwellings have lower exit rates from unemployment, consistent with rent control reducing geographic mobility.

Data
10% random sample of the Danish adult population from administrative registers (Statistics Denmark), Housing unit characteristics for dwellings occupied by the sample, Weekly labour market event histories, Danish Tax Authorities 1999 hedonic model for owner-occupied housing (to predict uncontrolled rent)
Key variables
  • Outcome: unemployment duration in weeks (exit to job in local vs national labour market)
  • Explanatory: rent control benefit decile (predicted uncontrolled rent minus actual rent), time-varying
  • Mobility: job finding with move to another of 51 commuting areas
  • Tenure type: private rental housing vs other
Period
1997–2000
Sample
14,645 persons contributing 31,966 unemployment spells Inflow sample of unemployment spells 1997–2000 from a 10% random sample of the Danish adult population (IZA DP 842 working-paper version). source
How variables are defined (6)
  • Unemployment duration and exit destination Unemployment and benefits
    Flow sample of unemployment spells starting 1997-2000, from weekly labour-market event histories; duration measured in weeks, with destination employment recorded. Temporary layoffs (return to the previous employer, about 40% of spells) are treated as right-censored, as are exits to states outside the labour market.
    Registers: 10% sample of Danish adult population (Statistics Denmark registers)
    working paper · Section 4.1 'Unemployment spells and geographical mobility'
  • Local labour market (commuting area) Geography and neighbourhood
    Local labour markets are groups of municipalities between which the internal migration rate is 50% higher than the external migration rate (Andersen 2000), giving 51 commuting areas in Denmark.
    Registers: Population registers
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Geographically mobile job finding Geography and neighbourhood
    An unemployed worker is geographically mobile if he or she gets a job and moves to another commuting area within the window from 8 weeks before to 52 weeks after the start of the job spell; otherwise a job exit is local.
    Registers: Population registers, Weekly event histories
    working paper · Section 4.1
  • Rent control benefit and decile of rent control degree Wealth, debt and consumption
    Rent control benefit = predicted uncontrolled rent minus actual rent; uncontrolled rent from the Danish Tax Authorities' 1999 hedonic model for owner-occupied housing (sales 1996-1999, dwelling traits, more than 50,000 geographic areas) times an estimate of user cost; missing actual rents (about 50% of units) imputed by Heckman two-step. The regressor is the decile of the rent control degree (benefit / uncontrolled rent), using 1999 decile limits applied to 1997, 1998 and 2000; time-varying across housing units via moving dates.
    Registers: Housing unit characteristics (Statistics Denmark), DTA 1999 hedonic model
    working paper · Section 4.2 'The rent control benefit'
  • Replacement rate Unemployment and benefits
    Ratio of UI benefits received to the most recent wage.
    Registers: Statistics Denmark registers
    working paper · Section 4.3 'Explanatory variables'
  • Private rental housing tenure Geography and neighbourhood
    Housing market split into owner-occupied (51%), co-operative (6%), public rental (19%) and private rental (18%); analysis concerns private rental units, where rents are regulated except in dwellings built after 1991.
